[L39] ## 1. Idea

[L41] By a *braid group* [[Artin (1925)](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/braid+group#Artin25)] one means the [group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/group) of joint continuous *motions* [cf. [Goldsmith (1981)](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/braid+group#Goldsmith81)] of a fixed number `n+1` of non-coincident points in the [plane](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/plane), from any fixed [configuration](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/configuration+space+of+points) back to that fixed configuration. The “[worldlines](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/worldlines)” traced out by such points in space-time under such an operation look like a braid with `n+1` strands, whence the name.

[L43] [image](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/GenericBraidGroupElement-230205.jpg)

[L45] As with actual braids, here it is understood that two such operations are identified if they differ only by continuous deformations of the “strands” without breaking or intersecting these, hence that one identifies those such systems of [worldlines](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/worldlines) which are [isotopic](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/isotopy) in `ℝ3`. (This is just the kind of invariance considered for [link diagrams](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/link+diagrams) — such as under [Reidemeister moves](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Reidemeister+moves) — and in fact every link diagram may be obtained by “closing up” a braid diagram, in the evident sense.)

[L47] A quick way of saying this with precision is to observe that a braid group is thus the [*fundamental group*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/fundamental+group) `π1` of a [configuration space of points](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/configuration+space+of+points) in the plane (see [below](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/braid+group#AsFundamentalGroupOfConfigurationSpace) for more).

[L49] Here it makes a key difference whether:

[L51] - one considers the points in a configuration as *ordered* (labeled by numbers `1,⋯,n+1`) in which case one speaks of the [*pure braid group*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/pure+braid+group),
[L52] - or as indistinguishable (albeit in any case with distinct positions!) in which case one speaks of the *braid group* proper.

[L54] Namely, after traveling along a general braid `b` the order of the given points may come out permuted by a [permutation](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/permutation) `perm(b)`, and the braid is called *pure* precisely if this permutation is trivial:

[L56] [image](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/BraidGroupFibration-230205.jpg)

[L58] More explicitly, braid groups admit [finite presentations](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/finitely+presented+group) by [generators and relations](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/generators+and+relations). To these we now turn first:

[L60] ## 2. Definitions and characterizations

[L62] - [*Via generators and relations*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/braid+group#ByGeneratorsAndRelations)

[L67] ### *Via generators and relations*

[L69] #### Presentation of general braids

[L71] We discuss the braid group as a [finitely generated group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/finitely+generated+group) ([Artin 1925, (5)-(6)](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/braid+group#Artin25); [Artin 1947, (18)-(19)](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/braid+group#Artin47); review in, e.g.: [Fox & Neuwirth 1962, §7](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/braid+group#FoxNeuwirth62)):

[L73] ***Definition 2.1***. ***(Artin presentation)***

[L75] The ***Artin braid group***, `Br(n+1)`, on `n+1` strands is the [finitely generated group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/finitely+generated+group) given via [generators and relations](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/generators+and+relations) by (this and the following graphics are taken from [Myers et al. (2023)](https://ncatlab.org/schreiber/show/Topological+Quantum+Gates+in+Homotopy+Type+Theory)):

[L77] - generators:

  (1)
[L80]   ```math
[L81]   bii=1,…,n
  ```

[L84] svgsvg

[L86] - relations I:

  (2)
[L89]   ```math
[L90]   ∀i+1<jbi⋅bj=bj⋅bi
  ```

svg

[L95] - relations II ([Yang-Baxter equation](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Yang-Baxter+equation))
[L96]   ```math
[L97]   ∀1≤i<nbi⋅bi+1⋅bi=bi+1⋅bi⋅bi+1
  ```

svg



[L104] #### Presentation of pure braids

[L106] Similarly, the [pure braid group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/pure+braid+group) has a [finite presentation](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/finitely+presented+group).

[L108] One possible set of generators (also originally considered by Artin) are the “weave” braids where one strands lassos exactly one other strand:

svg

[L112] In terms of these generators, the [pure braid group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/pure+braid+group) is obained by quotienting out the following relations — an optimization of Artin’s original pure braid relations, due to [Lee (2010, Thm. 1.1, Rem. 3.1)](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/braid+group#Lee10):

[L114] [image](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/PureBraidGroupPresentation-230205b.jpg)

[L116] svgsvgsvgsvgsvg

[L118] Here we repeatedly used products of pure braid generators of the following form:

svg

[L122] ### *As fundamental group of a configuration space of points*

[L124] Geometrically, one may understand the group of braids in `ℝ3` as the [fundamental group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/fundamental+group) of the [configuration space of points](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/configuration+space+of+points) in the [plane](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/plane) `ℝ2` (traditionally regarded as the [complex plane](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/complex+plane) `ℂ` in this context, though the [complex structure](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/complex+structure) plays no role in the definition of the braid group as such).

[L126] (originally due to [Hurwitz 1891, §II](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/braid+group#Hurwitz1891), then re-discovered/re-vived in [Fadell & Neuwirth 1962, p. 118](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/braid+group#FadellNeuwirth62), [Fox & Neuwirth 1962, §7](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/braid+group#FoxNeuwirth62), review includes [Birman 1975, §1](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/braid+group#Birman75), [Williams 2020, pp. 9](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/braid+group#Williams20))

[L128] ***In the plane***

[L130] We say this in more detail:

[L132] Let `Cn↪ℂn` denote the space of [configurations of n ordered points](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/configuration+space+of+points) in the [complex plane](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/complex+plane), whose elements are those [n-tuples](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/n-tuples) `(z1,…,zn)` such that `zi≠zj` whenever `i≠j`. In other words, `Cn` is the [complement](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/complement) of the [fat diagonal](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/fat+diagonal):

[L134] ```math
[L135] Cn≔ℂn∖Δℂn.
```

[L138] The [symmetric group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/symmetric+group) `Sn` [acts](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/group+action) on `Cn` by [permuting](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/permutation) coordinates. Let:

[L140] - `Cn/Sn` denote the [quotient](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/quotient) by this group action, hence the [orbit](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/orbit) space (the space of `n`-element subsets of `ℂ` if one likes),
[L141] - `[z1,…,zn]` denote the image of `(z1,…,zn)` under the quotient [coprojection](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/coprojection) `π:Cn→Cn/Sn` (i.e. its the [equivalence class](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/equivalence+class)).

[L143] We understand `p=(1,2,…,n)` as the basepoint for `Cn`, and `[p]=[1,2,…n]` as the basepoint for the [configuration space of unordered points](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/configuration+space+of+unordered+points) `Cn/Sn`, making it a [pointed topological space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/pointed+topological+space).

[L145] ***Definition 2.2***.

[L147] The *braid group* is the [fundamental group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/fundamental+group) of the [configuration space of n unordered points](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/configuration+space+of+unordered+points):

[L149] ```math
[L150] Br(n)≔π1(Cn/Sn,[p])
```

[L153] The *pure braid group* is the [fundamental group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/fundamental+group) of the [configuration space of n ordered points](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/configuration+space+of+ordered+points):

[L155] ```math
[L156] PBr(n)≔π1(Cn,p).
```



[L161] Evidently a braid `β` is represented by a path `α:I→Cn/Sn` with `α(0)=[p]=α(1)`. Such a path may be uniquely lifted through the [covering](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/covering) projection `π:Cn→Cn/Sn` to a path `α˜` such that `α˜(0)=p`. The end of the path `α˜(1)` has the same underlying subset as `p` but with coordinates permuted: `α˜(1)=(σ(1),σ(2),…,σ(n))`. Thus the braid `β` is exhibited by `n` non-intersecting strands, each one connecting an `i` to `σ(i)`, and we have a map `β↦σ` appearing as the quotient map of an exact sequence

[L163] ```math
[L164] 1→PBr(n)→Br(n)→Sym(n)→1
```

[L167] which is part of a [long exact homotopy sequence](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/long+exact+sequence+of+homotopy+groups) corresponding to the [fibration](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/fibration) `π:Cn→Cn/Sn`.

[L169] ***In general surfaces or graphs***

[L171] Since the notion of a [configuration space of points](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/configuration+space+of+points) makes sense for points in any [topological space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/topological+space), not necessarily the [plane](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/plane) `ℝ2`, the [above](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/braid+group#GeometricDefinition) geometric definition has an immediate generalization:

[L173] For `Σ` any [surface](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/surface), the [fundamental group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/fundamental+group) of the (ordered) [configuration space of points](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/configuration+space+of+points) in `Σ` may be regarded as generalized (pure) braid group, called a *surface braid group*. (See the [*spherical braid group*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/spherical+braid+group) for the case that the surface in question is the [2-sphere](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/2-sphere).)

[L175] These surface braid groups are of interest in [3d topological field theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/3d+topological+field+theory) and in particular in [topological quantum computation](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/topological+quantum+computation) where it models [non-abelian anyons](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/non-abelian+anyons).

[L177] Yet more generally, one may consider the fundamental group of the configuration space of points of any topological space `X`.

[L179] For example for `X` a 1-dimensional [CW-complex](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/CW-complex), hence an ([undirected](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/undirected+graph)) [graph](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/graph), one speaks of *graph braid groups* (e.g. [Farley & Sabalka 2009](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/braid+group#FarleySabalka2009)).

[L181] > The following should maybe not be here in the Definition-section, but in some Properties- or Examples-section, or maybe in a dedicated entry on *graph braid groups*[*?*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/new/graph+braid+groups):

[L183] It has been shown ([An & Maciazek 2006](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/braid+group#AnMaciazek2006), using discrete [Morse theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Morse+theory) and combinatorial analysis of small graphs) that graph braid groups are generated by particular particle moves with the following description:

[L185] 1. Star-type generators: exchanges of particle pairs on vertices of the particular graph
[L186] 2. loop type generators: circular moves of a single particle around a simple cycle of the graph

[L188] ### *Braid groups as mapping class groups of punctured surfaces*

[L190] The [braid groups](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/braid+groups) are equivalently given by [mapping class groups](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/mapping+class+groups) of [punctured](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/punctured) [surfaces](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/surfaces). [[Birman 1969](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/braid+group#Birman69)]

[L192] #### For plain braid groups

[L194] The braid group `Br(n)` may be alternatively described as the [mapping class group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/mapping+class+group) of a 2-disk `D2` with `n` punctures. [[Birman 1969](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/braid+group#Birman69)]

[L196] (review includes [Birman 1975 §4](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/braid+group#Birman75), [González-Meneses 2011 §1.4](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/braid+group#Gonz%C3%A1lez-Meneses11), [Massuyeau 2021 §3.3](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/braid+group#Massuyeau21), [Abadie 2022 §1.3](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/braid+group#Abadie22))

[L198] Concretely, consider

[L200] 1. `D2∖{z1,⋯,zn}`

[L202]    denoting the [complement](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/complement)

This is an nLab overview of the **braid group**, and it’s actually a pretty rich doorway into several things you’ve been circling: worldline topology, surface/spherical braids, anyonic exchange structure, mapping-class viewpoints, and eventually framed/loop braids. I’m reading it as a mathematical object first, then I’ll separate what looks genuinely useful for H(s)H from what is just neighboring vocabulary.

[L120]
[L121] A quick way of saying this with precision is to observe that a braid group is thus the [*fundamental group*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/fundamental+group) `π1` of a [configuration space of points](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/configuration+space+of+points) in the plane (see [below](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/braid+group#AsFundamentalGroupOfConfigurationSpace) for more).
[L122]
[L123] Here it makes a key difference whether:
[L124]
[L125] - one considers the points in a configuration as *ordered* (labeled by numbers `1,⋯,n+1`) in which case one speaks of the [*pure braid group*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/pure+braid+group),
[L126] - or as indistinguishable (albeit in any case with distinct positions!) in which case one speaks of the *braid group* proper.
[L127]
[L128] Namely, after traveling along a general braid `b` the order of the given points may come out permuted by a [permutation](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/permutation) `perm(b)`, and the braid is called *pure* precisely if this permutation is trivial:

[L197]
[L198] Partly motivated by the possibility of [quantum computation](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/quantum+computation) eventually breaking the security of [cryptography](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/cryptography) based on [abelian groups](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/abelian+groups), such as [elliptic curves](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/elliptic+curves), there are proposals to use [non-abelian](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/non-abelian+group) [braid groups](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/braid+groups) for purposes of [cryptography](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/cryptography) (“post-quantum cryptography”).
[L199]
[L200] #### Via Conjugacy Search
[L201]
[L202] An early proposal was to use the *Conjugacy Search Problem* in [braid groups](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/braid+groups) as a computationally hard problem for cryptography. This approach, though, was eventually found not to be viable.

thoughts.summary: Explained braid groups and their mathematical context

parts:
This is the nLab entry on the **braid group**, and there’s more here for your purposes than the name alone suggests. At bottom, braid groups are a rigorous way of answering:

> If several identifiable things move around one another without colliding, which histories of motion are genuinely different, and which are merely deformable versions of the same history?

The page starts with exactly the spacetime interpretation that makes the subject intuitive: take several noncoincident points moving in a plane. Their histories through time become strands in three-dimensional spacetime. Two histories count as the same braid if one can be continuously deformed into the other without strands crossing or breaking. fileciteturn0file0L41-L47

That gives a surprisingly deep equivalence:

\[
B_n \cong \pi_1(\mathrm{Conf}_n(\mathbb{R}^2)/S_n).
\]

In words: the braid group is the fundamental group of the **configuration space** of \(n\) unordered noncolliding points. If the individual points retain their labels, you instead get the **pure braid group** \(PB_n\). fileciteturn0file0L122-L156

That distinction is useful. A general braid can exchange the identities/positions of strands; a pure braid must bring each labeled strand back to its own position. Algebraically there is an exact sequence

\[
1\rightarrow PB_n\rightarrow B_n\rightarrow S_n\rightarrow1,
\]

so you can think of a braid as containing more information than merely the final permutation. The permutation tells you **where everybody ended up**; the braid remembers **how they got there**. fileciteturn0file0L161-L167

The algebra itself is extremely economical. \(B_n\) is generated by elementary crossings

\[
\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\ldots,\sigma_{n-1},
\]

where \(\sigma_i\) means, roughly, strand \(i\) passes strand \(i+1\) in one orientation. The defining relations are

\[
\sigma_i\sigma_j=\sigma_j\sigma_i,\qquad |i-j|>1
\]

and

\[
\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i
=
\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}.
\]

That second relation is the braid/Yang–Baxter relation. fileciteturn1file7L253-L280

Visually, it says that two apparently different sequences of three adjacent exchanges are topologically the same motion. This is one reason braid groups suddenly connect knot theory, statistical mechanics, quantum groups, Yang–Baxter equations, anyons, and topological quantum computing. The document explicitly follows those connections into braid-group representations and quantum gates. fileciteturn1file1L32-L47

There is a particularly nice low-\(n\) progression. \(B_1\) is trivial. \(B_2\cong\mathbb Z\): with only two strands, the invariant essentially counts signed winding/crossing. \(B_3\) is the first seriously noncommutative case, and the page notes that \(B_3\) is also the trefoil knot group. fileciteturn1file2L81-L108

But the part I think is considerably more interesting for H(s)H begins when the article stops assuming the points live in an ordinary plane.

The configuration-space definition generalizes immediately. Put the moving points on some surface \(\Sigma\), and you get a **surface braid group**. Put them on \(S^2\), and you get a **spherical braid group**. The article explicitly points out their appearance in 3-dimensional topological field theory and non-Abelian anyon models. fileciteturn2file0L25-L33

And it generalizes farther still: the underlying space does not even have to be a surface. The page mentions **graph braid groups**, where allowable motion is constrained to a graph. Interestingly, their generators break naturally into exchange-like motions at vertices and loop-like motions around cycles. fileciteturn2file0L31-L40

That is already close to something I'd flag for your finite-core work: **the topology of the allowed carrier changes the algebra of possible histories.** You do not first prescribe an abstract particle algebra and then make things move. You can instead specify a configuration space and ask what its allowable continuous motions generate.

There is another equivalence in the article that I suspect may eventually be even more useful to you than the pictures of braids:

\[
B_n \simeq \mathrm{MCG}(D^2-\{n\text{ punctures}\}).
\]

A braid group can be understood as the **mapping-class group of a punctured disk**. In other words, instead of asking how strands move, ask which globally distinct deformations of a punctured surface exist. Those are two descriptions of the same structure. fileciteturn0file0L188-L230

And yet another:

\[
B_n\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Aut}(F_n),
\]

a faithful action on the automorphisms of a free group. So the same object can be viewed as:

motion histories → topology of configuration space → deformations of a punctured surface → algebraic transformations of a free group.

That multiplicity of representations is important. It means "braiding" isn't fundamentally about drawing intertwined ropes. The rope picture is one realization of a deeper structure.

For H(s)H, though, there is one major caveat I'd put in red ink.

**Ordinary Artin braid groups are probably not the eventual object you want.**

Classical braiding is naturally about pointlike objects moving in **two spatial dimensions**, whose histories are one-dimensional strands in \(2+1\)-dimensional spacetime. In three unrestricted spatial dimensions, point particles can generally move around one another and undo apparent braidings; the surviving exchange structure collapses much closer to ordinary permutation structure.

But H(s)H has repeatedly been dealing with **extended filaments/worldtubes, intrinsic rotation, framing, closed carriers, shells and embedded structures**. Once the moving objects themselves have extent, the topology changes.

And the nLab page gives two conspicuous signposts in exactly that direction:

- **framed braid groups**
- **loop braid groups** fileciteturn2file2L136-L148 fileciteturn2file1L115-L125

A framed braid adds something like an orientation/twist degree of freedom to each strand. Merely exchanging two strands no longer exhausts the state: each strand may also rotate about its own longitudinal axis.

That immediately sounds closer to your decomposition into **translation/exchange + intrinsic rotation/twist** than ordinary \(B_n\).

And a **loop braid group** replaces point particles by loops moving through three-dimensional space. Loops can pass around one another, and—depending on the precise version—can have motions unavailable to point braids. For a theory whose fundamental geometrical objects are filamentary, tubular, closed, nested, or recursively wound, that may be a much better mathematical neighborhood.

So I would currently draw the relationship this way:

\[
\text{Artin braids}
\longrightarrow
\text{surface/spherical braids}
\longrightarrow
\text{framed braids}
\longrightarrow
\text{motion/loop braid groups}
\]

not as a proposed H(s)H derivation, but as an increasingly plausible sequence of **candidate calculational grammars**.

There is also a very interesting conceptual match with what you've been doing with the finite core and \(P\). Suppose your canonical local configuration is \(P\), and allowed evolution consists of a small finite set of elementary moves. Then instead of immediately assigning continuous field variables to every microscopic detail, one could ask whether the evolution history admits a word

\[
P
\xrightarrow{g_{i_1}}
P_1
\xrightarrow{g_{i_2}}
P_2
\xrightarrow{g_{i_3}}\cdots
\]

in some motion group, with different apparent sequences identified whenever the geometry says they are continuously equivalent.

Then your proposed quantities like angle deviation, asymmetry, bifurcation, rotation, reconnection, etc. would not necessarily all be **generators**. Some might instead be:

1. continuous parameters attached to generators,
2. framing variables,
3. invariants of a braid/motion class,
4. transition conditions between classes,
5. or energetic weights assigned after the topology has been classified.

That distinction could clean up the architecture considerably.

And there is one especially appealing possibility: the braid relation itself is a model of **path independence under locally different decompositions**,

\[
\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i
=
\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}.
\]

You have been trying to determine when apparently different decompositions of the same canonical \(P\)-evolution should count as genuinely different states versus merely different descriptions of one evolution. Braid/motion-group machinery is almost tailor-made for posing that question rigorously.

I would therefore classify this article as **not merely a background reference on braids**, but a map pointing toward a mathematical program:

**construct the configuration space of the actual H(s)H finite object first; then calculate its motion group rather than assuming that its motion group is \(B_n\).**

That is the interesting move.

The page itself even contains recent references through 2026, including Cohen and Pakianathan's *Configuration Spaces and Braid Groups*, so whoever assembled the version you pasted has kept the bibliography quite current. fileciteturn2file0L76-L94

If I were choosing the next thing to inspect from this tree, I would go straight to **framed braid groups and loop braid groups**, with **spherical braid groups** alongside them because of your sphere/core constructions. Those three are considerably closer to the geometry you've actually been building than vanilla Artin braids.

Abstract: (APS)

The experiments of Tuve, Heydenburg and Hafstad and those of White are discussed by means of the standard theory of scattering in central fields. The theoretical formulas are presented in a form convenient for numerical computation and are supplemented by tables. These are arranged so as to enable an experimentalist to compute the effect of phase shifts due to angular momenta L=0,ℏ,2ℏ, and to infer these phase shifts from the experimental material (Tables I, II, III, IV, V, VI, VII, VIII, IX). Tables of necessary Coulomb wave functions are also given for zero angular momentum. By means of these the interaction energy can be computed from the experimental material (Tables X, XI, XII, XIII). Statistical fluctuations make conclusions drawn from White's data somewhat uncertain. The experiments of Tuve, Heydenburg and Hafstad are comparatively free of statistical effects and their comparison with theory shows that (a) There is an unmistakable difference between the observed scattering and that to be expected according to Mott's formula which uses the inverse square law. (b) This difference can be explained by using practically entirely effects of the phase shift in the partial wave having L=0 (head on collisions; s wave distortions). The distortion of p and d waves (L=ℏ,2ℏ) is secondary and the experimental accuracy does not yet suffice to enable their quantitative determination. (c) The variation of the scattering anomaly with proton energy is in approximate agreement with that to be expected from an interaction potential independent of the energy. (d) For a given range of nuclear forces the interaction potential is accurately determined by the data. The values obtained are in good agreement with those found by Feenberg and Knipp and by Bethe from the mass defects of H2, H3, He4 provided the mass defect calculations are made on the basis of a proton-neutron interaction which depends on the relative orientation of the spins of proton and neutron in accordance with Wigner's explanation of the large scattering of slow neutrons by hydrogen. Mass defect calculations based on a proton-neutron interaction indicated by the binding energy of H2 without dependence on the spin orientation give a much lower value for the interaction between like particles than that obtained from the proton-proton scattering experiments. The "like-particle" interaction for a Gauss error potential is 39mc2e−17r2 with 8.97×10−13 cm as the unit of length and the interaction energy is 11.1 mev for a potential which is constant (except for its Coulombian part) within a distance e2mc2=2.82×10−13 cm. (e) The interaction between protons as derived from the scattering experiments is found to be very nearly equal to that between a proton and a neutron in the corresponding condition of relative spin orientation and angular momentum (S1 state). The proton-neutron values which come closest to being equal to the proton-proton values are those obtained by Fermi and Amaldi from the scattering and absorption of slow neutrons. The close agreement between the empirical values of the proton-proton and proton-neutron interactions in S1 states suggests that aside from Coulombian and spin effects the interactions between heavy particles are independent of their charge and that the apparent preference for equal numbers of protons and neutrons in the building up of nuclei is conditioned more by the operation of the exclusion principle than by the greater values of proton-neutron forces.

Abstract: (APS)

The various types of exchange forces that are being used in current discussions of nuclear structure may all be simply expressed in terms of a formalism which attributes five coordinates to each "heavy" particle and applies the Pauli exclusion principle to all the particles in the system. The simplest assumption for the interaction law is that which implies equality of proton-proton and neutron-neutron forces and also equality with the proton-neutron forces of corresponding symmetry. This is in accord with the empirical knowledge of these interactions at present.

## Abstract

A comparison of Fermi's formula for the distribution in energy of the electrons and positrons emitted by radioactive bodies with the observed spectra seems to show that a basic factor in it, the statistical factor, is not asymmetric enough. Since about the same degree of asymmetry is common to the spectra of light and heavy nuclei and of positron and electron emitters, it cannot be ascribed to another factor in the Fermi formula, depending on the nuclear field. A weight factor is introduced to provide the required asymmetry by changing the form of the Fermi interaction energy. It is shown that two almost equivalent points of view can be employed in attacking this problem and that a certain uniqueness in the form of the interaction law can be obtained within the requirements laid down by Fermi. The modified distribution formula, which holds strictly only for light nuclei, is then shown to give a much more satisfactory agreement with the data than the original formula.

## Zusammenfassung

Eine quantitative Theorie des β-Zerfalls wird vorgeschlagen, in welcher man die Existenz des Neutrinos annimmt, und die Emission der Elektronen und Neutrinos aus einem Kern beim β-Zerfall mit einer ähnlichen Methode behandelt, wie die Emission eines Lichtquants aus einem angeregten Atom in der Strahlungstheorie. Formeln für die Lebensdauer und für die Form des emittierten kontinuierlichen β- Strahlenspektrums werden abgeleitet und mit der Erfahrung verglichen.

Abstract: (APS)

The representation of Fermi particles by two-component Pauli spinors satisfying a second order differential equation and the suggestion that in β decay these spinors act without gradient couplings leads to an essentially unique weak four-fermion coupling. It is equivalent to equal amounts of vector and axial vector coupling with two-component neutrinos and conservation of leptons. (The relative sign is not determined theoretically.) It is taken to be "universal"; the lifetime of the μ agrees to within the experimental errors of 2%. The vector part of the coupling is, by analogy with electric charge, assumed to be not renormalized by virtual mesons. This requires, for example, that pions are also "charged" in the sense that there is a direct interaction in which, say, a π0 goes to π− and an electron goes to a neutrino. The weak decays of strange particles will result qualitatively if the universality is extended to include a coupling involving a Λ or Σ fermion. Parity is then not conserved even for those decays like K→2π or 3π which involve no neutrinos. The theory is at variance with the measured angular correlation of electron and neutrino in He6, and with the fact that fewer than 10−4 pion decay into electron and neutrino.

## Abstract

A two-component theory of the neutrino is discussed. The theory is possible only if parity is not conserved in interactions involving the neutrino. Various experimental implications are analyzed. Some general remarks concerning nonconservation are made.

## Abstract

The decay of a polarized muon is studied in the case of the general four-component neutrino theory with the most general parity-nonconserving interaction. A three-parameter formula for the decay-electron distribution is obtained as a generalization of the Michel formula for an unpolarized muon. This general formula is examined to determine to what extent the observed spectrum enables one to decide whether any particular theory is correct or not. It is seen, among other things, that by the observation of the muon decay spectrum alone one cannot test the validity of the two-component neutrino theory. To facilitate a possible accurate experimental test of the two-component neutrino theory, the radiative correction for the decay of a polarized muon is worked out to the lowest order in 𝛼. Although the correction is rather complicated, it can still be expressed approximately by the three-parameter formula mentioned above. It is found, in particular, that the corrected Michel parameter for the two-component theory is 0.706 when a neutrino and an antineutrino are emitted in the final state, which is 6% smaller than the value 0.75 predicted by the simple theory.

## Abstract

The decay of a polarized muon is studied in the case of the general four-component neutrino theory with the most general parity-nonconserving interaction. A three-parameter formula for the decay-electron distribution is obtained as a generalization of the Michel formula for an unpolarized muon. This general formula is examined to determine to what extent the observed spectrum enables one to decide whether any particular theory is correct or not. It is seen, among other things, that by the observation of the muon decay spectrum alone one cannot test the validity of the two-component neutrino theory. To facilitate a possible accurate experimental test of the two-component neutrino theory, the radiative correction for the decay of a polarized muon is worked out to the lowest order in 𝛼. Although the correction is rather complicated, it can still be expressed approximately by the three-parameter formula mentioned above. It is found, in particular, that the corrected Michel parameter for the two-component theory is 0.706 when a neutrino and an antineutrino are emitted in the final state, which is 6% smaller than the value 0.75 predicted by the simple theory.

[L8] Abstract
[L9] One of us (L.S.) and H. Verlinde independently conjectured a holographic duality
[L10] between the double-scaled SYK model at infinite temperature and dimensionally
[L11] reduced (2 + 1)-dimensional de Sitter space [1]-[8]. Beyond the statement that such
[L12] a duality exists there was deep disagreement between the two proposals [9]. In this
[L13] note, we trace the origin of the disagreement to a superficial similarity between two
[L14] q-deformed algebraic structures: the algebra of “chords” in DSSYK, and the algebra
[L15] of line operators in the Chern-Simons formulation of 3D de Sitter gravity. Assuming
[L16] that these two structures are the same requires an identification of parameters [7][10]
[L17] which leads to a collapse of the separation of scales [9]—the separation being required
[L18] by the semiclassical limit [3][9]. Dropping that assumption restores the separation
[L19] of scales but leaves unexplained the relation between chords and Chern-Simons line
[L20] operators.
[L21] In this note we point out the existence of a third q-deformed algebra that appears
[L22] in DSSYK: the algebra of “wee-chords.” Identifying the Chern-Simons line operators
[L23] with wee-chords removes the discrepancy and leads to a satisfying relation between
[L24] the two sides of the duality.

[L17] [Wikipedia](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Page) enforces its entries to adopt an [NPOV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia\:Neutral_point_of_view) – a *neutral point of view*. This is appropriate for an encyclopedia.

[L19] However, [the nLab is not Wikipedia](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/About), nor is it an encyclopedia, although it does aspire to provide a useful reference in many areas (among its other purposes). In particular, many parts of the `n`Lab *have* a particular point of view, which we may call the ***`n`******-point of view*** (`n`POV) or the [***higher structures***](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+structures)*** point of view***, encompassing [higher algebraic](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+algebra), [homotopical](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+theory), or [n-](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+category+theory) [categorical](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/category+theory) point of views.

[L21] To some extent the `n`POV is just the observation that [homotopy theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+theory)/[algebraic topology](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/algebraic+topology), ([homotopy](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+type+theory)) [type theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/type+theory), ([higher](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+category+theory)) [category theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/category+theory) and ([higher](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+algebra)) [categorical algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/categorical+algebra) have a plethora of useful applications.

[L30] *Higher geometry* or *homotopical geometry* is the study of concepts of [space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/space) and [geometry](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/geometry) in the context of [higher category theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+category+theory) and [homotopy theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+theory).

[L32] ***Slogan***. higher geometry = [geometry](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/geometry) + [homotopy theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+theory)/[higher category theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+category+theory)

[L22] ## 1. Idea

[L24] The *Whitehead tower* of a [pointed](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/pointed+object) [homotopy type](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+type) `X` is an interpolation of the point inclusion `*→X` by a sequence of homotopy types

[L26] ```math
[L27] *→⋯→X(2)→X(1)→X(0)≃X
```

[L30] that are obtained from right to left by *removing *[*homotopy groups*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+groups)* from below*, hence such that

[L32] - each `X(n)` is `(n−1)`-[connected](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/n-simply+connected+space)
[L33] - and each [morphism](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/morphism) `X(n+1)→X(n)` induces an [isomorphism](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/isomorphism) on all [homotopy groups](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+groups) in degree `k≥(n+1)` (and the inclusion `1→πn(X(n))` in degree `n` as well as the identity `1=1` in degree `k<n`).

[L35] The notion of Whitehead tower is [dual](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/duality) to the notion of [*Postnikov tower*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Postnikov+tower), which instead is a factorization of the terminal morphism `X→*` into a tower, where homotopy groups are *added* from right to left.

[L37] In fact, the Whitehead tower may be constructed by taking each stage `X(n+1)→X` to be the [*homotopy fiber*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+fiber) of the corresponding map into the `(n+1)`st stage

[L50] Abstract:

[L52] The first part of this thesis contains two new techniques for the calculation of scattering amplitudes in quantum field theories. These methods were inspired by the recent proposal of a correspondence between the weakly coupled regime of the maximally supersymmetric four dimensional gauge theory and a string theory in twistor space. We show how generalised unitarity cuts in D = 4 − 2² dimensions can be used to calculate efficiently complete one-loop scattering amplitudes in non-supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory. This approach naturally generates the rational terms in the amplitudes, as well as the cut-constructible parts. We then show that the ideas of the Britto, Cachazo, Feng and Witten tree-level on-shell recursion relation can also be applied to the calculation of finite one-loop amplitudes in pure Einstein gravity. The second part of this thesis is a study of the nonabelian phenomena associated with D-branes. Specifically we study the nonabelian bionic brane intersection in which a stack of many coincident D1-branes expand via a non-commutative spherical configuration into a collection of higher dimensional D-branes orthogonal to the original stack of D1-branes. We suggest a construction of monopoles in dimension 2k+1 from fuzzy funnels. We then perform two charge calculations related to this construction. This leads to a new formula for the symmetrised trace quantity. This new formula for the symmetrised trace is then used to study the collapse of a spherical bound state of D0-branes.

[L50] Abstract:

[L52] The first part of this thesis contains two new techniques for the calculation of scattering amplitudes in quantum field theories. These methods were inspired by the recent proposal of a correspondence between the weakly coupled regime of the maximally supersymmetric four dimensional gauge theory and a string theory in twistor space. We show how generalised unitarity cuts in D = 4 − 2² dimensions can be used to calculate efficiently complete one-loop scattering amplitudes in non-supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory. This approach naturally generates the rational terms in the amplitudes, as well as the cut-constructible parts. We then show that the ideas of the Britto, Cachazo, Feng and Witten tree-level on-shell recursion relation can also be applied to the calculation of finite one-loop amplitudes in pure Einstein gravity. The second part of this thesis is a study of the nonabelian phenomena associated with D-branes. Specifically we study the nonabelian bionic brane intersection in which a stack of many coincident D1-branes expand via a non-commutative spherical configuration into a collection of higher dimensional D-branes orthogonal to the original stack of D1-branes. We suggest a construction of monopoles in dimension 2k+1 from fuzzy funnels. We then perform two charge calculations related to this construction. This leads to a new formula for the symmetrised trace quantity. This new formula for the symmetrised trace is then used to study the collapse of a spherical bound state of D0-branes.

[L15] will be put forward, in which the similarity to Dirac’s equation of the
[L16] electron is emphasized. Although it would not seem to be so from previous

[L18] yields more than a mere restatement of old results. In the former presenta￾tion of the theory a number of points concerning the particle aspect of the
[L19] meson undoubtedly remained somewhat obscure. For instance, the correct
[L20] transition to the non-relativistic wave mechanics of a particle of spin 1
[L21] has never been completely given, and it can hardly be claimed that in the
[L22] meson case the use of the term “ spin ” as distinct from polarization has been
[L23] fully justified. In addition, the relation—so important in non-relativistic
[L24] wave mechanics and in Dirac’s theory—which interprets the value of any
[L25] observable as the average of the corresponding operator over the given
[L26] probability distribution of the particle, hitherto appeared to possess no
[L27] counterpart in meson theory. The object of the following is to remedy these
[L28] omissions.
[L29] The meson equations will appear as equations of the Dirac type, but will
[L30] involve matrices obeying a different scheme of commutation rules. These
[L31] rules were first given by Duffin (1938).* A treatment of similar character
[L32] has also been developed by Belinfante (1939), who, however, presents the
[L33] matter in an entirely different form, namely in a generalized spinor notation.

[L38] matrices. Duffin confines himself to stating the representations, which in

[L40] only one of them, and the representation used by de Broglie is actually

[L44] ## 1. Idea
[L45]
[L46] A closed *Jacobi diagram* is a connected undirected [graph](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/graph) with oriented trivalent vertices and with an embedded oriented [circle](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/circle), regarded modulo cyclic identifications, if any.
[L47]
[L48] Here is a picture of a typical Jacobi diagram:
[L49]
[L50] [image](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/JacobiDiagram.jpg)
[L51]
[L52] Here the internal lines need not form a [tree](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/tree); the following is also a Jacobi diagram:
[L53]
[L54] [image](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/OneLoopJacobiDiagram.jpg)
[L55]
[L56] > graphics from [Sati-Schreiber 19c](https://ncatlab.org/schreiber/show/Differential+Cohomotopy+implies+intersecting+brane+observables)
[L57]
[L58] If all the [vertices](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/vertices) sit on the circle, Jacobi diagrams specialize to [chord diagrams](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/chord+diagrams).
[L59]
[L60] Half the number of vertices of a Jacobi diagram is called its *order*
[L61]
[L62] ```math
[L63] order(Γ)≔#Vertices(Γ)/2
[L64] ```
[L65]
[L66] For example, these are the two closed Jacobi diagrams with 2 vertices (order 1):
[L67]
[L68] [image](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/JacobiDiagramsOfOrder1.jpg)
[L69]
[L70] and these are are the 10 closed Jacobi diagrams with 4 vertices (order 2):
[L71]
[L72] [image](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/JacobiDiagramsOfOrder2.jpg)
[L73]
[L74] > graphics grabbed from [Chmutov-Duzhin-Mostovoy 11](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Jacobi+diagram#ChmutovDuzhinMostovoy11)
[L75]
[L76] In applications to [Vassiliev invariants](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Vassiliev+invariants) in [knot theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/knot+theory), Jacobi diagrams play the role of connected [Feynman diagrams](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Feynman+diagrams) for [Chern-Simons theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Chern-Simons+theory) in the presence of one [Wilson line](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Wilson+line) (the circle is then the knot/Wilson line).
[L77]
[L78] ***Terminology.*** Jacobi diagrams have originally been called “chinese character diagrams” ([Bar-Natan 95, Def. 1.8](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Jacobi+diagram#BarNatan95)) or “[Feynman diagrams](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Feynman+diagrams) for [Chern-Simons theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Chern-Simons+theory)” ([Kricker-Spence-Aitchison 97](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Jacobi+diagram#KrickerSpenceAitchison97)) or “circle diagrams” ([Kneissler 97](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Jacobi+diagram#Kneissler97)) or “round diagrams” ([Willerton 99](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Jacobi+diagram#Willerton99)). The term “Jacobi diagram” ([Chmutov-Duzhin-Mostovoy 11, Chapter 5](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Jacobi+diagram#ChmutovDuzhinMostovoy11), [Jackson-Moffat 19, Section 13](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Jacobi+diagram#JacksonMoffat19)) alludes to the [Jacobi identity](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Jacobi+identity) – here also called the [STU relation](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/STU+relation) – via the fact that these diagrams are naturally labelled by a [Lie algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+algebra) equipped with a [Lie algebra representation](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+algebra+representation) (which is really just the [interaction](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/interaction)-aspect of their interpretation as [Chern-Simons theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Chern-Simons+theory) [Feynman diagrams](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Feynman+diagrams)…).
[L79]

[L110] # nLabnPOV
[L111]
[L112] |  [Home Page](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/HomePage "Home page") | [All Pages](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/all_pages "List of all pages") | [Latest Revisions](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/latest_revisions "Latest edits and page creations") | [Discuss this page](https://nforum.ncatlab.org/discussion/584/#Item_15 "Discuss this page in its dedicated thread on the nForum") | 
[L113]
[L114] ### *Context*
[L115]
[L116] #### Algebra
[L117]
[L118] #### Homotopy theory
[L119]
[L120] #### Type theory
[L121]
[L122] #### Category theory
[L123]
[L124] #### Higher category theory
[L125]
[L126] [Wikipedia](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Page) enforces its entries to adopt an [NPOV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia\:Neutral_point_of_view) – a *neutral point of view*. This is appropriate for an encyclopedia.
[L127]
[L128] However, [the nLab is not Wikipedia](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/About), nor is it an encyclopedia, although it does aspire to provide a useful reference in many areas (among its other purposes). In particular, many parts of the `n`Lab *have* a particular point of view, which we may call the ***`n`******-point of view*** (`n`POV) or the [***higher structures***](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+structures)*** point of view***, encompassing [higher algebraic](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+algebra), [homotopical](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+theory), or [n-](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+category+theory) [categorical](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/category+theory) point of views.
[L129]
[L130] To some extent the `n`POV is just the observation that [homotopy theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+theory)/[algebraic topology](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/algebraic+topology), ([homotopy](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+type+theory)) [type theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/type+theory), ([higher](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+category+theory)) [category theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/category+theory) and ([higher](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+algebra)) [categorical algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/categorical+algebra) have a plethora of useful applications.
[L131]
[L132] # Contents
[L133]
[L134] - [1. Idea](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/nPOV#idea)
[L135]   - [Category theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/nPOV#category_theory_2)
[L136]   - [Higher algebra/Homotopy theory/Type theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/nPOV#higher_algebrahomotopy_theorytype_theory)
[L137] - [2. The role of the ](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/nPOV#RoleOfnPOV)[`n`](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/nPOV#RoleOfnPOV)[POV](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/nPOV#RoleOfnPOV)
[L138]   - [Category theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/nPOV#category_theory_3)
[L139] - [3. Examples](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/nPOV#examples)
[L140]
[L141] ## 1. Idea
[L142]
[L143] Around the [nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/HomePage) it is widely believed that [homotopy theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+theory)/[algebraic topology](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/algebraic+topology), ([homotopy](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+type+theory)) [type theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/type+theory), ([higher](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+category+theory)) [category theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/category+theory) and ([higher](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+algebra)) [categorical algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/categorical+algebra) provide a point of view on [Mathematics](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Mathematics), [Physics](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Physics) and [Philosophy](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Philosophy) which is a valuable unifying point of view for the understanding of the concepts involved.
[L144]
[L145] In particular, at the `n`Lab, there is no commitment to being neutral. There are certainly other valid points of view on mathematics, but describing them and being neutral towards them is not the purpose of the `n`Lab. Rather, the `n`Lab starts from the premise that homotopy theory/algebraic topology, (homotopy) type theory, (higher) category theory and (higher) categorical algebra are a useful point of view, and one of its aims is to expose this point of view generally and in a multitude of examples, and thereby accumulate evidence for it.
[L146]
[L147] If you feel skeptical about the `n`-point of view, you should still find the `n`Lab useful, as the largest site for detailed category-theoretic and homotopy-theoretic information online. You are very much welcome to contribute relevant content even if you are such a skeptic.
[L148]
[L149] ### *Category theory*
[L150]
[L151] As recalled in parts on the page on [category theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/category+theory), category theorists have early on, beginning in the 1960s, proclaimed the advantages of category theory over other points of view. It has been observed that this claim, or at least the way it has been put forward, has contributed to a certain alienation of category theory in parts of the mathematical community. That may be true and is understandable. But since a claim is not false *just* because it is put forward with possibly unpleasant boldness, all evidence for the claim deserves to be collected and exposed. We hope the `n`Lab to play a role in this effort.
[L152]
[L153] In particular, there have been dramatic developments since the 1960s. Back then promoting category theory may have been as visionary as the invention of [complex numbers](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/complex+numbers) was in the 16th century. But just as the early rejections of the complex numbers appear strangely out of place from today’s perspective, where their ubiquity proves their reality to the point that it is hard to imagine how life must have been before their conception, so developments of category theory and its applications in the last years have in many areas brought it to the point that rejecting its prevalence amounts (we believe) to rejecting the obvious and ubiquitous. But also mathematics as a whole has drastically grown since then, and while category theory has become an entirely obvious ingredient in areas such as [homotopy theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+theory), [homological algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homological+algebra), [algebraic geometry](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/algebraic+geometry) and even fields like [topological quantum field theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/topological+quantum+field+theory), its similar role to be played in many other areas has often not found wide recognition yet. But this is gradually changing.
[L154]
[L155] ### *Higher algebra/Homotopy theory/Type theory*
[L156]
[L157] From the perspective of [higher algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+algebra), [homotopy theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+theory), and [type theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/type+theory), the fundamental objects of mathematics are [homotopy types](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+types) or [`∞`](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/infinity-groupoid)[-groupoids](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/infinity-groupoid), and the `n`-truncated versions of them, the [`n`](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/n-groupoid)[-groupoids](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/n-groupoid), due to their differing treatment of [equality](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/equality)/[equivalence](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/equivalence) of such objects. This perspective is somewhat different from the perspective of category theory, as category theory takes `n`-categories to be more fundamental than `n`-groupoids, while these branches of mathematics view `n`-categories merely as `n`-groupoids with additional higher structure on top of the [core](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/core) `n`-groupoid. In particular, `n`-categories are merely specific kinds of [directed ](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/directed+%28n%2Cr%29-graph)[`(n,r)`](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/directed+%28n%2Cr%29-graph)[-graphs](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/directed+%28n%2Cr%29-graph).
[L158]
[L159] On the other hand, from this perspective, if one were to take the directed structure to be more fundamental as one does in category theory, then the fundamental structures would end up being `n`-[posets](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/n-poset) rather than `n`-[categories](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/n-category); in particular, taking [preorder](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/preorder) to be more fundamental than [equivalence relations](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/equivalence+relations)/[equality](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/equality).
[L160]
[L161] ## 2. The role of the `n`POV
[L162]
[L163] ### *Category theory*
[L164]
[L165] Practitioners of category theory have often attempted to express the striking power of category theory (or general conceptual methods), sometimes through aphorism, sometimes through metaphor. Early on, [Peter Freyd](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Peter+Freyd) wrote
[L166]
[L167] > Perhaps the purpose of categorical algebra is to show that which is trivial is trivially trivial.
[L168]
[L169] This can be taken to mean that one thing category theory does is help make the softer bits seem utterly natural and obvious, so as to quickly get to the heart of the matter, isolating the hard nuggets, which one may then attack with abandon. This is an invaluable service category theory performs for mathematics; therefore, category theory is plain good pragmatics.
[L170]
[L171] However, it is also possible to take it a step beyond the pragmatic attitude, and see category theory (and now higher category theory) as exemplifying a style for doing even hard mathematics, as in the style for which Grothendieck is renowned. Paraphrasing from Colin McLarty’s [excellent essay](http://webusers.imj-prg.fr/~leila.schneps/grothendieckcircle/Mathbiographies/mclarty1.pdf), let us regard the aforementioned pragmatic attitude as leading up to the *hammer-and-chisel principle*: if you think of a theorem to be proved as a nut to be opened, so as to reach “the nourishing flesh protected by the shell” (Grothendieck), then one thing to do is “put the cutting edge of the chisel against the shell and strike hard. If needed, begin again at many different points until the shell cracks – and you are satisfied.” Grothendieck points to Serre as a master of this technique. He then says:
[L172]
[L173] > I can illustrate the second approach with the same image of a nut to be opened. The first analogy which came to my mind is of immersing the nut in some softening liquid, and why not simply water? From time to time you rub so the liquid penetrates better, and otherwise you let time pass. The shell becomes more flexible through weeks and months – when the time is ripe, hand pressure is enough, the shell opens like a perfectly ripened avocado!
[L174] >
[L175] > A different image came to me a few weeks ago. The unknown thing to be known appeared to me as some stretch of earth or hard marl, resisting penetration… the sea advances insensibly in silence, nothing seems to happen, nothing moves, the water is so far off you hardly hear it… yet it finally surrounds the resistant substance. (Translated from the French by McLarty)
[L176]
[L177] This arresting metaphor of “la mer qui monte” (“[the rising sea](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/the+rising+sea)”), which over time changes the very form of the resistant substance, is very much in the style of Grothendieck himself. McLarty quotes Deligne as saying that a typical Grothendieck proof consists of a long series of trivial steps where “nothing seems to happen, and yet at the end a highly non-trivial theorem is there.”
[L178]
[L179] ## 3. Examples
[L180]
[L181] For an (incomplete) list of examples of topics for which the `n`POV has proven to be a useful perspective, see
[L182]

[L204]
[L205] **Redirected from "higher structures".**
[L206]
[L207] ### *Context*
[L208]
[L209] #### Higher category theory
[L210]
[L211] #### Homotopy theory
[L212]
[L213] # Contents
[L214]
[L215] - [1. Idea](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+structure#idea)
[L216] - [2. Related entries](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+structure#related_entries)
[L217] - [3. References](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+structure#references)
[L218]
[L219] ## 1. Idea
[L220]
[L221] The term *higher structure*
[L222]
[L223] > (as used in numerous conference titles starting in the 2010s, e.g. [CGX 11](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+structure#CGX11), [BBM 16](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+structure#BBM16), [SBBM 18](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+structure#SBBM18), [JSSW 18](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+structure#JSSW18) and by a journal titled [*Higher Structures*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+structure#HSJ))
[L224]
[L225] has come to mean essentially what elsewhere had been and still is called:
[L226]
[L227] - [*categorified*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/categorification)* *[*mathematical structure*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/mathematical+structure) or [*mathematical structure*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/mathematical+structure)* *[*in*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/internalization)* *[*higher category theory*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+category+theory),
[L228]
[L229] or, more specifically:
[L230]
[L231] - [*mathematical structure*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/mathematical+structure)* *[*in*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/internalization)* *[*(∞,1)-category theory*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-category+theory),
[L232]
[L233] hence:
[L234]
[L235] - [*mathematical structure*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/mathematical+structure)* *[*in*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/internalization)* *[*homotopy theory*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+theory) ([higher algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+algebra)/[homotopical algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopical+algebra), [higher geometry](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+geometry)/[derived geometry](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/derived+algebraic+geometry), etc.),
[L236]
[L237] where the identies/laws of ordinary [mathematical structures](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/mathematical+structures) may hold only up to [coherent](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/coherence+law) [higher homotopies](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+homotopies).
[L238]
[L239] For example, [L-∞ algebras](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/L-%E2%88%9E+algebras), which are [Lie algebra objects](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+algebra+objects) [in](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/internalization) the [(∞,1)-](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-category)[category of chain complexes](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/category+of+chain+complexes), would be a core topic in *higher structures in *[*Lie theory*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+theory) (elsewhere: [*∞-Lie theory*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%E2%88%9E-Lie+theory)). Further basic classes of higher structures in [higher algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+algebra) (“[brave new algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/brave+new+algebra)”) are [`A∞`](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/A-infinity+algebras)[ algebras](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/A-infinity+algebras) and [`E∞`](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/E-infinity+algebras)[-algebras](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/E-infinity+algebras).
[L240]
[L241] Similarly there are higher structures in [topology](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/topology)/[geometry](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/geometry), for instance [principal ](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/principal+infinity-bundles)[`∞`](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/principal+infinity-bundles)[-bundles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/principal+infinity-bundles) generalizing [principal bundles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/principal+bundles) etc.
[L242]

[L301] # nLabhigher geometry
[L302]
[L303] |  [Home Page](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/HomePage "Home page") | [All Pages](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/all_pages "List of all pages") | [Latest Revisions](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/latest_revisions "Latest edits and page creations") | [Discuss this page](https://nforum.ncatlab.org/discussion/2084/#Item_37 "Discuss this page in its dedicated thread on the nForum") | 
[L304]
[L305] ### *Context*
[L306]
[L307] #### Higher geometry
[L308]
[L309] ***higher geometry*** `←` [Isbell duality](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Isbell+duality) `→` [higher algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+algebra)
[L310]
[L311] ---
[L312]
[L313] # Contents
[L314]
[L315] - [1. Idea](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+geometry#idea)
[L316]   - [Slogan](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+geometry#slogan)
[L317] - [2. Formalizations](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+geometry#Formalizations)
[L318]   - [Gros (∞,1)-toposes](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+geometry#GrosHigherToposes)
[L319]   - [Petit (∞,1)-toposes](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+geometry#PetitHigherToposes)
[L320] - [3. Relation between these approaches](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+geometry#relation_between_these_approaches)
[L321] - [4. Examples](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+geometry#Examples)
[L322]   - [List of examples](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+geometry#list_of_examples)
[L323]   - [Noncommutative algebraic geometry](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+geometry#NoncommutativeAlgebraicGeometry)
[L324]   - [Connes-style noncommutative geometry](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+geometry#ConnesStyleNoncommutativeGeometry)
[L325] - [5. Related concepts](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+geometry#related_concepts)
[L326] - [6. References](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+geometry#Lurie)
[L327]
[L328] ## 1. Idea
[L329]
[L330] *Higher geometry* or *homotopical geometry* is the study of concepts of [space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/space) and [geometry](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/geometry) in the context of [higher category theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+category+theory) and [homotopy theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+theory).
[L331]
[L332] ***Slogan***. higher geometry = [geometry](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/geometry) + [homotopy theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+theory)/[higher category theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+category+theory)
[L333]
[L334] Higher geometry subsumes notably the theory of [orbifolds](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/orbifolds) and [geometric stacks](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/geometric+stacks), as well as the theory of more general [stacks](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/stacks) such as [moduli stacks](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/moduli+stacks), and generalizes all this to [∞-stacks](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%E2%88%9E-stacks) and [derived stacks](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/derived+stacks). This way higher geometry includes what is called [*derived geometry*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/derived+geometry) and it subsumes at least parts of (derived) [noncommutative geometry](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/noncommutative+geometry). Many other phenomena are naturally part of higher geometry, see the list of [Examples](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+geometry#Examples) below.
[L335]
[L336] In any given instance of higher geometry, one starts with a notion of “local models” for the geometry. An *affine space* will then be a formal dual of such a local model, and a general [space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/space) will be formed by “gluing” these affine spaces in some appropriate way. There are two ways of formalizing this idea, coming from [Alexander Grothendieck](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Alexander+Grothendieck)‘s two definitions of [scheme](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/scheme) in [algebraic geometry](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/algebraic+geometry) via [locally ringed spaces](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/locally+ringed+spaces) and [functors of points](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/functors+of+points). Both are built on [(∞,1)-topos theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-topos+theory): in one direction, a [petit](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/petit+topos) [(∞,1)-topos](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-topos) (with some additional [structure](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/structured+%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-topos)) encodes a [space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/space) itself; in another direction, a [space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/space) is an object of a [gros](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/gros+topos) [(∞,1)-topos](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-topos) of [∞-stacks](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%E2%88%9E-stacks) on some [(∞,1)-site](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-site). We discuss these axiomatizations below in [*Formalization*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+geometry#Formalizations).
[L337]
[L338] These approaches do not apply to [noncommutative algebraic geometry](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/noncommutative+algebraic+geometry), which requires a different approach to deal with a more complicated notion of gluing; we discuss this below in [*Noncommutative algebraic geometry*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+geometry#NoncommutativeAlgebraicGeometry).
[L339]
[L340] ## 2. Formalizations
[L341]
[L342] We discuss two different (but closely related) formalizations of these ideas.
[L343]
[L344] In
[L345]
[L346] - [*Gros (∞,1)-topos*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+geometry#GrosHigherToposes)
[L347]
[L348] we discuss the approach of considering one big [(∞,1)-topos](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-topos) `H` (with “big”/[gros](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/gros+topos) being formalized for instance by [cohesion](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/cohesion)) such that (some of) its objects are to be regarded as higher geometric spaces.
[L349]
[L350] In
[L351]
[L352] - [*Petit (∞,1)-toposes*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+geometry#PetitHigherToposes)
[L353]
[L354] we discuss the approach of encoding a would-be higher geometric space `X` by a [structured (∞,1)-topos](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/structured+%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-topos) to be thought of as the [petit](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/petit+topos) [(∞,1)-topos](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-topos) of [(∞,1)-sheaves](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-sheaves) `(Sh∞(X),𝒪X)` of `X`, canonically equipped with a [structure sheaf](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/structure+sheaf) `𝒪X`.
[L355]
[L356] ### *Gros (∞,1)-toposes*
[L357]
[L358] Let `𝒢` be an [(∞,1)-site](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-site) whose objects are to be viewed as “local models” or “test spaces” for a geometry. Within the context of this geometry, we make the following definitions:
[L359]
[L360] An ***affine space*** is a formal dual of an object of `𝒢`, so that the (∞,1)-category of affine spaces is the [opposite](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/opposite+%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-category) of `𝒢`. A ***stack*** is an [∞-stack](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%E2%88%9E-stack) on `𝒢`, so that the (∞,1)-category of stacks is the [gros](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/gros+topos) [(∞,1)-sheaf (∞,1)-topos](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-sheaf+%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-topos) on `𝒢`. Finally, a ***space*** is a [stack](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/stack) `X` that has a cover by a family of affine spaces `(fi:Ui→X)i`, where each `fi` belongs to some nice class of morphisms (e.g. [open immersions](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/open+immersions), [etale morphisms](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/etale+morphisms) or [smooth morphisms](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/smooth+morphisms)).
[L361]
[L362] When the underlying (∞,1)-category of `𝒢` is the (∞,1)-category of [commutative algebras in a symmetric monoidal (∞,1)-category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/commutative+algebras+in+a+symmetric+monoidal+%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-category), this is known as [*homotopical algebraic geometry*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopical+algebraic+geometry). When it is the (∞,1)-category of [algebras over a Lawvere theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/algebras+over+a+Lawvere+theory), this is discussed at [derived geometry](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/derived+geometry).
[L363]
[L364] Following [Bill Lawvere](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Bill+Lawvere), one may ask for a set of [axioms](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/axioms) on the [(∞,1)-sheaf (∞,1)-topos](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-sheaf+%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-topos) `Sh∞(𝒢)` that ensure that it is appropriate to view [(∞,1)-sheaves](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-sheaves) on `𝒢` as generalized geometric spaces. One such set of axioms is [*cohesion*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/cohesion).
[L365]
[L366] ### *Petit (∞,1)-toposes*
[L367]
[L368] As above, let `𝒢` be an [(∞,1)-category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-category) whose objects will be viewed as “local models” for the kind of geometry to be developed. Following [Jacob Lurie](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Jacob+Lurie) (based on the theory of geometry via [ringed toposes](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/ringed+toposes) by [Alexander Grothendieck](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Alexander+Grothendieck) and [Monique Hakim](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Monique+Hakim)), a `𝒢`-[structured (∞,1)-topos](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/structured+%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-topos) is the data of an [(∞,1)-topos](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-topos) together with a [structure sheaf](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/structure+sheaf) valued in `𝒢`. Given an appropriate choice of `𝒢`, one gets the following hierarchy of generalized spaces this way:
[L369]
[L370] - [test spaces](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/geometry+%28for+structured+%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-toposes%29)`↪`
[L371]
[L372]   [spaces locally equivalent to test spaces](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/generalized+scheme)
[L373]
[L374]   `↪` [concrete spaces with structure sheaves taking values in test spaces](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/structured+%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-topos) `↪` [spaces probeable by test spaces](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%E2%88%9E-stack).
[L375]
[L376] technically modeled by:
[L377]
[L378] - [geometry (for structured (∞,1)-toposes)](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/geometry+%28for+structured+%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-toposes%29)`𝒢`
[L379]
[L380]   `↪`
[L381]
[L382]   [generalized scheme](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/generalized+scheme)s
[L383]
[L384]   `↪` formal duals to `𝒢`-[structured (∞,1)-topos](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/structured+%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-topos)es `↪` [(∞,1)-topos](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-topos) of [∞-stack](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%E2%88%9E-stack)s on `𝒢`.
[L385]
[L386] A plethora of proposals for formalizations of higher geometry find their home in this pattern, for instance most of the concepts listed at [generalized smooth space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/generalized+smooth+space).
[L387]
[L388] ## 3. Relation between these approaches
[L389]
[L390] Given a gros [cohesive (∞,1)-topos](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/cohesive+%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-topos) `H` and an object `X∈H`, one may in turn assign to `X` a petit [structured (∞,1)-topos](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/structured+%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-topos) `ShH(X)` of [internal sheaves](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/internal+sheaves) over `X`. See at [*differential cohesion*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/differential+cohesion) for how this works. This connects the “gros” perspective back to the “petit” perspective.
