[L427]
[L428] ## 1. Idea
[L429]
[L430] Traditional [prequantum geometry](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/prequantum+geometry) is the [differential geometry](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/differential+geometry) of [smooth manifolds](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/smooth+manifolds) which are equipped with a [*twist*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/twisted+cohomology) in the form of a [principal U(1)-bundle](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/principal+U%281%29-bundle) and a circle-[principal connection](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/principal+connection). In the context of [*geometric quantization*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/geometric+quantization) of [symplectic manifolds](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/symplectic+manifolds) these arise as [*prequantum bundles*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/prequantum+bundles). Equivalently, prequantum geometry is the [*contact geometry*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/contact+geometry) of the total spaces of these bundles, equipped with their [Ehresmann connection](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Ehresmann+connection) [differential 1-form](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/differential+1-form) and thought of as [*regular contact manifolds*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/regular+contact+manifolds). Prequantum geometry notably studies the [automorphisms](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/automorphisms) of [prequantum bundles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/prequantum+bundles) covering [diffeomorphisms](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/diffeomorphisms) of the base – the [*prequantum operators*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/prequantum+operators) or [*contactomorphisms*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/contactomorphisms) – and the [action](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/action) of these on the space of [sections](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/sections) of the [associated](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/associated+bundle) [line bundle](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/line+bundle) – the [*prequantum states*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/prequantum+states). This is an intermediate step in the genuine [*geometric quantization*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/geometric+quantization) of the [curvature](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/curvature) [differential 2-form](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/differential+2-form) of these bundles, which is obtained by “dividing the above data in half” ([polarization](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/polarization)), important for instance in the the [*orbit method*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/orbit+method).
[L431]
[L432] But prequantum geometry is of interest in its own right. For instance the above automorphism group naturally provides the [Lie integration](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+integration) of the [Poisson bracket](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Poisson+bracket) [Lie algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+algebra) of the underlying [symplectic manifold](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/symplectic+manifold), together with the canonical injection into the [group of bisections](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/group+of+bisections) of the [Lie integration](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+integration) of the [*Atiyah Lie algebroid*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Atiyah+Lie+algebroid) which is associated with the given circle bundle, all of which are fundamental objects of interest in the study of [line bundles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/line+bundles) over [manifolds](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/manifolds).
[L433]
[L434] For a plethora of applications in [differential geometry](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/differential+geometry), one wants to generalize this to [*higher differential geometry*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+differential+geometry) (see at [*motivation for higher differential geometry*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/motivation+for+higher+differential+geometry)) and accordingly study *higher prequantum geometry*.
[L435]
[L436] ## 2. Motivation and survey of results
[L437]
[L438] ### *Ordinary prequantum geometry in terms of automorphisms in slices*
[L439]
[L440] A sequence of time-honored traditional concepts in [geometric quantization](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/geometric+quantization)/[prequantum geometry](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/prequantum+geometry) is
[L441]
[L442] | [Lie groups](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+groups):[Heisenberg group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Heisenberg+group)`↪`[quantomorphism group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/quantomorphism+group)`↪`[gauge group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/gauge+group) |                                                                                |     |                                                                          |     |                                                                      |
[L443] | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
[L444] | [Lie algebras](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+algebras):                                                                                                                                                                                                       | [Heisenberg Lie algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Heisenberg+Lie+algebra) | `↪` | [Poisson Lie algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Poisson+Lie+algebra) | `↪` | twisted [vector fields](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/vector+fields) |
[L445]
[L446] For instance in the [geometric quantization](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/geometric+quantization) of the [electrically](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/electromagnetic+field) [charged](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/charged+particle) [particle](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/particle) [sigma-model](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/sigma-model) we have a [prequantum circle bundle](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/prequantum+circle+bundle) `P` with [connection on a bundle](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/connection+on+a+bundle) `∇` on a [cotangent bundle](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/cotangent+bundle) `X=T*Y` which is essentially the [pullback](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/pullback) of the [electromagnetic field](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/electromagnetic+field)-bundle on [target](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/target+space) [spacetime](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/spacetime) `Y`. Its [*quantomorphism group*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/quantomorphism+group) is the group of [diffeomorphisms](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/diffeomorphisms) `P→≃P` of the total space of the prequantum bundle which preserve the connection (also called the [*contactomorphism*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/contactomorphism) of `(P,∇)` regarded as a [regular contact manifold](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/regular+contact+manifold)). For the following it is convenient to say this using the language of [*moduli stacks*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/moduli+stacks): we may regard `X` as a [representable](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/representable+functor) [sheaf](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/sheaf) on the [site](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/site) of [smooth manifolds](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/smooth+manifolds) (a “[smooth space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/smooth+space)”) and then moreover as a [representable](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/representable+functor) [stack](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/stack) on this site (a “[smooth groupoid](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/smooth+groupoid)”) and make use of the tautological existence of the [moduli stack](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/moduli+stack) of `U(1)`-[principal connections](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/principal+connections), which we write `BU(1)conn` (we don’t need further details right now, but they can be found for instance at [*circle n-bundle with connection*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/circle+n-bundle+with+connection) for details). By definition this is such that for any `X` a map `∇:X→BU(1)conn` is equivalently a `U(1)`-[principal connection](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/principal+connection) and such that a [homotopy](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy) `η:∇1→∇2` between two such maps is equivalently a [gauge transformation](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/gauge+transformation) between two such connections. With this formulation a [quantomorphism](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/quantomorphism) of the [prequantum bundle](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/prequantum+bundle) `∇` is equivalently a diagram of the form as on the right of
[L447]
[L448] ```math
[L449] QuantMorph(∇)={X→≃ϕX↘⇙η↙BU(1)conn}
[L450] ```
[L451]
[L452] in the [(2,1)-category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%282%2C1%29-category) of [stacks](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/stacks), namely a [diffeomorphism](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/diffeomorphism) `ϕ:X→≃X` of the base space of the bundle together with a [gauge transformation](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/gauge+transformation) of `U(1)`-[principal connections](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/principal+connections) `η:ϕ*∇→≃∇`.
[L453]
[L454] The [quantomorphism group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/quantomorphism+group) is naturally an ([infinite dimensional](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/infinite-dimensional+Lie+group)) [Lie group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+group). Its [Lie algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+algebra) is the [Poisson bracket](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Poisson+bracket) [Lie algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+algebra). If `X` is equipped with the structure of a [Lie group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+group) itself (notably if it is a [vector space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/vector+space)), then the sub-Lie algebra of that on the [invariant vectors](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/invariant+differential+form) is the [Heisenberg Lie algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Heisenberg+Lie+algebra) and the Lie group corresponding to that is the [Heisenberg group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Heisenberg+group).
[L455]
[L456] One also says that a triangular diagram as above is an autoequivalence of the “modulating” map `∇:X→BU(1)conn` in the [*slice (2,1)-category*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/slice+%28infinity%2C1%29-category) of [stacks](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/stacks)/[smooth groupoids](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/smooth+groupoids) over `BU(1)conn`.
[L457]
[L458] Such autoequivalences in slices are familiar from basic concepts of [Lie groupoid](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+groupoid) theory. For `𝒢=(𝒢1→→𝒢0)` a [Lie groupoid](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+groupoid), we may regard the inclusion of its manifold of objects as an [atlas](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/atlas) being a map `p𝒢:𝒢0→𝒢`. Regarding this atlas as an object in the [slice (2,1)-category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/slice+%28infinity%2C1%29-category) of [stacks](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/stacks)/[smooth groupoids](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/smooth+groupoids) over `𝒢`, its autoequivalences are diagrams as on the right of
[L459]
[L460] ```math
[L461] BiSect(p𝒢)={𝒢0→ϕ𝒢0↘⇙η↙𝒢}.
[L462] ```
[L463]
[L464] This is a [diffeomorphism](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/diffeomorphism) `ϕ:𝒢0→≃𝒢0` of the [smooth manifold](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/smooth+manifold) of [objects](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/objects) equipped with a [natural transformation](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/natural+transformation) `η` whose component map is a [smooth function](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/smooth+function) that assigns to each point `q∈𝒢0` a [morphism](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/morphism) in `𝒢` of the form `ηq:q→ϕ(q)`. This collection of data is known as a [*bisection*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/bisection) of a [Lie groupoid](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+groupoid). Bisections naturally form a group `BiSect(p𝒢)` , which is all the more manifest if we understand them as autoequivalences of the atlas in the slice, called the [group of bisections](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/group+of+bisections).
[L465]
[L466] This perspective of regarding maps of [smooth groupoids](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/smooth+groupoids) as objects in the slice over their codomain (an elementary step in [higher category theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+category+theory)/[higher topos theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%28infinity%2C1%29-topos+theory), but not common in traditional differential geometry) turns out to be useful and drives all of the refinements, generalizations and theorems that we discuss in the following: we will see that higher [prequantum geometry](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/prequantum+geometry) is essentially the geometry insice [higher slice categories](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/slice+%28infinity%2C1%29-topos) of [higher stacks](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/infinity-stack) over [higher moduli stacks](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/moduli+infinity-stack) of [higher principal connections](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/principal+infinity-connection).
[L467]
[L468] Before we get there, notice the following…
[L469]
[L470] ### *The need for higher prequantum bundles*

[L21] #### Higher category theory
[L22]
[L23] This entry lists aspects of [fundamental physics](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/fundamental+physics) from the [nPOV](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/nPOV): its description in terms of [category theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/category+theory) and [higher category theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+category+theory). For a more coherent exposition, starting with introduction of the very basics, see also at [*geometry of physics*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/geometry+of+physics).

[L56] ## 1. The basic structures
[L57]
[L58] We discuss the setting in which fundamental physics takes place.
[L59]
[L60] ### *Dynamics in space*
[L61]
[L62] Physics is *dynamics* in *spaces* .
[L63]
[L64] [Higher topos theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+topos+theory) provides the formalizations of this most fundamental aspect of physics.
[L65]
[L66] - A general context for [***space***](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/space)***s*** is a [big](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/big+topos) [(∞,1)-topos](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-topos) `H`.
[L67] - A general context for [***geometrical***](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+geometry)*** spaces*** is a [local (∞,1)-topos](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/local+%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-topos).
[L68] - A general context for geometrical spaces and ***processes*** in these spaces is a [cohesive (∞,1)-topos](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/cohesive+%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-topos).
[L69]
[L70] An example of relevance for much of physics is the cohesive `(∞,1)`-topos `H=` [∞LieGrpd](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%E2%88%9ELieGrpd) of [∞-Lie groupoid](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%E2%88%9E-Lie+groupoid)s. This contains
[L71]
[L72] - [smooth manifold](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/smooth+manifold)s;
[L73] - [orbifold](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/orbifold)s;
[L74] - [diffeological space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/diffeological+space)s;
[L75] - smooth [path space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/path+space)s;
[L76]
[L77] In its [Cahiers topos](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Cahiers+topos)-version it contains also
[L78]
[L79] - [infinitesimal space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/infinitesimal+space)s;
[L80] - such as [∞-Lie algebroid](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%E2%88%9E-Lie+algebroid)s.
[L81] - [de Rham space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/de+Rham+space)s, smooth [D-module](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/D-module)s;
[L82]
[L83] In its full [derived geometry](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/derived+geometry)-version it contains also
[L84]
[L85] - [derived ∞-Lie algebroid](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/derived+%E2%88%9E-Lie+algebroid)s such as the [BV-BRST complex](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/BV-BRST+complex)es of [gauge theories](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/gauge+theories).
[L86]
[L87] Every `(∞,1)`-topos comes with its intrinsic notion of [cohomology](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/cohomology). This encodes ***kinematics*** in physics. Such as [orientation](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/orientation); [spin structure](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/spin+structure)s; [string structure](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/string+structure)s, [fivebrane structure](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/fivebrane+structure)s.
[L88]
[L89] Every cohesive `(∞,1)`-topos is in particular a [locally ∞-connected (∞,1)-topos](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/locally+%E2%88%9E-connected+%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-topos). For these their intrinsic cohomology refines to [differential cohomology in an (∞,1)-topos](https://ncatlab.org/schreiber/show/differential+cohomology+in+an+%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-topos) classifying [connections on ∞-bundles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/connections+on+%E2%88%9E-bundles). This encodes ***dynamics*** in physics: a connection on a principal `∞`-bundle is a [***gauge field***](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/gauge+field) which exerts [***force***](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/force)s. Such as:
[L90]
[L91] - the [electromagnetic field](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/electromagnetic+field), [Yang-Mills field](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Yang-Mills+field), the field of [gravity](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/gravity), of [supergravity](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/supergravity), the [Kalb-Ramond field](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Kalb-Ramond+field), the [supergravity C-field](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/supergravity+C-field), the [RR-field](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/RR-field).
[L92]
[L93] In every such connected `(∞,1)`-topos every [characteristic class](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/characteristic+class) gives rise to its [∞-Chern-Weil homomorphism](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%E2%88%9E-Chern-Weil+homomorphism) that sends gauge fields encoded as [∞-connections](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/connections+on+%E2%88%9E-bundles) on [principal ∞-bundles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/principal+%E2%88%9E-bundles) to [circle n-bundles with connection](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/circle+n-bundles+with+connection). Such as:
[L94]
[L95] - the [Chern-Simons circle 3-bundle](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Chern-Simons+circle+3-bundle) known from the [Green-Schwarz mechanism](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Green-Schwarz+mechanism) or the [Chern-Simons circle 7-bundle](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Chern-Simons+circle+7-bundle) known from [dual heterotic string theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/dual+heterotic+string+theory).
[L96]
[L97] Under the [higher parallel transport](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/higher+parallel+transport) of these circle `n`-bundles with connection, this assignment is the [action functional](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/action+functional) for the [∞-Chern-Simons theory](https://ncatlab.org/schreiber/show/%E2%88%9E-Chern-Simons+theory) of the corresponding characteristic class. This includes as special cases various [sigma-model](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/sigma-model) [quantum field theories](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/quantum+field+theories) such as:
[L98]
[L99] - [Dijkgraaf-Witten theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Dijkgraaf-Witten+theory), ordinary [Chern-Simons theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Chern-Simons+theory), all versions of [AKSZ theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/AKSZ+theory), (Chern-Simons-)[supergravity](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/supergravity), [BF-theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/BF-theory) coupled to [topological Yang-Mills theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/topological+Yang-Mills+theory) with cosmological constant.
[L100]
[L101] These are all [topological quantum field theories](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/topological+quantum+field+theories). But by the [holographic principle of higher category theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/holographic+principle+of+higher+category+theory) we have that on their boundaries live non-topological theories:
[L102]
[L103] - on the boundary of [Chern-Simons theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Chern-Simons+theory) sits the [Wess-Zumino-Witten model](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Wess-Zumino-Witten+model).
[L104] - on the boundary of the [A-model](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/A-model) sits the [quantum mechanics](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/quantum+mechanics) dynamics of any classical [symplectic](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/symplectic+manifold) [phase space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/phase+space) and on the boundary of the [Poisson sigma-model](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Poisson+sigma-model) that of a [Poisson manifold](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Poisson+manifold) phase space.
[L105]
[L106] ### *Quantum dynamics*
[L107]
[L108] The [quantum mechanics](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/quantum+mechanics) associated with such [sigma-model](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/sigma-model)s is the collection of data given by
[L109]
[L110] - on each closed piece `Σd−n` of worldvolume [cobordism](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/cobordism) of codimension `n` the [n-vector space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/n-vector+space) of [state](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/state)s of the system;

[L126] ### *Context*
[L127]
[L128] #### Homotopy theory
[L129]

[L142]
[L143] ## 1. Idea
[L144]
[L145] The *Whitehead tower* of a [pointed](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/pointed+object) [homotopy type](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+type) `X` is an interpolation of the point inclusion `*→X` by a sequence of homotopy types
[L146]
[L147] ```math
[L148] *→⋯→X(2)→X(1)→X(0)≃X
[L149] ```
[L150]
[L151] that are obtained from right to left by *removing *[*homotopy groups*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+groups)* from below*, hence such that
[L152]
[L153] - each `X(n)` is `(n−1)`-[connected](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/n-simply+connected+space)
[L154] - and each [morphism](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/morphism) `X(n+1)→X(n)` induces an [isomorphism](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/isomorphism) on all [homotopy groups](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+groups) in degree `k≥(n+1)` (and the inclusion `1→πn(X(n))` in degree `n` as well as the identity `1=1` in degree `k<n`).
[L155]
[L156] The notion of Whitehead tower is [dual](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/duality) to the notion of [*Postnikov tower*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Postnikov+tower), which instead is a factorization of the terminal morphism `X→*` into a tower, where homotopy groups are *added* from right to left.
[L157]
[L158] In fact, the Whitehead tower may be constructed by taking each stage `X(n+1)→X` to be the [*homotopy fiber*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+fiber) of the corresponding map into the `(n+1)`st stage of the [Postnikov tower](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Postnikov+tower).
[L159]
[L160] ## 2. Definition
[L161]
[L162] The construction of Whitehead towers is traditionally done for [topological spaces](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/topological+spaces) regarded up to [weak homotopy equivalence](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/weak+homotopy+equivalence), hence as objects of the [(∞,1)-category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-category) [Top](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Top). The discussion directly generalizes to any [(∞,1)-topos](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-topos).
[L163]
[L164] The ***Whitehead tower*** of a [pointed](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/pointed+object) [homotopy type](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+type) `X` is a sequence of [homotopy types](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+types)
[L165]
[L166] ```math
[L167] *→⋯→X(2)→X(1)→X(0)≃X
[L168] ```
[L169]
[L170] where [the](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/generalized+the) space `X(n)` is [the](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/generalized+the) [homotopy fiber](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+fiber) of [the](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/generalized+the) map `X→X(n+1)` into the item `X(n+1)` in the [Postnikov tower](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Postnikov+tower) of `X`.
[L171]
[L172] Here each [homotopy pullback](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+pullback)
[L173]
[L174] ```math
[L175] X(n)→*↓↓X→X(n+1)
[L176] ```
[L177]
[L178] in the [(∞,1)-category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-category) [Top](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Top) may be computed (as described at [homotopy pullback](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+pullback)) as an ordinary [pullback](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/pullback) in the 1-[category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/category) [Top](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Top) of a fibrantly replaced diagram, for instance with the point `*` replaced by the path fibration `PX(n+1)≃*`, which is a [Hurewicz fibration](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Hurewicz+fibration) `PX(n+1)→X(n+1)`. In this case also the ordinary [pullback](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/pullback) `X(n)→X`
[L179]
[L180] ```math
[L181] X(n)→PX(n+1)↓↓X→X(n+1)
[L182] ```
[L183]
[L184] is a fibration, and this is often taken as part of the definition of the Whitehead tower.
[L185]
[L186] From this perspective the *Whitehead tower* of a [pointed space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/pointed+space) `(X,x)` is a sequence of fibrations
[L187]
[L188] ```math
[L189] …→X⟨n⟩→…→X⟨1⟩→X⟨0⟩→X
[L190] ```
[L191]
[L192] where each `X⟨n⟩→X⟨n−1⟩` induces isomorphisms on [homotopy group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+group)s `πi` for `i>n` and such that `X⟨n⟩` is `n`-[connected](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/n-connected) (has trivial [homotopy group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+group)s `πi` for `i≤n`). The homotopy long exact sequence then shows that the fiber of `X⟨n⟩→X⟨n−1⟩` is a `K(πn−1(X,x),n−1)` [Eilenberg-Mac Lane space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Eilenberg-Mac+Lane+space). One has a model for `K(πn−1(X,x),n−1)` which is an abelian topological group; this has a remarkable consequence when `(X,x)=(G,e)` is a [topological group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/topological+group). Indeed, in this case one sees inductively that `G⟨n⟩` has a model which is a topological group, which is an abelian group extension:
[L193]
[L194] ```math
[L195] 1→K(πn−1(X,x),n−1)→G⟨n⟩→G⟨n−1⟩→1
[L196] ```
[L197]
[L198] For instance, the [string group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/string+group) can be realized as a topological group as a `K(ℤ,2)`-extension of the [spin group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/spin+group).
[L199]
[L200] For `n=0` we require that `X⟨0⟩↪X` is the inclusion of the path-component of `x`. Really this is defined up to [homotopy](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+%28as+an+operation%29), but we have a canonical model. If `X` is locally connected and semilocally path-connected, then `X⟨1⟩` can be chosen as the [universal covering space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/universal+covering+space).
[L201]
[L202] In traditional models this construction is highly non-[functor](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/functor)ial, except for nice spaces in low dimensions as remarked above.
[L203]
[L204] ## 3. Constructions
[L205]
[L206] ### *Whitehead’s construction*
[L207]
[L208] [Whitehead 1952](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Whitehead+tower#Whitehead) answered the question, posed by [Witold Hurewicz](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Witold+Hurewicz), of the existence of what we would now call `n`-connected 'covers' of a given space `X`, taking this to mean a fibration `X⟨n⟩→X` with `X⟨n⟩` `n`-connected and otherwise inducing isomorphisms on homotopy groups.
[L209]
[L210] The construction proceeds as follows (using modern terminology). Given a pointed space `(X,x)`,
[L211]
[L212] - Choose a representative for the [Postnikov section](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Postnikov+section) `Xn` such that `X↪Xn` is a closed subspace (I would be tempted to make it a closed cofibration, but I don’t know any reason for this to be necessary -DMR).
[L213] - Form the `∞`-connected cover of `Xn`, i.e. the [path fibration](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/path+fibration) `PXn`. This is a [Hurewicz fibration](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Hurewicz+fibration).
[L214] - Pull this back to `X`, to get `p:X⟨n⟩→X`, which is still a fibration. The induced maps on long exact sequences in homotopy can be compared, and show that `p` has the desired properties.
[L215]
[L216] This gives us a single `n`-connected cover, but by considering the [Postnikov tower](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Postnikov+tower)
[L217]
[L218] ```math
[L219] X→(…→Xn→Xn−1→…→X1→X0)
[L220] ```

[L264]   - [In quantum anomaly cancellation](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/spin+structure#in_quantum_anomaly_cancellation)
[L265]
[L266] ## 1. Idea
[L267]
[L268] A *spin structure* on a [manifold](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/manifold) `X` with an [orientation](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/orientation) is a [lift](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/lift) `g^` of the [classifying map](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/classifying+map) `g:X→BSO(n)` of its [tangent bundle](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/tangent+bundle) through the second step `BSpin(n)→BSO(n)` in the [Whitehead tower](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Whitehead+tower) of `O(n)` to the [classifying space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/classifying+space) of the [spin group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/spin+group):
[L269]
[L270] ```math
[L271] BSpin(n)g^↗↓X→gBSO(n)
[L272] ```
[L273]
[L274] Spin structures derive their name from the fact that their existence on a space `X` make the [quantum anomaly](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/quantum+anomaly) for spinning particles propagating on `X` vanish. See there.
[L275]
[L276] ## 2. Definition
[L277]
[L278] Let `n∈ℕ`, write
[L279]
[L280] ```math
[L281] ℤ2→Spin(n)→SO(n)
[L282] ```
[L283]
[L284] for the [spin group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/spin+group) [group extension](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/group+extension) of the [special orthogonal group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/special+orthogonal+group) in [dimension](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/dimension) `n`. (All of the following also applies verbatim for [Lorentzian signature](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lorentzian+signature)).
[L285]
[L286] ### *Topological*
[L287]
[L288] ***Definition 2.1***. Write
[L289]
[L290] ```math
[L291] SO(n)˜≔[ℤ2→Spin(n)]
[L292] ```
[L293]
[L294] for the [crossed module](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/crossed+module) of [smooth groups](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/smooth+groups) induced by the [spin](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/spin+group) [group extension](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/group+extension). Write
[L295]
[L296] ```math
[L297] Bℤ2≔[ℤ2→1]
[L298] ```
[L299]
[L300] for the [crossed module](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/crossed+module) given by shifting up the [group of order two](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/group+of+order+two) in degree. Finally write
[L301]
[L302] ```math
[L303] SO(n)˜↓SO(n)
[L304] ```
[L305]
[L306] for the canonical morphism of [crossed modules](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/crossed+modules) which is the [terminal](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/terminal+object) morphism in degree-1 and the defining projection in degree 0, and write
[L307]
[L308] ```math
[L309] w˜2:SO(n)˜=[ℤ2→Spin(n)]⟶[ℤ2→1]=Bℤ2
[L310] ```
[L311]
[L312] for the canonical morphism of [crossed modules](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/crossed+modules) which is the identity in degree 1 and the [terminal](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/terminal+object) map in degree 0.
[L313]
[L314] ***Proposition 2.2****. In the *[*span*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/span)*/*[*zig-zag*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/zig-zag)
[L315]
[L316] ```math
[L317] SO(n)˜⟶w2˜Bℤ2↓≃SO(n)
[L318] ```
[L319]
[L320] *the left leg is a *[*weak equivalence*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/weak+equivalence)* of *[*smooth groupoids*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/smooth+groupoids)* (under the identification of *[*crossed modules*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/crossed+modules)* with *[*strict 2-groups*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/strict+2-groups)*). Under *[*delooping*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/delooping)* it presents a morphism of *[*smooth 2-groupoids*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/smooth+2-groupoids)* of the form*
[L321]
[L322] ```math
[L323] w2:BSO(n)⟶B2ℤ2
[L324] ```
[L325]
[L326] *from the universal *[*moduli stack*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/moduli+stack)* of smooth **`SO(n)`**-*[*principal bundles*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/principal+bundles)* to that of **`Bℤ2`**-*[*principal 2-bundles*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/principal+2-bundles)* (**`ℤ2`**-*[*bundle gerbes*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/bundle+gerbes)*). The *[*homotopy fiber*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+fiber)* of this map in *[*Smooth∞Grpd*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Smooth%E2%88%9EGrpd)* is **`BSpin(n)`**, for the *[*spin group*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/spin+group)* regarded as a *[*smooth group*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/smooth+group)*. Under *[*geometric realization of cohesive ∞-groupoids*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/geometric+realization+of+cohesive+%E2%88%9E-groupoids)* **`|−|:Smooth∞Grpd⟶∞Grpd`** this maps ti the universal *[*second Stiefel-Whitney class*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/second+Stiefel-Whitney+class)
[L327]
[L328] ```math
[L329] |w2|≃w2:BSO(n)⟶K(ℤ2,2).
[L330] ```

[L60] Abstract:
[L61]
[L62] The first part of this thesis contains two new techniques for the calculation of scattering amplitudes in quantum field theories. These methods were inspired by the recent proposal of a correspondence between the weakly coupled regime of the maximally supersymmetric four dimensional gauge theory and a string theory in twistor space. We show how generalised unitarity cuts in D = 4 − 2² dimensions can be used to calculate efficiently complete one-loop scattering amplitudes in non-supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory. This approach naturally generates the rational terms in the amplitudes, as well as the cut-constructible parts. We then show that the ideas of the Britto, Cachazo, Feng and Witten tree-level on-shell recursion relation can also be applied to the calculation of finite one-loop amplitudes in pure Einstein gravity. The second part of this thesis is a study of the nonabelian phenomena associated with D-branes. Specifically we study the nonabelian bionic brane intersection in which a stack of many coincident D1-branes expand via a non-commutative spherical configuration into a collection of higher dimensional D-branes orthogonal to the original stack of D1-branes. We suggest a construction of monopoles in dimension 2k+1 from fuzzy funnels. We then perform two charge calculations related to this construction. [L181] Abstract:
[L182]
[L183] The first part of this thesis contains two new techniques for the calculation of scattering amplitudes in quantum field theories. These methods were inspired by the recent proposal of a correspondence between the weakly coupled regime of the maximally supersymmetric four dimensional gauge theory and a string theory in twistor space. We show how generalised unitarity cuts in D = 4 − 2² dimensions can be used to calculate efficiently complete one-loop scattering amplitudes in non-supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory. This approach naturally generates the rational terms in the amplitudes, as well as the cut-constructible parts. We then show that the ideas of the Britto, Cachazo, Feng and Witten tree-level on-shell recursion relation can also be applied to the calculation of finite one-loop amplitudes in pure Einstein gravity. The second part of this thesis is a study of the nonabelian phenomena associated with D-branes. Specifically we study the nonabelian bionic brane intersection in which a stack of many coincident D1-branes expand via a non-commutative spherical configuration into a collection of higher dimensional D-branes orthogonal to the original stack of D1-branes. We suggest a construction of monopoles in dimension 2k+1 from fuzzy funnels. We then perform two charge calculations related to this construction. This leads to a new formula for the symmetrised trace quantity. This new formula for the symmetrised trace is then used to study the collapse of a spherical bound state of D0-branes.

[L432] Gravitation 267
[L433] 1. Introduction
[L434] The quantum theory ofgravitation has been discussed in lectures by various
[L435] authors, notably Feynman in a course given at CalTec in the academic year
[L436] 1962-1963, and De Witt, at the 1963 Les Houches school. Since then a cer￾tain amount of progress has been made, and it seems proper to emphasize the
[L437] recent developments in this course.
[L438] The progress mentioned stems basically from two facts. One, we now un￾derstand much better how to quantize a gauge theory, that is a theory with a
[L439] Lagrangian possessing an invariance with respect to certain local (i.e. space￾time dependent) transformations. Secondly, the dimensional regularization
[L440] method turns out to be a powerful tool in handling infinities, and since infini￾ties are plentiful in gravitation theory such a tool is indispensable.
[L441] In these lectures we will approach the theory ofgravitation from the point
[L442] ofview ofquantum field theory. This in itselfposes directly a restriction,
[L443] namely that we abandon from the start things like curved space and Mach's
[L444] principle. Of course, the theory that emerges is in the classical limit nothing
[L445] but Einstein's theory; but the interpretation is really quite different. We refer
[L446] to the book by Weinberg for the classical theory of gravitation developed
[L447] from this point of view.
[L448] Our starting point will be that gravitation is caused by a particle of spin two.
[L449] The reasons for that have been given at many occasions, and may be summa￾rized as follows:
[L450] (i) The gravitational field cannot be described by a vector field such as the
[L451] e.m. field because then particles and antiparticles would behave differently,
[L452] contrary to experiment.
[L453] (ii) The gravitational field cannot be described by a scalar field. The reason
[L454] for this is that we know that gravity couples to energy, which is not a scalar
[L455] quantity.

[L8] Abstract
[L9] One of us (L.S.) and H. Verlinde independently conjectured a holographic duality
[L10] between the double-scaled SYK model at infinite temperature and dimensionally
[L11] reduced (2 + 1)-dimensional de Sitter space [1]-[8]. Beyond the statement that such
[L12] a duality exists there was deep disagreement between the two proposals [9]. In this
[L13] note, we trace the origin of the disagreement to a superficial similarity between two
[L14] q-deformed algebraic structures: the algebra of “chords” in DSSYK, and the algebra
[L15] of line operators in the Chern-Simons formulation of 3D de Sitter gravity. Assuming
[L16] that these two structures are the same requires an identification of parameters [7][10]
[L17] which leads to a collapse of the separation of scales [9]—the separation being required
[L18] by the semiclassical limit [3][9]. Dropping that assumption restores the separation
[L19] of scales but leaves unexplained the relation between chords and Chern-Simons line
[L20] operators.
[L21] In this note we point out the existence of a third q-deformed algebra that appears
[L22] in DSSYK: the algebra of “wee-chords.” Identifying the Chern-Simons line operators
[L23] with wee-chords removes the discrepancy and leads to a satisfying relation between
[L24] the two sides of the duality.

[L21] ## 1. Idea
[L22]
[L23] A *spin structure* on a [manifold](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/manifold) `X` with an [orientation](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/orientation) is a [lift](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/lift) `g^` of the [classifying map](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/classifying+map) `g:X→BSO(n)` of its [tangent bundle](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/tangent+bundle) through the second step `BSpin(n)→BSO(n)` in the [Whitehead tower](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Whitehead+tower) of `O(n)` to the [classifying space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/classifying+space) of the [spin group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/spin+group):
[L24]
[L25] ```math
[L26] BSpin(n)g^↗↓X→gBSO(n)
[L27] ```
[L28]
[L29] Spin structures derive their name from the fact that their existence on a space `X` make the [quantum anomaly](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/quantum+anomaly) for spinning particles propagating on `X` vanish. See there.
[L30] [match 1 | match_lines 282 | shown_lines 277-302]
[L31]
[L32] In the context of [quantum field theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/quantum+field+theory) the existence of a spin structure on a [Riemannian manifold](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Riemannian+manifold) `X` arises notably as the condition for [quantum anomaly](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/quantum+anomaly) cancellation of the [sigma-model](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/sigma-model) for the spinning particle – the superparticle – propagating on `X`.
[L33]
[L34] It is the generalization of this anomaly computation from the worldlines of superparticles to super[string](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/string+theory)s that leads to [string structure](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/string+structure), and then further the generalizaton to the worldvolume anomaly of fivebranes that leads to [fivebrane structure](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/fivebrane+structure).
[L35]

[L44] ```
[L45]
[L46] where the stages are the deloopings of
[L47]

[L139] ## 3. Constructions
[L140]
[L141] ### *Whitehead’s construction*
[L142]
[L143] [Whitehead 1952](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Whitehead+tower#Whitehead) answered the question, posed by [Witold Hurewicz](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Witold+Hurewicz), of the existence of what we would now call `n`-connected 'covers' of a given space `X`, taking this to mean a fibration `X⟨n⟩→X` with `X⟨n⟩` `n`-connected and otherwise inducing isomorphisms on homotopy groups.
[L144]
[L145] The construction proceeds as follows (using modern terminology). Given a pointed space `(X,x)`,
[L146]
[L147] - Choose a representative for the [Postnikov section](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Postnikov+section) `Xn` such that `X↪Xn` is a closed subspace (I would be tempted to make it a closed cofibration, but I don’t know any reason for this to be necessary -DMR).
[L148] - Form the `∞`-connected cover of `Xn`, i.e. the [path fibration](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/path+fibration) `PXn`. This is a [Hurewicz fibration](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Hurewicz+fibration).
[L149] - Pull this back to `X`, to get `p:X⟨n⟩→X`, which is still a fibration. The induced maps on long exact sequences in homotopy can be compared, and show that `p` has the desired properties.
[L150]
[L151] This gives us a single `n`-connected cover, but by considering the [Postnikov tower](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Postnikov+tower)
[L152]
[L153] ```math

[L206] ## 5. Whitehead tower in general `(∞,1)`-toposes
[L207]
[L208] While a notion of [Postnikov tower in an (∞,1)-category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Postnikov+tower+in+an+%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-category) depends on the *categorical* [homotopy groups in an (∞,1)-category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+groups+in+an+%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-topos), the notion of Whitehead tower makes good sense with respect to the *geometric* homotopy groups.
[L209]
[L210] A good notion of geometric [homotopy groups in an (∞,1)-topos](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+groups+in+an+%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-topos) exist in a [locally contractible (∞,1)-topos](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/locally+contractible+%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-topos). The notion of Whitehead tower in this context is discussed at
[L211]
[L212] - [Whitehead tower in an (∞,1)-topos](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Whitehead+tower+in+an+%28%E2%88%9E%2C1%29-topos).
[L213]
[L214] ## 6. Related concepts
[L215]
[L216] - Applying the [Hurewicz theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Hurewicz+theorem) stagewise to a [Whitehead tower](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Whitehead+tower) yields an method for computing the [homotopy groups](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/homotopy+groups) of the original [space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/space). This process, or rather the refinement thereof for Whitehead towers generalized to [Adams resolutions](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Adams+resolutions), is formalized by the [*Adams spectral sequence*](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Adams+spectral+sequence), see there for more.

thoughts.summary: Clarified sources, themes, links, models, and claims

parts:
There are several different literatures piled together here, but they are not random. Taken as a set, they trace a fairly coherent mathematical migration in twentieth- and twenty-first-century physics:

\[
\text{particle labels}
\;\longrightarrow\;
\text{representations}
\;\longrightarrow\;
\text{symmetry groups}
\;\longrightarrow\;
\text{bundles/connections}
\;\longrightarrow\;
\text{topology and homotopy}
\;\longrightarrow\;
\text{higher geometric structures}.
\]

And running across that progression is another theme that I think is particularly important: **an object that initially looks like a separate physical ingredient can sometimes turn out to be a sector, representation, obstruction, holonomy, or invariant of a more general mathematical structure.**

That does *not* mean all of these authors are saying the same thing. They aren't. In fact, one of your most useful sources here is explicitly about the danger of making exactly that mistake.

### The 1930s material: particle type starts becoming algebra

Duffin and Kemmer are an unusually interesting part of this pile.

Kemmer's 1939 *The Particle Aspect of Meson Theory* starts from the contemporary realization that relativistic quantum theories can support integral and half-integral spin and immediately connects integer spin with Bose statistics and half-integer spin with Fermi statistics. fileciteturn8file4L547-L555

But his more interesting move is methodological. He takes something analogous to the Dirac equation and replaces Dirac's matrix algebra with a different algebra whose commutation rules had been given by Duffin in 1938. He explicitly says he wants a formulation independent of a particular matrix representation and remarks that this may simplify treatment of higher spins. fileciteturn8file4L593-L623

What comes out of that algebra is not arbitrary. Its irreducible representations separate into the familiar scalar and vector possibilities: Kemmer identifies the 10-dimensional representation with the Proca spin-1 theory and the 5-dimensional one with the Klein-Gordon scalar theory. fileciteturn4file8L415-L447

That is a very clean historical example of

\[
\boxed{\text{particle sector} \leftarrow \text{representation of an underlying algebra}}
\]

rather than starting by declaring "here is a scalar particle" and "here is a vector particle" as unrelated primitives.

Kemmer also derives a genuine spin operator from the angular-momentum decomposition and gets eigenvalues \(+1,0,-1\), rather than merely counting three polarization states and calling that spin. fileciteturn4file5L278-L291

So Duffin–Kemmer is one of the strongest items in your bundle if you're interested in the question, "How much apparent particle taxonomy can arise from the algebra of a more economical object?"

It doesn't answer the H(s)H question. But it demonstrates that this is a perfectly serious mathematical question.

### Spin geometry is a different, deeper level of the same story

The nLab "Spin geometry" page you pasted is basically a reference scaffold for Lawson and Michelsohn's 1989 book rather than an exposition in its own right. But its chapter sequence tells you exactly what spin geometry is about:

quadratic metric structure → Clifford algebra → Pin/Spin groups → representations → spin structures on manifolds → spinor bundles → spin connections → Dirac operators → index theory.

The central construction is

\[
\mathrm{Spin}(n)\longrightarrow SO(n),
\]

a double covering. A spinor does not transform as an ordinary vector under rotations; it transforms under the double cover. This is where the familiar \(2\pi\) sign change and \(4\pi\) return of a spin-\(\tfrac12\) state lives mathematically.

On a manifold, you cannot simply assume spinors exist globally. You need a **spin structure**: roughly, you need to lift the \(SO(n)\) frame structure to a \(\mathrm{Spin}(n)\) structure. The uploaded nLab source states this quite explicitly as a lift

\[
X\to BSO(n)
\]

through

\[
B\mathrm{Spin}(n)\to BSO(n).
\]

fileciteturn7file2L266-L284

For an oriented manifold the obstruction is the second Stiefel–Whitney class \(w_2\).

This is worth separating sharply from three things that sound similar:

| Term | What it actually means |
|---|---|
| particle **spin** | representation of spacetime rotation/Lorentz symmetry |
| **spin structure** | global topological lifting condition that permits spinor fields |
| geometric **twist/framing** | orientation of an extended curve/tube's local frame |

Those can interact mathematically, but they are not synonyms.

Likewise, "higher spin" in particle physics—spin \(3/2,2,5/2,\ldots\)—is not the same thing as the "higher spin structures" on the nLab page. The latter means further stages beyond Spin in an obstruction-theoretic tower.

### The Whitehead tower is especially interesting, but easy to overread

The Whitehead material gives you:

\[
O
\leftarrow SO
\leftarrow Spin
\leftarrow String
\leftarrow Fivebrane
\leftarrow \cdots
\]

with successive lifting conditions controlled by characteristic classes. The nLab source associates the successive lifts with orientation, spin structure, string structure and fivebrane structure. fileciteturn11file2L155-L194

The spin-structure page makes the physical motivation more concrete: spin structure appears in anomaly cancellation for a spinning point particle; analogous anomaly questions for strings lead to string structures, and for fivebranes to fivebrane structures. fileciteturn11file0L32-L56

This is genuinely suggestive if you're interested in a progression

\[
\text{point history}\to\text{extended history}\to\text{higher-dimensional history}.
\]

But the rigorous caution is important: a Whitehead tower is **not a hierarchy of physical scales or nested physical objects**. It is a hierarchy of connected covers/lifting problems in homotopy theory. Any identification with physical nesting would have to be constructed separately.

### Then there is the other "spin": isospin

The old nuclear papers show a parallel evolution.

The proton and neutron increasingly came to be treated as members of an approximately symmetric multiplet. "Isotopic spin" or **isospin** uses mathematics resembling ordinary angular momentum, but it is an **internal** symmetry. It is not rotation in ordinary space.

That is crucial.

Gell-Mann's 1953 *Isotopic Spin and New Unstable Particles* sits in this development. The Breit–Condon–Present proton-scattering material you pasted is even earlier: experimentally, they find that corresponding proton-proton and proton-neutron interactions come out very nearly equal when spin state is held appropriately fixed, apart from Coulomb and spin effects. Cassen and Condon then package exchange-force schemes in a more abstract coordinate formalism.

So empirically motivated particle distinctions were already being reorganized according to symmetry.

That path eventually becomes

\[
\text{isospin symmetry}
\rightarrow
\text{internal Lie groups}
\rightarrow
\text{Yang--Mills gauge symmetry}.
\]

The Glashow–Gell-Mann 1961 paper in your files makes that transition explicit: they consider vector-boson theories invariant under coordinate-dependent continuous transformations and show that the "simple" cases correspond to simple Lie algebras. They also note that putting in ordinary vector-boson mass terms destroys this local gauge invariance. fileciteturn7file4L469-L506

So this is another instance where what we call "forces" increasingly become encoded by the transformation structure of a field.

### The weak-interaction sequence adds chirality

Your Fermi → Konopinski/Uhlenbeck → Lee/Yang → Kinoshita/Sirlin → Feynman/Gell-Mann material is another coherent historical chain.

Fermi in 1934 models beta decay as a contact process involving electron and neutrino creation, deliberately analogous in some respects to photon emission.

Konopinski and Uhlenbeck modify the interaction to repair the spectral shape.

Then parity violation changes the problem radically. Lee and Yang's two-component-neutrino paper is explicitly possible only when parity is not conserved.

Feynman and Gell-Mann's 1958 *Theory of Fermi Interaction* then organizes the weak interaction essentially into equal vector and axial-vector pieces acting on two-component neutrinos—the immediate ancestor of the familiar \(V-A\) chiral weak interaction.

This is where another distinction becomes indispensable:

\[
\text{curve handedness}
\neq
\text{spinor chirality}
\neq
\text{helicity}
\neq
\text{parity violation}.
\]

They can correlate under particular conditions. For a massless fermion, for example, helicity and chirality line up in the familiar way. But a right- or left-handed geometric helix is not automatically a left- or right-handed Weyl representation.

If an H(s)H construction is ultimately supposed to produce weak chirality from geometric handedness, that translation is one of the places where the model has to do actual work rather than rely on vocabulary.

### Pauli gives the corresponding hard constraint for statistics

The 1940 Pauli paper you included is important for similar reasons.

Spin-statistics in relativistic QFT is not merely the statement "twisty things with half-integer winding happen to anticommute." Pauli's argument connects half-integral spin to Fermi statistics and integral spin to Bose statistics under conditions involving relativistic covariance, energy positivity and spacelike commutativity/locality.

So if some braid/framing/worldtube construction eventually reproduces fermionic exchange, that's interesting—but the serious benchmark is whether its effective theory also reproduces the relevant locality/Lorentz/positivity structure.

That is a much more useful target than visual similarity.

### Veltman's gravity lectures are perhaps the most striking methodological parallel

Veltman deliberately starts from almost the opposite end of the usual GR presentation.

He says that for these lectures he will begin from quantum field theory, set curved-space interpretation aside at the start, and take gravity to be mediated by a spin-2 field—while noting that the classical theory that emerges is Einstein gravity. fileciteturn10file2L254-L270

Then something remarkable happens.

A straightforward massless spin-2 propagator is not acceptable by itself. Gauge invariance is needed to decouple unphysical components, much as in electromagnetism. Closing and extending that gauge transformation structure then produces the machinery from which Veltman develops finite transformations, covariant derivatives, and finally the Riemann tensor.

In his construction, the Riemann tensor appears because he needs a combination of derivatives and connection-like objects whose non-tensorial pieces cancel. fileciteturn10file4L438-L455

And later he makes a particularly strong statement: gauge invariance fixes the gravitational coupling to matter universally; he identifies that with the essence of the equivalence principle. fileciteturn10file4L470-L477

So schematically his route is

\[
\text{massless spin 2}
\rightarrow
\text{consistency}
\rightarrow
\text{gauge redundancy}
\rightarrow
\text{connection}
\rightarrow
\text{curvature tensor}
\rightarrow
\text{GR}.
\]

That doesn't establish that spacetime curvature is "really" something else. Veltman is constructing a QFT representation of the same physics. But methodologically, it is a very good demonstration that one can recover geometrical machinery **from consistency requirements on a non-geometrically-presented starting system**.

For your purposes, that is much more interesting than another paper simply assuming a curved metric.

### Braids → Jacobi diagrams → Lie algebra → Chern–Simons

The Jacobi-diagram material connects directly to the braid material from the previous turn.

A Jacobi diagram is a trivalent oriented graph associated with an oriented circle. If all the vertices lie on that circle, it specializes to a chord diagram. fileciteturn6file0L44-L58

In perturbative Chern–Simons theory, these diagrams function as connected Feynman diagrams attached to a Wilson loop. The STU/Jacobi relations encode Lie-algebraic identities. fileciteturn6file0L76-L78

That makes them a genuine bridge:

\[
\boxed{
\text{knot/braid topology}
\leftrightarrow
\text{graphs}
\leftrightarrow
\text{Lie algebra}
\leftrightarrow
\text{gauge-theory observables}
}
\]

This is more substantial than "physics sometimes draws braided things."

Weight systems can assign algebraic quantities to these diagrams, and finite-type/Vassiliev invariants then organize knot information perturbatively. That gives you an established mathematical mechanism for turning topology into calculable algebraic observables.

### The Susskind–Rahman paper is almost a methodological warning written specifically for this sort of exploration

This paper deserves special attention.

They notice two algebraic structures that look remarkably alike: the \(q\)-deformed chord algebra of double-scaled SYK and a \(q\)-deformed algebra of Chern–Simons line operators in de Sitter gravity.

The tempting move is to identify them.

They explicitly say that doing so is wrong: the parameter identification collapses a required separation of scales. Their resolution is to introduce a third algebra, the "wee-chord" algebra, which looks similar but belongs to the appropriate scale sector. fileciteturn9file0L9-L24

For ordinary \(p\)-chords, an intersection contributes

\[
q(\Delta_1,\Delta_2)=q^{\Delta_1\Delta_2},
\qquad
q=e^{-\lambda},
\]

and as \(q\to1\), the chords effectively pass through one another without interaction. fileciteturn9file2L174-L190

Their wee chords have finite \(O(1)\) fermion weight and a corresponding intersection factor approximately

\[
q_{\rm wee}(n,m)\simeq e^{-2nm/N}.
\]

fileciteturn9file2L204-L264

The lesson is excellent:

\[
\boxed{\text{same-looking algebra} \not\Rightarrow \text{same physical structure}.}
\]

Scale, parameter maps and limiting behavior have to agree too.

Their conclusion says exactly that the \(p\)-chord and wee-chord observable algebras can both show chord-like \(q\)-deformations while describing decoupled scale sectors, and that the earlier direct identification with the wrong chord algebra had to be rejected. fileciteturn9file1L85-L109

That's an unusually good methodological template for comparing H(s)H constructions to existing physics: structural resemblance earns an investigation; parameter/limit consistency decides whether the resemblance survives.

### Higher geometry is the packaging language above all of this

The nLab pages then jump another abstraction level.

"Higher structures" means, roughly, ordinary mathematical structures promoted into a setting where equalities may themselves have transformations between them, and those transformations may have transformations between *them*, coherently. The source says ordinary identities may hold only up to coherent higher homotopies. fileciteturn6file2L221-L241

Higher geometry is then geometry done in this homotopical/higher-categorical setting. Instead of only manifolds and bundles, one gets stacks, higher stacks, derived spaces, higher bundles, higher gauge transformations, etc. fileciteturn6file3L328-L336

Higher prequantum geometry starts with the familiar quantum-geometric package

\[
U(1)\text{ bundle}+\text{connection}
\]

and promotes it to \(n\)-bundles/gerbes and higher connections appropriate to extended field theories. fileciteturn6file4L428-L434

This is why the collection starts naturally pulling together things like:

gauge fields, holonomy, spin structures, anomalies, Chern–Simons theory, Wilson lines, extended objects, cobordisms, and higher categories.

The nLab's own `nPOV` page is worth remembering, however, because it explicitly says this is a **point of view**, not a neutral encyclopedia organization. It deliberately treats homotopy and higher-category theory as a unifying language. fileciteturn6file1L126-L145

So the nLab connections are useful mathematical maps; they should not themselves be counted as empirical evidence that nature is fundamentally higher-categorical.

### The fuzzy-funnel item is more peripheral, but visually/structurally interesting

The McNamara thesis record—and three of your pasted files are duplicates of that same record—has a second half dealing with non-Abelian D-branes. Coincident D1-branes expand into a **noncommutative spherical configuration** representing higher-dimensional branes, and the thesis studies fuzzy funnels and collapse of a spherical D0-brane bound state. fileciteturn8file0L60-L72

That is certainly structurally adjacent to "extended constituents → collective spherical object."

But it comes with a lot of string-theory machinery. I would put it in the "interesting analogue / possible mathematical resource" bin, not the "close correspondence" bin.

### What the whole pile amounts to

I think there are really **four mature mathematical mechanisms** represented here that are worth distinguishing.

First, **representation selection**: one algebra or symmetry structure possesses inequivalent representations, and those representations appear as different particle types. Duffin–Kemmer and ordinary Lorentz/Spin representation theory live here.

Second, **topological lifting and obstruction**: not every local transformation structure extends globally. Orientation, spin, string and fivebrane structures arise as successive lifting conditions. Whitehead towers, characteristic classes and anomalies live here.

Third, **connection and holonomy**: local internal state is transported through space; curvature measures failure to return trivially, and Wilson loops/holonomies encode integrated information. Gauge theory, spin connections and Chern–Simons theory live here.

Fourth, **configuration/motion topology**: histories of objects can fall into inequivalent topological classes, and diagrams/algebras can encode those classes. Braids, framed braids, loop braids, Jacobi diagrams and chord algebras live here.

Those four are capable of interacting with one another. Modern geometry supplies languages in which they *do* interact.

But there's no licensed shortcut from that fact to

\[
\text{one finite geometric mechanism}=\text{Standard Model + gravity}.
\]

The interesting question is whether a sufficiently constrained finite geometry generates all four mechanisms rather than having them inserted independently.

And within the finite-core/worldtube direction you've been constructing, I think these sources substantially sharpen what that question should mean. Instead of asking vaguely whether the geometry "looks like spin" or "looks like gauge theory," you can ask something much harder and much more useful:

Does its actual configuration space have the required motion group?  
Do its allowed transformations possess representations corresponding to the observed sectors?  
Does its framing admit a genuine Spin-like double cover?  
Do closed transports produce the correct holonomy algebra?  
Do parity/chiral sectors transform like the relevant Lorentz representations?  
Can an effective massless spin-2 sector force universal coupling in the Veltman sense?  
Can intersection/reconnection statistics produce an algebra with controlled deformation parameters?  
And when two mathematical structures look the same, do their scales and limiting behavior agree—as Rahman and Susskind demand before identifying them?

That, to me, is the coherent research program hiding inside this otherwise rather wild pile of tabs. memcite

Force accounting

The current goal is mechanism minimization. Most named mechanisms should be demoted to regimes or observables of one underlying object.

Primitive mechanism:

    finite-core worldtubes in a growth-asymmetric 4D substrate resist, stir, braid, and project.

Candidate mappings:
