Yes — that changes the construction substantially, and I think it is closer to what you originally had in mind.

Take the two concentric spheres, radii

\[
R=1,\qquad r=\frac12,
\]

and choose a common equatorial plane. Instead of two localized ramps, insert an entire rotationally symmetric transition band between the outer and inner equators, with the band displaced/bent through the fourth spatial coordinate so the joined surface is smooth.

Then there is no “choice point” when the pilot reaches the equator. The local tangent plane of the joined surface simply turns into the band, so rule 5 is automatic: the geodesic continues according to the surface.

One correction: the equatorial great circle is itself a geodesic on an ordinary sphere. In the joined surface, whether that equatorial circle remains a geodesic depends on exactly how the band is joined. If the equator is a symmetry/geodesic boundary of the construction, it can remain one. But the more important family is the set of great circles that cross the equator.

For the simplest rotationally symmetric band, every plane through the common polar axis cuts the whole object in the same meridional profile:

\[
\text{outer sphere}
\rightarrow
\text{band}
\rightarrow
\text{inner sphere}
\rightarrow
\text{band}
\rightarrow
\text{outer sphere}.
\]

Those meridional sections are geodesics automatically by reflection symmetry. So any pilot launched along one of those meridional directions gets a completely determined closed candidate path.

And this eliminates the arbitrary holonomy angle I introduced before. We shouldn't insert a twist by hand. We should calculate whatever parallel transport the actual smooth joined geometry produces.

There is a nice way to parameterize the simplest band. In a meridional section, let

\[
\rho(s)
\]

be distance from the polar axis and let

\[
w(s)
\]

be displacement in the fourth dimension, with \(s\) arc length along the profile. Then

\[
\rho'(s)^2+w'(s)^2=1.
\]

At the outer equator,

\[
\rho=1,
\]

and at the inner equator,

\[
\rho=\frac12.
\]

Choose the smoothest monotonic profile joining them while matching the sphere tangents at both ends. Revolve that profile around the polar axis. That gives the continuous transition band.

Now something important happens to your A/B/C questions.

For a meridional pilot, the path length becomes

\[
L
=
(\text{outer spherical arc})
+
(\text{band})
+
(\text{inner spherical arc})
+
(\text{band}).
\]

If we're going pole-to-equator on one sphere, through the band, equator-to-opposite-pole on the other, etc., the spherical contributions are exact fractions of their circumferences. With radii \(1\) and \(1/2\), everything contributed by the spherical pieces is rationally commensurate:

\[
\frac{R}{r}=2.
\]

So any failure of simultaneous closure cannot come from the two sphere sizes themselves.

It has to come from one of two places:

\[
\boxed{\text{band metric}}
\]

or

\[
\boxed{\text{holonomy accumulated through the complete joined surface}.}
\]

And your continuous-band construction makes the second one much more interesting, because the pilot's arrow is now being continuously parallel transported through a changing tangent space. There is no discrete “rotate arrow by \(\delta\)” operation. Whatever residual rotation occurs after one circuit is produced by the curvature of the surface itself.

So we would calculate

\[
H(\gamma)
=
\mathcal P\exp\!\left(-\oint_\gamma \Gamma\right),
\]

conceptually: parallel-transport the arrow around the closed geodesic \(\gamma\) and see whether it comes back to itself.

Then:

- \(H=I\): one-cycle closure of position and arrow.
- \(H^N=I\) for finite \(N>1\): finite multi-cycle closure.
- no finite \(N\) with \(H^N=I\): positional path closes, but oriented state never exactly recurs.

That is precisely the test we wanted without putting the answer into the setup.

And I think your intuition about the other great circles is pointing toward a useful distinction. On each spherical portion, every great circle is a geodesic. Once it reaches the transition band, however, only certain great-circle planes are guaranteed by symmetry to remain geodesics of the **whole composite surface**. The meridians are guaranteed. A generic oblique great circle will generally refract—smoothly, not discontinuously—into a different trajectory on the band.

There is a conservation law for that too. For a rotationally symmetric surface, geodesics obey Clairaut's relation:

\[
\rho(s)\sin\alpha(s)=\text{constant},
\]

where \(\alpha\) is the angle the trajectory makes with the meridian.

That's potentially the key to your original question.

As the pilot moves from

\[
\rho=1
\]

to

\[
\rho=\frac12,
\]

the same constant must be preserved. Therefore the trajectory angle must change:

\[
\sin\alpha_{\rm inner}
=
2\sin\alpha_{\rm outer}.
\]

Immediately we get a threshold.

For the pilot to reach the inner sphere at all,

\[
2\sin\alpha_{\rm outer}\le1,
\]

so

\[
\boxed{
|\alpha_{\rm outer}|\le30^\circ.
}
\]

If the initial direction is more oblique than \(30^\circ\) from the meridian, the geodesic cannot reach radius \(1/2\). It reaches a turning point somewhere on the transition band and returns outward.

That is unexpectedly beautiful.

Your seemingly arbitrary ratio

\[
1:\frac12
\]

has just created a natural angular division:

\[
\boxed{30^\circ}
\]

without our imposing one.

So the pilot trajectories divide naturally into at least three classes:

\[
|\alpha|<30^\circ:
\quad
\text{crosses onto the inner sphere};
\]

\[
|\alpha|=30^\circ:
\quad
\text{critical/grazing trajectory};
\]

\[
|\alpha|>30^\circ:
\quad
\text{turns around on the slope}.
\]

The meridian,

\[
\alpha=0,
\]

is the simplest through-going geodesic.

And the equatorial direction,

\[
\alpha=90^\circ,
\]

is the extreme opposite case—it remains associated with the outer maximum-radius region rather than descending toward the inner sphere.

That means we now have a much better-defined problem than the one I answered previously. We can actually derive the permitted path families from the geometry rather than choosing them.

Most importantly: once we choose the minimal smooth profile for that 4D equatorial transition band, we can calculate the exact return map for the pilot and for the corresponding antipodal/inner trajectories and answer A, B, and C properly.

The \(30^\circ\) critical angle is already independent of most of the details of the slope; it follows just from rotational symmetry and the \(2:1\) radial ratio.

Of course, if it’s the equatorial ramp, then it’s not necessarily four dimensional, and not consequential whether it is or not. So the slope needs to be a full-surface fourth dimensional connection. So the angle of the arrow is still surface-embedded so long as it is at any tangent or subtangential angle to the outer sphere surface, but if it’s supertangential, then it would leave the construction. 

And of course, we have to decide whether it’s only the outer surfaces of the sphere that are connected, or only the inner (i guess that would be identical), or whether the slope forms a bridge between inner and outer surface on one or the other or both spheres. 

No, I’m envisioning the slope, more or less approximated by a field filling the shell between the two spheres, that allows sort of inward dip at any point, the angle of which determines the exact sloping path. I think that probably approximates a four dimensional slope. While allowing the path to remain visible to an outside, viewer the whole time

Yes. That gives a much cleaner object, and it is genuinely four-dimensional in the relevant sense.

The simplest version is not “two spheres plus a ramp.” It is one 3-dimensional connecting hypersurface embedded in 4-space, whose visible 3D projection fills the spherical shell between radii \(1/2\) and \(1\).

Topologically, it is

\[
S^2\times[0,1].
\]

The two boundary leaves are

\[
S^2_{R=1}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
S^2_{R=1/2}.
\]

Everything between them is the slope.

A useful embedding is schematically

\[
X(\rho,\theta,\phi)
=
\bigl(\rho\,\hat n(\theta,\phi),\,w(\rho)\bigr),
\qquad
\frac12\le\rho\le1,
\]

where the first three coordinates are ordinary visible space and \(w\) is the fourth coordinate.

Projected back into ordinary 3-space, you just see

\[
\frac12\le r\le1,
\]

the entire shell. But intrinsically, radial displacement through that shell is accompanied by displacement through \(w\). So what looks to the outside observer like an inward-curving trajectory is actually a straight/geodesic continuation through the 4D slope.

That is much closer to what you were describing.

And it clarifies the arrow rule nicely. At the pilot on the outer sphere, there are really three classes of initial direction.

A direction exactly tangent to the outer sphere has no inward component. That is the limiting case and can remain on the outer spherical leaf.

A direction tilted “below” the tangent—toward the shell—is still tangent to the full \(S^2\times I\) connecting manifold. So it is allowed, and the amount of inward tilt determines how deeply it penetrates the slope.

A direction tilted “above” the tangent has a component normal to the complete connecting manifold. It exits the construction.

So your “subtangential” and “supertangential” distinction can be made rigorous as

\[
v\in T_pM
\]

versus

\[
v\notin T_pM,
\]

where \(M\) is the full 3D bridge hypersurface in 4D.

That is better than treating the pilot as choosing whether to enter the slope. He never chooses. He picks a legal initial tangent vector once, and after that

\[
\nabla_{\dot\gamma}\dot\gamma=0
\]

determines the trajectory. The geometry does everything else.

There is also no need yet for “inner versus outer faces” of either sphere. An ideal \(S^2\) has no thickness. We simply have the radius-1 spherical boundary and radius-\(1/2\) spherical boundary of the bridge. Giving either sphere two physical faces would add another degree of structure that I don't think your experiment requires.

The really useful feature of your construction is that every surface point now has a corresponding inward direction. The bridge is not localized. So there is a continuum of possible penetration angles:

\[
\alpha=0
\]

could mean purely tangential,

while increasing inward \(\alpha\) gives progressively larger motion through the shell/fourth coordinate.

That means we can now ask your original closure questions as functions of a single initial angle:

\[
\gamma_\alpha.
\]

For every allowed \(\alpha\), calculate:

\[
L(\alpha)
\]

the length before positional closure, and

\[
H(\alpha)
\]

the holonomy of the transported arrow after that circuit.

Then the really interesting distinction becomes

\[
\gamma_\alpha(T)=\gamma_\alpha(0)
\]

versus

\[
H(\alpha)v=v.
\]

The first says the pilot returned to his starting location.

The second says his direction/frame returned too.

And then the finite-cycle question becomes

\[
H(\alpha)^N=I.
\]

If such a finite \(N\) exists, that trajectory has finite holonomic closure. If not, it can return spatially while its transported orientation continues cycling indefinitely.

One particularly nice thing about this construction is that the fourth dimension can be visually hidden without hiding the path. The observer sees the 3D projection

\[
\pi(\gamma)=(x,y,z),
\]

which remains continuously inside the visible shell. The actual path is

\[
\gamma=(x,y,z,w).
\]

So there are no disappearing segments or visually mysterious jumps. The 4D component shows up as apparent inward curvature/slope.

And I now think we should not prescribe the bridge as \(w=f(r)\) arbitrarily if we're interested in the closure result. That would bake a particular metric into the experiment. The cleaner thing is to ask for the **minimal rotationally symmetric smooth bridge** satisfying:

\[
R_{\rm outer}=1,\qquad
R_{\rm inner}=\frac12,
\]

smooth attachment at both spherical leaves, no preferred longitude or latitude, monotonic radial transition, and minimum additional geometric structure.

Then derive its metric and shoot geodesics through it as a function of initial angle.

That would give us exactly what you originally wanted: the possible closed paths and their angular relationships without selecting the answers beforehand.

And yes—this is now much more recognizably a “4D slope”: not a ramp sitting somewhere on the spheres, but a **full \(S^2\)-worth of slopes simultaneously**, whose 3D projection occupies the entire shell.
Ok. I think this is a good point to return to our examination of these braid guys lol

Lol, yes. And we’re coming back to them with a much better diagnostic now.

The key change is that I would no longer ask, “Are they doing something that resembles strands?” I’d ask:

\[
\boxed{\text{What exactly closes, what exactly is transported, and what survives one cycle?}}
\]

Because our last several turns separated three things that braid/higher-geometry writing often lets blur together:

\[
\text{trajectory topology}
\neq
\text{metric geometry}
\neq
\text{holonomy}.
\]

Ordinary braid theory mostly answers the first question: given several objects that cannot pass through one another, which histories can be continuously deformed into which other histories? Its basic object is a configuration-space motion class. That’s why \(B_n\) is fundamentally a \(\pi_1\): it records closed loops through configuration space.

But our pilot construction immediately asks more than that. Two paths can belong to the same topological motion class and nevertheless have different:

- lengths,
- curvatures,
- transported orientations,
- accumulated phase,
- frame rotations,
- winding ratios,
- finite versus infinite recurrence.

That last distinction is exactly where **framing and holonomy** come in.

So framed braid theory now looks considerably more relevant than bare braid theory. A bare braid says, roughly,

> “this strand went around that strand this way.”

A framed braid additionally remembers something like

> “and the strand itself rotated by this much while doing it.”

That is much closer to our arrow-bearing pilot. Two centerline trajectories could be identical while their frames finish differently.

Then loop braid groups become interesting because their basic objects aren't points but extended loops moving through 3-space. That gives the “strand guys” a way to retain nontrivial motion topology in three spatial dimensions where ordinary point braiding becomes comparatively trivial.

But there’s a limitation we can now state very sharply:

\[
\boxed{\text{A braid group doesn't tell you whether the transported frame closes.}}
\]

For that you need a connection/transport rule and its holonomy.

Likewise:

\[
\boxed{\text{Holonomy doesn't by itself tell you the braid class.}}
\]

You can have zero holonomy around a topologically nontrivial loop, or nonzero holonomy around a contractible loop if the connection has curvature.

That means the architecture probably separates naturally into layers:

\[
\text{configuration space}
\]

tells us what motions are available;

\[
\pi_1(\mathcal C)
\]

classifies topological cycles;

\[
\text{framing}
\]

retains orientation/twist information;

\[
\text{connection}
\]

specifies how the frame evolves;

\[
\text{holonomy}
\]

tells us the residual transformation after closure.

And then the thing we just discovered about rational versus irrational closure comes after all of those:

\[
H^N=I
\]

for some finite \(N\), versus no such finite \(N\).

That is an actual finite/infinite recurrence criterion.

So when we go back through their material, I particularly want to watch for places where they quietly identify different senses of “closure.” In this literature, “loop,” “closed,” “identity,” “equivalence,” “lift,” and “holonomy” can sound as though they are describing one phenomenon, but mathematically they're very different.

Also, the Jacobi diagrams now look somewhat different to me. They aren't primarily describing trajectories. They're an algebraic way of recording interaction/combinatorial structure attached to knots or Wilson lines. So I would put them downstream:

\[
\text{actual motion}
\rightarrow
\text{motion class}
\rightarrow
\text{holonomy/framing}
\rightarrow
\text{diagrammatic invariant}.
\]

Not the other way around.

And the “higher” guys become potentially useful at exactly one point: if our permitted histories can actually change topology—reconnection, bifurcation, one loop becoming two, carriers collapsing, etc.—then a single fixed braid group is no longer enough. A group assumes we're moving around inside one configuration type and eventually returning.

Once we permit

\[
n\rightarrow n+1
\]

or

\[
\text{linked}\rightarrow\text{unlinked},
\]

we need something that can represent maps **between different configuration spaces**, not just loops inside one of them. That's where tangles, cobordisms, groupoids and eventually higher categories could genuinely earn their keep instead of merely decorating the discussion.

So I think our revised reading order should effectively be:

\[
\boxed{
\text{braid}
\to
\text{framed braid}
\to
\text{loop braid}
\to
\text{holonomy}
\to
\text{topology-changing histories}
}
\]

And throughout, apply the sheep-counting rule:

> What is the actual object? What physical/geometric distinction survives? What calculation becomes possible because we retained it?

That should make the braid guys considerably easier to interrogate than they were the first time through.

[L21] The ability to control and manipulate time-reversal (T) symmetry-breaking phases with near-zero net
[L22] magnetization is a sought-after goal in spintronic devices. The recently discovered hexagonal altermagnet
[L23] manganese telluride (α-MnTe) is a prime example. It has a compensated altermagnetic ground state where
[L24] the magnetic moments are aligned in each layer and stacked antiparallel along the c axis, yet it exhibits a
[L25] spontaneous anomalous Hall effect (AHE) that breaks the T-symmetry with a vanishingly small c-axis
[L26] ferromagnetic moment. However, the presence of three 120° separated in-plane magnetic domains presents
[L27] a challenge in understanding the origin of the AHE and the effective control of the altermagnetic state. Here
[L28] we use neutron scattering to show that symmetry breaking anisotropic strain, induced by compressive
[L29] uniaxial pressure along the nearest-neighbor (NN) Mn-Mn bond directions, detwins α-MnTe into a single
[L30] in-plane magnetic domain. This control over in-plane domains allows us to unambiguously establish that
[L31] the in-plane moments are aligned along the next-nearest-neighbor (NNN) Mn-Mn bond direction,
[L32] irrespective of the applied strain directions. Mounting the sample on a piezoelectric strain cell along
[L33] both NN and NNN directions can drive the sample into a single-domain state that significantly sharpens the
[L34] AHE hysteresis loop and extends the AHE to lower temperatures. Furthermore, tuning the uniaxial strain
[L35] reverses the sign of the AHE near room temperature. Remarkably, this is achieved without altering the
[L36] altermagnetic phase-transition temperature. Combined with our phenomenological model, we propose that
[L37] these effects result from the modification of the electronic Berry curvature by a combination of both spin￾orbit coupling and strain. [L9] Monoidal categories with additional structure such as a braiding or some form of duality
[L10] abound in quantum topology. They often appear in tandem with Frobenius algebras inside
[L11] them. Motivations for this range from the theory of module categories to the construction
[L12] of correlators in conformal field theory. We generalize the Baez-Dolan microcosm principle
[L13] to consistently describe all these types of algebras by extending it to cyclic and modular
[L14] algebras in the sense of Getzler-Kapranov. Our main result links the microcosm principle for
[L15] cyclic algebras to the one for modular algebras via Costello’s modular envelope. The result
[L16] can be understood as a local-to-global construction or an integration procedure for various
[L17] flavors of Frobenius algebras that substantially generalizes and unifies the available (and often
[L18] intrinsically semisimple) methods using for example triangulations or classical skein theory.
[L19] As the main application of this rather abstract result, we solve the problem of classifying
[L20] consistent systems of correlators for open conformal field theories and show that the genus
[L21] zero correlators for logarithmic conformal field theories constructed by Fuchs-Schweigert can
[L22] be uniquely extended to handlebodies. This establishes a very general correspondence between
[L23] full genus zero conformal field theory in dimension two and skein theory in dimension three.

[L10] Topological quantum computation provides an elegant way around decoherence, as one encodes quantum
[L11] information in a non-local fashion that the environment finds difficult to corrupt. Here we establish that one of
[L12] the key operations—braiding of non-Abelian anyons—can be implemented in one-dimensional semiconductor
[L13] wire networks. Previous work1,2 provided a recipe for driving semiconducting wires into a topological phase
[L14] supporting long-sought particles known as Majorana fermions that can store topologically protected quantum
[L15] information. Majorana fermions in this setting can be transported, created, and fused by applying locally tunable
[L16] gates to the wire. More importantly, we show that networks of such wires allow braiding of Majorana fermions
[L17] and that they exhibit non-Abelian statistics like vortices in a p + ip superconductor. We propose experimental
[L18] setups that enable the Majorana fusion rules to be probed, along with networks that allow for efficient exchange
[L19] of arbitrary numbers of Majorana fermions. This work paves a new path forward in topological quantum com￾putation that benefits from physical transparency and experimental realism.
[L20] PACS numbers:
[L21] The experimental realization of a quantum computer ranks
[L22] among the foremost outstanding problems in condensed mat￾ter physics, particularly in light of the revolutionary rewards
[L23] the achievement of this goal promises. Typically, decoher￾ence presents the primary obstacle to fabricating a scalable
[L24] quantum computer. In this regard topological quantum com￾puting holds considerable promise, as here one embeds quan￾tum information in a non-local, intrinsically decoherence-free

[L10] may lead to the formation of a helical liquid in single-channel quantum wires. In a helical liquid,
[L11] electrons with opposite velocities have opposite spin precessions. We argue that zero-energy Ma￾jorana bound states are formed in various situations when the wire is situated in proximity to a
[L12] conventional s-wave superconductor. This occurs when the external magnetic field, the supercon￾ducting gap, or the chemical potential vary along the wire. We discuss experimental consequences
[L13] of the formation of the helical liquid and the Majorana bound states.
[L14] States of matter that support Majorana fermions have
[L15] received much attention in the context of quantum com￾putation. A widely separated pair of Majorana bound
[L16] states forms a nonlocal fermionic state which is immune
[L17] to local sources of decoherence, thus providing a platform
[L18] for fault-tolerant quantum memory. Moreover, since Ma￾jorana states realize a representation of the non-Abelian
[L19] braid group, topological quantum information processing
[L20] can, in principle, be effected by braiding operations [1].
[L21] A realization of such states where they can be readily
[L22] moved around and manipulated is therefore highly desir￾able.
[L23] There are several suggestions for physical systems that
[L24] support Majorana states, for particular ways to manip￾ulate them, and for measuring their properties. These
[L25] include fractional quantum Hall states at filling factor
[L26] ν = 5/2 [2], p-wave superconductors [3], surfaces of
[L27] three-dimensional topological insulators in proximity to
[L28] a superconductor [4], and helical edge modes of two￾dimensional topological insulators in proximity to a fer￾romagnet and a superconductor [5]. Recently, it was
[L29] suggested that a semiconducting thin film sandwiched
[L30] between an s-wave superconductor and a magnetic insu￾lator [6] will host Majorana states associated with super￾conducting vortices. All these proposals, however, would
[L31] be experimentally extremely challenging.

[L33] wires may be decisively simpler. Here we show that quan￾tum wires with strong spin-orbit coupling, such as InAs
[L34] or InSb wires, and banded carbon nanotubes form a he￾lical liquid, similar to the edges of a topological insula￾tor. Consequently, these wires support Majorana states
[L35] when they are in proximity to s-wave superconductors,
[L36] and a magnetic field. Most importantly, we explain how

[L38] a chemical potential, which could be simply produced

[L20] The nLab is a collaborative wiki. It grew out of the desire (I, II) to have a place for development (the “Lab” in “
n

n

n

The

n
[L34] Lab” (short for “
n
[L36] -Category Lab”, but perhaps less restrictive) was dreamt up by Lisa Raphals (John Baez‘s wife).

[L44] 2. What the 
n
[L46] Lab is
[L47] The most apt analogy for the 
n
[L49] Lab is of a group lab book. A lab book for a research scientist is a place where they write down anything that they consider relevant for their work; a group lab book is one that several researchers with common interests use. The material recorded in a lab book can include:

[L51] Notes from seminars
[L52] Notes from papers and books
[L53] Summaries of known work
[L54] Observations and results from experiments
[L55] Ideas for future work
[L56] Apart from not having actual physical experiments, this matches the content of the 
n
[L58] Lab fairly well. The key difference between the 
n
[L60] Lab and an “ordinary” lab book is that it is public. By making it public we hope to achieve two things:

[L62] To enable others to benefit from our work while it is still being done.
[L63] To benefit from the work of others while we are doing it.
[L64] There is much more to a research project than that which appears in the final paper and we believe that since our results and our final proofs will be public, then both we and those who might read such a paper can benefit from beginning the interaction much earlier in its development.

[L66] Thus by making our lab book public, we hope that casual passers-by will stop, read, and scribble something on it that will help us do our research.

[L68] There are three things to say about this that are worth making very clear.

[L70] Our reasons for having the 
n
[L72] Lab are ultimately selfish. We have set it up and run it to make it easier to our research.
[L73] But to make it work properly in public, we need to make it attractive to others so that they will stop by, read our jottings, and scribble something of their own.
[L74] We aim to achieve a system whereby those who put most in are also those who get most out.
[L75] 3. Who Are We?

[L81] 7. Discussion
[L82] Quantum groups and braid groups play important roles in physics. Taken as a flavour sym￾metry, SUq(3) leads to exceptionally accurate baryon mass formulas. It would be interesting to

[L85] networks by representations of SUq(2) introduces a (positive) cosmological constant. At the same

[L87] network.

[L108] wire networks. Previous work1,2 provided a recipe for driving semiconducting wires into a topological phase
[L109] supporting long-sought particles known as Majorana fermions that can store topologically protected quantum
[L110] information. Majorana fermions in this setting can be transported, created, and fused by applying locally tunable
[L111] gates to the wire. More importantly, we show that networks of such wires allow braiding of Majorana fermions
[L112] and that they exhibit non-Abelian statistics like vortices in a p + ip superconductor. We propose experimental
[L113] setups that enable the Majorana fusion rules to be probed, along with networks that allow for efficient exchange
[L114] of arbitrary numbers of Majorana fermions. This work paves a new path forward in topological quantum com￾putation that benefits from physical transparency and experimental realism.

[L193] 1. Anyon braiding
[L194] In quantum physics, braid group statistics or anyon statistics (sometimes: plektons) refers to an exotic kind of particle statistics where the braiding of the worldlines of certain effective particles (“anyons”) in an effectively 1+2-dimensional spacetime has the effect of transforming the quantum state of the total quantum system by unitary operators which constitute a linear representation of the braid group – a braid representation.
[L195]
[L196] Often this is motivated as a generalization of the boson- or fermion-“statistics” which enters the spin-statistics theorem, see below.
[L197]
[L198] But the actual mathematical nature of anyons must be different from that of elements of boson/fermion-Fock spaces and often remains somewhat vague in existing discussions.

[L376] 1. Anyon braiding
[L377] In quantum physics, braid group statistics or anyon statistics (sometimes: plektons) refers to an exotic kind of particle statistics where the braiding of the worldlines of certain effective particles (“anyons”) in an effectively 1+2-dimensional spacetime has the effect of transforming the quantum state of the total quantum system by unitary operators which constitute a linear representation of the braid group – a braid representation.
[L378]
[L379] Often this is motivated as a generalization of the boson- or fermion-“statistics” which enters the spin-statistics theorem, see below.
[L380]
[L381] But the actual mathematical nature of anyons must be different from that of elements of boson/fermion-Fock spaces and often remains somewhat vague in existing discussions. One may recognize two different more concrete conceptualizations of anyons in the literature:
[L382]
[L383] anyonic quanta much like boson/fermion quanta but subject to an additional global interaction by Aharonov-Bohm phases due to a flat fictitious gauge field which is sourced by and coupled to each of the quanta;
[L384]
[L385] (this goes back to Arovas, Schrieffer, Wilczek & Zee 1985, further developed in Chen, Wilczek, Witten & Halperin 1989, see below)
[L386]
[L387] anyonic defects like vortices or other solitons, whose position is a classical parameter to the quantum system, the adiabatic movement of which acts by Berry phases on the quantum ground state.
[L388]
[L389] (e.g. Arovas, Schrieffer & Wilczek 1984, see further below)
[L390]
[L391] The concept of anyons is particularly well motivated in solid state physics, where effectively 2-dimensional quantum materials are common place (eg. graphene) or where particles may otherwise be constrained to move in a plane, such as in the quantum Hall effect. There is a multitude of models in condensed matter theory (mostly lattice models, such as string-net models) which theoretically realize anyon braid group statistics, and there are some first experimental indications of anyonic phenomena in actual materials (see the references under Experimental Realization) below.
[L392]
[L393] Specifically, in the context of topological phases of matter, the (potential) presence of anyons has come to be known as the case of topological order, see there for more.
[L394]
[L395] Besides general curiosity, much of the interest in anyonic braid group statistics lies in the fact that these braid representations are imagined to potentially serve as quantum gates in topological quantum computers. See there for more.
[L396]

[L437] 3. The Helon model
[L438] The Helon model of Bilson-Thompson maps the simplest non-trivial braids consisting of three
[L439] (twisted) ribbons and two crossings to the first generation of SM fermions. There are exactly 15
[L440] states in the model with no place for a right-handed neutrino. Quantized electric charges of particles
[L441] are represented by integral twists of the ribbons of the braids; The color charges of quarks and
[L442] gluons are accounted for by the permutations of twists on certain braids; and simple topological
[L443] processes are identified with the electroweak interaction, the color interaction, and conservation
[L444] laws.
[L445] These braided structures may be embedded within a larger network of braided ribbons. Such
[L446] a braided ribbon network (BRN) is a generalization of a spin network, fundamental in LQG. The
[L447] embedding of the braids into BRNs make it possible to develop a unified theory of matter and
[L448] spacetime in which both are emergent from the BRN [29]. The representation of first generation
[L449] SM fermions in terms of braids and an illustration of the embedding of such a braid into a BRN are
[L450] shown in Figure 1.
[L451] Figure 1: The Helon model of Bilson-Thompson in which the first generation SM fermions are represented
[L452] as braids of three (possibly twisted) ribbons, and the embedding of such braids into a braided ribbon network.
[L453] Sources, [10] and [29].
[L454] 4. Normed division algebras
[L455] A division algebra is an algebra over a field where division is always possible, with the excep￾tion of division by zero. Nature admits only four normed division algebras over the reals, the real
[L456] numbers R, the complex numbers C, the quaternions Q and the octonions O. Starting from the real
[L457] numbers and generalizing to the complex numbers, one has to give up the ordered property of the
[L458] reals.

[L482] 7. Discussion
[L483] Quantum groups and braid groups play important roles in physics. Taken as a flavour sym￾metry, SUq(3) leads to exceptionally accurate baryon mass formulas. It would be interesting to
[L484] consider the deformation of other internal symmetries in the SM and extend previous work to cal￾culate cross sections and branching ratios of particles when one assumes underlying quantum group
[L485] symmetries. Quantum groups have also played a role in LQG where labelling the edges of spin
[L486] networks by representations of SUq(2) introduces a (positive) cosmological constant. At the same
[L487] time, doing so requires replacing the ended of the network by ribbons, giving a braided ribbon
[L488] network.
[L489] 7Quantum groups and braid groups Niels G. Gresnigt
[L490] The main idea presented here is that the Clifford Braiding Theorem it is possible to investigate
[L491] the braid content of the description of SM symmetries based on the NDAs and compare it to the
[L492] braided structures found in the Helon model. Remarkably, we find that the braid groups representa￾tions admitted by the complex numbers and quaternions are precisely those braid groups present in
[L493] the Helon model. Further work to investigate the connections between the two models, in particular
[L494] the role of the octonions and the braid group they represent, is ongoing.
[L495] The choice of braid group structure in the Helon model is somewhat arbitrary, chosen because
[L496] it is the seemingly simplest possibility. Using NDAs provides a justification for why one should
[L497] consider braids consisting of three ribbons, rather than any other number of ribbons. That is, the
[L498] four NDAs dictate which braid groups one should consider. What is still needed is a mechanism
[L499] to determine which elements within each braid groups should be considered. It may be speculated
[L500] that this could be determined by the finite order of the braid generators as represented by the NDAs.
[L501] In these cases the order of each generator is eight, in contrast to the standard braid generators which
[L502] have infinite order. This is currently work in progress.

[L645] 1. Idea
[L646] Around the nLab it is widely believed that homotopy theory/algebraic topology, (homotopy) type theory, (higher) category theory and (higher) categorical algebra provide a point of view on Mathematics, Physics and Philosophy which is a valuable unifying point of view for the understanding of the concepts involved.
[L647]
[L648] In particular, at the 
[L649] n
[L650] Lab, there is no commitment to being neutral. There are certainly other valid points of view on mathematics, but describing them and being neutral towards them is not the purpose of the 
[L651] n
[L652] Lab. Rather, the 
[L653] n
[L654] Lab starts from the premise that homotopy theory/algebraic topology, (homotopy) type theory, (higher) category theory and (higher) categorical algebra are a useful point of view, and one of its aims is to expose this point of view generally and in a multitude of examples, and thereby accumulate evidence for it.
[L655]
[L656] If you feel skeptical about the 
[L657] n
[L658] -point of view, you should still find the 
[L659] n
[L660] Lab useful, as the largest site for detailed category-theoretic and homotopy-theoretic information online. You are very much welcome to contribute relevant content even if you are such a skeptic.
[L661]
[L662] Category theory
[L663] As recalled in parts on the page on category theory, category theorists have early on, beginning in the 1960s, proclaimed the advantages of category theory over other points of view. It has been observed that this claim, or at least the way it has been put forward, has contributed to a certain alienation of category theory in parts of the mathematical community. That may be true and is understandable. But since a claim is not false just because it is put forward with possibly unpleasant boldness, all evidence for the claim deserves to be collected and exposed. We hope the 
[L664] n
[L665] Lab to play a role in this effort.
[L666]
[L667] In particular, there have been dramatic developments since the 1960s. Back then promoting category theory may have been as visionary as the invention of complex numbers was in the 16th century.

[L720] Abstract
[L721] We study interactions amongst topologically conserved excitations of quantum theories of gravity, in particular the braid excitations of four valent spin networks. These have been shown previously to propagate and interact under evolution rules of spin foam models. We show that the dynamics of these braid excitations can be described by an effective theory based on Feynman diagrams. In this language, braids which are actively interacting are analogous to bosons, in that the topological conservation laws permit them to be singly created and destroyed. Exchanges of these excitations give rise to interactions between braids which are charged under the topological conservation rules.

[L724] Introduction
[L725] A substantial amount of work [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9] has been done recently towards emergent matter as topological invariants of framed spin networks, embedded in a topological three-manifold [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], [7], [8] and unembedded [9], as fundamental states of quantum gravity and quantum geometry. Some papers study the case of framed three-valent spin networks [1], [2], [3], [9], which were motivated by the pioneer work of Bilson-Thompson [10]. Others investigate the three-strand braids of four-valent spin networks embedded in a topological three manifold [5], [6], [7], [8].
[L726] The aim of this paper is to present an effective description of these emergent local excitations [1], [5], [11] in the language of Feynman diagrams. As an analogy effective emergent degrees of freedom have been realized in condensed matter physics. For example, there are emergent quasiparticles as collective modes in some condensed matter systems, such as phonons and rotons in superfluid He4. Another example is the string-net condensation which gives rise to low energy effective gauge theories [14].
[L727] The three-valent case considered in [1], [2], [3] is limited by lack of creation and annihilation of the topological invariants [2] which are considered corresponding to Standard Model particles [3]. This partly motivates our work in the four-valent case [4], [5], [6], [7], [8] in which the topological excitations can propagate and interact under the dual Pachner moves [5]. The four-valent spin networks here can be understood as those naturally occur in spin foam models [12], or in a more generic sense as the original proposal of spin networks put forward by Penrose [13].

[L93] Originally this was considered just an intermediate technical step to separate the issue of “UV-divergences” (the definition of the S-matrix at coinciding interaction points) from the “IR-divergences”, namely from the issue of taking the “adiabatic limit” of the S-matrix in which the adiabatic switching is removed and interactions are considered over all of spacetime.
[L94]
[L95] But it had been observed already in Il’in-Slavnov 78 that for realistic quantum observables which are supported in a compact region of spacetime (corresponding to an experimental setup of finite extension in space and time) all that matters is that the interaction is “switched on” in the causal closure of the support of the observable, while outside its support it may be “adiabatically switched off” at will without actually changing the value of the observables (up to canonical unitary equivalence, see here). Moreover, the system of spacetime localized perturbative quantum observables obtained this way from the causal S-matrix turns out to satisfy axioms that had earlier been proposed in Haag-Kastler 64 to provide a complete mathematical characterization of the physical content of a pQFT: they form a local net of observables. This will be explained in detail in the next part of this series.
[L96]
[L97] Haag-Kastler originally aimed, ambitiously, for the axiomatization of the non-perturbative quantum field theory, and hence required the algebras of observables in the local net to be -algebras. Their formulation of non-perturbative quantum field theory via local nets of -algebras came to be known as algebraic quantum field theory (AQFT). Here in perturbation theory, these algebras are just formal power series algebras (in the coupling constant and in Plancks’s constant), but otherwise, they satisfy the original Haag-Kastler axioms. This way pQFT in the rigorous guise of causal perturbation theory came to be called perturbative algebraic quantum field theory (pAQFT, Brunetti-Dütsch-Fredenhagen 09).
[L98]
[L99] The terminology overlaps a bit.

[L533] In any case, the presence of strong electromagnetic fields (potential) tend to enhance such effects.
[L534]
[L535] When the U(1) symmetry is broken the corresponding (Noether) charge current is not conserved. Although the fermionic charge density and number density of the fermions is not conserved locally in this model, the equations suggest interpreting the terms of geometric origin as effective charge currents that compensate and balance the non-conservation of the usual charge current. In other words, by following this interpretation the space-time geometrodynamics would gain physical features, such as effective mass, spin or charge currents, when it couples to matter. When these terms are considered, then a new conserved quantity is clear. Another way to see this is to deduce the phenomenology associated to such an interpretation and search for possible observational tests of the predictions. In this context, this type of models where the stress-energy tensor or the charge current is not conserved in the usual sense, predict the creation of particles from the energy available in the space-time geometrodynamics, in strong gravity environments.
[L536]
[L537] When the contribution from the bosonic sector to the spin tensor is taken into account, then the bosonic field propagates on a RC spacetime and backreact on its geometry. Since torsion in EC theory is given by an algebraic expression of the matter fields, one then gets non-minimal couplings between these but also self-interactions. Therefore, we obtain effectively a non-linear dynamical equations for the bosonic fields. In fact, just as in the case of fermions where a linear Dirac field in RC space-time of the EC theory is equivalent to a non-linear spinor in GR, also here the linear electromagnetic Lagrangian in the RC space-time leads to an effective non-linear electrodynamics in GR. Non-linear dynamics in the matter fields can emerge naturally from the (minimal) couplings of these fields with the extended space-time geometries of gauge theories of gravity.
[L538]
[L539] In the case of fermionic fields in EC theory, torsion effects can also become significant in environments where the density is lower than Cartan’s density. This is not so commonly mentioned in the literature, on the contrary, much emphasis is put on the fact that in EC theory the effects of torsion in Einstein’s equations, i.e., for the metric, are only significant at extremely high densities such as those found in the very early Universe or inside black holes. Since the Cartan equations imply K\sim \kappa ^{2}\breve{s}, after its substitution in the Dirac equation i\hbar \gamma ^{\lambda } D_{\lambda }\psi -m\psi =0, one obtains the (cubic) Hehl–Datta equation where the torsion-induced term will become significant at (spin) densities comparable to any strong-gravity regime where GR effects become important.
[L540]
[L541] Let us stress that the Hehl–Datta term, which is related to an effective axial–axial (spin–spin) repulsive interaction, has been studied in connection to different physical mechanisms important for particle physics and cosmology, such as non-singular black holes, matter/anti-matter asymmetry and energy-levels, etc. Analogously, in our U(1) symmetry-breaking model similar cubic terms are present that are quadratic in the electromagnetic four-potential. In this case, these torsion-induced corrections scale with \kappa ^{4}, which means that the corresponding physical effects (on the energy levels, generalized effective Feynmann diagrams, etc) will only become relevant at extremely high densities (Cartan’s density or above, but still lower than Planck density).

[L625] The introduction of the cipher 0 or the group concept was general nonsense too, and mathematics was more or less stagnating for thousands of years because nobody was around to take such childish steps…
[L626]
[L627] The nPOV
[L628] The vast applicability and expressiveness of category theory leads to the observation that most structures in mathematics are best understood from a category theoretic or higher category theoretic viewpoint. This is the nPOV.
[L629]
[L630] 2. The central constructions
[L631]
[L632] Presheaves
[L633]
[L634] Much of the power of category theory rests in the fact that it reflects on itself. For instance that functors between two categories form themselves a category: the functor category.
[L635]
[L636] This leads to the notion of presheaf categories and sheaf toposes. Much of category theory is topos theory.
[L637]
[L638] Under Isbell duality this sets the stage for everything in mathematics related to space and algebra and their duality.
[L639]
[L640] Universal constructions
[L641]
[L642] Elementary as it is, the definition of a category supports a powerful set of constructions: universal constructions. These include
[L643]
[L644] limit and colimit;
[L645]
[L646] adjunction;
[L647]
[L648] Kan extension
[L649]
[L650] end and coend.
[L651]
[L652] All these are special cases of each other and thus reflect different aspect of one single phenomenon. Applying category theory means applying these constructions in specific situations and using general abstract theorems for deducing statements about concrete contexts.
[L653]
[L654] The central theorems
[L655]
[L656] Category theory has a handful of central lemmas and theorems. Their proof is typically easy, sometimes almost tautological. Their power rests in the fact that they apply over and over again all over mathematics. Many concrete constructions get simplified by observing that they are but special realizations of these general abstract results in category theory. Among these central theorems are
[L657]
[L658] first and foremost: the Yoneda lemma;
[L659]
[L660] Isbell duality;
[L661]
[L662] the Grothendieck construction;
[L663]
[L664] the adjoint functor theorem;
[L665]
[L666] the monadicity theorem;
[L667]
[L668] Tannaka duality.
[L669]
[L670] 3. Applications
[L671]
[L672] For a detailed list of applications see
[L673]
[L674] applications of (higher) category theory.
[L675] In pure mathematics
[L676]
[L677] Apart from its general role in mathematics, category theory provides the high-level language for
[L678]
[L679] logic / type theory
[L680]
[L681] higher algebra
[L682]
[L683] higher geometry .
[L684]
[L685] Outside of mathematics
[L686]
[L687] Outside of pure mathematics, category theory finds major applications in
[L688]
[L689] fundamental physics – see higher category theory and physics
[L690]
[L691] theoretical computer science
[L692]
[L693] and is increasingly finding applications in such diverse areas as chemistry, network theory and natural language processing. Further information can be found on the applied category theory page.
[L694]
[L695] 4. Contrast to theories of other objects
[L696]
[L697] Category theory vs. set theory
[L698]
[L699] Here set theory is assumed to be a theory of the usual concept of sets, that is material set theory.
[L700]
[L701] No one of these is more fundamental than the other as a foundation of mathematics. Category theory is a holistic (structural) approach to mathematics that can (through such methods as Lawvere’s ETCS) provide foundations of mathematics and (through algebraic set theory) reproduce all the different axiomatic set theories; elementary category theory does not need the concept of set to be formulated. Set theory is an analytic approach (element-wise) and can reproduce category theory by simply defining all the concepts in the usual way, as long as one include a technique to handle large categories (for instance by using classes instead of sets, or by including as an axiom that an uncountable inaccessible cardinal exists or even that Grothendieck universes exist).

thoughts.content: I’m seeing a real pattern, but not one uniform story: older foundations are being reused across modern work on topology, quantum information, particle symmetries, and quantum gravity. The citation surge likely reflects convergence among these research communities.

parts:
Yes. And after going through the bundle, I think there are two separate things going on here that are worth distinguishing.

First, this is much less a random cloud of “braid guys” than it looked at first. There is an identifiable intellectual pipeline running from old spin/statistics/symmetry work, through topology and configuration spaces, into anyons/topological matter, and then into a much more speculative branch that asks whether particles themselves could be braided structures.

Second, that citation-rise pattern is real-looking, but I would not yet attribute it specifically to this community. Some of it will be general growth in publication volume and electronic citation indexing. But the timing is conspicuous because roughly the same period saw topology, Berry phase, anyons, topological quantum computation, Majoranas, Chern–Simons theory, spin networks, and topological phases become much more central to physics. The bundle itself is full of that migration.

And one thing in the copypasta resolves our earlier “underground” impression rather decisively. nLab literally says it originated as an indexed working archive around the n-Category Café, and calls itself a **public group lab book**, containing seminar notes, paper notes, known work, observations and future ideas. It says its purpose is to make its own researchers’ work easier, not to function primarily as public education. fileciteturn12file13L20-L34 fileciteturn12file13L44-L74 And its `nPOV` page explicitly says neutrality is not its purpose: it begins from the premise that homotopy theory, higher category theory, etc. provide a valuable unifying viewpoint and aims to accumulate evidence for that viewpoint. fileciteturn13file9L622-L665

So we weren't imagining the register. We're basically reading somebody else's open research-room whiteboard.

But the biggest surprise in what you uploaded is Gresnigt's 2017 paper, because this is no longer merely “braids are a convenient algebra.”

The abstract explicitly says it is connecting Standard Model symmetries to a description in which **elementary matter is represented as braided objects**. fileciteturn12file0L2-L11 And then it gets considerably more literal. The Bilson-Thompson Helon model maps simple three-ribbon braids onto first-generation fermions; integral twists represent electric charge; permutations of twists represent color; and topological processes are associated with interactions and conservation laws. The braids are then embedded in braided ribbon networks, with the proposal that matter and spacetime could both emerge from the network. fileciteturn13file6L437-L452

That's much closer to what I thought we *weren't* seeing.

Still not your construction: these are framed/twisted ribbons in spin-network/topological-manifold settings, not finite-core 4D strands following the kind of full-shell slope we've just been constructing. But it absolutely is “particle identity as braid/twist structure,” rather than merely using braid groups to classify particle exchanges.

And the paper is candid about the weak spot. It says the original choice of braid structure in the Helon model was “somewhat arbitrary,” chosen as the seemingly simplest possibility; the proposed division-algebra connection is meant to justify three ribbons, but the mechanism selecting the actual braid-group elements is still missing. fileciteturn13file7L482-L502

That's exactly the place where I would press them.

The other physically serious braid branch is different and much better established: anyons and Majorana systems. Here the braid isn't supposed to be what an electron is. Instead, exchanging effective excitations produces a nontrivial transformation of the quantum state. nLab itself describes anyonic statistics as worldline braiding in effectively \(1+2\) dimensions acting through a unitary representation of the braid group, and distinguishes quasiparticle-like anyons from defects such as vortices whose adiabatic motion produces Berry phases. fileciteturn13file5L376-L395

And here our holonomy discussion suddenly becomes directly relevant.

The Alicea–Oreg–Refael–von Oppen–Fisher paper physically transports Majorana modes through wire junctions. During an exchange, the superconducting phase changes continuously; a \(2\pi\) phase change changes the sign of the Majorana operator, so they introduce branch cuts to keep track of the state. fileciteturn15file2L201-L253 The resulting exchange acts as

\[
\gamma_1\rightarrow\gamma_2,\qquad
\gamma_2\rightarrow-\gamma_1,
\]

implemented by a nontrivial unitary transformation. fileciteturn15file5L388-L435 They also explicitly get a topologically originating \(4\pi\) periodicity. fileciteturn15file3L265-L274

That is basically a concrete realization of the distinction we just reached with the pilot:

\[
\boxed{\text{the path can close while the transported state does not.}}
\]

Or more accurately, after one exchange the physical configuration may look equivalent while the state has acquired a nontrivial transformation. Repeat the motion and closure can occur only after a larger cycle.

That's exactly where braid theory, holonomy, and spin-like double-cover behavior start touching each other.

The copypasta then pushes outward from there. There are mapping-class groups and Dehn twists—ways of classifying globally inequivalent transformations of surfaces. There are cobordisms—ways of treating entire histories connecting one boundary configuration to another. There are Chern–Simons connections, where knot/braid information and gauge holonomy are intimately linked. There is the higher-category program attempting to put all those transformations and transformations-between-transformations into one formal language.

And there is a separate speculative quantum-gravity branch that is strikingly close to particle mechanics. One paper excerpt in the copypasta studies **topologically conserved braid excitations of framed spin networks**, lets neighboring braids interact, merge, decay and exchange braid excitations, and then constructs “braid Feynman diagrams” as an effective description of their dynamics. fileciteturn14file0L10-L33 Another excerpt explicitly describes the broader effort as “emergent matter as topological invariants of framed spin networks” embedded in a topological three-manifold. fileciteturn13file10L699-L727

So I would now divide the population we have been calling “the braid guys” into three quite different camps:

1. **Mathematical braid people:** configuration spaces, braid groups, mapping-class groups, homology, knot invariants. No claim that particles are literally braids.
2. **Established topological-physics people:** anyons, Berry phases, Chern numbers, Majoranas, topological phases. Braiding has measurable consequences, but the “braid” normally describes exchange history/configuration-space topology.
3. **Emergent-particle/topological-unification people:** Bilson-Thompson, braided ribbon networks, some spin-network/LQG work, division-algebra/braid attempts. Here the braid/twist itself is being promoted toward particle structure.

The third group is the one we were actually looking for.

And now the citation graphs.

You're right that several old papers show a very conspicuous late revival. Pauli's 1940 spin-statistics paper sits nearly flat for decades and then climbs strongly after roughly the turn of the century. Kemmer's 1939 paper behaves similarly, though with more earlier activity. Wigner's nuclear-symmetry paper really takes off in the last couple of decades. Stückelberg's graph has an especially dramatic modern rise. Feynman–Gell-Mann is somewhat different—it was already a heavily cited foundational paper, although it too gets a modern surge.

The copypasta itself shows why some of that old literature is being revisited. Its braid-statistics bibliography explicitly runs from Pauli-style boson/fermion statistics into Leinaas–Myrheim, Wilczek, Aharonov–Bohm phases, Berry phases and modern anyons. fileciteturn14file10L666-L705 And the same file contains the old Wigner, Stückelberg, Schwinger, Gell-Mann, Kemmer/Majorana material embedded inside modern symmetry/topology trails. fileciteturn14file8L551-L590 fileciteturn14file11L719-L778

Meanwhile the *current* end of that literature is no longer merely formal. The nLab material lists 2023–2025 anyonic interference/braiding experiments in quantum-Hall systems and graphene. fileciteturn13file14L887-L925

So my provisional interpretation of that citation hump is:

\[
\text{old symmetry/statistics foundations}
\longrightarrow
\text{modern topology of quantum states}
\longrightarrow
\text{experimentally accessible topological matter}.
\]

Not “everyone suddenly decided the 1930s guys were secretly braid theorists.” More that modern physics has become interested in questions for which those old papers are again natural foundational citations.

There's another document in your pile that is almost comically appropriate to our earlier discussion. McLarty's essay on Grothendieck describes the “rising sea” method: rather than attack one theorem directly, build a sufficiently broad theory that the theorem becomes almost trivial inside it. It quotes the idea of constructing an entire mathematical “world,” a topos, potentially as large as the universe of sets, adapted even to one problem. fileciteturn12file8L48-L60

That is basically the intellectual temperament we were detecting in nLab before we knew its genealogy.

And here is where I think our pilot/sphere exercise gives us an unusually good instrument for reading them. We can now ask every braid construction:

\[
\text{What physically/geometrically closes?}
\]

\[
\text{What is merely identified as equivalent?}
\]

\[
\text{What gets transported around the cycle?}
\]

\[
\text{What residual transformation remains after return?}
\]

\[
\text{Is that residual finite-order, infinite-order, or continuous?}
\]

That immediately distinguishes a braid-class statement from a holonomy statement from a metric/path-length statement from a particle-identity claim.

And the Majorana material already demonstrates that those distinctions matter enormously.

So my assessment has changed somewhat: there really **is** a research lineage here investigating surprisingly close relatives of what we've been talking about. But it's fragmented across very different meanings of “braid.” The genuinely interesting job is to find exactly where someone stops using the braid as bookkeeping for exchange and starts letting **finite geometric structure, twist, closure and transport constitute the state itself**.

That's where I want to dig next.

It’s SAT stamp collecting. Only a whole community of people classifying and calculating various types of filament structures. A hundred years ago, this was the direction of 4-dimensional physics thinking. But it was out of style, and got a bad name, in part because of the co-opting of the 4th dimension by spiritualists and charlatans. So, they stopped talking about it like Minkowski did and started wrapping it in knot theory and generalizing dimensionality. But it’s been *active as hell*

parts:
Yes — with one important historical correction. The continuity you’re seeing is real enough to investigate seriously, but I would not yet say “they stopped talking about 4D filaments and hid it inside knot theory.” That is stronger than the evidence supports.

What does look well supported is this:

There was already a 19th-century physical-filament program. Kelvin’s vortex-atom idea explicitly tried to model atoms as knots in a continuous medium, and Tait’s early knot tables grew directly out of that effort. Knot theory then survived as mathematics after the physical vortex-atom model fell away. citeturn964666search32turn964666search7

At almost the same historical moment, higher-dimensional geometry really did get heavily entangled with spiritualism and occult claims. Zöllner famously used knots supposedly produced at séances as evidence for a fourth spatial dimension, and historians explicitly describe that episode as drawing higher-dimensional space into occultist discourse. citeturn964666search0turn964666search2 So your cultural-history instinct there is not fanciful at all.

Then the language changed. By the early 20th century, topology, knot groups, homology, braid groups, mapping-class groups, etc. became mathematically respectable ways of discussing exactly the properties of strands that survive continuous deformation, without requiring anyone to say “these are literal 4D physical filaments.” Artin formalized braid groups in the 1920s; later topology developed the invariant machinery around them. fileciteturn12file5L17-L41

And then physics comes roaring back into it.

The major modern reconnection really accelerates in the 1980s: Jones invariants, statistical mechanics, Witten’s Chern–Simons/QFT interpretation, low-dimensional topology, anyons, quantum Hall physics, topological phases, Majoranas, topological quantum computation. Atiyah described the new situation explicitly as quantum field theory becoming deeply tied to geometry and topology in dimensions 2, 3, and 4. citeturn964666search4

And your uploaded corpus goes farther still. It is not merely studying abstract knot invariants. It contains people proposing:

\[
\text{elementary particle} \leftrightarrow \text{braided/twisted ribbon structure},
\]

with charge represented by ribbon twist, color by twist permutations, interactions by topological operations, and matter/spacetime both emerging from braided ribbon networks. fileciteturn13file6L437-L452

It contains braid excitations of framed spin networks that propagate, interact, merge, decay, and get represented by their own effective Feynman diagrams. fileciteturn14file0L10-L33

It contains actual physical braid phenomena in anyons and Majoranas, where moving things around closed or exchanging paths changes quantum states through phase/holonomy-like transformations. fileciteturn13file5L376-L395

And the Gresnigt paper literally calls quantum groups and braid groups candidates for “fundamental symmetries” and connects division algebras to elementary matter represented as braided objects. fileciteturn12file0L2-L11

So “SAT stamp collecting” is actually a pretty perceptive description of the corpus from your point of view. They have spent generations cataloguing:

- strand crossings,
- twist,
- writhe,
- linking,
- framing,
- orientation,
- chirality,
- closed-loop classes,
- surface mappings,
- braid composition,
- holonomy/Berry phase,
- cobordisms,
- topology-changing histories,
- representations of those structures,
- and increasingly their possible particle/field interpretations.

That is very close to a systematic taxonomy of filament behavior.

Where I think your historical hypothesis gets especially interesting is that there may not have been one clean suppression-and-rebranding event. It may be more like divergence and reconvergence.

Something like:

\[
\text{physical vortex/filament speculation}
\]

splits into

\[
\begin{cases}
\text{topology/knot theory as pure mathematics},\\
\text{4D spacetime/relativity},\\
\text{field theory and representation theory},
\end{cases}
\]

and then during the late 20th century those branches begin recombining:

\[
\text{knot theory}
+
\text{QFT}
+
\text{gauge connections}
+
\text{holonomy}
+
\text{spin}
+
\text{topological phases}
+
\text{extended objects}.
\]

That history is demonstrable.

The stronger sociological proposition—

> “people deliberately stopped saying 4D strands because fourth-dimensional language had become contaminated by spiritualists”

—is plausible enough to investigate, especially because historians document an actual cultural contamination of the fourth dimension by spiritualism. citeturn964666search1turn964666search3 But we’d need correspondence, textbooks, reviews, rhetoric from physicists/mathematicians, perhaps changes in terminology, to establish causal influence rather than chronological coincidence.

What I find much harder to dismiss now is your other point:

**the program never went dormant.**

At least the broader topological/strand-structure program plainly did not. It changed mathematical languages and research communities, but the citation histories and the material you collected show sustained development and then a major late-century/21st-century acceleration.

And the nLab material makes the continuity unusually visible because those people deliberately collect links across what conventional disciplinary history keeps separated. Their lab-book model is practically designed to reveal long conceptual genealogies. fileciteturn12file13L44-L66

The surprising thing, looking at it from SAT/H(s)H, is that your archive and theirs seem to be exploring many of the same **degrees of freedom**, despite starting from almost opposite ends.

You started largely from a geometrical/mechanical construction and kept discovering the need to distinguish twist, braid, holonomy, closure, chirality, finite-core interaction, bifurcation, etc.

They started largely by abstractly classifying precisely those distinctions and only later asked how some of them might instantiate physics.

That is why it looks like stamp collecting from where you're standing.

They already have an enormous catalog of the possible stamps.

What they generally do **not** appear to have is your single finite mechanical object whose behavior is supposed to generate the catalog.

And that may be the most productive way to read this whole literature: not as competing theories, and certainly not as evidence for H(s)H, but as a century-plus inventory of mathematical distinctions that a serious finite-strand construction might have to reproduce or explain.

The historical thesis itself is now worth doing properly. I’d specifically test whether the vocabulary migrated from “higher-dimensional physical geometry” toward “topology/configuration space/internal symmetry” during roughly 1890–1930, and whether authors explicitly linked that linguistic shift to the occult/spiritualist reputation of higher dimensions. That would tell us whether your “hidden in plain sight” impression is merely structural continuity or an actual intellectual genealogy.

[L120] PREFACE.


[L123] The MSS. which formed the basis of this book were committed to us by the
[L124] author, on his leaving England for a distant foreign appointment. It was
[L125] his wish that we should construct upon them a much more complete
[L126] treatise than we have effected, and with that intention he asked us to
[L127] make any changes or additions we thought desirable. But long alliance
[L128] with him in this work has convinced us that his thought (especially that
[L129] of a general philosophical character) loses much of its force if
[L130] subjected to any extraneous touch.

[L132] This feeling has induced us to print Part I. almost exactly as it came
[L133] from his hands, although it would probably have received much
[L134] rearrangement if he could have watched it through the press himself.

[L136] Part II. has been written from a hurried sketch, which he considered
[L137] very inadequate, and which we have consequently corrected and
[L138] supplemented. Chapter XI. of this part has been entirely re-written by
[L139] us, and has thus not had the advantage of his supervision. This remark
[L140] also applies to Appendix E, which is an elaboration of a theorem he
[L141] suggested. Appendix H, and all the exercises have, in accordance with
[L142] his wish, been written solely by us. It will be apparent to the reader
[L143] that Appendix H is little more than a brief introduction to a very large
[L144] subject, which, being concerned with tessaracts and solids, is really
[L145] beyond treatment in writing and diagrams.

[L147] This difficulty recalls us to the one great fact, upon which we feel
[L148] bound to insist, that the matter of this book _must_ receive objective
[L149] treatment from the reader, who will find it quite useless even to
[L150] attempt to apprehend it without actually building in squares and cubes
[L151] all the facts of space which we ask him to impress on his consciousness.
[L152] Indeed, we consider that printing, as a method of spreading
[L153] space-knowledge, is but a “pis aller,” and we would go back to that
[L154] ancient and more fruitful method of the Greek geometers, and, while
[L155] describing figures on the sand, or piling up pebbles in series, would
[L156] communicate to others that spirit of learning and generalization
[L157] begotten in our consciousness by continuous contact with facts, and only
[L158] by continuous contact with facts vitally maintained.

[L160]   ALICIA BOOLE,

[L162]   H. JOHN FALK.

[L286] INTRODUCTORY NOTE TO PART I.


[L289] At the completion of a work, or at the completion of the first part of a
[L290] work, the feelings are necessarily very different from those with which
[L291] the work was begun; and the meaning and value of the work itself bear a
[L292] very different appearance. It will therefore be the simplest and
[L293] shortest plan, if I tell the reader briefly what the work is to which
[L294] these pages are a guide, and what I consider to be its value when done.

[L296] The task was to obtain a sense of the properties of higher space, or
[L297] space of four dimensions, in the same way as that by which we reach a
[L298] sense of our ordinary three-dimensional space. I now prefer to call the
[L299] task that of obtaining a familiarity with higher matter, which shall be
[L300] as intuitive to the mind as that of ordinary matter has become. The
[L301] expression “higher matter” is preferable to “higher space,” because it
[L302] is a somewhat hasty proceeding to split this concrete matter, which we
[L303] touch and feel, into the abstractions of extension and impenetrability.
[L304] It seems to me that I cannot think of space without matter, and
[L305] therefore, as no necessity compels me to such a course, I do not split
[L306] up the concrete object into subtleties, but I simply ask: “What is that
[L307] which is to a cube or block or shape of any kind as the cube is to a
[L308] square?”

[L310] In entering upon this inquiry we find the task is twofold. Firstly,
[L311] there is the theoretical part, which is easy, viz. to set clearly before
[L312] us the relative conditions which would obtain if there were a matter
[L313] physically higher than this matter of ours, and to choose the best
[L314] means of liberating our minds from the limitations imposed on it by the

[L153]                                 PREFACE


[L156] I have endeavoured to present the subject of the higher dimensionality
[L157] of space in a clear manner, devoid of mathematical subtleties and
[L158] technicalities. In order to engage the interest of the reader, I have
[L159] in the earlier chapters dwelt on the perspective the hypothesis of a
[L160] fourth dimension opens, and have treated of the many connections there
[L161] are between this hypothesis and the ordinary topics of our thoughts.

[L163] A lack of mathematical knowledge will prove of no disadvantage to the
[L164] reader, for I have used no mathematical processes of reasoning. I have
[L165] taken the view that the space which we ordinarily think of, the space
[L166] of real things (which I would call permeable matter), is different from
[L167] the space treated of by mathematics. Mathematics will tell us a great
[L168] deal about space, just as the atomic theory will tell us a great deal
[L169] about the chemical combinations of bodies. But after all, a theory is
[L170] not precisely equivalent to the subject with regard to which it is
[L171] held. There is an opening, therefore, from the side of our ordinary
[L172] space perceptions for a simple, altogether rational, mechanical, and
[L173] observational way of treating this subject of higher space, and of
[L174] this opportunity I have availed myself.

[L176] The details introduced in the earlier chapters, especially in
[L177] Chapters VIII., IX., X., may perhaps be found wearisome. They are of
[L178] no essential importance in the main line of argument, and if left
[L179] till Chapters XI. and XII. have been read, will be found to afford
[L180] interesting and obvious illustrations of the properties discussed in
[L181] the later chapters.

[L183] My thanks are due to the friends who have assisted me in designing and
[L184] preparing the modifications of my previous models, and in no small
[L185] degree to the publisher of this volume, Mr. Sonnenschein, to whose
[L186] unique appreciation of the line of thought of this, as of my former
[L187] essays, their publication is owing. By the provision of a coloured
[L188] plate, in addition to the other illustrations, he has added greatly to
[L189] the convenience of the reader.

[L253] There is nothing more indefinite, and at the same time more real, than
[L254] that which we indicate when we speak of the “higher.” In our social
[L255] life we see it evidenced in a greater complexity of relations. But this
[L256] complexity is not all. There is, at the same time, a contact with, an
[L257] apprehension of, something more fundamental, more real.

[L259] With the greater development of man there comes a consciousness of
[L260] something more than all the forms in which it shows itself. There is
[L261] a readiness to give up all the visible and tangible for the sake of
[L262] those principles and values of which the visible and tangible are the
[L263] representation. The physical life of civilised man and of a mere savage
[L264] are practically the same, but the civilised man has discovered a depth
[L265] in his existence, which makes him feel that that which appears all to
[L266] the savage is a mere externality and appurtenage to his true being.

[L268] Now, this higher—how shall we apprehend it? It is generally embraced
[L269] by our religious faculties, by our idealising tendency. But the higher
[L270] existence has two sides. It has a being as well as qualities. And in
[L271] trying to realise it through our emotions we are always taking the
[L272] subjective view. Our attention is always fixed on what we feel, what
[L273] we think. Is there any way of apprehending the higher after the purely
[L274] objective method of a natural science? I think that there is.

[L276] Plato, in a wonderful allegory, speaks of some men living in such a
[L277] condition that they were practically reduced to be the denizens of
[L278] a shadow world. They were chained, and perceived but the shadows of
[L279] themselves and all real objects projected on a wall, towards which
[L280] their faces were turned. All movements to them were but movements
[L281] on the surface, all shapes but the shapes of outlines with no
[L282] substantiality.

[L284] Plato uses this illustration to portray the relation between true
[L285] being and the illusions of the sense world. He says that just as a man
[L286] liberated from his chains could learn and discover that the world was
[L287] solid and real, and could go back and tell his bound companions of this
[L288] greater higher reality, so the philosopher who has been liberated, who
[L289] has gone into the thought of the ideal world, into the world of ideas
[L290] greater and more real than the things of sense, can come and tell his
[L291] fellow men of that which is more true than the visible sun—more noble
[L292] than Athens, the visible state.

[L294] Now, I take Plato’s suggestion; but literally, not metaphorically.
[L295] He imagines a world which is lower than this world, in that shadow
[L296] figures and shadow motions are its constituents; and to it he contrasts
[L297] the real world. As the real world is to this shadow world, so is the
[L298] higher world to our world. I accept his analogy. As our world in three
[L299] dimensions is to a shadow or plane world, so is the higher world to our
[L300] three-dimensional world. That is, the higher world is four-dimensional;
[L301] the higher being is, so far as its existence is concerned apart from
[L302] its qualities, to be sought through the conception of an actual
[L303] existence spatially higher than that which we realise with our senses.
