[L54]                      What is the Fourth Dimension?


[L57]                                CHAPTER I.

[L59] At the present time our actions are largely influenced by our theories.
[L60] We have abandoned the simple and instinctive mode of life of the earlier
[L61] civilisations for one regulated by the assumptions of our knowledge and
[L62] supplemented by all the devices of intelligence. In such a state it is
[L63] possible to conceive that a danger may arise, not only from a want of
[L64] knowledge and practical skill, but even from the very presence and
[L65] possession of them in any one department, if there is a lack of
[L66] information in other departments. If, for instance, with our present
[L67] knowledge of physical laws and mechanical skill, we were to build houses
[L68] without regard to the conditions laid down by physiology, we should
[L69] probably—to suit an apparent convenience—make them perfectly
[L70] draught-tight, and the best-constructed mansions would be full of
[L71] suffocating chambers. The knowledge of the construction of the body and
[L72] the conditions of its health prevent it from suffering injury by the
[L73] development of our powers over nature.

[L75] In no dissimilar way the mental balance is saved from the dangers
[L76] attending an attention concentrated on the laws of mechanical science by
[L77] a just consideration of the constitution of the knowing faculty, and the
[L78] conditions of knowledge. Whatever pursuit we are engaged in, we are
[L79] acting consciously or unconsciously upon some theory, some view of
[L80] things. And when the limits of daily routine are continually narrowed by
[L81] the ever-increasing complication of our civilisation, it becomes doubly
[L82] important that not one only but every kind of thought should be shared
in.

[L85] There are two ways of passing beyond the domain of practical certainty,
[L86] and of looking into the vast range of possibility. One is by asking,
[L87] “What is knowledge? What constitutes experience?” If we adopt this
[L88] course we are plunged into a sea of speculation. Were it not that the
[L89] highest faculties of the mind find therein so ample a range, we should
[L90] return to the solid ground of facts, with simply a feeling of relief at
[L91] escaping from so great a confusion and contradictoriness.

[L93] The other path which leads us beyond the horizon of actual experience is
[L94] that of questioning whatever seems arbitrary and irrationally limited in
[L95] the domain of knowledge. Such a questioning has often been successfully
[L96] applied in the search for new facts. For a long time four gases were
[L97] considered incapable of being reduced to the liquid state. It is but
[L98] lately that a physicist has succeeded in showing that there is no such
[L99] arbitrary distinction among gases. Recently again the question has been
[L100] raised, “Is there not a fourth state of matter?” Solid, liquid, and
[L101] gaseous states are known. Mr. Crookes attempts to demonstrate the
[L102] existence of a state differing from all of these. It is the object of
[L103] these pages to show that, by supposing away certain limitations of the
[L104] fundamental conditions of existence as we know it, a state of being can
[L105] be conceived with powers far transcending our own. When this is made
[L106] clear it will not be out of place to investigate what relations would
[L107] subsist between our mode of existence and that which will be seen to be
[L108] a possible one.

[L110] In the first place, what is the limitation that we must suppose away?

[L112] An observer standing in the corner of a room has three directions
[L113] naturally marked out for him; one is upwards along the line of meeting
[L114] of the two walls; another is forwards where the floor meets one of the
[L115] walls; a third is sideways where the floor meets the other wall. He can
[L116] proceed to any part of the floor of the room by moving first the right
[L117] distance along one wall, and then by turning at right angles and walking
[L118] parallel to the other wall. He walks in this case first of all in the
[L119] direction of one of the straight lines that meet in the corner of the
[L120] floor, afterwards in the direction of the other. By going more or less
[L121] in one direction or the other, he can reach any point on the floor, and
[L122] any movement, however circuitous, can be resolved into simple movements
[L123] in these two directions.

[L125] But by moving in these two directions he is unable to raise himself in
[L126] the room. If he wished to touch a point in the ceiling, he would have to
[L127] move in the direction of the line in which the two walls meet. There are
[L128] three directions then, each at right angles to both the other, and
[L129] entirely independent of one another. By moving in these three directions
[L130] or combinations of them, it is possible to arrive at any point in a
[L131] room. And if we suppose the straight lines which meet in the corner of
[L132] the room to be prolonged indefinitely, it would be possible by moving in
[L133] the direction of those three lines, to arrive at any point in space.
[L134] Thus in space there are three independent directions, and only three;
[L135] every other direction is compounded of these three. The question that
[L136] comes before us then is this. “Why should there be three and only three
[L137] directions?” Space, as we know it, is subject to a limitation.

[L139] In order to obtain an adequate conception of what this limitation is, it
[L140] is necessary to first imagine beings existing in a space more limited
[L141] than that in which we move. Thus we may conceive a being who has been
[L142] throughout all the range of his experience confined to a single straight
[L143] line. Such a being would know what it was to move to and fro, but no
[L144] more. The whole of space would be to him but the extension in both
[L145] directions of the straight line to an infinite distance. It is evident
[L146] that two such creatures could never pass one another. We can conceive
[L147] their coming out of the straight line and entering it again, but they
[L148] having moved always in one straight line, would have no conception of
[L149] any other direction of motion by which such a result could be effected.
[L150] The only shape which could exist in a one-dimensional existence of this
[L151] kind would be a finite straight line. There would be no difference in
[L152] the shapes of figures; all that could exist would simply be longer or
[L153] shorter straight lines.

[L155] Again, to go a step higher in the domain of a conceivable existence.
[L156] Suppose a being confined to a plane superficies, and throughout all the
[L157] range of its experience never to have moved up or down, but simply to
[L158] have kept to this one plane. Suppose, that is, some figure, such as a
[L159] circle or rectangle, to be endowed with the power of perception; such a
[L160] being if it moves in the plane superficies in which it is drawn, will
[L161] move in a multitude of directions; but, however varied they may seem to
[L162] be, these directions will all be compounded of two, at right angles to
[L163] each other. By no movement so long as the plane superficies remains
[L164] perfectly horizontal, will this being move in the direction we call up
[L165] and down. And it is important to notice that the plane would be
[L166] different, to a creature confined to it, from what it is to us. We think
[L167] of a plane habitually as having an upper and a lower side, because it is
[L168] only by the contact of solids that we realize a plane. But a creature
[L169] which had been confined to a plane during its whole existence would have
[L170] no idea of there being two sides to the plane he lived in. In a plane
[L171] there is simply length and breadth. If a creature in it be supposed to
[L172] know of an up or down he must already have gone out of the plane.

[L174] Is it possible, then, that a creature so circumstanced would arrive at
[L175] the notion of there being an up and down, a direction different from
[L176] those to which he had been accustomed, and having nothing in common with
[L177] them? Obviously nothing in the creature’s circumstances would tell him
[L178] of it. It could only be by a process of reasoning on his part that he
[L179] could arrive at such a conception. If he were to imagine a being
[L180] confined to a single straight line, he might realise that he himself
[L181] could move in two directions, while the creature in a straight line
[L182] could only move in one. Having made this reflection he might ask, “But
[L183] why is the number of directions limited to two? Why should there not be
[L184] three?”

[L186] A creature (if such existed), which moves in a plane would be much more
[L187] fortunately circumstanced than one which can only move in a straight
[L188] line. For, in a plane, there is a possibility of an infinite variety of
[L189] shapes, and the being we have supposed could come into contact with an
[L190] indefinite number of other beings. He would not be limited, as in the
[L191] case of the creature in a straight line, to one only on each side of
him.

[L194] It is obvious that it would be possible to play curious tricks with a
[L195] being confined to a plane. If, for instance, we suppose such a being to
[L196] be inside a square, the only way out that he could conceive would be
[L197] through one of the sides of the square. If the sides were impenetrable,
[L198] he would be a fast prisoner, and would have no way out.

[L200] What his case would be we may understand, if we reflect what a similar
[L201] case would be in our own existence. The creature is shut in in all the
[L202] directions he knows of. If a man is shut in in all the directions he
[L203] knows of, he must be surrounded by four walls, a roof and a floor. A
[L204] two-dimensional being inside a square would be exactly in the same
[L205] predicament that a man would be, if he were in a room with no opening on
[L206] any side. Now it would be possible to us to take up such a being from
[L207] the inside of the square, and to set him down outside it. A being to
[L208] whom this had happened would find himself outside the place he had been
[L209] confined in, and he would not have passed through any of the boundaries
[L210] by which he was shut in. The astonishment of such a being can only be
[L211] imagined by comparing it to that which a man would feel, if he were
[L212] suddenly to find himself outside a room in which he had been, without
[L213] having passed through the window, doors, chimney or any opening in the
[L214] walls, ceiling or floor.

[L216] Another curious thing that could be effected with a two-dimensional
[L217] being, is the following. Conceive two beings at a great distance from
[L218] one another on a plane surface. If the plane surface is bent so that
[L219] they are brought close to one another, they would have no conception of
[L220] their proximity, because to each the only possible movements would seem
[L221] to be movements in the surface. The two beings might be conceived as so
[L222] placed, by a proper bending of the plane, that they should be absolutely
[L223] in juxtaposition, and yet to all the reasoning faculties of either of
[L224] them a great distance could be proved to intervene. The bending might be
[L225] carried so far as to make one being suddenly appear in the plane by the
[L226] side of the other. If these beings were ignorant of the existence of a
[L227] third dimension, this result would be as marvellous to them, as it would
[L228] be for a human being who was at a great distance—it might be at the
[L229] other side of the world—to suddenly appear and really be by our side,

[L62] Overview 
[L63] Part I: GEB 
[L64] Introduction: A Musico-Logical Offering. The book opens with the story of Bach's Musical 
[L65] Offering. Bach made an impromptu visit to King Frederick the Great of Prussia, and was 
[L66] requested to improvise upon a theme presented by the King. His improvisations formed the basis 
[L67] of that great work. The Musical Offering and its story form a theme upon which I "improvise" 
[L68] throughout the book, thus making a sort of "Metamusical Offering". Self-reference and the 
[L69] interplay between different levels in Bach are discussed: this leads to a discussion of parallel 
[L70] ideas in Escher's drawings and then Gödel’s Theorem. A brief presentation of the history of logic 
[L71] and paradoxes is given as background for Gödel’s Theorem. This leads to mechanical reasoning 
[L72] and computers, and the debate about whether Artificial Intelligence is possible. I close with an 
[L73] explanation of the origins of the book-particularly the why and wherefore of the Dialogues. 
[L74] Three-Part Invention. Bach wrote fifteen three-part inventions. In this three-part Dialogue, the 
[L75] Tortoise and Achilles-the main fictional protagonists in the Dialogues-are "invented" by Zeno (as 
[L76] in fact they were, to illustrate Zeno's paradoxes of motion). Very short, it simply gives the flavor 
[L77] of the Dialogues to come. 
[L78] Chapter I: The MU-puzzle. A simple formal system (the MIL'-system) is presented, and the reader 
[L79] is urged to work out a puzzle to gain familiarity with formal systems in general. A number of 
[L80] fundamental notions are introduced: string, theorem, axiom, rule of inference, derivation, formal 
[L81] system, decision procedure, working inside/outside the system. 
[L82] Two-Part Invention. Bach also wrote fifteen two-part inventions. This two-part Dialogue was written 
[L83] not by me, but by Lewis Carroll in 1895. Carroll borrowed Achilles and the Tortoise from Zeno, 
[L84] and I in turn borrowed them from Carroll. The topic is the relation between reasoning, reasoning 
[L85] about reasoning, reasoning about reasoning about reasoning, and so on. It parallels, in a way, 
[L86] Zeno's paradoxes about the impossibility of motion, seeming to show, by using infinite regress, 
[L87] that reasoning is impossible. It is a beautiful paradox, and is referred to several times later in the 
book. 
[L89] Chapter II: Meaning and Form in Mathematics. A new formal system (the pq-system) is 
[L90] presented, even simpler than the MIU-system of Chapter I. Apparently meaningless at first, its 
[L91] symbols are suddenly revealed to possess meaning by virtue of the form of the theorems they 
[L92] appear in. This revelation is the first important insight into meaning: its deep connection to 
[L93] isomorphism. Various issues related to meaning are then discussed, such as truth, proof, symbol 
[L94] manipulation, and the elusive concept, "form". 
[L95] Sonata for Unaccompanied Achilles. A Dialogue which imitates the Bach Sonatas for 
[L96] unaccompanied violin. In particular, Achilles is the only speaker, since it is a transcript of one 
[L97] end of a telephone call, at the far end of which is the Tortoise. Their conversation concerns the 
[L98] concepts of "figure" and "ground" in various

[L102] Achilles' lines form a "figure", and the Tortoise's lines-implicit in Achilles' lines-form a "ground". 
[L103] Chapter III: Figure and Ground. The distinction between figure and ground in art is compared to 
[L104] the distinction between theorems and nontheorems in formal systems. The question "Does a 
[L105] figure necessarily contain the same information as its ground%" leads to the distinction between 
[L106] recursively enumerable sets and recursive sets. 
[L107] Contracrostipunctus. This Dialogue is central to the book, for it contains a set of paraphrases of 
[L108] Gödel’s self-referential construction and of his Incompleteness Theorem. One of the paraphrases 
[L109] of the Theorem says, "For each record player there is a record which it cannot play." The 
[L110] Dialogue's title is a cross between the word "acrostic" and the word "contrapunctus", a Latin word 
[L111] which Bach used to denote the many fugues and canons making up his Art of the Fugue. Some 
[L112] explicit references to the Art of the Fugue are made. The Dialogue itself conceals some acrostic 
[L113] tricks. 
[L114] Chapter IV: Consistency, Completeness, and Geometry. The preceding Dialogue is explicated to 
[L115] the extent it is possible at this stage. This leads back to the question of how and when symbols in 
[L116] a formal system acquire meaning. The history of Euclidean and non-Euclidean geometry is given, 
[L117] as an illustration of the elusive notion of "undefined terms". This leads to ideas about the 
[L118] consistency of different and possibly "rival" geometries. Through this discussion the notion of 
[L119] undefined terms is clarified, and the relation of undefined terms to perception and thought 
[L120] processes is considered. 
[L121] Little Harmonic Labyrinth. This is based on the Bach organ piece by the same name. It is a playful 
[L122] introduction to the notion of recursive-i.e., nested structures. It contains stories within stories. The 
[L123] frame story, instead of finishing as expected, is left open, so the reader is left dangling without 
[L124] resolution. One nested story concerns modulation in music-particularly an organ piece which 
[L125] ends in the wrong key, leaving the listener dangling without resolution. 
[L126] Chapter V: Recursive Structures and Processes. The idea of recursion is presented in many 
[L127] different contexts: musical patterns, linguistic patterns, geometric structures, mathematical 
[L128] functions, physical theories, computer programs, and others. 
[L129] Canon by Intervallic Augmentation. Achilles and the Tortoise try to resolve the question, "Which 
[L130] contains more information-a record, or the phonograph which plays it This odd question arises 
[L131] when the Tortoise describes a single record which, when played on a set of different 
[L132] phonographs, produces two quite different melodies: B-A-C-H and C-A-G-E. It turns out, 
[L133] however, that these melodies are "the same", in a peculiar sense. 
[L134] Chapter VI: The Location of Meaning. A broad discussion of how meaning is split among coded 
[L135] message, decoder, and receiver. Examples presented include strands of DNA, undeciphered 
[L136] inscriptions on ancient tablets, and phonograph records sailing out in space. The relationship of 
[L137] intelligence to "absolute" meaning is postulated.

[L139] Bach's Chromatic Fantasy and Fugue. It concerns the proper way to manipulate sentences so as

[L145] Chapter VII: The Propositional Calculus. It is suggested how words such as .,and" can be

[L65] PREFACE


[L68] THE book which is herewith presented to the public has few
[L69] contemporaries of a like nature; it deserves special attention inasmuch
[L70] as it is illuminated by the name _Albert Einstein_, and deals with a
[L71] personality whose achievements mark a turning-point in the development
[L72] of science.

[L74] Every investigator, who enlarges our vision by some permanent discovery,
[L75] becomes a milestone on the road to knowledge, and great would be the
[L76] array of those who have defined the stages of the long avenue of
[L77] research. One might endeavour, then, to decide to whom mankind owes the
[L78] greater debt, to Euclid or to Archimedes, to Plato or to Aristotle, to
[L79] Descartes or to Pascal, to Lagrange or to Gauss, to Kepler or to
[L80] Copernicus. One would have to investigate--as far as this is
[L81] possible--in how far each outstanding personality was in advance of his
[L82] time, whether some contemporary might not have had the equal good
[L83] fortune to stumble on the same discovery, and whether, indeed, the time
[L84] had not come when it must inevitably have been revealed. If we then
[L85] further selected only those who saw far beyond their own age into the
[L86] inimitable future of knowledge, this great number of celebrities would
[L87] be considerably diminished. We should glance away from the milestones,
[L88] and fix our gaze on the larger signs that denote the lines of
[L89] demarcation of the sciences, and among them we should find the name of
[L90] Albert Einstein. We may find it necessary to proceed to a still more
[L91] rigorous classification; Science, herself, may rearrange her
[L92] chronological table later, and reckon the time at which Einstein's
[L93] doctrine first appeared as the beginning of an important era.

[L95] This would in itself justify--nay, render imperative--the writing of
[L96] a book _about_ Einstein. But this need has already been satisfied on
[L97] several occasions, and there is even now a considerable amount of
[L98] literature about him. At the end of this generation we shall possess a
[L99] voluminous library composed entirely of books about Einstein. The
[L100] present book will differ from most of these, in that Einstein here
[L101] occurs not only objectively but also subjectively. We shall, of course,
[L102] speak of him here too, but we shall also hear him speak himself, and
[L103] there can be no doubt that all who are devoted to the world thought can
[L104] but gain by listening to him.

[L106] The title agrees with the circumstance to which this book owes its
[L107] birth. And in undertaking to address itself to the circle of readers as
[L108] to an audience, it promises much eloquence that came from Einstein's own
[L109] lips, during hours of social intercourse, far removed from academic
[L110] purposes and not based on any definite scheme intended for instruction.
[L111] It will, therefore, be neither a course of lectures nor anything similar
[L112] aiming at a systematic order and development. Nor is it a mere
[L113] phonographic record, for this is made impossible if for no other reason
[L114] than that whoever has the good fortune to converse with this man, finds
[L115] every minute far too precious to waste it in snatching moments to take
[L116] shorthand notes. What he has heard and discussed crystallizes itself in
[L117] subsequent notes, and to some extent he relies on his memory, which
[L118] would have to be extraordinarily lax if it managed to forget the
[L119] essentials of such conversations.

[L121] But these essentials could not be attained by clinging closely to the
[L122] exact terms of utterance. This would be a gain neither for the scheme of
[L123] the book nor for the reader who wishes to follow a great thinker in all
[L124] the ramifications of his ideas. It must be reiterated that this book is
[L125] intended neither as a textbook nor as a guide leading to a complete
[L126] system of thought; nor, above all, is it in any way due to Einstein, nor
[L127] desired by him. Any value and attraction of the book is rather to be
[L128] sought in its kaleidoscopic nature, its loose connexion, which expresses
[L129] a general meaning without being narrowed to pedantic limits by a
[L130] restriction to literal repetition. It is just this absence of the method
[L131] that is rightly demanded of a textbook, which may enable these
[L132] conversations to pass on to the world a little of the pleasure which
[L133] they originally gave me. Perhaps they will even be sufficient to furnish
[L134] the reader with a picture of the eminent scientist, sufficient to give
[L135] him a glimpse of his personality, without demanding a detailed study to
[L136] secure this end. Even here I should like to state that the range of
[L137] Einstein's genius extends much further than is generally surmised by
[L138] those who have busied themselves only with the actual physical theory.
[L139] It sends out rays in all directions, and brings into view wonderful
[L140] cosmic features under his stimulus--features which are, of course,
[L141] embedded in the very refractory mathematical shell of his physics which
[L142] embraces the whole world. But only minds of the distant future, perhaps,
[L143] will be in a position to realize that _all_ our mental knowledge is
[L144] illuminated by the light of his doctrine.

[L146] Einstein's mission is that of a king who is pursuing building operations
[L147] on a large scale; carters and workmen, each in their own line, receive
[L148] employment for decades ahead. But apart from the technical work, there
[L149] may still be room for non-technical account, which, without following a
[L150] definite programme, yet pursues a definite object, to offer Einsteiniana
[L151] in an easily intelligible and ever-changing form, to represent him, as
[L152] it were, wandering over fields and meadows, and every now and then
[L153] stooping to pluck some problem in the guise of a flower. Seeing that he
[L154] granted me the pleasure of accompanying him on these excursions, it was
[L155] not within my sphere to expect in addition that he would direct his
[L156] steps according to a preconceived plan. Often enough the goal vanished,
[L157] and there remained nothing but the pleasure of the rambles themselves
[L158] with the consciousness of their purpose. As Schopenhauer remarks, one
[L159] who walks for leisure can never be said to be making detours; and this
[L160] holds true independently of the nature of the country that happens to be
[L161] traversed at the moment. If I just now mentioned walks on meadowy
[L162] slopes, this is not to be understood literally. In Einstein's company
[L163] one encounters from moment to moment quite suddenly some adventure which
[L164] destroys our comparison with idyllic rambles. Abysmal depths appear, and
[L165] one has to pass along dangerous pathways. It is at these moments that
[L166] unexpected views present themselves, and many strips of landscape that,
[L167] according to our previous estimate, appeared to be situated on higher
[L168] slopes, are now discovered reposing far below. We are familiar with the
[L169] "Wanderer Fantasie" of Schubert; its tonal disposition is realistic,
[L170] conforming to Nature, yet its general expression is transcendental: so
[L171] is a ramble with Einstein; he remains firmly implanted in reality, but
[L172] the distant views that he points out stretch into transcendental
[L173] regions. He seems to me to be essentially as much an artist as a
[L174] discoverer, and if some sense of this heaven-sent combination of gifts
[L175] should be inspired by this book, it alone would justify the publication
[L176] of these talks.




[L181] TRANSLATOR'S NOTE


[L184] IT is scarcely necessary to enlarge on the scope and design of the
[L185] present book, which manifest themselves at a glance.

[L187] The author merits our thanks for making accessible to us material about
[L188] Einstein which, in the ordinary course of events, would ever remain
[L189] unknown. An account of Einstein's work would be incomplete without a
[L190] sketch of his personality. Mr. Moszkowski invites us to ramble with
[L191] Einstein into realms not confined to pure physics. Many subjects that
[L192] have a peculiar interest at the present critical stage of the world's
[L193] history receive illuminating attention. It is hoped that the appearance
[L194] of the book in English will stimulate further interest in the
[L195] thought-world of a great scientist.

[L197] Warm thanks are due to Mr. Raymond Kershaw, B.A., and to my sister, Miss

[L10] Is there anything analogous to this within the range of our observation?
[L11]
[L12] An electric current answers this description in every respect.
[L13] Electricity does not flow through a wire. Its effect travels both ways
[L14] from the starting point along the wire. The spark which shows its
[L15] passing midway in its circuit is later than that which occurs at points
[L16] near its starting point on either side of it.
[L17]
[L18] Moreover, it is known that the action of the current is not in the
[L19] wire. It is in the region enclosed by the wire, this is the field of
[L20] force, the locus of the exhibition of the effects of the current.
[L21]
[L22] And the necessity of a conducting circuit for a current is exactly
[L23] that which we should expect if it were a four-dimensional vortex.
[L24] According to Maxwell every current forms a closed circuit, and this,
[L25] from the four-dimensional point of view, is the same as saying a vortex
[L26] must have its ends on a boundary of the fluid.
[L27]
[L28] Thus, on the hypothesis of a fourth dimension, the rotation of the
[L29] fluid ether would give the phenomenon of an electric current. We must
[L30] suppose the ether to be full of movement, for the more we examine into
[L31] the conditions which prevail in the obscurity of the minute, the more
[L32] we find that an unceasing and perpetual motion reigns. Thus we may say
[L33] that the conception of the fourth dimension means that there must be a
[L34] phenomenon which presents the characteristics of electricity.
[L35]
[L36] We know now that light is an electro-magnetic action, and that so far
[L37] from being a special and isolated phenomenon this electric action is
[L38] universal in the realm of the minute. Hence, may we not conclude that,
[L39] so far from the fourth dimension being remote and far away, being a
[L40] thing of symbolic import, a term for the explanation of dubious facts
[L41] by a more obscure theory, it is really the most important fact within
[L42] our knowledge. Our three-dimensional world is superficial. These
[L43] processes, which really lie at the basis of all phenomena of matter,
[L44] escape our observation by their minuteness, but reveal to our intellect
[L45] an amplitude of motion surpassing any that we can see. In such shapes
[L46] and motions there is a realm of the utmost intellectual beauty, and one
[L47] to which our symbolic methods apply with a better grace than they do to
[L48] those of three dimensions.
[L49]
[L50]
[L51]
[L52]
[L53]                              CHAPTER VIII
[L54]
[L55]                  THE USE OF FOUR DIMENSIONS IN THOUGHT
[L56]
[L57]
[L58] Having held before ourselves this outline of a conjecture of the world
[L59] as four-dimensional, having roughly thrown together those facts of
[L60] movement which we can see apply to our actual experience, let us pass
[L61] to another branch of our subject.
[L62]
[L63] The engineer uses drawings, graphical constructions, in a variety of
[L64] manners. He has, for instance, diagrams which represent the expansion
[L65] of steam, the efficiency of his valves. These exist alongside the
[L66] actual plans of his machines. They are not the pictures of anything
[L67] really existing, but enable him to think about the relations which
[L68] exist in his mechanisms.
[L69]
[L70] And so, besides showing us the actual existence of that world which
[L71] lies beneath the one of visible movements, four-dimensional space
[L72] enables us to make ideal constructions which serve to represent the
[L73] relations of things, and throw what would otherwise be obscure into a
[L74] definite and suggestive form.
[L75]
[L76] From amidst the great variety of instances which lies before me I will
[L77] select two, one dealing with a subject of slight intrinsic interest,
[L78] which however gives within a limited field a striking example of the
[L79] method of drawing conclusions and the use of higher space figures.[1]

[L147] There are therefore four possibilities with regard to this fourth
[L148] variable as with regard to the premisses.
[L149]
[L150] We have used up our dimensions of space in representing the phases of
[L151] the premisses and the conclusion in respect of mood, and to represent
[L152] in an analogous manner the variations in figure we require a fourth
[L153] dimension.
[L154]
[L155] Now in bringing in this fourth dimension we must make a change in our
[L156] origins of measurement analogous to that which we made in passing from
[L157] the plane to the solid.
[L158]
[L159] This fourth dimension is supposed to run at right angles to any of the
[L160] three space dimensions, as the third space dimension runs at right
[L161] angles to the two dimensions of a plane, and thus it gives us the
[L162] opportunity of generating a new kind of volume. If the whole cube moves
[L163] in this dimension, the solid itself traces out a path, each section of
[L164] which, made at right angles to the direction in which it moves, is a
[L165] solid, an exact repetition of the cube itself.
[L166]
[L167] The cube as we see it is the beginning of a solid of such a kind. It
[L168] represents a kind of tray, as the square face of the cube is a kind of
[L169] tray against which the cube rests.
[L170]
[L171] Suppose the cube to move in this fourth dimension in four stages,
[L172] and let the hyper-solid region traced out in the first stage of its
[L173] progress be characterised by this, that the terms of the syllogism
[L174] are in the first figure, then we can represent in each of the three
[L175] subsequent stages the remaining three figures. Thus the whole cube
[L176] forms the basis from which we measure the variation in figure. The
[L177] first figure holds good for the cube as we see it, and for that
[L178] hyper-solid which lies within the first stage; the second figure holds
[L179] good in the second stage, and so on.
[L180]
[L181] Thus we measure from the whole cube as far as figures are concerned.
[L182]
[L183] But we saw that when we measured in the cube itself having three
[L184] variables, namely, the two premisses and the conclusion, we measured
[L185] from three planes. The base from which we measured was in every case
[L186] the same.
[L187]
[L188] Hence, in measuring in this higher space we should have bases of the
[L189] same kind to measure from, we should have solid bases.
[L190]
[L191] The first solid base is easily seen, it is the cube itself. The other
[L192] can be found from this consideration.
[L193]
[L194] That solid from which we measure figure is that in which the remaining
[L195] variables run through their full range of varieties.
[L196]
[L197] Now, if we want to measure in respect of the moods of the major
[L198] premiss, we must let the minor premiss, the conclusion, run through
[L199] their range, and also the order of the terms. That is we must take as
[L200] basis of measurement in respect to the moods of the major that which
[L201] represents the variation of the moods of the minor, the conclusion and
[L202] the variation of the figures.
[L203]
[L204] Now the variation of the moods of the minor and of the conclusion are
[L205] represented in the square face on the left of the cube. Here are all
[L206] varieties of the minor premiss and the conclusion. The varieties of
[L207] the figures are represented by stages in a motion proceeding at right
[L208] angles to all space directions, at right angles consequently to the
[L209] face in question, the left-hand face of the cube.
[L210]
[L211] Consequently letting the left-hand face move in this direction we get
[L212] a cube, and in this cube all the varieties of the minor premiss, the
[L213] conclusion, and the figure are represented.
[L214]
[L215] Thus another cubic base of measurement is given to the cube, generated
[L216] by movement of the left-hand square in the fourth dimension.

[L226] Let us now take our eight coloured cubes, which form a cube in
[L227] space, and ask what additions we must make to them to represent
[L228] the simplest collection of four-dimensional bodies—namely, a group
[L229] of them of the same extent in every direction. In plane space we
[L230] have four squares. In solid space we have eight cubes. So we should
[L231] expect in four-dimensional space to have sixteen four-dimensional
[L232] bodies-bodies which in four-dimensional space correspond to cubes in
[L233] three-dimensional space, and these bodies we call tesseracts.
[L234]
[L235] Given then the null, white, red, yellow cubes, and those which make up
[L236] the block, we notice that we represent perfectly well the extension
[L237] in three directions (fig. 98). From the null point of the null cube,
[L238] travelling one inch, we come to the white cube; travelling one inch
[L239] away we come to the yellow cube; travelling one inch up we come to the
[L240] red cube. Now, if there is a fourth dimension, then travelling from the
[L241] same null point for one inch in that direction, we must come to the
[L242] body lying beyond the null region.
[L243]
[L244] [Illustration: Fig. 98.]
[L245]
[L246] I say null region, not cube; for with the introduction of the fourth
[L247] dimension each of our cubes must become something different from cubes.
[L248] If they are to have existence in the fourth dimension, they must be
[L249] “filled up from” in this fourth dimension.
[L250]
[L251] Now we will assume that as we get a transference from null to white
[L252] going in one way, from null to yellow going in another, so going
[L253] from null in the fourth direction we have a transference from null
[L254] to blue, using thus the colours white, yellow, red, blue, to denote
[L255] transferences in each of the four directions—right, away, up, unknown
[L256] or fourth dimension.
[L257]
[L258] [Illustration: Fig. 99.
[L259]
[L260] A plane being’s representation of a block of eight cubes by two sets of
[L261] four squares.]
[L262]
[L263] Hence, as the plane being must represent the solid regions, he would
[L264] come to by going right, as four squares lying in some position in his
[L265] plane, arbitrarily chosen, side by side with his original four squares,
[L266] so we must represent those eight four-dimensional regions, which we
[L267] should come to by going in the fourth dimension from each of our eight
[L268] cubes, by eight cubes placed in some arbitrary position relative to our
[L269] first eight cubes.
[L270]
[L271] [Illustration: Fig. 100.]
[L272]
[L273] Our representation of a block of sixteen tesseracts by two blocks of
[L274] eight cubes.[3]
[L275]
[L276]  [3] The eight cubes used here in 2 can be found in the second of the
[L277]  model blocks. They can be taken out and used.
[L278]
[L279] Hence, of the two sets of eight cubes, each one will serve us as a
[L280] representation of one of the sixteen tesseracts which form one single
[L281] block in four-dimensional space. Each cube, as we have it, is a tray,
[L282] as it were, against which the real four-dimensional figure rests—just
[L283] as each of the squares which the plane being has is a tray, so to
[L284] speak, against which the cube it represents could rest.
[L285]
[L286] If we suppose the cubes to be one inch each way, then the original
[L287] eight cubes will give eight tesseracts of the same colours, or the
[L288] cubes, extending each one inch in the fourth dimension.
[L289]
[L290] But after these there come, going on in the fourth dimension, eight
[L291] other bodies, eight other tesseracts. These must be there, if we
[L292] suppose the four-dimensional body we make up to have two divisions, one
[L293] inch each in each of four directions.

[L367] three dimensions only is a mere abstraction; all material objects
[L368] must then have a slight four-dimensional thickness. In this case the
[L369] above statement will undergo modification. The material cube which is
[L370] used as the model of the boundary of a tesseract will have a slight
[L371] thickness in the fourth dimension, and when the cube is presented to
[L372] us in another aspect, it would not be a mere surface. But it is most
[L373] convenient to regard the cubes we use as having no extension at all in
[L374] the fourth dimension. This consideration serves to bring out a point
[L375] alluded to before, that, if there is a fourth dimension, our conception
[L376] of a solid is the conception of a mere abstraction, and our talking
[L377] about real three-dimensional objects would seem to a four-dimensional

[L424] As the plane being can think of the cube as consisting of sections,
[L425] each like a figure he knows, extending away from his plane, so we can
[L426] think of a higher solid as composed of sections, each like a solid
[L427] which we know, but extending away from our space.
[L428]
[L429] Thus, taking a higher cube, we can look on it as starting from a cube
[L430] in our space and extending in the unknown dimension.
[L431]
[L432] [Illustration: Fig. 12.]
[L433]
[L434] Take the face A and conceive it to exist as simply a face, a square
[L435] with no thickness. From this face the cube in our space extends by the
[L436] occupation of space which we can see.
[L437]
[L438] But from this face there extends equally a cube in the unknown
[L439] dimension. We can think of the higher cube, then, by taking the set
[L440] of sections A, B, C, D, etc., and considering that from each of them
[L441] there runs a cube. These cubes have nothing in common with each other,
[L442] and of each of them in its actual position all that we can have in our
[L443] space is an isolated square. It is obvious that we can take our series
[L444] of sections in any manner we please. We can take them parallel, for
[L445] instance, to any one of the three isolated faces shown in the figure.
[L446] Corresponding to the three series of sections at right angles to each
[L447] other, which we can make of the cube in space, we must conceive of the
[L448] higher cube, as composed of cubes starting from squares parallel to the
[L449] faces of the cube, and of these cubes all that exist in our space are
[L450] the isolated squares from which they start.
[L451]
[L452]
[L453]
[L454]
[L455]                               CHAPTER III
[L456]
[L457]            THE SIGNIFICANCE OF A FOUR-DIMENSIONAL EXISTENCE
[L458]
[L459]
[L460] Having now obtained the conception of a four-dimensional space, and
[L461] having formed the analogy which, without any further geometrical
[L462] difficulties, enables us to enquire into its properties, I will refer
[L463] the reader, whose interest is principally in the mechanical aspect,
[L464] to Chapters VI. and VII. In the present chapter I will deal with
[L465] the general significance of the enquiry, and in the next with the
[L466] historical origin of the idea.
[L467]
[L468] First, with regard to the question of whether there is any evidence
[L469] that we are really in four-dimensional space, I will go back to the
[L470] analogy of the plane world.
[L471]
[L472] A being in a plane world could not have any experience of
[L473] three-dimensional shapes, but he could have an experience of
[L474] three-dimensional movements.
[L475]
[L476] We have seen that his matter must be supposed to have an extension,
[L477] though a very small one, in the third dimension. And thus, in the
[L478] small particles of his matter, three-dimensional movements may well
[L479] be conceived to take place. Of these movements he would only perceive
[L480] the resultants. Since all movements of an observable size in the plane
[L481] world are two-dimensional, he would only perceive the resultants in
[L482] two dimensions of the small three-dimensional movements. Thus, there
[L483] would be phenomena which he could not explain by his theory of
[L484] mechanics—motions would take place which he could not explain by his
[L485] theory of motion. Hence, to determine if we are in a four-dimensional
[L486] world, we must examine the phenomena of motion in our space. If

[L502] Similarly, taking a plane—this is by definition not curved in any way,
[L503] known or unknown, and it can only be conceived to be bent by ampler
[L504] space being conceived, and its being imagined as having force applied to
[L505] it so as to become a bent thing in this ampler space. In this case the
[L506] term “plane” is not the correct name.

[L508] And so about our three-dimensional space; we cannot be robbed of that
[L509] idea, although it might conceivably be proved that our earth and our
[L510] whole universe were on a curved thing in 4 space.
[L511]
[L512] We will then keep the term “space” for the ordinary conception; and call
[L513] it 1, 2, 3, 4 space, according to the number of supposed independent
[L514] directions.
[L515]
[L516] A curved line or surface or solid we will call a 1, 2, or 3 thing,
[L517] according to the number of dimensions in it.
[L518]
[L519] A straight line is a 1 thing possible in 1 space. A circle is a 1 thing
[L520] possible in 2 space. At any point of it a being in it is limited to
[L521] motion in one direction, while the circle itself involves two
[L522] dimensions. The surface of a sphere is a 2 thing possible in 3 space.
[L523] The rind of an orange, or the orange itself, is a 3 thing possible in 3
[L524] space.

[L527] thing, involves the conception of 3 space, and cannot be understood
[L528] without the use of the idea of 3 space. It is a 2 thing because at any
[L529] point of the surface a being can only move in two independent
[L530] directions. A crooked line drawn on the surface of a sphere is a 1 thing
[L531] in a 2 thing in 3 space.
[L532]
[L533] Another very common misconception is occasioned by the use of a figure
[L534] of this kind [Illustration: symbol] to represent a “knot” in 2 space.

[L536] It obviously corresponds in 2 space to an iron rod welded together at
[L537] the crossing place of the loop, so that it is indistinguishable which is
[L538] the one free end, which the other. At the crossing point the two lines
[L539] represented by the two ink marks must be absolutely one and the same.
[L540]
[L541] If one line be supposed to go over the other, by however small a
[L542] distance, it would leave the plane. It would suddenly become invisible
[L543] to the creature in the plane, and it would appear again at the other
[L544] side of the line it crossed as if it came from nowhere.
[L545]

[L547] brick wall, then beyond the brick wall the rest of the pole
[L548] appearing—not going through the brick wall, nor coming round it—but
[L549] somehow appearing; part of the same pole moving when it moved, obviously
[L550] connected with it, and yet with no joining part which we could possibly
[L551] discover.
[L552]
[L553] Again, it sometimes appears to be thought that the fourth dimension is
[L554] in some way different from the three which we know. But there is nothing

[L573] He must also acquire a distinct notion about his plane world, he must
[L574] no longer believe that it is the all of space, but that space extends
[L575] on both sides of it. In order, then, to prevent his moving off in this
[L576] unknown direction, he must assume a sheet, an extended solid sheet, in
[L577] two dimensions, against which, in contact with which, all his movements
[L578] take place.
[L579]
[L580] When we come to think of a four-dimensional solid, what are the
[L581] corresponding assumptions which we must make?
[L582]
[L583] We must suppose a sense which we have not, a sense of direction
[L584] wanting in us, something which a being in a four-dimensional world
[L585] has, and which we have not. It is a sense corresponding to a new space
[L586] direction, a direction which extends positively and negatively from
[L587] every point of our space, and which goes right away from any space
[L588] direction we know of. The perpendicular to a plane is perpendicular,
[L589] not only to two lines in it, but to every line, and so we must conceive
[L590] this fourth dimension as running perpendicularly to each and every line
[L591] we can draw in our space.
[L592]
[L593] And as the plane being had to suppose something which prevented his
[L594] moving off in the third, the unknown dimension to him, so we have to
[L595] suppose something which prevents us moving off in the direction unknown
[L596] to us. This something, since we must be in contact with it in every one
[L597] of our movements, must not be a plane surface, but a solid; it must be
[L598] a solid, which in every one of our movements we are against, not in.
[L599] It must be supposed as stretching out in every space dimension that we
[L600] know; but we are not in it, we are against it, we are next to it, in
[L601] the fourth dimension.
[L602]
[L603] That is, as the plane being conceives himself as having a very small
[L604] thickness in the third dimension, of which he is not aware in his
[L605] sense experience, so we must suppose ourselves as having a very small
[L606] thickness in the fourth dimension, and, being thus four-dimensional
[L607] beings, to be prevented from realising that we are such beings by a
[L608] constraint which keeps us always in contact with a vast solid sheet,
[L609] which stretches on in every direction. We are against that sheet, so
[L610] that, if we had the power of four-dimensional movement, we should
[L611] either go away from it or through it; all our space movements as we
[L612] know them being such that, performing them, we keep in contact with
[L613] this solid sheet.
[L614]
[L615] Now consider the exposition a plane being would make for himself as to
[L616] the question of the enclosure of a square, and of a cube.
[L617]
[L618] He would say the square A, in Fig. 96, is completely enclosed by the
[L619] four squares, A far, A near, A above, A below, or as they are written
[L620] A_n_, A_f_, A_a_, A_b_.
[L621]
[L622] [Illustration: Fig. 96.]
[L623]
[L624] If now he conceives the square A to move in the, to him, unknown
[L625] dimension it will trace out a cube, and the bounding squares will
[L626] form cubes. Will these completely surround the cube generated by A?
[L627] No; there will be two faces of the cube made by A left uncovered;
[L628] the first, that face which coincides with the square A in its first
[L629] position; the next, that which coincides with the square A in its
[L630] final position. Against these two faces cubes must be placed in order
[L631] to completely enclose the cube A. These may be called the cubes left
[L632] and right or A_l_ and A_r_. Thus each of the enclosing squares of the
[L633] square A becomes a cube and two more cubes are wanted to enclose the
[L634] cube formed by the movement of A in the third dimension.

[L778] Here we see that there is no obstacle to prevent the rods turning

[L789] three-dimensional. If the matter had a small thickness in the fourth
[L790] dimension, there would be a slight thickness in fig. 12 above the
[L791] plane of the paper—a thickness equal to the thickness of the matter

[L796]
[L797] Let us now consider, not a merely extensible body, but a liquid one. A
[L798] mass of rotating liquid, a whirl, eddy, or vortex, has many remarkable
[L799] properties. On first consideration we should expect the rotating mass
[L800] of liquid immediately to spread off and lose itself in the surrounding
[L801] liquid. The water flies off a wheel whirled round, and we should expect
[L802] the rotating liquid to be dispersed. But see the eddies in a river
[L803] strangely persistent. The rings that occur in puffs of smoke and last
[L804] so long are whirls or vortices curved round so that their opposite ends
[L805] join together. A cyclone will travel over great distances.
[L806]
[L807] Helmholtz was the first to investigate the properties of vortices.
[L808] He studied them as they would occur in a perfect fluid—that is, one
[L809] without friction of one moving portion or another. In such a medium
[L810] vortices would be indestructible. They would go on for ever, altering
[L811] their shape, but consisting always of the same portion of the fluid.
[L812] But a straight vortex could not exist surrounded entirely by the fluid.
[L813] The ends of a vortex must reach to some boundary inside or outside the
[L814] fluid.
[L815]
[L816] A vortex which is bent round so that its opposite ends join is capable
[L817] of existing, but no vortex has a free end in the fluid. The fluid
[L818] round the vortex is always in motion, and one produces a definite
[L819] movement in another.
[L820]
[L821] Lord Kelvin has proposed the hypothesis that portions of a fluid
[L822] segregated in vortices account for the origin of matter. The properties
[L823] of the ether in respect of its capacity of propagating disturbances
[L824] can be explained by the assumption of vortices in it instead of by a
[L825] property of rigidity. It is difficult to conceive, however, of any
[L826] arrangement of the vortex rings and endless vortex filaments in the
[L827] ether.

[L829] Now, the further consideration of four-dimensional rotations shows the
[L830] existence of a kind of vortex which would make an ether filled with a
[L831] homogeneous vortex motion easily thinkable.

[L905] Again, just as the plane being can represent any motion in his space by
[L906] two axes, so we can represent any motion in our three-dimensional space
[L907] by means of three axes. There is no point in our space to which we
[L908] cannot move by some combination of movements on the directions marked
[L909] out by these axes.
[L910]
[L911] On the assumption of a fourth dimension we have to suppose a fourth
[L912] axis, which we will call AW. It must be supposed to be at right angles
[L913] to each and every one of the three axes AX, AY, AZ. Just as the two
[L914] axes, AX, AZ, determine a plane which is similar to the original plane
[L915] on which we supposed the plane being to exist, but which runs off from
[L916] it, and only meets it in a line; so in our space if we take any three
[L917] axes such as AX, AY, and AW, they determine a space like our space
[L918] world. This space runs off from our space, and if we were transferred
[L919] to it we should find ourselves in a space exactly similar to our own.
[L920]
[L921] We must give up any attempt to picture this space in its relation
[L922] to ours, just as a plane being would have to give up any attempt to
[L923] picture a plane at right angles to his plane.
[L924]
[L925] Such a space and ours run in different directions from the plane of AX
[L926] and AY. They meet in this plane but have nothing else in common, just
[L927] as the plane space of AX and AY and that of AX and AZ run in different
[L928] directions and have but the line AX in common.
[L929]
[L930] Omitting all discussion of the manner on which a plane being might be
[L931] conceived to form a theory of a three-dimensional existence, let us
[L932] examine how, with the means at his disposal, he could represent the
[L933] properties of three-dimensional objects.
[L934]
[L935] There are two ways in which the plane being can think of one of our
[L936] solid bodies. He can think of the cube, fig. 8, as composed of a number

[L982] An inspection of above figures will give an answer to many questions
[L983] about the tesseract. If we have a tesseract one inch each way, then it
[L984] can be represented as a cube—a cube having white, yellow, red axes,
[L985] and from this cube as a beginning, a volume extending into the fourth
[L986] dimension. Now suppose the tesseract to pass transverse to our space,
[L987] the cube of the red, yellow, white axes disappears at once, it is
[L988] indefinitely thin in the fourth dimension. Its place is occupied by
[L989] those parts of the tesseract which lie further away from our space in
[L990] the fourth dimension. Each one of these sections will last only for
[L991] one moment, but the whole of them will take up some appreciable time
[L992] in passing. If we take the rate of one inch a minute the sections will
[L993] take the whole of the minute in their passage across our space, they
[L994] will take the whole of the minute except the moment which the beginning
[L995] cube and the end cube occupy in their crossing our space. In each one
[L996] of the cubes, the section cubes, we can draw lines in all directions
[L997] except in the direction occupied by the blue line, the fourth
[L998] dimension; lines in that direction are represented by the transition
[L999] from one section cube to another. Thus to give ourselves an adequate
[L1000] representation of the tesseract we ought to have a limitless number of
[L1001] section cubes intermediate between the first bounding cube, the ochre
[L1002] cube, and the last bounding cube, the other ochre cube. Practically

[L10] Hence a system of molecules with the A motion would not destroy it in
[L11] one another, and would impart it to a body in contact with them. Thus A
[L12] and B motions possess the first requisite which must be demanded in any
[L13] mode of motion representative of electricity.
[L14]
[L15] Let us trace out the consequences of defining positive electricity as
[L16] an A motion and negative electricity as a B motion. The combination of
[L17] positive and negative electricity produces a current. Imagine a vortex
[L18] in the ether of the A kind and unite with this one of the B kind. An
[L19] A motion and B motion produce rotation round a plane, which is in the
[L20] ether a vortex round an axial surface. It is a vortex of the kind we
[L21] represent as a part of a sphere turning inside out. Now such a vortex
[L22] must have its rim on a boundary of the ether—on a body in the ether.
[L23]
[L24] Let us suppose that a conductor is a body which has the property of
[L25] serving as the terminal abutment of such a vortex. Then the conception
[L26] we must form of a closed current is of a vortex sheet having its edge
[L27] along the circuit of the conducting wire. The whole wire will then be
[L28] like the centres on which a spindle turns in three-dimensional space,
[L29] and any interruption of the continuity of the wire will produce a
[L30] tension in place of a continuous revolution.
[L31]
[L32] As the direction of the rotation of the vortex is from a three-space
[L33] direction into the fourth dimension and back again, there will be no
[L34] direction of flow to the current; but it will have two sides, according
[L35] to whether _z_ goes to _w_ or _z_ goes to negative _w_.
[L36]
[L37] We can draw any line from one part of the circuit to another; then the
[L38] ether along that line is rotating round its points.
[L39]
[L40] This geometric image corresponds to the definition of an electric
[L41] circuit. It is known that the action does not lie in the wire, but in
[L42] the medium, and it is known that there is no direction of flow in the
[L43] wire.
[L44]
[L45] No explanation has been offered in three-dimensional mechanics of how
[L46] an action can be impressed throughout a region and yet necessarily
[L47] run itself out along a closed boundary, as is the case in an electric
[L48] current. But this phenomenon corresponds exactly to the definition of a
[L49] four-dimensional vortex.
[L50]
[L51] If we take a very long magnet, so long that one of its poles is
[L52] practically isolated, and put this pole in the vicinity of an electric
[L53] circuit, we find that it moves.
[L54]
[L55] Now, assuming for the sake of simplicity that the wire which determines
[L56] the current is in the form of a circle, if we take a number of small
[L57] magnets and place them all pointing in the same direction normal to
[L58] the plane of the circle, so that they fill it and the wire binds them
[L59] round, we find that this sheet of magnets has the same effect on
[L60] the magnetic pole that the current has. The sheet of magnets may be
[L61] curved, but the edge of it must coincide with the wire. The collection
[L62] of magnets is then equivalent to the vortex sheet, and an elementary
[L63] magnet to a part of it. Thus, we must think of a magnet as conditioning
[L64] a rotation in the ether round the plane which bisects at right angles
[L65] the line joining its poles.

[L149] The shape of the vortex may alter, but it always consists of the same
[L150] particles of the fluid.
[L151]
[L152] Now, a very remarkable fact about such a vortex is that the ends of the
[L153] vortex cannot remain suspended and isolated in the fluid. They must
[L154] always run to the boundary of the fluid. An eddy in water that remains
[L155] half way down without coming to the top is impossible.
[L156]
[L157] The ends of a vortex must reach the boundary of a fluid—the boundary
[L158] may be external or internal—a vortex may exist between two objects
[L159] in the fluid, terminating one end on each object, the objects being
[L160] internal boundaries of the fluid. Again, a vortex may have its ends
[L161] linked together, so that it forms a ring. Circular vortex rings of
[L162] this description are often seen in puffs of smoke, and that the smoke
[L163] travels on in the ring is a proof that the vortex always consists of
[L164] the same particles of air.
[L165]
[L166] Let us now enquire what a vortex would be in a four-dimensional fluid.
[L167]
[L168] We must replace the line axis by a plane axis. We should have therefore
[L169] a portion of fluid rotating round a plane.
[L170]
[L171] We have seen that the contour of this plane corresponds with the ends
[L172] of the axis line. Hence such a four-dimensional vortex must have its
[L173] rim on a boundary of the fluid. There would be a region of vorticity
[L174] with a contour. If such a rotation were started at one part of a
[L175] circular boundary, its edges would run round the boundary in both
[L176] directions till the whole interior region was filled with the vortex
[L177] sheet.
[L178]
[L179] A vortex in a three-dimensional liquid may consist of a number of
[L180] vortex filaments lying together producing a tube, or rod of vorticity.
[L181]
[L182] In the same way we can have in four dimensions a number of vortex
[L183] sheets alongside each other, each of which can be thought of as a
[L184] bowl-shaped portion of a spherical shell turning inside out. The
[L185] rotation takes place at any point not in the space occupied by the
[L186] shell, but from that space to the fourth dimension and round back again.
[L187]
[L188] Is there anything analogous to this within the range of our observation?
[L189]
[L190] An electric current answers this description in every respect.
[L191] Electricity does not flow through a wire. Its effect travels both ways
[L192] from the starting point along the wire. The spark which shows its
[L193] passing midway in its circuit is later than that which occurs at points
[L194] near its starting point on either side of it.
[L195]
[L196] Moreover, it is known that the action of the current is not in the
[L197] wire. It is in the region enclosed by the wire, this is the field of
[L198] force, the locus of the exhibition of the effects of the current.
[L199]
[L200] And the necessity of a conducting circuit for a current is exactly
[L201] that which we should expect if it were a four-dimensional vortex.
[L202] According to Maxwell every current forms a closed circuit, and this,
[L203] from the four-dimensional point of view, is the same as saying a vortex
[L204] must have its ends on a boundary of the fluid.
[L205]
[L206] Thus, on the hypothesis of a fourth dimension, the rotation of the
[L207] fluid ether would give the phenomenon of an electric current. We must
[L208] suppose the ether to be full of movement, for the more we examine into
[L209] the conditions which prevail in the obscurity of the minute, the more
[L210] we find that an unceasing and perpetual motion reigns. Thus we may say
[L211] that the conception of the fourth dimension means that there must be a
[L212] phenomenon which presents the characteristics of electricity.
[L213]
[L214] We know now that light is an electro-magnetic action, and that so far
[L215] from being a special and isolated phenomenon this electric action is
[L216] universal in the realm of the minute.

[L271]                  THE USE OF FOUR DIMENSIONS IN THOUGHT
[L272]
[L273]
[L274] Having held before ourselves this outline of a conjecture of the world
[L275] as four-dimensional, having roughly thrown together those facts of
[L276] movement which we can see apply to our actual experience, let us pass
[L277] to another branch of our subject.

[L279] The engineer uses drawings, graphical constructions, in a variety of
[L280] manners. He has, for instance, diagrams which represent the expansion

[L282] actual plans of his machines. They are not the pictures of anything

[L285]
[L286] And so, besides showing us the actual existence of that world which
[L287] lies beneath the one of visible movements, four-dimensional space

[L323] over it is found to be rotating in the opposite direction. Now, if
[L324] rotation in one direction corresponds to positive electricity, rotation
[L325] in the opposite direction corresponds to negative electricity, and the
[L326] smallest electrified particles would have their charges reversed by
[L327] being turned over—an absurd supposition.
[L328]
[L329] If we fix on a mode of motion as a definition of electricity, we must
[L330] have two varieties of it, one for positive and one for negative; and a
[L331] body possessing the one kind must not become possessed of the other by
[L332] any change in its position.
[L333]
[L334] All three-dimensional motions are compounded of rotations and
[L335] translations, and none of them satisfy this first condition for serving
[L336] as a definition of electricity.
[L337]
[L338] But consider the double rotation of the A and B kinds. A body rotating
[L339] with the A motion cannot have its motion transformed into the B kind
[L340] by being turned over in any way. Suppose a body has the rotation _x_
[L341] to _y_ and _z_ to _w_. Turning it about the _xy_ plane, we reverse the
[L342] direction of the motion _x_ to _y_. But we also reverse the _z_ to _w_
[L343] motion, for the point at the extremity of the positive _z_ axis is
[L344] now at the extremity of the negative _z_ axis, and since we have not
[L345] interfered with its motion it goes in the direction of position _w_.
[L346] Hence we have _y_ to _x_ and _w_ to _z_, which is the same as _x_ to
[L347] _y_ and _z_ to _w_. Thus both components are reversed, and there is the
[L348] A motion over again. The B kind is the semi-negative, with only one
[L349] component reversed.
[L350]
[L351] Hence a system of molecules with the A motion would not destroy it in
[L352] one another, and would impart it to a body in contact with them. Thus A
[L353] and B motions possess the first requisite which must be demanded in any
[L354] mode of motion representative of electricity.
[L355]
[L356] Let us trace out the consequences of defining positive electricity as
[L357] an A motion and negative electricity as a B motion. The combination of
[L358] positive and negative electricity produces a current. Imagine a vortex
[L359] in the ether of the A kind and unite with this one of the B kind. An
[L360] A motion and B motion produce rotation round a plane, which is in the
[L361] ether a vortex round an axial surface. It is a vortex of the kind we
[L362] represent as a part of a sphere turning inside out. Now such a vortex
[L363] must have its rim on a boundary of the ether—on a body in the ether.

[L373] If a current is started in a circuit, we must imagine vortices like
[L374] bowls turning themselves inside out, starting from the contour. In
[L375] reaching a parallel circuit, if the vortex sheet were interrupted and
[L376] joined momentarily to the second circuit by a free rim, the axis plane
[L377] would lie between the two circuits, and a point on the second circuit
[L378] opposite a point on the first would correspond to a point opposite
[L379] to it on the first; hence we should expect a current in the opposite
[L380] direction in the second circuit. Thus the phenomena of induction are
[L381] not inconsistent with the hypothesis of a vortex about an axial plane.
[L382]
[L383] In four-dimensional space, in which all four dimensions were
[L384] commensurable, the intensity of the action transmitted by the medium
[L385] would vary inversely as the cube of the distance. Now, the action of
[L386] a current on a magnetic pole varies inversely as the square of the
[L387] distance; hence, over measurable distances the extension of the ether
[L388] in the fourth dimension cannot be assumed as other than small in
[L389] comparison with those distances.
[L390]
[L391] If we suppose the ether to be filled with vortices in the shape of
[L392] four-dimensional spheres rotating with the A motion, the B motion would
[L393] correspond to electricity in the one-fluid theory. There would thus
[L394] be a possibility of electricity existing in two forms, statically,
[L395] by itself, and, combined with the universal motion, in the form of a
[L396] current.
[L397]
[L398] To arrive at a definite conclusion it will be necessary to investigate
[L399] the resultant pressures which accompany the collocation of solid
[L400] vortices with surface ones.
[L401]
[L402] To recapitulate:
[L403]
[L404] The movements and mechanics of four-dimensional space are definite and
[L405] intelligible. A vortex with a surface as its axis affords a geometric
[L406] image of a closed circuit, and there are rotations which by their
[L407] polarity afford a possible definition of statical electricity.[7]
[L408]
[L409]  [7] These double rotations of the A and B kinds I should like to call
[L410]  Hamiltons and co-Hamiltons, for it is a singular fact that in his
[L411]  “Quaternions” Sir Wm. Rowan Hamilton has given the theory of either
[L412]  the A or the B kind. They follow the laws of his symbols, I, J, K.
[L413]
[L414] Hamiltons and co-Hamiltons seem to be natural units of geometrical
[L415] expression. In the paper in the “Proceedings of the Royal Irish
[L416] Academy,” Nov. 1903, already alluded to, I have shown something of the
[L417] remarkable facility which is gained in dealing with the composition of
[L418] three- and four-dimensional rotations by an alteration in Hamilton’s
[L419] notation, which enables his system to be applied to both the A and B
[L420] kinds of rotations.
[L421]
[L422] The objection which has been often made to Hamilton’s system, namely,
[L423] that it is only under special conditions of application that his
[L424] processes give geometrically interpretable results, can be removed, if
[L425] we assume that he was really dealing with a four-dimensional motion,

[L427] recognition.

[L454] Helmholtz was the first to investigate the properties of vortices.
[L455] He studied them as they would occur in a perfect fluid—that is, one
[L456] without friction of one moving portion or another. In such a medium
[L457] vortices would be indestructible. They would go on for ever, altering
[L458] their shape, but consisting always of the same portion of the fluid.
[L459] But a straight vortex could not exist surrounded entirely by the fluid.
[L460] The ends of a vortex must reach to some boundary inside or outside the
[L461] fluid.
[L462]
[L463] A vortex which is bent round so that its opposite ends join is capable
[L464] of existing, but no vortex has a free end in the fluid. The fluid
[L465] round the vortex is always in motion, and one produces a definite
[L466] movement in another.
[L467]
[L468] Lord Kelvin has proposed the hypothesis that portions of a fluid
[L469] segregated in vortices account for the origin of matter. The properties
[L470] of the ether in respect of its capacity of propagating disturbances
[L471] can be explained by the assumption of vortices in it instead of by a
[L472] property of rigidity. It is difficult to conceive, however, of any
[L473] arrangement of the vortex rings and endless vortex filaments in the
[L474] ether.
[L475]
[L476] Now, the further consideration of four-dimensional rotations shows the
[L477] existence of a kind of vortex which would make an ether filled with a
[L478] homogeneous vortex motion easily thinkable.
[L479]
[L480] To understand the nature of this vortex, we must go on and take a
[L481] step by which we accept the full significance of the four-dimensional
[L482] hypothesis. Granted four-dimensional axes, we have seen that a rotation
[L483] of one into another leaves two unaltered, and these two form the axial
[L484] plane about which the rotation takes place. But what about these two?
[L485] Do they necessarily remain motionless? There is nothing to prevent a
[L486] rotation of these two, one into the other, taking place concurrently
[L487] with the first rotation. This possibility of a double rotation deserves
[L488] the most careful attention, for it is the kind of movement which is
[L489] distinctly typical of four dimensions.
[L490]
[L491] Rotation round a plane is analogous to rotation round an axis. But in
[L492] three-dimensional space there is no motion analogous to the double
[L493] rotation, in which, while axis 1 changes into axis 2, axis 3 changes
[L494] into axis 4.
[L495]
[L496] Consider a four-dimensional body, with four independent axes, _x_,
[L497] _y_, _z_, _w_. A point in it can move in only one direction at a given
[L498] moment. If the body has a velocity of rotation by which the _x_ axis
[L499] changes into the _y_ axis and all parallel sections move in a similar
[L500] manner, then the point will describe a circle. If, now, in addition
[L501] to the rotation by which the _x_ axis changes into the _y_ axis the
[L502] body has a rotation by which the _z_ axis turns into the _w_ axis, the
[L503] point in question will have a double motion in consequence of the two
[L504] turnings. The motions will compound, and the point will describe a
[L505] circle, but not the same circle which it would describe in virtue of
[L506] either rotation separately.

[L516] As the plane being can think of the cube as consisting of sections,
[L517] each like a figure he knows, extending away from his plane, so we can
[L518] think of a higher solid as composed of sections, each like a solid
[L519] which we know, but extending away from our space.
[L520]
[L521] Thus, taking a higher cube, we can look on it as starting from a cube
[L522] in our space and extending in the unknown dimension.

[L525]
[L526] Take the face A and conceive it to exist as simply a face, a square
[L527] with no thickness. From this face the cube in our space extends by the
[L528] occupation of space which we can see.
[L529]
[L530] But from this face there extends equally a cube in the unknown
[L531] dimension. We can think of the higher cube, then, by taking the set
[L532] of sections A, B, C, D, etc., and considering that from each of them
[L533] there runs a cube. These cubes have nothing in common with each other,
[L534] and of each of them in its actual position all that we can have in our
[L535] space is an isolated square. It is obvious that we can take our series
[L536] of sections in any manner we please. We can take them parallel, for
[L537] instance, to any one of the three isolated faces shown in the figure.
[L538] Corresponding to the three series of sections at right angles to each
[L539] other, which we can make of the cube in space, we must conceive of the
[L540] higher cube, as composed of cubes starting from squares parallel to the
[L541] faces of the cube, and of these cubes all that exist in our space are
[L542] the isolated squares from which they start.
[L543]
[L544]
[L545]
[L546]
[L547]                               CHAPTER III
[L548]
[L549]            THE SIGNIFICANCE OF A FOUR-DIMENSIONAL EXISTENCE
[L550]
[L551]
[L552] Having now obtained the conception of a four-dimensional space, and
[L553] having formed the analogy which, without any further geometrical
[L554] difficulties, enables us to enquire into its properties, I will refer
[L555] the reader, whose interest is principally in the mechanical aspect,
[L556] to Chapters VI. and VII. In the present chapter I will deal with
[L557] the general significance of the enquiry, and in the next with the
[L558] historical origin of the idea.
[L559]
[L560] First, with regard to the question of whether there is any evidence
[L561] that we are really in four-dimensional space, I will go back to the
[L562] analogy of the plane world.
[L563]
[L564] A being in a plane world could not have any experience of
[L565] three-dimensional shapes, but he could have an experience of
[L566] three-dimensional movements.
[L567]
[L568] We have seen that his matter must be supposed to have an extension,
[L569] though a very small one, in the third dimension. And thus, in the
[L570] small particles of his matter, three-dimensional movements may well
[L571] be conceived to take place. Of these movements he would only perceive
[L572] the resultants. Since all movements of an observable size in the plane
[L573] world are two-dimensional, he would only perceive the resultants in
[L574] two dimensions of the small three-dimensional movements. Thus, there
[L575] would be phenomena which he could not explain by his theory of
[L576] mechanics—motions would take place which he could not explain by his
[L577] theory of motion. Hence, to determine if we are in a four-dimensional
[L578] world, we must examine the phenomena of motion in our space. If
[L579] movements occur which are not explicable on the suppositions of our
[L580] three-dimensional mechanics, we should have an indication of a possible
[L581] four-dimensional motion, and if, moreover, it could be shown that such
[L582] movements would be a consequence of a four-dimensional motion in the
[L583] minute particles of bodies or of the ether, we should have a strong
[L584] presumption in favour of the reality of the fourth dimension.

[L657] If we suppose the spherical shell to be of four-dimensional matter, our
[L658] representation will be a little different. Let us suppose there to be a
[L659] small thickness to the matter in the fourth dimension. This would make
[L660] no difference in fig. 44, for that merely shows the view in the _xyz_
[L661] space. But when the _x_ axis is let drop, and the _w_ axis comes in,
[L662] then the rods CD and EF which represent the matter of the shell, will
[L663] have a certain thickness perpendicular to the plane of the paper on

[L665] they will show this thickness when looked at from the direction of the
[L666] _w_ axis.
