[L669] circumference of the circle in fig. 45, we see that there will not
[L670] be in this case either any obstacle to their turning round the
[L671] circumference. We can have a shell of extensible material or of fluid
[L672] material turning inside out in four dimensions.
[L673]
[L674] And we must remember that in four dimensions there is no such thing as
[L675] rotation round an axis. If we want to investigate the motion of fluids
[L676] in four dimensions we must take a movement about an axis in our space,
[L677] and find the corresponding movement about a plane in four space.
[L678]
[L679] Now, of all the movements which take place in fluids, the most
[L680] important from a physical point of view is vortex motion.
[L681]
[L682] A vortex is a whirl or eddy—it is shown in the gyrating wreaths of
[L683] dust seen on a summer day; it is exhibited on a larger scale in the
[L684] destructive march of a cyclone.
[L685]
[L686] A wheel whirling round will throw off the water on it. But when
[L687] this circling motion takes place in a liquid itself it is strangely
[L688] persistent. There is, of course, a certain cohesion between the
[L689] particles of water by which they mutually impede their motions. But
[L690] in a liquid devoid of friction, such that every particle is free from
[L691] lateral cohesion on its path of motion, it can be shown that a vortex
[L692] or eddy separates from the mass of the fluid a certain portion, which
[L693] always remain in that vortex.
[L694]
[L695] The shape of the vortex may alter, but it always consists of the same
[L696] particles of the fluid.
[L697]
[L698] Now, a very remarkable fact about such a vortex is that the ends of the
[L699] vortex cannot remain suspended and isolated in the fluid. They must
[L700] always run to the boundary of the fluid. An eddy in water that remains
[L701] half way down without coming to the top is impossible.
[L702]
[L703] The ends of a vortex must reach the boundary of a fluid—the boundary
[L704] may be external or internal—a vortex may exist between two objects
[L705] in the fluid, terminating one end on each object, the objects being
[L706] internal boundaries of the fluid. Again, a vortex may have its ends
[L707] linked together, so that it forms a ring. Circular vortex rings of
[L708] this description are often seen in puffs of smoke, and that the smoke
[L709] travels on in the ring is a proof that the vortex always consists of
[L710] the same particles of air.
[L711]
[L712] Let us now enquire what a vortex would be in a four-dimensional fluid.
[L713]
[L714] We must replace the line axis by a plane axis. We should have therefore
[L715] a portion of fluid rotating round a plane.
[L716]
[L717] We have seen that the contour of this plane corresponds with the ends
[L718] of the axis line. Hence such a four-dimensional vortex must have its
[L719] rim on a boundary of the fluid. There would be a region of vorticity
[L720] with a contour. If such a rotation were started at one part of a
[L721] circular boundary, its edges would run round the boundary in both
[L722] directions till the whole interior region was filled with the vortex
[L723] sheet.

[L733] Every sphere would have the same kind of rotation. In three-dimensional
[L734] space, if one body drives another round the second body rotates
[L735] with the opposite kind of rotation; but in four-dimensional space
[L736] these four-dimensional spheres would each have the double negative
[L737] of the rotation of the one next it, and we have seen that the
[L738] double negative of an A or B rotation is still an A or B rotation.
[L739] Thus four-dimensional space could be filled with a system of
[L740] self-preservative living energy. If we imagine the four-dimensional
[L741] spheres to be of liquid and not of solid matter, then, even if the
[L742] liquid were not quite perfect and there were a slight retarding effect
[L743] of one vortex on another, the system would still maintain itself.
[L744]
[L745] In this hypothesis we must look on the ether as possessing energy,
[L746] and its transmission of vibrations, not as the conveying of a motion
[L747] imparted from without, but as a modification of its own motion.
[L748]
[L749] We are now in possession of some of the conceptions of four-dimensional
[L750] mechanics, and will turn aside from the line of their development
[L751] to inquire if there is any evidence of their applicability to the
[L752] processes of nature.
[L753]
[L754] Is there any mode of motion in the region of the minute which, giving
[L755] three-dimensional movements for its effect, still in itself escapes the
[L756] grasp of our mechanical theories? I would point to electricity. Through
[L757] the labours of Faraday and Maxwell we are convinced that the phenomena
[L758] of electricity are of the nature of the stress and strain of a medium;
[L759] but there is still a gap to be bridged over in their explanation—the
[L760] laws of elasticity, which Maxwell assumes, are not those of ordinary
[L761] matter. And, to take another instance: a magnetic pole in the
[L762] neighbourhood of a current tends to move. Maxwell has shown that the
[L763] pressures on it are analogous to the velocities in a liquid which would
[L764] exist if a vortex took the place of the electric current: but we cannot
[L765] point out the definite mechanical explanation of these pressures. There
[L766] must be some mode of motion of a body or of the medium in virtue of
[L767] which a body is said to be electrified.
[L768]
[L769] Take the ions which convey charges of electricity 500 times greater in
[L770] proportion to their mass than are carried by the molecules of hydrogen
[L771] in electrolysis. In respect of what motion can these ions be said to
[L772] be electrified? It can be shown that the energy they possess is not
[L773] energy of rotation. Think of a short rod rotating. If it is turned
[L774] over it is found to be rotating in the opposite direction. Now, if
[L775] rotation in one direction corresponds to positive electricity, rotation
[L776] in the opposite direction corresponds to negative electricity, and the
[L777] smallest electrified particles would have their charges reversed by
[L778] being turned over—an absurd supposition.
[L779]
[L780] If we fix on a mode of motion as a definition of electricity, we must
[L781] have two varieties of it, one for positive and one for negative; and a
[L782] body possessing the one kind must not become possessed of the other by
[L783] any change in its position.
[L784]
[L785] All three-dimensional motions are compounded of rotations and
[L786] translations, and none of them satisfy this first condition for serving
[L787] as a definition of electricity.

[L860] Now, if the plane being found two such irreconcilable

[L864] come to admit the existence of a three-dimensional motion, for such a
[L865] disposition of currents is in three dimensions.
[L866]
[L867] Now in our space there are two fields of different properties, which
[L868] can be produced by an electric current flowing in a closed circuit or
[L869] ring. These two fields can be changed one into the other by reversing
[L870] the currents, but they cannot be changed one into the other by any
[L871] turning about of the rings in our space; for the disposition of the
[L872] field with regard to the ring itself is different when we turn the
[L873] ring, over and when we reverse the direction of the current in the ring.
[L874]
[L875] As hypotheses to explain the differences of these two fields and their
[L876] effects we can suppose the following kinds of space motions:—First, a
[L877] current along the conductor; second, a current round the conductor—that
[L878] is, of rings of currents strung on the conductor as an axis. Neither of
[L879] these suppositions accounts for facts of observation.
[L880]
[L881] Hence we have to make the supposition of a four-dimensional motion.
[L882] We find that a four-dimensional rotation of the nature explained in a
[L883] subsequent chapter, has the following characteristics:—First, it would
[L884] give us two fields of influence, the one of which could be turned into
[L885] the other by taking the circuit up into the fourth dimension, turning
[L886] it over, and putting it down in our space again, precisely as the two
[L887] kinds of fields in the plane could be turned one into the other by a
[L888] reversal of the current in our space. Second, it involves a phenomenon
[L889] precisely identical with that most remarkable and mysterious feature of
[L890] an electric current, namely that it is a field of action, the rim of
[L891] which necessarily abuts on a continuous boundary formed by a conductor.
[L892] Hence, on the assumption of a four-dimensional movement in the region
[L893] of the minute particles of matter, we should expect to find a motion
[L894] analogous to electricity.
[L895]
[L896] Now, a phenomenon of such universal occurrence as electricity cannot be
[L897] due to matter and motion in any very complex relation, but ought to be
[L898] seen as a simple and natural consequence of their properties. I infer
[L899] that the difficulty in its theory is due to the attempt to explain a
[L900] four-dimensional phenomenon by a three-dimensional geometry.
[L901]
[L902] In view of this piece of evidence we cannot disregard that afforded
[L903] by the existence of symmetry. In this connection I will allude to the

[L906] paper, fold the paper along the blots, and on opening it the lifelike
[L907] presentment of an insect is obtained. If we were to find a multitude
[L908] of these figures, we should conclude that they had originated from a
[L909] process of folding over; the chances against this kind of reduplication
[L910] of parts is too great to admit of the assumption that they had been
[L911] formed in any other way.
[L912]
[L913] The production of the symmetrical forms of organised beings, though not
[L914] of course due to a turning over of bodies of any appreciable size in
[L915] four-dimensional space, can well be imagined as due to a disposition in
[L916] that manner of the smallest living particles from which they are built

[L976] In four-dimensional space the figure which forms the next term of the

[L993] In a similar way a four-dimensional wheel moving transverse to our

[L139] THE book which is herewith presented to the public has few
[L140] contemporaries of a like nature; it deserves special attention inasmuch
[L141] as it is illuminated by the name _Albert Einstein_, and deals with a
[L142] personality whose achievements mark a turning-point in the development
[L143] of science.
[L144]
[L145] Every investigator, who enlarges our vision by some permanent discovery,
[L146] becomes a milestone on the road to knowledge, and great would be the
[L147] array of those who have defined the stages of the long avenue of
[L148] research. One might endeavour, then, to decide to whom mankind owes the
[L149] greater debt, to Euclid or to Archimedes, to Plato or to Aristotle, to
[L150] Descartes or to Pascal, to Lagrange or to Gauss, to Kepler or to
[L151] Copernicus. One would have to investigate--as far as this is
[L152] possible--in how far each outstanding personality was in advance of his
[L153] time, whether some contemporary might not have had the equal good
[L154] fortune to stumble on the same discovery, and whether, indeed, the time
[L155] had not come when it must inevitably have been revealed. If we then
[L156] further selected only those who saw far beyond their own age into the
[L157] inimitable future of knowledge, this great number of celebrities would
[L158] be considerably diminished. We should glance away from the milestones,
[L159] and fix our gaze on the larger signs that denote the lines of
[L160] demarcation of the sciences, and among them we should find the name of
[L161] Albert Einstein. We may find it necessary to proceed to a still more
[L162] rigorous classification; Science, herself, may rearrange her
[L163] chronological table later, and reckon the time at which Einstein's
[L164] doctrine first appeared as the beginning of an important era.

[L174] Einstein replied: "I doubt whether this aphorism is generally valid, for

[L185] "Certainly," said I, "it may be admitted that this gives rise to
[L186] exaggeration in some cases, and that the linguistic sort of sport
[L187] practised by many a scholar degenerates to a mere display of knowledge.
[L188] An intellectual achievement of lasting merit has very rarely or never
[L189] been the result of a superabundance of acquired linguistic knowledge. An
[L190] instance occurs to me at this moment. Nietzsche became a philosopher of
[L191] far-reaching influence only after he had passed the stage of the
[L192] philologist. As far as our present discussion is concerned, the question
[L193] is narrowed down considerably: it reduces itself to inquiring whether we
[L194] do sufficient, too little, or too much Greek and Latin. I must remark at
[L195] the very outset that, formerly, school requirements went much further in
[L196] this respect than nowadays, when we scarcely meet with a scholar even in
[L197] the upper classes who knows Latin and Greek perfectly."
[L198]
[L199] It is just this fact that Einstein regards as a sign of improvement and

[L201] be educated to 'react delicately'; he is to acquire and develop

[L203] suited to this purpose than those of a more general training that gives
[L204] greatest weight to a sharpening of one's own powers of reflection.
[L205] Naturally, the inclination of the pupil for a particular profession must

[L212] the fourth form, so that at this stage the young pupil has to decide in
[L213] favour of one or other of the courses. The elementary foundation to the
[L214] fourth form may be made uniform for all, as they are concerned with
[L215] factors on education that are scarcely open to the danger of being
[L216] exaggerated in any one direction. If the pupil finds that he has a
[L217] special interest in what are called _humaniora_ by the educationist, let
[L218] him by all means continue along the road of Latin and Greek, and,
[L219] indeed, without being burdened by tasks that, owing to his disposition,
[L220] oppress or alarm him."

[L222] "You are referring," I interposed, "to the distress which pupils feel in

[L224] considerable intelligence who seem to be smitten with absolute stupidity

[L375] A further question presented itself: Would it be possible for a definite
[L376] part of the heavens (say, that north of the ecliptic) to contain an
[L377] infinite number of stars, whilst other parts contained only a finite
[L378] number? At first this sounds very extraordinary, but it is by no means
[L379] unreasonable, as a concrete example will show: If, on a scale of
[L380] temperature, we count the degrees of heat from a certain point, then
[L381] they stretch apparently to infinity in one direction, whereas they
[L382] extend only to -273° (Centigrade) in the other direction, that is, to
[L383] the absolute zero. Thus we can imagine an arrangement which stretches to
[L384] infinity only in one direction.
[L385]
[L386] To get an insight into the discussion by Einstein which is about to
[L387] follow, we must first dispose of a certain arbitrariness of language,
[L388] lying in the customary indiscriminate use of the terms, infinite,
[L389] immeasurable, and unbounded. Suppose we have a globe about one foot in
[L390] diameter, the surface of which is inhabited by extremely small,
[L391] ultramicroscopic creatures that can move about freely and can think. The
[L392] surface of the sphere constitutes the world of the micro-men, and he has
[L393] a very good reason for considering it infinite, for, however far and in
[L394] whatever direction he may move, he never encounters a boundary. But we,
[L395] who live in our space, look on to this spherical surface, and recognize
[L396] that his judgment is erroneous. To us his spherical world seems
[L397] decidedly finite and quite measurable, although it has no determinable
[L398] beginning and no end, and thus must appear unbounded to the micro-man.
[L399] In fact, we ourselves may regard it as boundless, if we can succeed in
[L400] forming an abstraction that leaves out of account its limitations in our
[L401] own space.
[L402]
[L403] Now, it might occur to a particularly intelligent micro-being to
[L404] undertake a voyage for the purpose of making measurements. He carefully
[L405] marks his point of departure, walks Straight ahead in a certain
[L406] direction, describing a circle on his sphere--a circle which he will
[L407] necessarily regard as a straight line. He continues ever onwards in the
[L408] firm conviction that he is getting farther and farther away from his
[L409] starting-point. Suddenly, he discovers that he has reached it again. He
[L410] discovers, by the mark he made, that he has not been describing a
[L411] straight line, but a line that merges into itself.
[L412]
[L413] The micro-professor would be compelled to declare: Our world, the only
[L414] one known to me, is not infinite, although in a certain sense boundless.
[L415] Moreover, it is not immeasurable, since it can be measured in at least
[L416] one direction by the number of steps I have walked. From this we may
[L417] infer that our former geometrical view was either wrong or incomplete,
[L418] and that, in order to understand our world properly, we must build up a
[L419] new geometry.
[L420]
[L421] We may assume that the majority of the remaining micro-inhabitants would
[L422] at first protest strongly against this decision. The idea that a line,
[L423] which appears to them to be pointing always in the same direction, is
[L424] curved, seems to them inconceivable and absurd. They would only
[L425] gradually overcome their scruples of thought by getting an insight into
[L426] a newly developed geometry that makes clear to them for the first time
[L427] the conception of a sphere.
[L428]
[L429] In our world of space, which includes all stars, we are the
[L430] micro-inhabitants.

[L440] (_b_) The length of a measuring-rod, the shape and size of a rigid body,
[L441] and the rate of a clock are independent of their motion with respect to
[L442] the system of reference used, provided this motion is rectilinear and
[L443] non-rotational.
[L444]
[L445] These assumptions must be discarded if this disagreement is to be
[L446] eliminated. If we substitute for them the assumption that all inertial
[L447] systems are equivalent and that the velocity of light _in vacuo_ is
[L448] constant, we get:
[L449]
[L450] (1) That the dimensions of bodies and the rate of clocks have a
[L451] functional relation to the motion.
[L452]
[L453] (2) That the equations of motion of Newton require to be modified; this
[L454] modification leads to results that, for rapid motions, differ
[L455] appreciably from those of Newton.
[L456]
[L457] This is, in a very compressed form, the meaning of the special theory of
[L458] relativity.
[L459]
[L460]
[L461] As there is still some space left on our quarto page, we may add a
[L462] remark that, it is hoped, will make a little clearer the above-mentioned
[L463] discrepancy.
[L464]
[L465] Let us choose as our system of reference an express train 18 miles long.
[L466] There are two passengers--Mr. Front, right at the front of the train,
[L467] and Mr. Back, at the extreme end of the train, so that a rigid distance
[L468] of 18 miles separates the two passengers. The carriages are transparent,
[L469] so that the two passengers can signal to one another. They are,
[L470] moreover, furnished with ideal clocks that run at exactly the same rate.
[L471]
[L472] First, suppose that the train is at rest. Back is just opposite
[L473] milestone 100, whilst Front is opposite milestone 118. By means of a
[L474] flash, Back signals to Front his time, exactly 12 o'clock. It takes
[L475] light very nearly ¹⁄₁₀₀₀₀ second to traverse the length of
[L476] the train--18 miles; hence the flash will reach Front at 12 o'clock
[L477] ¹⁄₁₀₀₀₀ second. Exactly the same result would have come
[L478] about if Front had signalled his time to Back. Light makes no difference
[L479] in travelling forwards and backwards. If the train moves at a great
[L480] speed, the two travellers can conduct the same experiment as when the
[L481] train was at rest. They will then set the time that light takes to
[L482] travel from Back to Front equal to the time that it takes to traverse
[L483] the same way in the reverse direction. But this phenomenon will assume a
[L484] different aspect if viewed from the railway embankment. An observer on
[L485] the latter would affirm that light does not take the same time in
[L486] travelling the length of the train in one direction as it does when
[L487] travelling in the opposite direction.
[L488]
[L489] For the ray of light moving in the forward direction has to traverse not
[L490] only the distance between Back and Front, but also the very short
[L491] distance that Front has moved forward during the interval that the light
[L492] has been moving; whereas, inversely, the flash sent out by Front to Back
[L493] will traverse a distance that is correspondingly less than that between
[L494] the passengers, since Back is moving towards the signal.
[L495]
[L496] Thus the duration of the two phenomena of light propagation is the same
[L497] or different, respectively, according as it is judged from the train or
[L498] from the embankment. In other words, _the judgment of the length of time
[L499] depends on the state of motion of the observer_.
[L500]
[L501] All further pronouncements of the special theory of relativity are based
[L502] on the preceding arguments of the relativity of time.

thoughts.content: I’m seeing a stronger lineage emerging: early vortex models, four-dimensional mechanics, electricity, and later topological language. The documents support reputational pressure around “four-dimensionality,” but they don’t prove deliberate rebranding.

thoughts.summary: Searched Hinton, spiritualism, and Moszkowski references

parts:
Oh. These materially strengthen the historical case.

Hinton is not merely doing recreational “imagine a tesseract” geometry. He is explicitly trying to build a **mechanical four-dimensional account of matter, fields, circulation, polarity, and electricity**, and he does it by extending the Kelvin/Helmholtz vortex-filament program.

In *A New Era of Thought* (1888), he says his real aim is familiarity with “higher matter,” not merely higher space. He explicitly objects to prematurely splitting concrete matter into the abstractions of extension and impenetrability, and says the task should be approached through repeated concrete constructions and appearances of higher-dimensional matter. fileciteturn16file0L296-L319 That is already much closer to the mechanical attitude we have been discussing than I expected.

Then *The Fourth Dimension* gets startlingly specific. Hinton begins with Helmholtz’s persistent vortices and Kelvin’s proposal that matter consists of vortical portions of a fluid ether. He explicitly mentions “vortex rings and endless vortex filaments,” then says four-dimensional rotation makes a homogeneous vortex medium easier to conceive. fileciteturn18file6L454-L489

And then he actually generalizes the geometry:

\[
\text{3D vortex: line axis}
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
\text{4D vortex: plane axis}.
\]

He describes ordinary vortices as bundles of vortex filaments making tubes or rods of vorticity, then says the 4D analogue is a collection of vortex **sheets**, with rotation proceeding out of our three-space into the fourth dimension and back. fileciteturn18file2L149-L186

Then he asks what observable phenomenon corresponds to it.

His answer is: **electric current**.

Not metaphorically. He says the closed-circuit requirement is what one would expect from a four-dimensional vortex, interprets the field enclosed by the conductor as the region of action, and proposes rotation of the ether through the fourth dimension as the mechanism. fileciteturn18file2L188-L212

It gets even closer. Positive and negative electricity are assigned two different kinds of **four-dimensional double rotation**. Combining them produces a vortex about an axial surface; the conductor acts as the boundary on which the vortex terminates. Hinton describes the current as a “vortex sheet” whose edge follows the conducting circuit. fileciteturn18file0L10-L49

And he is explicitly thinking in terms of the kind of boundary mechanics we've just spent several turns discussing. His vortex has to close on itself or terminate on an internal/external boundary; in four dimensions the line-axis becomes a plane-axis and its boundary becomes the rim of the vortex sheet. fileciteturn18file9L698-L723

Even the sphere construction we were just fooling with has an eerie predecessor here. Hinton takes a spherical shell, gives its matter a small fourth-dimensional thickness, and considers portions rotating through the fourth direction so that the sphere can effectively turn inside out. fileciteturn18file15L1073-L1111 He also explicitly says that if four-dimensional space exists, ordinary three-dimensional material bodies would have some fourth-dimensional thickness; purely 3D bodies would be abstractions. fileciteturn17file5L366-L379

And his argument for looking for the fourth dimension is mechanical rather than merely geometrical: if motions occur that three-dimensional mechanics cannot explain, and those motions follow naturally from minute four-dimensional motions of matter or ether, that would constitute evidence for the extra-dimensional hypothesis. fileciteturn18file7L552-L584

So I would now say something considerably stronger than I did before:

\[
\boxed{\text{There really was an explicit 4D mechanical-vortex/filament physics program before relativity.}}
\]

Not merely “higher-dimensional speculation.” Filaments, vortices, closed boundaries, fluids, rotations, polarity, fields, electricity, and finite fourth-dimensional material extension are all right there.

And your other historical claim gets a surprisingly direct piece of evidence from the Moszkowski book.

In a conversation presented as involving Einstein, Moszkowski explicitly raises the problem that Einsteinian four-dimensionality shares terminology with the “four-dimensionality of certain spiritistic pseudo-philosophers,” says occult circles were already invoking Einstein in connection with mediumistic experiments “flavoured with four-dimensionality,” and Einstein refuses to engage those people. fileciteturn20file4L318-L354

That is almost exactly the reputational collision you were talking about.

It does **not** yet establish:

\[
\text{spiritualists appropriated 4D}
\Rightarrow
\text{physicists deliberately renamed the program topology}.
\]

We would need correspondence, reviews, disciplinary rhetoric, textbooks, etc. to show that causal step.

But we now have direct primary-source evidence for both ends:

\[
\begin{array}{c}
\text{late-19th/early-20th c. explicit physical 4D mechanics}\\
\text{vortices + filaments + ether + fields + rotations}
\end{array}
\]

and simultaneously

\[
\begin{array}{c}
\text{“fourth dimension” becomes culturally entangled}\\
\text{with spiritism/mediums/occult claims}.
\end{array}
\]

Then, immediately afterward, the respectable physics vocabulary does indeed become Minkowski spacetime, tensors, fields, internal symmetries, topology, homotopy, knot theory, gauge connections, configuration spaces, etc.

And Moszkowski gives us another fascinating transition marker. He describes the Michelson–Morley failure as producing a “void” in the old ether picture, followed by Lorentz, Minkowski and Einstein. fileciteturn20file10L717-L768 Elsewhere he describes the emerging relativistic view as recognizing three-dimensionality as an abstraction from a four-dimensional world. fileciteturn20file3L238-L260

So there is a plausible historical fork around exactly the period you're pointing to:

\[
\text{Kelvin/Helmholtz/Hinton}
\]

\[
\text{4D medium + mechanical vortex structure}
\]

then

\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
&\text{crisis of mechanical ether}&\\
\swarrow&&\searrow\\
\text{relativistic 4D spacetime}&&\text{topology/knot algebra}
\end{array}
\]

and much later those branches start recombining through gauge theory, holonomy, Chern–Simons, spin networks, anyons, braided ribbons, and topological matter.

That is starting to look less like an analogy and more like an actual genealogy worth reconstructing.

There is another remarkable bridge to the modern braid material. Hinton explicitly distinguishes a purely representational use of four-dimensional constructions from a proposed physical one. He says engineers use diagrams that are not themselves pictures of existing things but represent relations; he then says four-dimensional constructions can be used in exactly that way **in addition to** the physical hypothesis he has just developed. fileciteturn18file3L274-L290

So even Hinton already has the distinction we've been hammering on:

\[
\text{4D as representational grammar}
\neq
\text{4D as physical-mechanical hypothesis}.
\]

That makes the later history especially interesting, because the mathematical branch can keep developing the grammar after physicists abandon or suspend the mechanical referent.

Then a century later people discover that the grammar describes actual measurable phenomena extraordinarily well.

That is your “stamp collection.”

The stamps survived even when the proposed album did not.

And then we get things like the modern Helon/ribbon work we just examined, where the stamps start being assembled back into candidate particle structures.

One more item from your pile matters philosophically rather than historically. *Gödel, Escher, Bach* is largely about formal systems, recursion, self-reference and the distinction between meaning and symbol manipulation; its overview explicitly treats infinite regress in reasoning and recursive nested structures as structures of formal description. fileciteturn16file3L78-L94 fileciteturn16file3L121-L137 So it belongs beside our earlier infinity discussion, but I wouldn't put it in the direct 4D-filament genealogy.

The Hinton material, though, absolutely belongs there.

In fact, the sentence I would now put at the top of our historical working document is:

\[
\boxed{
\textbf{By 1904–06 Hinton was explicitly attempting a finite mechanical physics of}
\\
\textbf{four-dimensional vortex structures, boundaries, double rotations,}
\\
\textbf{electromagnetism, and matter, extending the Kelvin–Helmholtz vortex program.}
}
\]

That is not SAT/H(s)H, and it doesn't validate SAT/H(s)H. But in terms of **structural ancestry**, this is no longer “hey, somebody used a knot once.”

This is genuinely close enough that I think we should reconstruct the whole line from Helmholtz → Kelvin/Tait → Newcomb/Hinton → Minkowski/Einstein → Artin/knot topology → gauge/holonomy/Chern–Simons → anyons/spin networks/Helon, and mark exactly where the mechanical object disappears, where it survives mathematically, and where it begins re-entering physics.

That could answer the historical question we've been circling with much more precision than “it went out of fashion.”
GEB has a place. It's hard-ish to explain. But not that hard. Here's some other older material, I suspect almost the counter-argument. But maybe not monolithically

[L68] THE book which is herewith presented to the public has few
[L69] contemporaries of a like nature; it deserves special attention inasmuch
[L70] as it is illuminated by the name _Albert Einstein_, and deals with a
[L71] personality whose achievements mark a turning-point in the development
[L72] of science.

[L74] Every investigator, who enlarges our vision by some permanent discovery,
[L75] becomes a milestone on the road to knowledge, and great would be the
[L76] array of those who have defined the stages of the long avenue of
[L77] research. One might endeavour, then, to decide to whom mankind owes the
[L78] greater debt, to Euclid or to Archimedes, to Plato or to Aristotle, to
[L79] Descartes or to Pascal, to Lagrange or to Gauss, to Kepler or to
[L80] Copernicus. One would have to investigate--as far as this is
[L81] possible--in how far each outstanding personality was in advance of his
[L82] time, whether some contemporary might not have had the equal good
[L83] fortune to stumble on the same discovery, and whether, indeed, the time
[L84] had not come when it must inevitably have been revealed. If we then
[L85] further selected only those who saw far beyond their own age into the
[L86] inimitable future of knowledge, this great number of celebrities would
[L87] be considerably diminished. We should glance away from the milestones,
[L88] and fix our gaze on the larger signs that denote the lines of
[L89] demarcation of the sciences, and among them we should find the name of
[L90] Albert Einstein. We may find it necessary to proceed to a still more
[L91] rigorous classification; Science, herself, may rearrange her
[L92] chronological table later, and reckon the time at which Einstein's
[L93] doctrine first appeared as the beginning of an important era.

[L95] This would in itself justify--nay, render imperative--the writing of
[L96] a book _about_ Einstein. But this need has already been satisfied on
[L97] several occasions, and there is even now a considerable amount of
[L98] literature about him. At the end of this generation we shall possess a
[L99] voluminous library composed entirely of books about Einstein. The
[L100] present book will differ from most of these, in that Einstein here
[L101] occurs not only objectively but also subjectively. We shall, of course,
[L102] speak of him here too, but we shall also hear him speak himself, and
[L103] there can be no doubt that all who are devoted to the world thought can
[L104] but gain by listening to him.

[L75] GENERAL CONCLUSIONS ON PART THIRD
[L76]
[L77] The principles of mechanics, then, present themselves to us under two
[L78] different aspects. On the one hand, they are truths founded on
[L79] experiment and approximately verified so far as concerns almost isolated
[L80] systems. On the other hand, they are postulates applicable to the
[L81] totality of the universe and regarded as rigorously true.
[L82]
[L83] If these postulates possess a generality and a certainty which are
[L84] lacking to the experimental verities whence they are drawn, this is
[L85] because they reduce in the last analysis to a mere convention which we
[L86] have the right to make, because we are certain beforehand that no
[L87] experiment can ever contradict it.
[L88]
[L89] This convention, however, is not absolutely arbitrary; it does not
[L90] spring from our caprice; we adopt it because certain experiments have
[L91] shown us that it would be convenient.
[L92]
[L93] Thus is explained how experiment could make the principles of mechanics,
[L94] and yet why it can not overturn them.
[L95]
[L96] Compare with geometry: The fundamental propositions of geometry, as for
[L97] instance Euclid's postulate, are nothing more than conventions, and it
[L98] is just as unreasonable to inquire whether they are true or false as to
[L99] ask whether the metric system is true or false.
[L100]
[L101] Only, these conventions are convenient, and it is certain experiments
[L102] which have taught us that.
[L103]
[L104] At first blush, the analogy is complete; the rôle of experiment seems
[L105] the same. One will therefore be tempted to say: Either mechanics must be
[L106] regarded as an experimental science, and then the same must hold for
[L107] geometry; or else, on the contrary, geometry is a deductive science, and
[L108] then one may say as much of mechanics.
[L109]
[L110] Such a conclusion would be illegitimate. The experiments which have led
[L111] us to adopt as more convenient the fundamental conventions of geometry
[L112] bear on objects which have nothing in common with those geometry
[L113] studies; they bear on the properties of solid bodies, on the rectilinear
[L114] propagation of light. They are experiments of mechanics, experiments of
[L115] optics; they can not in any way be regarded as experiments of geometry.
[L116] And even the principal reason why our geometry seems convenient to us is
[L117] that the different parts of our body, our eye, our limbs, have the
[L118] properties of solid bodies. On this account, our fundamental experiments
[L119] are preeminently physiological experiments, which bear, not on space
[L120] which is the object the geometer must study, but on his body, that is
[L121] to say, on the instrument he must use for this study.
[L122]
[L123] On the contrary, the fundamental conventions of mechanics, and the
[L124] experiments which prove to us that they are convenient, bear on exactly
[L125] the same objects or on analogous objects. The conventional and general
[L126] principles are the natural and direct generalization of the experimental
[L127] and particular principles.
[L128]
[L129] Let it not be said that thus I trace artificial frontiers between the
[L130] sciences; that if I separate by a barrier geometry properly so called
[L131] from the study of solid bodies, I could just as well erect one between
[L132] experimental mechanics and the conventional mechanics of the general
[L133] principles. In fact, who does not see that in separating these two
[L134] sciences I mutilate them both, and that what will remain of conventional
[L135] mechanics when it shall be isolated will be only a very small thing and
[L136] can in no way be compared to that superb body of doctrine called
[L137] geometry?
[L138]
[L139] One sees now why the teaching of mechanics should remain experimental.
[L140]
[L141] Only thus can it make us comprehend the genesis of the science, and that
[L142] is indispensable for the complete understanding of the science itself.

[L205] Mach's ether not only _conditions_ the
[L206] behaviour of inert masses, but _is also conditioned_ in its state
[L207] by them.
[L208]
[L209] Mach's idea finds its full development in the ether of the general
[L210] theory of relativity. According to this theory the metrical
[L211] qualities of the continuum of space-time differ in the environment
[L212] of different points of space-time, and are partly conditioned by the
[L213] matter existing outside of the territory under consideration.  This
[L214] space-time variability of the reciprocal relations of the standards
[L215] of space and time, or, perhaps, the recognition of the fact that
[L216] "empty space" in its physical relation is neither homogeneous nor
[L217] isotropic, compelling us to describe its state by ten functions (the
[L218] gravitation potentials g_(mn)), has, I think, finally disposed of
[L219] the view that space is physically empty. But therewith the
[L220] conception of the ether has again acquired an intelligible content,
[L221] although this content differs widely from that of the ether of the
[L222] mechanical undulatory theory of light.  The ether of the general
[L223] theory of relativity is a medium which is itself devoid of _all_
[L224] mechanical and kinematical qualities, but helps to determine
[L225] mechanical (and electromagnetic) events.
[L226]
[L227] What is fundamentally new in the ether of the general theory of
[L228] relativity as opposed to the ether of Lorentz consists in this, that
[L229] the state of the former is at every place determined by connections
[L230] with the matter and the state of the ether in neighbouring places,
[L231] which are amenable to law in the form of differential equations;
[L232] whereas the state of the Lorentzian ether in the absence of
[L233] electromagnetic fields is conditioned by nothing outside itself,
[L234] and is everywhere the same. The ether of the general theory of
[L235] relativity is transmuted conceptually into the ether of Lorentz if
[L236] we substitute constants for the functions of space which describe
[L237] the former, disregarding the causes which condition its state.
[L238] Thus we may also say, I think, that the ether of the general theory
[L239] of relativity is the outcome of the Lorentzian ether, through
[L240] relativation.
[L241]
[L242] As to the part which the new ether is to play in the physics of
[L243] the future we are not yet clear. We know that it determines the
[L244] metrical relations in the space-time continuum, e.g. the configurative
[L245] possibilities of solid bodies as well as the gravitational fields;
[L246] but we do not know whether it has an essential share in the structure
[L247] of the electrical elementary particles constituting matter. Nor do
[L248] we know whether it is only in the proximity of ponderable masses
[L249] that its structure differs essentially from that of the Lorentzian
[L250] ether; whether the geometry of spaces of cosmic extent is approximately
[L251] Euclidean. But we can assert by reason of the relativistic equations
[L252] of gravitation that there must be a departure from Euclidean
[L253] relations, with spaces of cosmic order of magnitude, if there exists
[L254] a positive mean density, no matter how small, of the matter in the
[L255] universe. In this case the universe must of necessity be spatially
[L256] unbounded and of finite magnitude, its magnitude being determined
[L257] by the value of that mean density.
[L258]
[L259] If we consider the gravitational field and the electromagnetic field
[L260] from the stand-point of the ether hypothesis, we find a remarkable
[L261] difference between the two. There can be no space nor any part
[L262] of space without gravitational potentials; for these confer upon
[L263] space its metrical qualities, without which it cannot be imagined
[L264] at all. The existence of the gravitational field is inseparably
[L265] bound up with the existence of space.

[L312] gases than to electrodynamics. In general, it appears to me that the original differences

[L324] III
[L325]
[L326] _The Principle of Reaction_
[L327]
[L328] Let us see what the principle of the equality of action and reaction
[L329] becomes in the theory of Lorentz. Consider an electron _A_ which for any
[L330] cause begins to move; it produces a perturbation in the ether; at the
[L331] end of a certain time, this perturbation reaches another electron _B_,
[L332] which will be disturbed from its position of equilibrium. In these
[L333] conditions there can not be equality between action and reaction, at
[L334] least if we do not consider the ether, but only the electrons, _which
[L335] alone are observable_, since our matter is made of electrons.
[L336]
[L337] In fact it is the electron _A_ which has disturbed the electron _B_;
[L338] even in case the electron _B_ should react upon _A_, this reaction could
[L339] be equal to the action, but in no case simultaneous, since the electron
[L340] _B_ can begin to move only after a certain time, necessary for the
[L341] propagation. Submitting the problem to a more exact calculation, we
[L342] reach the following result: Suppose a Hertz discharger placed at the
[L343] focus of a parabolic mirror to which it is mechanically attached; this
[L344] discharger emits electromagnetic waves, and the mirror reflects all
[L345] these waves in the same direction; the discharger therefore will radiate
[L346] energy in a determinate direction. Well, the calculation shows that _the
[L347] discharger recoils_ like a cannon which has shot out a projectile. In
[L348] the case of the cannon, the recoil is the natural result of the equality
[L349] of action and reaction. The cannon recoils because the projectile upon
[L350] which it has acted reacts upon it. But here it is no longer the same.
[L351] What has been sent out is no longer a material projectile: it is energy,
[L352] and energy has no mass: it has no counterpart. And, in place of a
[L353] discharger, we could have considered just simply a lamp with a reflector
[L354] concentrating its rays in a single direction.
[L355]
[L356] It is true that, if the energy sent out from the discharger or from the
[L357] lamp meets a material object, this object receives a mechanical push as
[L358] if it had been hit by a real projectile, and this push will be equal to
[L359] the recoil of the discharger and of the lamp, if no energy has been lost
[L360] on the way and if the object absorbs the whole of the energy. Therefore
[L361] one is tempted to say that there still is compensation between the
[L362] action and the reaction. But this compensation, even should it be
[L363] complete, is always belated. It never happens if the light, after
[L364] leaving its source, wanders through interstellar spaces without ever
[L365] meeting a material body; it is incomplete, if the body it strikes is not
[L366] perfectly absorbent.
[L367]
[L368] Are these mechanical actions too small to be measured, or are they
[L369] accessible to experiment? These actions are nothing other than those due
[L370] to the _Maxwell-Bartholi_ pressures; Maxwell had predicted these
[L371] pressures from calculations relative to electrostatics and magnetism;
[L372] Bartholi reached the same result by thermodynamic considerations.
[L373]
[L374] This is how the _tails of comets_ are explained. Little particles detach
[L375] themselves from the nucleus of the comet; they are struck by the light
[L376] of the sun, which pushes them back as would a rain of projectiles coming
[L377] from the sun. The mass of these particles is so little that this
[L378] repulsion sweeps it away against the Newtonian attraction; so in moving
[L379] away from the sun they form the tails.

[L483] That would save Newton's principle, but that is
[L484] not true. If energy in its diffusion remained always attached to some
[L485] material substratum, then matter in motion would carry along light with
[L486] it, and Fizeau has demonstrated that it does nothing of the sort, at
[L487] least for air. Michelson and Morley have since confirmed this. It might
[L488] be supposed also that the movements of matter proper are exactly
[L489] compensated by those of the ether; but that would lead us to the same
[L490] reflections as before now. The principle so understood will explain
[L491] everything, since, whatever might be the visible movements, we always
[L492] could imagine hypothetical movements which compensate them. But if it is
[L493] able to explain everything, this is because it does not enable us to
[L494] foresee anything; it does not enable us to decide between the different
[L495] possible hypotheses, since it explains everything beforehand. It
[L496] therefore becomes useless.
[L497]
[L498] And then the suppositions that it would be necessary to make on the
[L499] movements of the ether are not very satisfactory. If the electric
[L500] charges double, it would be natural to imagine that the velocities of
[L501] the diverse atoms of ether double also; but, for the compensation, it
[L502] would be necessary that the mean velocity of the ether quadruple.
[L503]
[L504] This is why I have long thought that these consequences of theory,
[L505] contrary to Newton's principle, would end some day by being abandoned,
[L506] and yet the recent experiments on the movements of the electrons issuing
[L507] from radium seem rather to confirm them.
[L508]
[L509] _Lavoisier's Principle._--I arrive at the principle of Lavoisier on the
[L510] conservation of mass. Certainly, this is one not to be touched without
[L511] unsettling all mechanics. And now certain persons think that it seems
[L512] true to us only because in mechanics merely moderate velocities are
[L513] considered, but that it would cease to be true for bodies animated by
[L514] velocities comparable to that of light. Now these velocities are
[L515] believed at present to have been realized; the cathode rays and those of
[L516] radium may be formed of very minute particles or of electrons which are
[L517] displaced with velocities smaller no doubt than that of light, but which
[L518] might be its one tenth or one third.
[L519]
[L520] These rays can be deflected, whether by an electric field, or by a
[L521] magnetic field, and we are able, by comparing these deflections, to
[L522] measure at the same time the velocity of the electrons and their mass
[L523] (or rather the relation of their mass to their charge). But when it was
[L524] seen that these velocities approached that of light, it was decided that
[L525] a correction was necessary. These molecules, being electrified, can not
[L526] be displaced without agitating the ether; to put them in motion it is
[L527] necessary to overcome a double inertia, that of the molecule itself and
[L528] that of the ether. The total or apparent mass that one measures is
[L529] composed, therefore, of two parts: the real or mechanical mass of the
[L530] molecule and the electrodynamic mass representing the inertia of the
[L531] ether.

[L650] To discuss this opinion, we should first ask ourselves what is the
[L651] nature of the geometric axioms.
[L652]
[L653] Are they synthetic _a priori_ judgments, as Kant said?
[L654]
[L655] They would then impose themselves upon us with such force that we could
[L656] not conceive the contrary proposition, nor build upon it a theoretic
[L657] edifice. There would be no non-Euclidean geometry.
[L658]
[L659] To be convinced of it take a veritable synthetic _a priori_ judgment,
[L660] the following, for instance, of which we have seen the preponderant rôle
[L661] in the first chapter:
[L662]
[L663] _If a theorem is true for the number 1, and if it has been proved that
[L664] it is true of n + 1 provided it is true of n, it will be true of all the
[L665] positive whole numbers._
[L666]
[L667] Then try to escape from that and, denying this proposition, try to found
[L668] a false arithmetic analogous to non-Euclidean geometry--it can not be
[L669] done; one would even be tempted at first blush to regard these judgments
[L670] as analytic.
[L671]
[L672] Moreover, resuming our fiction of animals without thickness, we can
[L673] hardly admit that these beings, if their minds are like ours, would
[L674] adopt the Euclidean geometry which would be contradicted by all their
[L675] experience.
[L676]
[L677] Should we therefore conclude that the axioms of geometry are
[L678] experimental verities? But we do not experiment on ideal straights or
[L679] circles; it can only be done on material objects. On what then could be
[L680] based experiments which should serve as foundation for geometry? The
[L681] answer is easy.
[L682]
[L683] We have seen above that we constantly reason as if the geometric figures
[L684] behaved like solids. What geometry would borrow from experience would
[L685] therefore be the properties of these bodies. The properties of light and
[L686] its rectilinear propagation have also given rise to some of the
[L687] propositions of geometry, and in particular those of projective
[L688] geometry, so that from this point of view one would be tempted to say
[L689] that metric geometry is the study of solids, and projective, that of
[L690] light.
[L691]
[L692] But a difficulty remains, and it is insurmountable. If geometry were an
[L693] experimental science, it would not be an exact science, it would be
[L694] subject to a continual revision. Nay, it would from this very day be
[L695] convicted of error, since we know that there is no rigorously rigid
[L696] solid.
[L697]
[L698] The _axioms of geometry therefore are neither synthetic_ a priori
[L699] _judgments nor experimental facts_.
[L700]
[L701] They are _conventions_; our choice among all possible conventions is
[L702] _guided_ by experimental facts; but it remains _free_ and is limited
[L703] only by the necessity of avoiding all contradiction. Thus it is that the
[L704] postulates can remain _rigorously_ true even though the experimental
[L705] laws which have determined their adoption are only approximative.
[L706]
[L707] In other words, _the axioms of geometry_ (I do not speak of those of
[L708] arithmetic) _are merely disguised definitions_.
[L709]
[L710] Then what are we to think of that question: Is the Euclidean geometry
[L711] true?
[L712]
[L713] It has no meaning.
[L714]
[L715] As well ask whether the metric system is true and the old measures
[L716] false; whether Cartesian coordinates are true and polar coordinates
[L717] false. One geometry can not be more true than another; it can only be
[L718] _more convenient_.
[L719]
[L720] Now, Euclidean geometry is, and will remain, the most convenient:

[L959] Thenceforth he
[L960] was certain of the possibility of a mechanical explanation.
[L961]
[L962] If he had explained this idea at the beginning of his book instead of
[L963] relegating it to an obscure part of the second volume, it would not have
[L964] escaped the majority of readers.
[L965]
[L966] If, then, a phenomenon admits of a complete mechanical explanation, it
[L967] will admit of an infinity of others, that will render an account equally
[L968] well of all the particulars revealed by experiment.
[L969]
[L970] And this is confirmed by the history of every branch of physics; in
[L971] optics, for instance, Fresnel believed vibration to be perpendicular to
[L972] the plane of polarization; Neumann regarded it as parallel to this
[L973] plane. An 'experimentum crucis' has long been sought which would enable
[L974] us to decide between these two theories, but it has not been found.
[L975]
[L976] In the same way, without leaving the domain of electricity, we may
[L977] ascertain that the theory of two fluids and that of the single fluid
[L978] both account in a fashion equally satisfactory for all the observed laws
[L979] of electrostatics.
[L980]
[L981] All these facts are easily explicable, thanks to the properties of the
[L982] equations of Lagrange which I have just recalled.
[L983]
[L984] It is easy now to comprehend what is Maxwell's fundamental idea.
[L985]
[L986] To demonstrate the possibility of a mechanical explanation of
[L987] electricity, we need not preoccupy ourselves with finding this
[L988] explanation itself; it suffices us to know the expression of the two
[L989] functions _T_ and _U_, which are the two parts of energy, to form with
[L990] these two functions the equations of Lagrange and then to compare these
[L991] equations with the experimental laws.
[L992]
[L993] Among all these possible explanations, how make a choice for which the
[L994] aid of experiment fails us? A day will come perhaps when physicists will
[L995] not interest themselves in these questions, inaccessible to positive
[L996] methods, and will abandon them to the metaphysicians. This day has not
[L997] yet arrived; man does not resign himself so easily to be forever
[L998] ignorant of the foundation of things.
[L999]
[L1000] Our choice can therefore be further guided only by considerations where
[L1001] the part of personal appreciation is very great; there are, however,
[L1002] solutions that all the world will reject because of their whimsicality,
[L1003] and others that all the world will prefer because of their simplicity.
[L1004]
[L1005] In what concerns electricity and magnetism, Maxwell abstains from making
[L1006] any choice. It is not that he systematically disdains all that is
[L1007] unattainable by positive methods; the time he has devoted to the kinetic
[L1008] theory of gases sufficiently proves that. I will add that if, in his
[L1009] great work, he develops no complete explanation, he had previously
[L1010] attempted to give one in an article in the _Philosophical Magazine_. The
[L1011] strangeness and the complexity of the hypotheses he had been obliged to
[L1012] make had led him afterwards to give this up.
[L1013]
[L1014] The same spirit is found throughout the whole work. What is essential,
[L1015] that is to say what must remain common to all theories, is made
[L1016] prominent; all that would only be suitable to a particular theory is
[L1017] nearly always passed over in silence. Thus the reader finds himself in
[L1018] the presence of a form almost devoid of matter, which he is at first
[L1019] tempted to take for a fugitive shadow not to be grasped. But the efforts
[L1020] to which he is thus condemned force him to think and he ends by
[L1021] comprehending what was often rather artificial in the theoretic
[L1022] constructs he had previously only wondered at.

[L10] The consideration of the general flux of events leads to this analysis
[L11] into an underlying eternal energy in whose nature there stands an
[L12] envisagement of the realm of all eternal objects. Such an envisagement
[L13] is the ground of the individualised thoughts which emerge as
[L14] thought-aspects grasped within the life-history of the subtler and more
[L15] complex enduring patterns. Also in the nature of the eternal activity
[L16] there must stand an envisagement of all values to be obtained by a real
[L17] togetherness of eternal objects, as envisaged in ideal situations. Such
[L18] ideal situations, apart from any reality, are devoid of intrinsic value,
[L19] but are valuable as elements in purpose. The individualised prehension
[L20] into individual events of aspects of these ideal situations takes the
[L21] form of individualised thoughts, and as such has intrinsic value. Thus
[L22] value arises because there is now a real togetherness of the ideal
[L23] aspects, as in thought, with the actual aspects, as in process of
[L24] occurrence. Accordingly no value is to be ascribed to the underlying
[L25] activity as divorced from the matter-of-fact events of the real world.
[L26]
[L27] Finally, to sum up this train of thought, the underlying activity, as
[L28] conceived apart from the fact of realisation, has three types of
[L29] envisagement. These are: first, the envisagement of eternal objects;
[L30] secondly, the envisagement of possibilities of value in respect to the
[L31] synthesis of eternal objects; and lastly, the envisagement of the actual
[L32] matter of fact which must enter into the total situation which is
[L33] achievable by the addition of the future. But in abstraction from
[L34] actuality, the eternal activity is divorced from value. For the
[L35] actuality is the value. The individual perception arising from enduring
[L36] objects will vary in its individual depth and width according to the way
[L37] in which the pattern dominates its own route. It may represent the
[L38] faintest ripple differentiating the general substrate energy; or, in the
[L39] other extreme, it may rise to conscious thought, which includes poising
[L40] before self-conscious judgment the abstract possibilities of value
[L41] inherent in various situations of ideal togetherness. The intermediate
[L42] cases will group round the individual perception as envisaging (without
[L43] self-consciousness) that one immediate possibility of attainment which
[L44] represents the closest analogy to its own immediate past, having regard
[L45] to the actual aspects which are there for prehension. The laws of
[L46] physics represent the harmonised adjustment of development which results
[L47] from this unique principle of determination. Thus dynamics is dominated
[L48] by a principle of least action, whose detailed character has to be
[L49] learnt from observation.
[L50]
[L51] The atomic material entities which are considered in physical science
[L52] are merely these individual enduring entities, conceived in abstraction
[L53] from everything except what concerns their mutual interplay in
[L54] determining each other’s historical routes of life-history. Such
[L55] entities are partially formed by the inheritance of aspects from their
[L56] own past. But they are also partially formed by the aspects of other
[L57] events forming their environments. The laws of physics are the laws
[L58] declaring how the entities mutually react among themselves. For physics
[L59] these laws are arbitrary, because that science has abstracted from what
[L60] the entities are in themselves. We have seen that this fact of what the
[L61] entities are in themselves is liable to modification by their
[L62] environments. Accordingly, the assumption that no modification of these
[L63] laws is to be looked for in environments, which have any striking
[L64] difference from the environments for which the laws have been observed
[L65] to hold, is very unsafe. The physical entities may be modified in very
[L66] essential ways, so far as these laws are concerned.

[L76] But it is the observer’s body that we want,
[L77] and not his mind. Even this body is only useful as an example of a very
[L78] familiar form of apparatus. On the whole, it is better to concentrate
[L79] attention on Michelson’s interferometer, and to leave Michelson’s body
[L80] and Michelson’s mind out of the picture. The question is, why did the
[L81] interferometer have black bands on its screen, and why did not these
[L82] bands slightly shift as the instrument turned. The new relativity
[L83] associates space and time with an intimacy not hitherto contemplated;
[L84] and presupposes that their separation in concrete fact can be achieved
[L85] by alternative modes of abstraction, yielding alternative meanings. But
[L86] each mode of abstraction is directing attention to something which is in
[L87] nature; and thereby is isolating it for the purpose of contemplation.
[L88] The fact relevant to experiment, is the relevance of the interferometer
[L89] to just one among the many alternative systems of these spatio-temporal
[L90] relations which hold between natural entities.
[L91]
[L92] What we must now ask of philosophy is to give us an interpretation of
[L93] the status in nature of space and time, so that the possibility of
[L94] alternative meanings is preserved. These lectures are not suited for the
[L95] elaboration of details; but there is no difficulty in pointing out where
[L96] to look for the origin of the discrimination between space and time. I
[L97] am presupposing the organic theory of nature, which I have outlined as a
[L98] basis for a thoroughgoing objectivism.
[L99]
[L100] An event is the grasping into unity of a pattern of aspects. The
[L101] effectiveness of an event beyond itself arises from the aspects of
[L102] itself which go to form the prehended unities of other events. Except
[L103] for the systematic aspects of geometrical shape, this effectiveness is
[L104] trivial, if the mirrored pattern attaches merely to the event as one
[L105] whole. If the pattern endures throughout the successive parts of the
[L106] event, and also exhibits itself in the whole, so that the event is the
[L107] life history of the pattern, then in virtue of that enduring pattern the
[L108] event gains in external effectiveness. For its own effectiveness is
[L109] reënforced by the analogous aspects of all its successive parts. The
[L110] event constitutes a patterned value with a permanence inherent
[L111] throughout its own parts; and by reason of this inherent endurance the
[L112] event is important for the modification of its environment.
[L113]
[L114] It is in this endurance of pattern that time differentiates itself from
[L115] space. The pattern is spatially _now_; and this temporal determination
[L116] constitutes its relation to each partial event. For it is reproduced in
[L117] this temporal succession of these spatial parts of its own life. I mean
[L118] that this particular rule of temporal order allows the pattern to be
[L119] reproduced in each temporal slice of its history. So to speak, each
[L120] enduring object discovers in nature and requires from nature a principle
[L121] discriminating space from time. Apart from the fact of an enduring
[L122] pattern this principle might be there, but it would be latent and
[L123] trivial. Thus the importance of space as against time, and of time as
[L124] against space, has developed with the development of enduring organisms.
[L125] Enduring objects are significant of a differentiation of space from time
[L126] in respect to the patterns ingredient within events; and conversely the
[L127] differentiation of space from time in the patterns ingredient within
[L128] events expresses the patience of the community of events for enduring
[L129] objects. There might be the community without objects, but there could
[L130] not be the enduring objects without the community with its peculiar
[L131] patience for them.
[L132]
[L133] It is very necessary that this point should not be misunderstood.

[L143] Accordingly, consciousness will be the function of knowing. But what is
[L144] known is already a prehension of aspects of the one real universe. These
[L145] aspects are aspects of other events as mutually modifying, each the
[L146] others. In the pattern of aspects they stand in their pattern of mutual
[L147] relatedness.
[L148]
[L149] The aboriginal data in terms of which the pattern weaves itself are the
[L150] aspects of shapes, of sense-objects, and of other eternal objects whose
[L151] self-identity is not dependent on the flux of things. Wherever such
[L152] objects have ingression into the general flux, they interpret events,
[L153] each to the other. They are here in the perceiver; but, as perceived by
[L154] him, they convey for him something of the total flux which is beyond
[L155] himself. The subject-object relation takes its origin in the double rôle
[L156] of these eternal objects. They are modifications of the subject, but
[L157] only in their character of conveying aspects of other subjects in the
[L158] community of the universe. Thus no individual subject can have
[L159] independent reality, since it is a prehension of limited aspects of
[L160] subjects other than itself.
[L161]
[L162] The technical phrase ‘subject-object’ is a bad term for the fundamental
[L163] situation disclosed in experience. It is really reminiscent of the
[L164] Aristotelian ‘subject-predicate.’ It already presupposes the
[L165] metaphysical doctrine of diverse subjects qualified by their private
[L166] predicates. This is the doctrine of subjects with private worlds of
[L167] experience. If this be granted, there is no escape from solipsism. The
[L168] point is that the phrase ‘subject-object’ indicates a fundamental entity
[L169] underlying the objects. Thus the ‘objects,’ as thus conceived, are
[L170] merely the ghosts of Aristotelian predicates. The primary situation
[L171] disclosed in cognitive experience is ‘ego-object amid objects.’ By this
[L172] I mean that the primary fact is an impartial world transcending the
[L173] ‘here-now’ which marks the ego-object, and transcending the ‘now’ which
[L174] is the spatial world of simultaneous realisation. It is a world also
[L175] including the actuality of the past, and the limited potentiality of the
[L176] future, together with the complete world of abstract potentiality, the
[L177] realm of eternal objects, which transcends, and finds exemplification in
[L178] and comparison with, the actual course of realisation. The ego-object,
[L179] as consciousness here-now, is conscious of its experient essence as
[L180] constituted by its internal relatedness to the world of realities, and
[L181] to the world of ideas. But the ego-object, in being thus constituted, is
[L182] within the world of realities, and exhibits itself as an organism
[L183] requiring the ingression of ideas for the purpose of this status among
[L184] realities. This question of consciousness must be reserved for treatment
[L185] on another occasion.
[L186]
[L187] The point to be made for the purposes of the present discussion is that
[L188] a philosophy of nature as organic must start at the opposite end to that
[L189] requisite for a materialistic philosophy. The materialistic starting
[L190] point is from independently existing substances, matter and mind. The
[L191] matter suffers modifications of its external relations of locomotion,
[L192] and the mind suffers modifications of its contemplated objects. There
[L193] are, in this materialistic theory, two sorts of independent substances,
[L194] each qualified by their appropriate passions. The organic starting point
[L195] is from the analysis of process as the realisation of events disposed in
[L196] an interlocked community. The event is the unit of things real. The
[L197] emergent enduring pattern is the stabilisation of the emergent
[L198] achievement so as to become a fact which retains its identity throughout
[L199] the process. It will be noted that endurance is not primarily the
[L200] property of enduring beyond itself, but of enduring within itself.

[L210] Such envisagement might
[L211] reach to the attainment of the poising of alternative values with
[L212] exercise of choice lying outside the physical laws, and expressible only
[L213] in terms of purpose. Apart from such remote possibilities, it remains an
[L214] immediate deduction that an individual entity, whose own life-history is
[L215] a part within the life-history of some larger, deeper, more complete
[L216] pattern, is liable to have aspects of that larger pattern dominating its
[L217] own being, and to experience modifications of that larger pattern
[L218] reflected in itself as modifications of its own being. This is the
[L219] theory of organic mechanism.
[L220]
[L221] According to this theory the evolution of laws of nature is concurrent
[L222] with the evolution of enduring pattern. For the general state of the
[L223] universe, as it now is, partly determines the very essences of the
[L224] entities whose modes of functioning these laws express. The general
[L225] principle is that in a new environment there is an evolution of the old
[L226] entities into new forms.
[L227]
[L228] This rapid outline of a thoroughgoing organic theory of nature enables
[L229] us to understand the chief requisites of the doctrine of evolution. The
[L230] main work, proceeding during this pause at the end of the nineteenth
[L231] century, was the absorption of this doctrine as guiding the methodology
[L232] of all branches of science. By a blindness which is almost judicial as
[L233] being a penalty affixed to hasty, superficial thinking, many religious
[L234] thinkers opposed the new doctrine; although, in truth, a thoroughgoing
[L235] evolutionary philosophy is inconsistent with materialism. The aboriginal
[L236] stuff, or material, from which a materialistic philosophy starts is
[L237] incapable of evolution. This material is in itself the ultimate
[L238] substance. Evolution, on the materialistic theory, is reduced to the
[L239] rôle of being another word for the description of the changes of the
[L240] external relations between portions of matter. There is nothing to
[L241] evolve, because one set of external relations is as good as any other
[L242] set of external relations. There can merely be change, purposeless and
[L243] unprogressive. But the whole point of the modern doctrine is the
[L244] evolution of the complex organisms from antecedent states of less
[L245] complex organisms. The doctrine thus cries aloud for a conception of
[L246] organism as fundamental for nature. It also requires an underlying
[L247] activity—a substantial activity—expressing itself in individual
[L248] embodiments, and evolving in achievements of organism. The organism is a
[L249] unit of emergent value, a real fusion of the characters of eternal
[L250] objects, emerging for its own sake.
[L251]
[L252] Thus in the process of analysing the character of nature in itself, we
[L253] find that the emergence of organisms depends on a selective activity
[L254] which is akin to purpose. The point is that the enduring organisms are
[L255] now the outcome of evolution; and that, beyond these organisms, there is
[L256] nothing else that endures. On the materialistic theory, there is
[L257] material—such as matter or electricity—which endures. On the organic
[L258] theory, the only endurances are structures of activity, and the
[L259] structures are evolved.
[L260]
[L261] Enduring things are thus the outcome of a temporal process; whereas
[L262] eternal things are the elements required for the very being of the
[L263] process. We can give a precise definition of endurance in this way: Let
[L264] an event A be pervaded by an enduring structural pattern. Then A can be
[L265] exhaustively subdivided into a temporal succession of events.

[L275] I also expressed my conviction that if we desired to obtain a more
[L276] fundamental expression of the concrete character of natural fact, the
[L277] element in this scheme which we should first criticise is the concept of
[L278] _simple location_. In view therefore of the importance which this idea
[L279] will assume in these lectures, I will repeat the meaning which I have
[L280] attached to this phrase. To say that a bit of matter has _simple
[L281] location_ means that, in expressing its spatio-temporal relations, it is
[L282] adequate to state that it is where it is, in a definite finite region of
[L283] space, and throughout a definite finite duration of time, apart from any
[L284] essential reference of the relations of that bit of matter to other
[L285] regions of space and to other durations of time. Again, this concept of
[L286] simple location is independent of the controversy between the absolutist
[L287] and the relativist views of space or of time. So long as any theory of
[L288] space, or of time, can give a meaning, either absolute or relative, to
[L289] the idea of a definite region of space, and of a definite duration of
[L290] time, the idea of simple location has a perfectly definite meaning. This
[L291] idea is the very foundation of the seventeenth century scheme of nature.
[L292] Apart from it, the scheme is incapable of expression. I shall argue that
[L293] among the primary elements of nature as apprehended in our immediate
[L294] experience, there is no element whatever which possesses this character
[L295] of simple location. It does not follow, however, that the science of the
[L296] seventeenth century was simply wrong. I hold that by a process of
[L297] constructive abstraction we can arrive at abstractions which are the
[L298] simply-located bits of material, and at other abstractions which are the
[L299] minds included in the scientific scheme. Accordingly, the real error is
[L300] an example of what I have termed: The Fallacy of Misplaced Concreteness.
[L301]
[L302] The advantage of confining attention to a definite group of
[L303] abstractions, is that you confine your thoughts to clear-cut definite
[L304] things, with clear-cut definite relations. Accordingly, if you have a
[L305] logical head, you can deduce a variety of conclusions respecting the
[L306] relationships between these abstract entities. Furthermore, if the
[L307] abstractions are well-founded, that is to say, if they do not abstract
[L308] from everything that is important in experience, the scientific thought
[L309] which confines itself to these abstractions will arrive at a variety of
[L310] important truths relating to our experience of nature. We all know those
[L311] clear-cut trenchant intellects, immovably encased in a hard shell of
[L312] abstractions. They hold you to their abstractions by the sheer grip of
[L313] personality.
[L314]
[L315] The disadvantage of exclusive attention to a group of abstractions,
[L316] however well-founded, is that, by the nature of the case, you have
[L317] abstracted from the remainder of things. In so far as the excluded
[L318] things are important in your experience, your modes of thought are not
[L319] fitted to deal with them. You cannot think without abstractions;
[L320] accordingly, it is of the utmost importance to be vigilant in critically
[L321] revising your _modes_ of abstraction. It is here that philosophy finds
[L322] its niche as essential to the healthy progress of society. It is the
[L323] critic of abstractions. A civilisation which cannot burst through its
[L324] current abstractions is doomed to sterility after a very limited period
[L325] of progress. An active school of philosophy is quite as important for
[L326] the locomotion of ideas, as is an active school of railway engineers for
[L327] the locomotion of fuel.
[L328]
[L329] Sometimes it happens that the service rendered by philosophy is entirely
[L330] obscured by the astonishing success of a scheme of abstractions in
[L331] expressing the dominant interests of an epoch.
