[L341] Thereby, modern philosophy has been ruined. It has oscillated in a
[L342] complex manner between three extremes. There are the dualists, who
[L343] accept matter and mind as on equal basis, and the two varieties of
[L344] monists, those who put mind inside matter, and those who put matter
[L345] inside mind. But this juggling with abstractions can never overcome the
[L346] inherent confusion introduced by the ascription of _misplaced
[L347] concreteness_ to the scientific scheme of the seventeenth century.
[L348]
[L349]
[L350]
[L351]
[L352]                                CHAPTER IV
[L353]
[L354]                          THE EIGHTEENTH CENTURY
[L355]
[L356]
[L357] In so far as the intellectual climates of different epochs can be
[L358] contrasted, the eighteenth century in Europe was the complete antithesis
[L359] to the Middle Ages. The contrast is symbolised by the difference between
[L360] the cathedral of Chartres and the Parisian salons, where D’Alembert
[L361] conversed with Voltaire. The Middle Ages were haunted with the desire to
[L362] rationalise the infinite: the men of the eighteenth century rationalised
[L363] the social life of modern communities, and based their sociological
[L364] theories on an appeal to the facts of nature. The earlier period was the
[L365] age of faith, based upon reason. In the later period, they let sleeping
[L366] dogs lie: it was the age of reason, based upon faith. To illustrate my
[L367] meaning:—St. Anselm would have been distressed if he had failed to find
[L368] a convincing argument for the existence of God, and on this argument he
[L369] based his edifice of faith, whereas Hume based his _Dissertation on the
[L370] Natural History of Religion_ upon his faith in the order of nature. In
[L371] comparing these epochs it is well to remember that reason can err, and
[L372] that faith may be misplaced.
[L373]
[L374] In my previous lecture I traced the evolution, during the seventeenth
[L375] century, of the scheme of scientific ideas which has dominated thought
[L376] ever since. It involves a fundamental duality, with _material_ on the
[L377] one hand, and on the other hand _mind_. In between there lie the
[L378] concepts of life, organism, function, instantaneous reality,
[L379] interaction, order of nature, which collectively form the Achilles heel
[L380] of the whole system.
[L381]
[L382] I also expressed my conviction that if we desired to obtain a more
[L383] fundamental expression of the concrete character of natural fact, the
[L384] element in this scheme which we should first criticise is the concept of
[L385] _simple location_. In view therefore of the importance which this idea
[L386] will assume in these lectures, I will repeat the meaning which I have
[L387] attached to this phrase. To say that a bit of matter has _simple
[L388] location_ means that, in expressing its spatio-temporal relations, it is
[L389] adequate to state that it is where it is, in a definite finite region of
[L390] space, and throughout a definite finite duration of time, apart from any
[L391] essential reference of the relations of that bit of matter to other
[L392] regions of space and to other durations of time. Again, this concept of
[L393] simple location is independent of the controversy between the absolutist
[L394] and the relativist views of space or of time. So long as any theory of
[L395] space, or of time, can give a meaning, either absolute or relative, to
[L396] the idea of a definite region of space, and of a definite duration of
[L397] time, the idea of simple location has a perfectly definite meaning. This
[L398] idea is the very foundation of the seventeenth century scheme of nature.
[L399] Apart from it, the scheme is incapable of expression. I shall argue that
[L400] among the primary elements of nature as apprehended in our immediate
[L401] experience, there is no element whatever which possesses this character
[L402] of simple location.

[L412] If the pattern endures throughout the successive parts of the
[L413] event, and also exhibits itself in the whole, so that the event is the
[L414] life history of the pattern, then in virtue of that enduring pattern the
[L415] event gains in external effectiveness. For its own effectiveness is
[L416] reënforced by the analogous aspects of all its successive parts. The
[L417] event constitutes a patterned value with a permanence inherent
[L418] throughout its own parts; and by reason of this inherent endurance the
[L419] event is important for the modification of its environment.
[L420]
[L421] It is in this endurance of pattern that time differentiates itself from
[L422] space. The pattern is spatially _now_; and this temporal determination
[L423] constitutes its relation to each partial event. For it is reproduced in
[L424] this temporal succession of these spatial parts of its own life. I mean
[L425] that this particular rule of temporal order allows the pattern to be
[L426] reproduced in each temporal slice of its history. So to speak, each
[L427] enduring object discovers in nature and requires from nature a principle
[L428] discriminating space from time. Apart from the fact of an enduring
[L429] pattern this principle might be there, but it would be latent and
[L430] trivial. Thus the importance of space as against time, and of time as
[L431] against space, has developed with the development of enduring organisms.
[L432] Enduring objects are significant of a differentiation of space from time
[L433] in respect to the patterns ingredient within events; and conversely the
[L434] differentiation of space from time in the patterns ingredient within
[L435] events expresses the patience of the community of events for enduring
[L436] objects. There might be the community without objects, but there could
[L437] not be the enduring objects without the community with its peculiar
[L438] patience for them.
[L439]
[L440] It is very necessary that this point should not be misunderstood.
[L441] Endurance means that a pattern which is exhibited in the prehension of
[L442] one event is also exhibited in the prehension of those of its parts
[L443] which are discriminated by a certain rule. It is not true that any part
[L444] of the whole event will yield the same pattern as does the whole. For
[L445] example, consider the total bodily pattern exhibited in the life of a
[L446] human body during one minute. One of the thumbs during the same minute
[L447] is part of the whole bodily event. But the pattern of this part is the
[L448] pattern of the thumb, and is not the pattern of the whole body. Thus
[L449] endurance requires a definite rule for obtaining the parts. In the above
[L450] example, we know at once what the rule is: You must take the life of the
[L451] whole body during any portion of that same minute; for example, during a
[L452] second or a tenth of a second. In other words, the meaning of endurance
[L453] presupposes a meaning for the lapse of time within the spatio-temporal
[L454] continuum.
[L455]
[L456] The question now arises whether all enduring objects discover the same
[L457] principle of differentiation of space from time; or even whether at
[L458] different stages of its own life-history one object may not vary in its
[L459] spatio-temporal discrimination. Up till a few years ago, everyone
[L460] unhesitatingly assumed that there was only one such principle to be
[L461] discovered. Accordingly, in dealing with one object, time would have
[L462] exactly the same meaning in reference to endurance as in dealing with
[L463] the endurance of another object. It would also follow then that spatial
[L464] relations would have one unique meaning. But now it seems that the
[L465] observed effectiveness of objects can only be explained by assuming that
[L466] objects in a state of motion relatively to each other are utilising, for
[L467] their endurance, meanings of space and of time which are not identical
[L468] from one object to another.

[L482] The second passage runs thus:
[L483]
[L484] “This peculiar property of quantities that no part of them is the
[L485] smallest possible part (no part indivisible) is called continuity. Time
[L486] and space are quanta continua, because there is no part of them that is
[L487] not enclosed between limits (points and moments), _no part that is not
[L488] itself again a space or a time. Space consists of spaces only, time of
[L489] times. Points and moments are only limits_, mere places of limitation,
[L490] and as places _presupposing always_ those intuitions which they are
[L491] meant to limit or to determine. Mere places or parts that might be given
[L492] before space or time, could never be compounded into space or time.”
[L493]
[L494] I am in complete agreement with the second extract if ‘time and space’
[L495] is the extensive continuum; but it is inconsistent with its predecessor.
[L496] For Zeno would object that a vicious infinite regress is involved. Every
[L497] part of time involves some smaller part of itself, and so on. Also this
[L498] series regresses backwards ultimately to nothing; since the initial
[L499] moment is without duration and merely marks the relation of contiguity
[L500] to an earlier time. Thus time is impossible, if the two extracts are
[L501] both adhered to. I accept the later, and reject the earlier, passage.
[L502] Realisation is the becoming of time in the field of extension. Extension
[L503] is the complex of events, _quâ_ their potentialities. In realisation the
[L504] potentiality becomes actuality. But the potential pattern requires a
[L505] duration; and the duration must be exhibited as an epochal whole, by the
[L506] realisation of the pattern. Thus time is the succession of elements in
[L507] themselves divisible and contiguous. A duration, in becoming temporal,
[L508] thereby incurs realisation in respect to some enduring object.
[L509] Temporalisation is realisation. Temporalisation is not another
[L510] continuous process. It is an atomic succession. Thus time is atomic
[L511] (_i.e._, epochal), though what is temporalised is divisible. This
[L512] doctrine follows from the doctrine of events, and of the nature of
[L513] enduring objects. In the next chapter we must consider its relevance to
[L514] the quantum theory of recent science.
[L515]
[L516] It is to be noted that this doctrine of the epochal character of time
[L517] does not depend on the modern doctrine of relativity, and holds
[L518] equally—and indeed, more simply—if this doctrine be abandoned. It does
[L519] depend on the analysis of the intrinsic character of an event,
[L520] considered as the most concrete finite entity.
[L521]
[L522] In reviewing this argument, note first that the second quotation from
[L523] Kant, on which it is based, does not depend on any peculiar Kantian
[L524] doctrine. The latter of the two is in agreement with Plato as against
[L525] Aristotle.[10] In the second place, the argument assumes that Zeno
[L526] understated his argument. He should have urged it against the current
[L527] notion of time in itself, and not against motion, which involves
[L528] relations between time and space. For, what becomes has duration. But no
[L529] duration can become until a smaller duration (part of the former) has
[L530] antecedently come into being [Kant’s earlier statement]. The same
[L531] argument applies to this smaller duration, and so on. Also the infinite
[L532] regress of these durations converges to nothing—and even on the
[L533] Aristotelian view there is no first moment. Accordingly time would be an
[L534] irrational notion. Thirdly, in the epochal theory Zeno’s difficulty is
[L535] met by conceiving temporalisation as the realisation of a complete
[L536] organism.

[L546] There are, however, some subordinate explanations to be made which bring
[L547] in the minor characteristics which I have already mentioned. First, as
[L548] regards time, if material has existed during any period, it has equally
[L549] been in existence during any portion of that period. In other words,
[L550] dividing the time does not divide the material. Secondly, in respect to
[L551] space, dividing the volume does divide the material. Accordingly, if
[L552] material exists throughout a volume, there will be less of that material
[L553] distributed through any definite half of that volume. It is from this
[L554] property that there arises our notion of density at a point of space.
[L555] Anyone who talks about density is not assimilating time and space to the
[L556] extent that some extremists of the modern school of relativists very
[L557] rashly desire. For the division of time functions, in respect to
[L558] material, quite differently from the division of space.
[L559]
[L560] Furthermore, this fact that the material is indifferent to the division
[L561] of time leads to the conclusion that the lapse of time is an accident,
[L562] rather than of the essence, of the material. The material is fully
[L563] itself in any sub-period however short. Thus the transition of time has
[L564] nothing to do with the character of the material. The material is
[L565] equally itself at an instant of time. Here an instant of time is
[L566] conceived as in itself without transition, since the temporal transition
[L567] is the succession of instants.
[L568]
[L569] The answer, therefore, which the seventeenth century gave to the ancient
[L570] question of the Ionian thinkers, ‘What is the world made of?’ was that
[L571] the world is a succession of instantaneous configurations of matter,—or
[L572] of material, if you wish to include stuff more subtle than ordinary
[L573] matter, the ether for example.
[L574]
[L575] We cannot wonder that science rested content with this assumption as to
[L576] the fundamental elements of nature. The great forces of nature, such as
[L577] gravitation, were entirely determined by the configurations of masses.
[L578] Thus the configurations determined their own changes, so that the circle
[L579] of scientific thought was completely closed. This is the famous
[L580] mechanistic theory of nature, which has reigned supreme ever since the
[L581] seventeenth century. It is the orthodox creed of physical science.
[L582] Furthermore, the creed justified itself by the pragmatic test. It
[L583] worked. Physicists took no more interest in philosophy. They emphasized
[L584] the anti-rationalism of the Historical Revolt. But the difficulties of
[L585] this theory of materialistic mechanism very soon became apparent. The
[L586] history of thought in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries is
[L587] governed by the fact that the world had got hold of a general idea which
[L588] it could neither live with nor live without.
[L589]
[L590] This simple location of instantaneous material configurations is what
[L591] Bergson has protested against, so far as it concerns time and so far as
[L592] it is taken to be the fundamental fact of concrete nature. He calls it a
[L593] distortion of nature due to the intellectual ‘spatialisation’ of things.
[L594] I agree with Bergson in his protest: but I do not agree that such
[L595] distortion is a vice necessary to the intellectual apprehension of
[L596] nature. I shall in subsequent lectures endeavour to show that this
[L597] spatialisation is the expression of more concrete facts under the guise
[L598] of very abstract logical constructions. There is an error; but it is
[L599] merely the accidental error of mistaking the abstract for the concrete.
[L600] It is an example of what I will call the ‘Fallacy of Misplaced
[L601] Concreteness.’ This fallacy is the occasion of great confusion in
[L602] philosophy. It is not necessary for the intellect to fall into the trap,
[L603] though in this example there has been a very general tendency to do so.

[L613] Science has never
[L614] shaken off the impress of its origin in the historical revolt of the
[L615] later Renaissance. It has remained predominantly an anti-rationalistic
[L616] movement, based upon a naïve faith. What reasoning it has wanted, has
[L617] been borrowed from mathematics which is a surviving relic of Greek
[L618] rationalism, following the deductive method. Science repudiates
[L619] philosophy. In other words, it has never cared to justify its faith or
[L620] to explain its meanings; and has remained blandly indifferent to its
[L621] refutation by Hume.
[L622]
[L623] Of course the historical revolt was fully justified. It was wanted. It
[L624] was more than wanted: it was an absolute necessity for healthy progress.
[L625] The world required centuries of contemplation of irreducible and
[L626] stubborn facts. It is difficult for men to do more than one thing at a
[L627] time, and that was the sort of thing they had to do after the
[L628] rationalistic orgy of the Middle Ages. It was a very sensible reaction;
[L629] but it was not a protest on behalf of reason.
[L630]
[L631] There is, however, a Nemesis which waits upon those who deliberately
[L632] avoid avenues of knowledge. Oliver Cromwell’s cry echoes down the ages,
[L633] ‘My brethren, by the bowels of Christ I beseech you, bethink you that
[L634] you may be mistaken.’
[L635]
[L636] The progress of science has now reached a turning point. The stable
[L637] foundations of physics have broken up: also for the first time
[L638] physiology is asserting itself as an effective body of knowledge, as
[L639] distinct from a scrap-heap. The old foundations of scientific thought
[L640] are becoming unintelligible. Time, space, matter, material, ether,
[L641] electricity, mechanism, organism, configuration, structure, pattern,
[L642] function, all require reinterpretation. What is the sense of talking
[L643] about a mechanical explanation when you do not know what you mean by
[L644] mechanics?
[L645]
[L646] The truth is that science started its modern career by taking over ideas
[L647] derived from the weakest side of the philosophies of Aristotle’s
[L648] successors. In some respects it was a happy choice. It enabled the
[L649] knowledge of the seventeenth century to be formularised so far as
[L650] physics and chemistry were concerned, with a completeness which has
[L651] lasted to the present time. But the progress of biology and psychology
[L652] has probably been checked by the uncritical assumption of half-truths.
[L653] If science is not to degenerate into a medley of _ad hoc_ hypotheses, it
[L654] must become philosophical and must enter upon a thorough criticism of
[L655] its own foundations.
[L656]
[L657] In the succeeding lectures of this course, I shall trace the successes
[L658] and the failures of the particular conceptions of cosmology with which
[L659] the European intellect has clothed itself in the last three centuries.
[L660] General climates of opinion persist for periods of about two to three
[L661] generations, that is to say, for periods of sixty to a hundred years.
[L662] There are also shorter waves of thought, which play on the surface of
[L663] the tidal movement. We shall find, therefore, transformations in the
[L664] European outlook, slowly modifying the successive centuries. There
[L665] persists, however, throughout the whole period the fixed scientific
[L666] cosmology which presupposes the ultimate fact of an irreducible brute
[L667] matter, or material, spread throughout space in a flux of
[L668] configurations. In itself such a material is senseless, valueless,
[L669] purposeless. It just does what it does do, following a fixed routine
[L670] imposed by external relations which do not spring from the nature of its
[L671] being. It is this assumption that I call ‘scientific materialism.’ Also
[L672] it is an assumption which I shall challenge as being entirely unsuited
[L673] to the scientific situation at which we have now arrived. It is not
[L674] wrong, if properly construed.

[L684] We must,
[L685] later on, consider this point in more detail.
[L686]
[L687] The same relegation of matter to the background occurs in connection
[L688] with the electromagnetic fields. The modern theory presupposes
[L689] happenings in that field which are divorced from immediate dependence
[L690] upon matter. It is usual to provide an ether as a substratum. But the
[L691] ether does not really enter into the theory. Thus again the notion of
[L692] material loses its fundamental position. Also, the atom is transforming
[L693] itself into an organism; and finally the evolution theory is nothing
[L694] else than the analysis of the conditions for the formation and survival
[L695] of various types of organisms. In truth, one most significant fact of
[L696] this later period is the advance in biological sciences. These sciences
[L697] are essentially sciences concerning organisms. During the epoch in
[L698] question, and indeed also at the present moment, the prestige of the
[L699] more perfect scientific form belongs to the physical sciences.
[L700] Accordingly, biology apes the manners of physics. It is orthodox to
[L701] hold, that there is nothing in biology but what is physical mechanism
[L702] under somewhat complex circumstances.
[L703]
[L704] One difficulty in this position is the present confusion as to the
[L705] foundational concepts of physical science. This same difficulty also
[L706] attaches to the opposed doctrine of vitalism. For, in this later theory,
[L707] the fact of mechanism is accepted—I mean, mechanism based upon
[L708] materialism—and an additional vital control is introduced to explain the
[L709] actions of living bodies. It cannot be too clearly understood that the
[L710] various physical laws which appear to apply to the behaviour of atoms
[L711] are not mutually consistent as at present formulated. The appeal to
[L712] mechanism on behalf of biology was in its origin an appeal to the
[L713] well-attested self-consistent physical concepts as expressing the basis
[L714] of all natural phenomena. But at present there is no such system of
[L715] concepts.
[L716]
[L717] Science is taking on a new aspect which is neither purely physical, nor
[L718] purely biological. It is becoming the study of organisms. Biology is the
[L719] study of the larger organisms; whereas physics is the study of the
[L720] smaller organisms. There is another difference between the two divisions
[L721] of science. The organisms of biology include as ingredients the smaller
[L722] organisms of physics; but there is at present no evidence that the
[L723] smaller of the physical organisms can be analysed into component
[L724] organisms. It may be so. But anyhow we are faced with the question as to
[L725] whether there are not primary organisms which are incapable of further
[L726] analysis. It seems very unlikely that there should be any infinite
[L727] regress in nature. Accordingly, a theory of science which discards
[L728] materialism must answer the question as to the character of these
[L729] primary entities. There can be only one answer on this basis. We must
[L730] start with the event as the ultimate unit of natural occurrence. An
[L731] event has to do with all that there is, and in particular with all other
[L732] events. This interfusion of events is effected by the aspects of those
[L733] eternal objects, such as colours, sounds, scents, geometrical
[L734] characters, which are required for nature and are not emergent from it.
[L735] Such an eternal object will be an ingredient of one event under the
[L736] guise, or aspect, of qualifying another event. There is a reciprocity of
[L737] aspects, and there are patterns of aspects. Each event corresponds to
[L738] two such patterns; namely, the pattern of aspects of other events which
[L739] it grasps into its own unity, and the pattern of its aspects which other
[L740] events severally grasp into their unities. Accordingly, a
[L741] non-materialistic philosophy of nature will identify a primary organism
[L742] as being the emergence of some particular pattern as grasped in the
[L743] unity of a real event.

[L797] The theory of relativity has justly excited a great amount of public
[L798] attention. But, for all its importance, it has not been the topic which
[L799] has chiefly absorbed the recent interest of physicists. Without question
[L800] that position is held by the quantum theory. The point of interest in
[L801] this theory is that, according to it, some effects which appear
[L802] essentially capable of gradual increase or gradual diminution are in
[L803] reality to be increased or decreased only by certain definite jumps. It
[L804] is as though you could walk at three miles per hour or at four miles per
[L805] hour, but not at three and a half miles per hour.
[L806]
[L807] The effects in question are concerned with the radiation of light from a
[L808] molecule which has been excited by some collision. Light consists of
[L809] waves of vibration in the electromagnetic field. After a complete wave
[L810] has passed a given point everything at that point is restored to its
[L811] original state and is ready for the next wave which follows on. Picture
[L812] to yourselves the waves on the ocean, and reckon from crest to crest of
[L813] successive waves. The number of waves which pass a given point in one
[L814] second is called the frequency of that system of waves. A system of
[L815] light-waves of definite frequency corresponds to a definite colour in
[L816] the spectrum. Now a molecule, when excited, vibrates with a certain
[L817] number of definite frequencies. In other words, there are a definite set
[L818] of modes of vibration of the molecule, and each mode of vibration has
[L819] one definite frequency.

[L229] The choice of the axioms and the investigation of their relations to one another
[L230] is a problem which, since the time of Euclid, has been discussed in numerous excellent
[L231] memoirs to be found in the mathematical literature.1 This problem is tantamount to the
[L232] logical analysis of our intuition of space.
[L233] The following investigation is a new attempt to choose for geometry a simple and
[L234] complete set of independent axioms and to deduce from these the most important geo￾metrical theorems in such a manner as to bring out as clearly as possible the significance
[L235] of the different groups of axioms and the scope of the conclusions to be derived from the
[L236] individual axioms.
[L237] 1Compare the comprehensive and explanatory report of G. Veronese, Grundz¨uge der Geometrie, Ger￾man translation by A. Schepp, Leipzig, 1894 (Appendix). See also F. Klein, “Zur ersten Verteilung des
[L238] Lobatschefskiy-Preises,” Math. Ann., Vol. 50.2
[L239] THE FIVE GROUPS OF AXIOMS.
[L240] § 1. THE ELEMENTS OF GEOMETRY AND THE FIVE GROUPS OF AXIOMS.
[L241] Let us consider three distinct systems of things. The things composing the first system,
[L242] we will call points and designate them by the letters A, B, C,. . . ; those of the second, we
[L243] will call straight lines and designate them by the letters a, b, c,. . . ; and those of the third
[L244] system, we will call planes and designate them by the Greek letters α, β, γ,. . . The points
[L245] are called the elements of linear geometry; the points and straight lines, the elements of
[L246] plane geometry; and the points, lines, and planes, the elements of the geometry of space
[L247] or the elements of space.
[L248] We think of these points, straight lines, and planes as having certain mutual relations,
[L249] which we indicate by means of such words as “are situated,” “between,” “parallel,” “con￾gruent,” “continuous,” etc. The complete and exact description of these relations follows
[L250] as a consequence of the axioms of geometry. These axioms may be arranged in five groups.
[L251] Each of these groups expresses, by itself, certain related fundamental facts of our intuition.
[L252] We will name these groups as follows:
[L253] I, 1–7. Axioms of connection.
[L254] II, 1–5. Axioms of order.
[L255] III. Axiom of parallels (Euclid’s axiom).
[L256] IV, 1–6. Axioms of congruence.
[L257] V. Axiom of continuity (Archimedes’s axiom).
[L258] § 2. GROUP I: AXIOMS OF CONNECTION.
[L259] The axioms of this group establish a connection between the concepts indicated above;
[L260] namely, points, straight lines, and planes. These axioms are as follows:
[L261] I, 1. Two distinct points A and B always completely determine a straight line a. We
[L262] write AB = a or BA = a.
[L263] Instead of “determine,” we may also employ other forms of expression; for example,
[L264] we may say A “lies upon” a, A “is a point of” a, a “goes through” A “and through” B,
[L265] a “joins” A “and” or “with” B, etc. If A lies upon a and at the same time upon another
[L266] straight line b, we make use also of the expression: “The straight lines” a “and” b “have
[L267] the point A in common,” etc.

[L353] the points of the segment AB or the points lying within the segment AB. All other points
[L354] of the straight line are referred to as the points lying outside the segment AB. The points
[L355] A and B are called the extremities of the segment AB.
[L356] II, 5. Let A, B, C be three points not lying in the same straight line and let a be a
[L357] straight line lying in the plane ABC and not passing through any of the points A,
[L358] B, C. Then, if the straight line a passes through a point of the segment AB, it will
[L359] also pass through either a point of the segment BC or a point of the segment AC.
[L360] Axioms II, 1–4 contain statements concerning the points of a straight line only, and,
[L361] hence, we will call them the linear axioms of group II. Axiom II, 5 relates to the
[L362] elements of plane geometry and, consequently, shall be called the plane axiom of
[L363] group II.
[L364] 2These axioms were first studied in detail by M. Pasch in his Vorlesungen ¨uber neuere Geometrie,
[L365] Leipsic, 1882. Axiom II, 5 is in particular due to him.5

[L368] By the aid of the four linear axioms II, 1–4, we can easily deduce the following theorems:
[L369] Theorem 3. Between any two points of a straight line, there always exists an

[L410] If we take as our axes in this new algebra of segments the co-ordinate axes already used
[L411] and consider the unit points E, E′ as suitably established, we see that the new algebra of
[L412] segments is nothing else than the system of co-ordinates previously employed.
[L413] In order to show that, for the new algebra of segments, the expression A(p1, p2, . . . , pr)
[L414] vanishes identically, it is sufficient to apply the theorems of Pascal and Desargues. Con￾sequently we see that:
[L415] Every proposition relative to points of intersection in the geometry in question must
[L416] always, by the aid of suitably constructed auxiliary points and straight lines, turn out to be
[L417] a combination of the theorems of Pascal and Desargues. Hence for the proof of the validity
[L418] of a theorem relating to points of intersection, we need not have resource to the theorems
[L419] of congruence.71
[L420] GEOMETRICAL CONSTRUCTIONS BASED UPON THE
[L421] AXIOMS I–V.
[L422] § 36. GEOMETRICAL CONSTRUCTIONS BY MEANS OF A STRAIGHT-EDGE
[L423] AND A TRANSFERER OF SEGMENTS.
[L424] Suppose we have given a geometry of space, in which all of the axioms I–V are valid. For
[L425] the sake of simplicity, we shall consider in this chapter a a plane geometry which is con￾tained in this geometry of space and shall investigate the question as to what elementary
[L426] geometrical constructions may be carried out in such a geometry.
[L427] Upon the basis of the axioms of group I, the following constructions are always possible.
[L428] Problem 1. To join two points with a straight line and to find the intersection of two
[L429] straight lines, the lines not being parallel.
[L430] Axiom III renders possible the following construction:
[L431] Problem 2. Through a given point to draw a parallel to a given straight line.
[L432] By the assistance of the axioms (IV) of congruence, it is possible to lay off segments
[L433] and angles; that is to say, in the given geometry we may solve the following problems:
[L434] Problem 3. To lay off from a given point upon a given straight line a given segment.
[L435] Problem 4. To lay off on a given straight line a given angle; or what is the same
[L436] thing, to construct a straight line which shall cut a given straight line at a given angle.
[L437] It is impossible to make any new constructions by the addition of the axioms of groups
[L438] II and V. Consequently, when we take into consideration merely the axioms of groups
[L439] I–V, all of those constructions and only those are possible, which may be reduced to the
[L440] problems 1–4 given above.
[L441] We will add to the fundamental problems 1–4 also the following:
[L442] Problem 5. To draw a perpendicular to a given straight line.
[L443] We see at once that this construction can be made in different ways by means of the
[L444] problems 1–4.
[L445] In order to carry out the construction in problem 1, we need to make use of only a
[L446] straight edge. An instrument which enables us to make the construction in problem 3, we
[L447] will call a transferer of segments. We shall now show that problems 2, 4, and 5 can be
[L448] reduced to the constructions in problems 1 and 3 and, consequently, all of the problems 1–
[L449] 5 can be completely constructed by means of a straight-edge and a transferer of segments.
[L450] We arrive, then, at the following result:
[L451] Theorem 40. Those problems in geometrical construction, which may be solved by
[L452] the assistance of only the axioms I–V, can always be carried out by the use of the
[L453] straight-edge and the transferer of segments.

[L497] The material contained in the following translation was given in substance by Professor Hilbert
[L498] as a course of lectures on euclidean geometry at the University of G¨ottingen during the winter
[L499] semester of 1898–1899. The results of his investigation were re-arranged and put into the form
[L500] in which they appear here as a memorial address published in connection with the celebration at
[L501] the unveiling of the Gauss-Weber monument at G¨ottingen, in June, 1899. In the French edition,
[L502] which appeared soon after, Professor Hilbert made some additions, particularly in the concluding
[L503] remarks, where he gave an account of the results of a recent investigation made by Dr. Dehn.
[L504] These additions have been incorporated in the following translation.
[L505] As a basis for the analysis of our intuition of space, Professor Hilbert commences his discussion
[L506] by considering three systems of things which he calls points, straight lines, and planes, and sets
[L507] up a system of axioms connecting these elements in their mutual relations. The purpose of his
[L508] investigations is to discuss systematically the relations of these axioms to one another and also the
[L509] bearing of each upon the logical development of euclidean geometry. Among the important results
[L510] obtained, the following are worthy of special mention:
[L511] 1. The mutual independence and also the compatibility of the given system of axioms is fully
[L512] discussed by the aid of various new systems of geometry which are introduced.
[L513] 2. The most important propositions of euclidean geometry are demonstrated in such a manner
[L514] as to show precisely what axioms underlie and make possible the demonstration.
[L515] 3. The axioms of congruence are introduced and made the basis of the definition of geometric
[L516] displacement.

[L518] of the euclidean geometry is clearly shown; for example, it is shown that the whole of the eu￾clidean geometry may be developed without the use of the axiom of continuity; the significance of

[L520] geometry of space, is made apparent, etc.

[L10] 2º There is no absolute time; to say two durations are equal is an
[L11] assertion which has by itself no meaning and which can acquire one only
[L12] by convention.
[L13]
[L14] 3º Not only have we no direct intuition of the equality of two
[L15] durations, but we have not even direct intuition of the simultaneity of
[L16] two events occurring in different places: this I have explained in an
[L17] article entitled _La mesure du temps_.[3]
[L18]
[L19]   [3] _Revue de Métaphysique et de Morale_, t. VI., pp. 1-13
[L20]       (January, 1898).
[L21]
[L22] 4º Finally, our Euclidean geometry is itself only a sort of convention
[L23] of language; mechanical facts might be enunciated with reference to a
[L24] non-Euclidean space which would be a guide less convenient than, but
[L25] just as legitimate as, our ordinary space; the enunciation would thus
[L26] become much more complicated, but it would remain possible.
[L27]
[L28] Thus absolute space, absolute time, geometry itself, are not conditions
[L29] which impose themselves on mechanics; all these things are no more
[L30] antecedent to mechanics than the French language is logically antecedent
[L31] to the verities one expresses in French.
[L32]
[L33] We might try to enunciate the fundamental laws of mechanics in a
[L34] language independent of all these conventions; we should thus without
[L35] doubt get a better idea of what these laws are in themselves; this is
[L36] what M. Andrade has attempted to do, at least in part, in his _Leçons de
[L37] mécanique physique_.
[L38]
[L39] The enunciation of these laws would become of course much more
[L40] complicated, because all these conventions have been devised expressly
[L41] to abridge and simplify this enunciation.
[L42]
[L43] As for me, save in what concerns absolute space, I shall ignore all
[L44] these difficulties; not that I fail to appreciate them, far from that;
[L45] but we have sufficiently examined them in the first two parts of the
[L46] book.
[L47]
[L48] I shall therefore admit, _provisionally_, absolute time and Euclidean
[L49] geometry.
[L50]
[L51] THE PRINCIPLE OF INERTIA.--A body acted on by no force can only move
[L52] uniformly in a straight line.
[L53]
[L54] Is this a truth imposed _a priori_ upon the mind? If it were so, how
[L55] should the Greeks have failed to recognize it? How could they have
[L56] believed that motion stops when the cause which gave birth to it ceases?
[L57] Or again that every body if nothing prevents, will move in a circle, the
[L58] noblest of motions?
[L59]
[L60] If it is said that the velocity of a body can not change if there is no
[L61] reason for it to change, could it not be maintained just as well that
[L62] the position of this body can not change, or that the curvature of its
[L63] trajectory can not change, if no external cause intervenes to modify
[L64] them?
[L65]
[L66] Is the principle of inertia, which is not an _a priori_ truth, therefore
[L67] an experimental fact? But has any one ever experimented on bodies
[L68] withdrawn from the action of every force? and, if so, how was it known
[L69] that these bodies were subjected to no force? The example ordinarily
[L70] cited is that of a ball rolling a very long time on a marble table; but
[L71] why do we say it is subjected to no force? Is this because it is too
[L72] remote from all other bodies to experience any appreciable action from
[L73] them? Yet it is not farther from the earth than if it were thrown freely
[L74] into the air; and every one knows that in this case it would experience
[L75] the influence of gravity due to the attraction of the earth.

[L85] Among these series, we have distinguished
[L86] those which of themselves alone can compensate an external change, and
[L87] which we have called 'displacements.' As we can not discriminate between
[L88] two displacements which are too close together, the totality of these
[L89] displacements presents the characteristics of a physical continuum;
[L90] experience teaches us that they are those of a physical continuum of six
[L91] dimensions; but we do not yet know how many dimensions space itself has,
[L92] we must first solve another question.
[L93]
[L94] What is a point of space? Everybody thinks he knows, but that is an
[L95] illusion. What we see when we try to represent to ourselves a point of
[L96] space is a black speck on white paper, a speck of chalk on a blackboard,
[L97] always an object. The question should therefore be understood as
[L98] follows:
[L99]
[L100] What do I mean when I say the object _B_ is at the same point that the
[L101] object _A_ occupied just now? Or further, what criterion will enable me
[L102] to apprehend this?
[L103]
[L104] I mean that, _although I have not budged_ (which my muscular sense tells
[L105] me), my first finger which just now touched the object _A_ touches at
[L106] present the object _B_. I could have used other criteria; for instance
[L107] another finger or the sense of sight. But the first criterion is
[L108] sufficient; I know that if it answers yes, all the other criteria will
[L109] give the same response. I know it _by experience_, I can not know it _a
[L110] priori_. For the same reason I say that touch can not be exercised at a
[L111] distance; this is another way of enunciating the same experimental fact.
[L112] And if, on the contrary, I say that sight acts at a distance, it means
[L113] that the criterion furnished by sight may respond yes while the others
[L114] reply no.
[L115]
[L116] And in fact, the object, although moved away, may form its image at the
[L117] same point of the retina. Sight responds yes, the object has remained at
[L118] the same point and touch answers no, because my finger which just now
[L119] touched the object, at present touches it no longer. If experience had
[L120] shown us that one finger may respond no when the other says yes, we
[L121] should likewise say that touch acts at a distance.
[L122]
[L123] In short, for each attitude of my body, my first finger determines a
[L124] point, and this it is, and this alone, which defines a point of space.
[L125]
[L126] To each attitude corresponds thus a point; but it often happens that the
[L127] same point corresponds to several different attitudes (in this case we
[L128] say our finger has not budged, but the rest of the body has moved). We
[L129] distinguish, therefore, among the changes of attitude those where the
[L130] finger does not budge. How are we led thereto? It is because often we
[L131] notice that in these changes the object which is in contact with the
[L132] finger remains in contact with it.
[L133]
[L134] Range, therefore, in the same class all the attitudes obtainable from
[L135] each other by one of the changes we have thus distinguished. To all the
[L136] attitudes of the class will correspond the same point of space.
[L137] Therefore to each class will correspond a point and to each point a
[L138] class. But one may say that what experience arrives at is not the point,
[L139] it is this class of changes or, better, the corresponding class of
[L140] muscular sensations.
[L141]
[L142] And when we say space has three dimensions, we simply mean that the
[L143] totality of these classes appears to us with the characteristics of a
[L144] physical continuum of three dimensions.
[L145]
[L146] One might be tempted to conclude that it is experience which has taught
[L147] us how many dimensions space has. But in reality here also our
[L148] experiences have bearing, not on space, but on our body and its
[L149] relations with the neighboring objects. Moreover they are excessively
[L150] crude.

[L160] When I say that such a part of such a body is in contact with such a
[L161] part of such another body, I enunciate a proposition which concerns the
[L162] mutual relations of these two bodies and not their relations with
[L163] space.
[L164]
[L165] I suppose you will grant me these are not geometric properties; at least
[L166] I am sure you will grant me these properties are independent of all
[L167] knowledge of metric geometry.
[L168]
[L169] This presupposed, I imagine that we have a solid body formed of eight
[L170] slender iron rods, _OA_, _OB_, _OC_, _OD_, _OE_, _OF_, _OG_, _OH_,
[L171] united at one of their extremities _O_. Let us besides have a second
[L172] solid body, for example a bit of wood, to be marked with three little
[L173] flecks of ink which I shall call [alpha], [beta], [gamma]. I further
[L174] suppose it ascertained that [alpha][beta][gamma] may be brought into
[L175] contact with _AGO_ (I mean [alpha] with _A_, and at the same time [beta]
[L176] with _G_ and [gamma] with _O_), then that we may bring successively into
[L177] contact [alpha][beta][gamma] with _BGO_, _CGO_, _DGO_, _EGO_, _FGO_,
[L178] then with _AHO_, _BHO_, _CHO_, _DHO_, _EHO_, _FHO_, then [alpha][gamma]
[L179] successively with _AB_, _BC_, _CD_, _DE_, _EF_, _FA_.
[L180]
[L181] These are determinations we may make without having in advance any
[L182] notion about form or about the metric properties of space. They in no
[L183] wise bear on the 'geometric properties of bodies.' And these
[L184] determinations will not be possible if the bodies experimented upon move
[L185] in accordance with a group having the same structure as the
[L186] Lobachevskian group (I mean according to the same laws as solid bodies
[L187] in Lobachevski's geometry). They suffice therefore to prove that these
[L188] bodies move in accordance with the Euclidean group, or at least that
[L189] they do not move according to the Lobachevskian group.
[L190]
[L191] That they are compatible with the Euclidean group is easy to see. For
[L192] they could be made if the body [alpha][beta][gamma] was a rigid solid of
[L193] our ordinary geometry presenting the form of a right-angled triangle,
[L194] and if the points _ABCDEFGH_ were the summits of a polyhedron formed of
[L195] two regular hexagonal pyramids of our ordinary geometry, having for
[L196] common base _ABCDEF_ and for apices the one _G_ and the other _H_.
[L197]
[L198] Suppose now that in place of the preceding determination it is observed
[L199] that as above [alpha][beta][gamma] can be successively applied to _AGO_,
[L200] _BGO_, _CGO_, _DGO_, _EGO_, _AHO_, _BHO_, _CHO_, _DHO_, _EHO_, _FHO_,
[L201] then that [alpha][beta] (and no longer [alpha][gamma]) can be
[L202] successively applied to _AB_, _BC_, _CD_, _DE_, _EF_ and _FA_.
[L203]
[L204] These are determinations which could be made if non-Euclidean geometry
[L205] were true, if the bodies [alpha][beta][gamma] and _OABCDEFGH_ were rigid
[L206] solids, and if the first were a right-angled triangle and the second a
[L207] double regular hexagonal pyramid of suitable dimensions.

[L217] MEASURABLE MAGNITUDE.--The magnitudes we have studied hitherto are not
[L218] _measurable_; we can indeed say whether a given one of these magnitudes
[L219] is greater than another, but not whether it is twice or thrice as great.
[L220]
[L221] So far, I have only considered the order in which our terms are ranged.
[L222] But for most applications that does not suffice. We must learn to
[L223] compare the interval which separates any two terms. Only on this
[L224] condition does the continuum become a measurable magnitude and the
[L225] operations of arithmetic applicable.
[L226]
[L227] This can only be done by the aid of a new and special _convention_. We
[L228] will _agree_ that in such and such a case the interval comprised between
[L229] the terms _A_ and _B_ is equal to the interval which separates _C_ and
[L230] _D_. For example, at the beginning of our work we have set out from the
[L231] scale of the whole numbers and we have supposed intercalated between two
[L232] consecutive steps _n_ intermediary steps; well, these new steps will be
[L233] by convention regarded as equidistant.
[L234]
[L235] This is a way of defining the addition of two magnitudes, because if the
[L236] interval _AB_ is by definition equal to the interval _CD_, the interval
[L237] _AD_ will be by definition the sum of the intervals _AB_ and _AC_.
[L238]
[L239] This definition is arbitrary in a very large measure. It is not
[L240] completely so, however. It is subjected to certain conditions and, for
[L241] example, to the rules of commutativity and associativity of addition.
[L242] But provided the definition chosen satisfies these rules, the choice is
[L243] indifferent, and it is useless to particularize it.
[L244]
[L245] VARIOUS REMARKS.--We can now discuss several important questions:
[L246]
[L247] 1º Is the creative power of the mind exhausted by the creation of the
[L248] mathematical continuum?
[L249]
[L250] No: the works of Du Bois-Reymond demonstrate it in a striking way.
[L251]
[L252] We know that mathematicians distinguish between infinitesimals of
[L253] different orders and that those of the second order are infinitesimal,
[L254] not only in an absolute way, but also in relation to those of the first
[L255] order. It is not difficult to imagine infinitesimals of fractional or
[L256] even of irrational order, and thus we find again that scale of the
[L257] mathematical continuum which has been dealt with in the preceding
[L258] pages.
[L259]
[L260] Further, there are infinitesimals which are infinitely small in relation
[L261] to those of the first order, and, on the contrary, infinitely great in
[L262] relation to those of order 1 + [epsilon], and that however small
[L263] [epsilon] may be. Here, then, are new terms intercalated in our series,
[L264] and if I may be permitted to revert to the phraseology lately employed

[L266] that thus has been created a sort of continuum of the third order.
[L267]

[L269] be imagining symbols without possible application, and no one will think

[L276] 2º Once in possession of the concept of the mathematical continuum, is

[L289] Thus if the principle of least action can not be satisfied, no
[L290] mechanical explanation is possible; if it can be satisfied, there is not
[L291] only one, but an infinity, whence it follows that as soon as there is
[L292] one there is an infinity of others.
[L293]
[L294] One more observation.
[L295]
[L296] Among the quantities that experiment gives us directly, we shall regard
[L297] some as functions of the coordinates of our hypothetical molecules;
[L298] these are our parameters _q_. We shall look upon the others as dependent
[L299] not only on the coordinates, but on the velocities, or, what comes to
[L300] the same thing, on the derivatives of the parameters _q_, or as
[L301] combinations of these parameters and their derivatives.
[L302]
[L303] And then a question presents itself: among all these quantities measured
[L304] experimentally, which shall we choose to represent the parameters _q_?
[L305] Which shall we prefer to regard as the derivatives of these parameters?
[L306] This choice remains arbitrary to a very large extent; but, for a
[L307] mechanical explanation to be possible, it suffices if we can make the
[L308] choice in such a way as to accord with the principle of least action.
[L309]
[L310] And then Maxwell asked himself whether he could make this choice and
[L311] that of the two energies _T_ and _U_, in such a way that the electrical
[L312] phenomena would satisfy this principle. Experiment shows us that the
[L313] energy of an electromagnetic field is decomposed into two parts, the
[L314] electrostatic energy and the electrodynamic energy. Maxwell observed
[L315] that if we regard the first as representing the potential energy _U_,
[L316] the second as representing the kinetic energy _T_; if, moreover, the
[L317] electrostatic charges of the conductors are considered as parameters _q_
[L318] and the intensities of the currents as the derivatives of other
[L319] parameters _q_; under these conditions, I say, Maxwell observed that the
[L320] electric phenomena satisfy the principle of least action. Thenceforth he
[L321] was certain of the possibility of a mechanical explanation.
[L322]
[L323] If he had explained this idea at the beginning of his book instead of
[L324] relegating it to an obscure part of the second volume, it would not have
[L325] escaped the majority of readers.
[L326]
[L327] If, then, a phenomenon admits of a complete mechanical explanation, it
[L328] will admit of an infinity of others, that will render an account equally
[L329] well of all the particulars revealed by experiment.
[L330]
[L331] And this is confirmed by the history of every branch of physics; in
[L332] optics, for instance, Fresnel believed vibration to be perpendicular to
[L333] the plane of polarization; Neumann regarded it as parallel to this
[L334] plane. An 'experimentum crucis' has long been sought which would enable
[L335] us to decide between these two theories, but it has not been found.
[L336]
[L337] In the same way, without leaving the domain of electricity, we may
[L338] ascertain that the theory of two fluids and that of the single fluid
[L339] both account in a fashion equally satisfactory for all the observed laws
[L340] of electrostatics.
[L341]
[L342] All these facts are easily explicable, thanks to the properties of the
[L343] equations of Lagrange which I have just recalled.
[L344]
[L345] It is easy now to comprehend what is Maxwell's fundamental idea.
[L346]
[L347] To demonstrate the possibility of a mechanical explanation of
[L348] electricity, we need not preoccupy ourselves with finding this
[L349] explanation itself; it suffices us to know the expression of the two
[L350] functions _T_ and _U_, which are the two parts of energy, to form with
[L351] these two functions the equations of Lagrange and then to compare these
[L352] equations with the experimental laws.

[L362] It may happen that among the numbers of the first class there is one
[L363] smaller than all the others; if, for example, we range in the first
[L364] class all numbers greater than 2, and 2 itself, and in the second class
[L365] all numbers less than 2, it is clear that 2 will be the least of all
[L366] numbers of the first class. The number 2 may be chosen as symbol of this
[L367] partition.
[L368]
[L369] It may happen, on the contrary, that among the numbers of the second
[L370] class is one greater than all the others; this is the case, for example,
[L371] if the first class comprehends all numbers greater than 2, and the
[L372] second all numbers less than 2, and 2 itself. Here again the number 2
[L373] may be chosen as symbol of this partition.
[L374]
[L375] But it may equally well happen that neither is there in the first class
[L376] a number less than all the others, nor in the second class a number
[L377] greater than all the others. Suppose, for example, we put in the first
[L378] class all commensurable numbers whose squares are greater than 2 and in
[L379] the second all whose squares are less than 2. There is none whose square
[L380] is precisely 2. Evidently there is not in the first class a number less
[L381] than all the others, for, however near the square of a number may be to
[L382] 2, we can always find a commensurable number whose square is still
[L383] closer to 2.
[L384]
[L385] In Dedekind's view, the incommensurable number
[L386]
[L387]   sqrt(2) or (2)^{1/2}
[L388]
[L389] is nothing but the symbol of this particular mode of partition of
[L390] commensurable numbers; and to each mode of partition corresponds thus a
[L391] number, commensurable or not, which serves as its symbol.
[L392]
[L393] But to be content with this would be to forget too far the origin of
[L394] these symbols; it remains to explain how we have been led to attribute
[L395] to them a sort of concrete existence, and, besides, does not the
[L396] difficulty begin even for the fractional numbers themselves? Should we
[L397] have the notion of these numbers if we had not previously known a matter
[L398] that we conceive as infinitely divisible, that is to say, a continuum?
[L399]
[L400] THE PHYSICAL CONTINUUM.--We ask ourselves then if the notion of the
[L401] mathematical continuum is not simply drawn from experience. If it were,
[L402] the raw data of experience, which are our sensations, would be
[L403] susceptible of measurement. We might be tempted to believe they really
[L404] are so, since in these latter days the attempt has been made to measure
[L405] them and a law has even been formulated, known as Fechner's law,
[L406] according to which sensation is proportional to the logarithm of the
[L407] stimulus.
[L408]
[L409] But if we examine more closely the experiments by which it has been
[L410] sought to establish this law, we shall be led to a diametrically
[L411] opposite conclusion. It has been observed, for example, that a weight
[L412] _A_ of 10 grams and a weight _B_ of 11 grams produce identical
[L413] sensations, that the weight _B_ is just as indistinguishable from a
[L414] weight _C_ of 12 grams, but that the weight _A_ is easily distinguished
[L415] from the weight _C_. Thus the raw results of experience may be expressed
[L416] by the following relations:
[L417]
[L418]   _A_ =_B_,   _B_ = _C_,   _A_ < _C_,
[L419]
[L420] which may be regarded as the formula of the physical continuum.
[L421]
[L422] But here is an intolerable discord with the principle of contradiction,
[L423] and the need of stopping this has compelled us to invent the
[L424] mathematical continuum.

[L507] But visual space is only one part of space, and in even the notion of
[L508] this space there is something artificial, as I have explained at the
[L509] beginning. The real space is motor space and this it is that we shall
[L510] examine in the following chapter.
[L511]
[L512]
[L513]
[L514]
[L515] CHAPTER IV
[L516]
[L517] SPACE AND ITS THREE DIMENSIONS
[L518]
[L519]
[L520] 1. _The Group of Displacements_
[L521]
[L522] Let us sum up briefly the results obtained. We proposed to investigate
[L523] what was meant in saying that space has three dimensions and we have
[L524] asked first what is a physical continuum and when it may be said to have
[L525] _n_ dimensions. If we consider different systems of impressions and
[L526] compare them with one another, we often recognize that two of these
[L527] systems of impressions are indistinguishable (which is ordinarily
[L528] expressed in saying that they are too close to one another, and that our
[L529] senses are too crude, for us to distinguish them) and we ascertain
[L530] besides that two of these systems can sometimes be discriminated from
[L531] one another though indistinguishable from a third system. In that case
[L532] we say the manifold of these systems of impressions forms a physical
[L533] continuum _C_. And each of these systems is called an _element_ of the
[L534] continuum _C_.
[L535]
[L536] How many dimensions has this continuum? Take first two elements _A_ and
[L537] _B_ of _C_, and suppose there exists a series [Sigma] of elements, all
[L538] belonging to the continuum _C_, of such a sort that _A_ and _B_ are the
[L539] two extreme terms of this series and that each term of the series is
[L540] indistinguishable from the preceding. If such a series [Sigma] can be
[L541] found, we say that _A_ and _B_ are joined to one another; and if any two
[L542] elements of _C_ are joined to one another, we say that _C_ is all of one
[L543] piece.
[L544]
[L545] Now take on the continuum _C_ a certain number of elements in a way
[L546] altogether arbitrary. The aggregate of these elements will be called a
[L547] _cut_. Among the various series [Sigma] which join _A_ to _B_, we shall
[L548] distinguish those of which an element is indistinguishable from one of
[L549] the elements of the cut (we shall say that these are they which _cut_
[L550] the cut) and those of which _all_ the elements are distinguishable from
[L551] all those of the cut. If _all_ the series [Sigma] which join _A_ to _B_
[L552] cut the cut, we shall say that _A_ and _B_ are _separated_ by the cut,
[L553] and that the cut _divides_ _C_. If we can not find on _C_ two elements
[L554] which are separated by the cut, we shall say that the cut _does not
[L555] divide_ _C_.
[L556]
[L557] These definitions laid down, if the continuum _C_ can be divided by cuts
[L558] which do not themselves form a continuum, this continuum _C_ has only
[L559] one dimension; in the contrary case it has several. If a cut forming a
[L560] continuum of 1 dimension suffices to divide _C_, _C_ will have 2
[L561] dimensions; if a cut forming a continuum of 2 dimensions suffices, _C_
[L562] will have 3 dimensions, etc. Thanks to these definitions, we can always
[L563] recognize how many dimensions any physical continuum has. It only
[L564] remains to find a physical continuum which is, so to speak, equivalent
[L565] to space, of such a sort that to every point of space corresponds an
[L566] element of this continuum, and that to points of space very near one
[L567] another correspond indistinguishable elements. Space will have then as
[L568] many dimensions as this continuum.

[L578] On the contrary, it may happen that the cut made is insufficient to
[L579] subdivide the continuum _C_. To classify the physical continua, we will
[L580] examine precisely what are the cuts which must be made to subdivide
[L581] them.
[L582]
[L583] If a physical continuum _C_ can be subdivided by a cut reducing to a
[L584] finite number of elements all distinguishable from one another (and
[L585] consequently forming neither a continuum, nor several continua), we
[L586] shall say _C_ is a _one-dimensional_ continuum.
[L587]
[L588] If, on the contrary, _C_ can be subdivided only by cuts which are
[L589] themselves continua, we shall say _C_ has several dimensions. If cuts
[L590] which are continua of one dimension suffice, we shall say _C_ has two
[L591] dimensions; if cuts of two dimensions suffice, we shall say _C_ has
[L592] three dimensions, and so on.
[L593]
[L594] Thus is defined the notion of the physical continuum of several
[L595] dimensions, thanks to this very simple fact that two aggregates of
[L596] sensations are distinguishable or indistinguishable.
[L597]
[L598] THE MATHEMATICAL CONTINUUM OF SEVERAL DIMENSIONS.--Thence the notion of
[L599] the mathematical continuum of _n_ dimensions has sprung quite naturally
[L600] by a process very like that we discussed at the beginning of this
[L601] chapter. A point of such a continuum, you know, appears to us as defined
[L602] by a system of _n_ distinct magnitudes called its coordinates.
[L603]
[L604] These magnitudes need not always be measurable; there is, for instance,
[L605] a branch of geometry independent of the measurement of these magnitudes,
[L606] in which it is only a question of knowing, for example, whether on a
[L607] curve _ABC_, the point _B_ is between the points _A_ and _C_, and not of
[L608] knowing whether the arc _AB_ is equal to the arc _BC_ or twice as great.
[L609] This is what is called _Analysis Situs_.
[L610]
[L611] This is a whole body of doctrine which has attracted the attention of
[L612] the greatest geometers and where we see flow one from another a series
[L613] of remarkable theorems. What distinguishes these theorems from those of
[L614] ordinary geometry is that they are purely qualitative and that they
[L615] would remain true if the figures were copied by a draughtsman so awkward
[L616] as to grossly distort the proportions and replace straights by strokes
[L617] more or less curved.
[L618]
[L619] Through the wish to introduce measure next into the continuum just
[L620] defined this continuum becomes space, and geometry is born. But the
[L621] discussion of this is reserved for Part Second.
[L622]

[L626] PART II

[L634] CHAPTER III
[L635]
[L636] THE NON-EUCLIDEAN GEOMETRIES
[L637]
[L638]
[L639] Every conclusion supposes premises; these premises themselves either are
[L640] self-evident and need no demonstration, or can be established only by
[L641] relying upon other propositions, and since we can not go back thus to
[L642] infinity, every deductive science, and in particular geometry, must rest
[L643] on a certain number of undemonstrable axioms. All treatises on geometry
[L644] begin, therefore, by the enunciation of these axioms. But among these
[L645] there is a distinction to be made: Some, for example, 'Things which are
[L646] equal to the same thing are equal to one another,' are not propositions
[L647] of geometry, but propositions of analysis. I regard them as analytic
[L648] judgments _a priori_, and shall not concern myself with them.
[L649]
[L650] But I must lay stress upon other axioms which are peculiar to geometry.
[L651] Most treatises enunciate three of these explicitly:
[L652]
[L653] 1º Through two points can pass only one straight;
[L654]
[L655] 2º The straight line is the shortest path from one point to another;
[L656]
[L657] 3º Through a given point there is not more than one parallel to a given
[L658] straight.

[L668] It is experimental physics that is entrusted with the purchases. It
[L669] alone, then, can enrich the library.
[L670]
[L671] As for mathematical physics, its task will be to make out the catalogue.
[L672] If the catalogue is well made, the library will not be any richer, but
[L673] the reader will be helped to use its riches.
[L674]
[L675] And even by showing the librarian the gaps in his collections, it will
[L676] enable him to make a judicious use of his funds; which is all the more
[L677] important because these funds are entirely inadequate.
[L678]
[L679] Such, then, is the rôle of mathematical physics. It must direct
[L680] generalization in such a manner as to increase what I just now called
[L681] the yield of science. By what means it can arrive at this, and how it
[L682] can do it without danger, is what remains for us to investigate.
[L683]
[L684] THE UNITY OF NATURE.--Let us notice, first of all, that every
[L685] generalization implies in some measure the belief in the unity and
[L686] simplicity of nature. As to the unity there can be no difficulty. If the
[L687] different parts of the universe were not like the members of one body,
[L688] they would not act on one another, they would know nothing of one
[L689] another; and we in particular would know only one of these parts. We do
[L690] not ask, then, if nature is one, but how it is one.
[L691]
[L692] As for the second point, that is not such an easy matter. It is not
[L693] certain that nature is simple. Can we without danger act as if it were?
[L694]
[L695] There was a time when the simplicity of Mariotte's law was an argument
[L696] invoked in favor of its accuracy; when Fresnel himself, after having
[L697] said in a conversation with Laplace that nature was not concerned about
[L698] analytical difficulties, felt himself obliged to make explanations, in
[L699] order not to strike too hard at prevailing opinion.
[L700]
[L701] To-day ideas have greatly changed; and yet, those who do not believe
[L702] that natural laws have to be simple, are still often obliged to act as
[L703] if they did. They could not entirely avoid this necessity without making
[L704] impossible all generalization, and consequently all science.
[L705]
[L706] It is clear that any fact can be generalized in an infinity of ways, and
[L707] it is a question of choice. The choice can be guided only by
[L708] considerations of simplicity. Let us take the most commonplace case,
[L709] that of interpolation. We pass a continuous line, as regular as
[L710] possible, between the points given by observation. Why do we avoid
[L711] points making angles and too abrupt turns? Why do we not make our curve
[L712] describe the most capricious zig-zags? It is because we know beforehand,
[L713] or believe we know, that the law to be expressed can not be so
[L714] complicated as all that.
[L715]
[L716] We may calculate the mass of Jupiter from either the movements of its
[L717] satellites, or the perturbations of the major planets, or those of the
[L718] minor planets. If we take the averages of the determinations obtained by
[L719] these three methods, we find three numbers very close together, but
[L720] different. We might interpret this result by supposing that the
[L721] coefficient of gravitation is not the same in the three cases. The
[L722] observations would certainly be much better represented. Why do we
[L723] reject this interpretation? Not because it is absurd, but because it is
[L724] needlessly complicated. We shall only accept it when we are forced to,
[L725] and that is not yet.
[L726]
[L727] To sum up, ordinarily every law is held to be simple till the contrary
[L728] is proved.

[L739] altogether arbitrary. The aggregate of these elements will be called a
[L740] _cut_. Among the various series [Sigma] which join _A_ to _B_, we shall
[L741] distinguish those of which an element is indistinguishable from one of
[L742] the elements of the cut (we shall say that these are they which _cut_
[L743] the cut) and those of which _all_ the elements are distinguishable from
[L744] all those of the cut. If _all_ the series [Sigma] which join _A_ to _B_
[L745] cut the cut, we shall say that _A_ and _B_ are _separated_ by the cut,
[L746] and that the cut _divides_ _C_. If we can not find on _C_ two elements
[L747] which are separated by the cut, we shall say that the cut _does not
[L748] divide_ _C_.
[L749]
[L750] These definitions laid down, if the continuum _C_ can be divided by cuts
[L751] which do not themselves form a continuum, this continuum _C_ has only
[L752] one dimension; in the contrary case it has several. If a cut forming a
[L753] continuum of 1 dimension suffices to divide _C_, _C_ will have 2
[L754] dimensions; if a cut forming a continuum of 2 dimensions suffices, _C_
[L755] will have 3 dimensions, etc. Thanks to these definitions, we can always
[L756] recognize how many dimensions any physical continuum has. It only
[L757] remains to find a physical continuum which is, so to speak, equivalent
[L758] to space, of such a sort that to every point of space corresponds an
[L759] element of this continuum, and that to points of space very near one
[L760] another correspond indistinguishable elements. Space will have then as
[L761] many dimensions as this continuum.
[L762]
[L763] The intermediation of this physical continuum, capable of
[L764] representation, is indispensable; because we can not represent space to
[L765] ourselves, and that for a multitude of reasons. Space is a mathematical
[L766] continuum, it is infinite, and we can represent to ourselves only
[L767] physical continua and finite objects. The different elements of space,
[L768] which we call points, are all alike, and, to apply our definition, it is
[L769] necessary that we know how to distinguish the elements from one another,
[L770] at least if they are not too close. Finally absolute space is nonsense,
[L771] and it is necessary for us to begin by referring space to a system of
[L772] axes invariably bound to our body (which we must always suppose put back
[L773] in the initial attitude).
[L774]
[L775] Then I have sought to form with our visual sensations a physical
[L776] continuum equivalent to space; that certainly is easy and this example
[L777] is particularly appropriate for the discussion of the number of
[L778] dimensions; this discussion has enabled us to see in what measure it is
[L779] allowable to say that 'visual space' has three dimensions. Only this
[L780] solution is incomplete and artificial. I have explained why, and it is
[L781] not on visual space but on motor space that it is necessary to bring our
[L782] efforts to bear. I have then recalled what is the origin of the
[L783] distinction we make between changes of position and changes of state.
[L784] Among the changes which occur in our impressions, we distinguish, first
[L785] the _internal_ changes, voluntary and accompanied by muscular
[L786] sensations, and the _external_ changes, having opposite characteristics.
[L787] We ascertain that it may happen that an external change may be
[L788] _corrected_ by an internal change which reestablishes the primitive
[L789] sensations. The external changes, capable of being corrected by an
[L790] internal change are called _changes of position_, those not capable of
[L791] it are called _changes of state_.

[L1074] The experiments which have led
[L1075] us to adopt as more convenient the fundamental conventions of geometry
[L1076] bear on objects which have nothing in common with those geometry
[L1077] studies; they bear on the properties of solid bodies, on the rectilinear
[L1078] propagation of light. They are experiments of mechanics, experiments of
[L1079] optics; they can not in any way be regarded as experiments of geometry.
[L1080] And even the principal reason why our geometry seems convenient to us is
[L1081] that the different parts of our body, our eye, our limbs, have the
[L1082] properties of solid bodies. On this account, our fundamental experiments
[L1083] are preeminently physiological experiments, which bear, not on space
[L1084] which is the object the geometer must study, but on his body, that is
[L1085] to say, on the instrument he must use for this study.
[L1086]
[L1087] On the contrary, the fundamental conventions of mechanics, and the
[L1088] experiments which prove to us that they are convenient, bear on exactly
[L1089] the same objects or on analogous objects. The conventional and general
[L1090] principles are the natural and direct generalization of the experimental
[L1091] and particular principles.
[L1092]
[L1093] Let it not be said that thus I trace artificial frontiers between the
[L1094] sciences; that if I separate by a barrier geometry properly so called
[L1095] from the study of solid bodies, I could just as well erect one between
[L1096] experimental mechanics and the conventional mechanics of the general
[L1097] principles. In fact, who does not see that in separating these two
[L1098] sciences I mutilate them both, and that what will remain of conventional
[L1099] mechanics when it shall be isolated will be only a very small thing and
[L1100] can in no way be compared to that superb body of doctrine called
[L1101] geometry?
[L1102]
[L1103] One sees now why the teaching of mechanics should remain experimental.
[L1104]
[L1105] Only thus can it make us comprehend the genesis of the science, and that
[L1106] is indispensable for the complete understanding of the science itself.
[L1107]
[L1108] Besides, if we study mechanics, it is to apply it; and we can apply it
[L1109] only if it remains objective. Now, as we have seen, what the principles
[L1110] gain in generality and certainty they lose in objectivity. It is,
[L1111] therefore, above all with the objective side of the principles that we
[L1112] must be familiarized early, and that can be done only by going from the
[L1113] particular to the general, instead of the inverse.
[L1114]
[L1115] The principles are conventions and disguised definitions. Yet they are
[L1116] drawn from experimental laws; these laws have, so to speak, been exalted
[L1117] into principles to which our mind attributes an absolute value.
[L1118]
[L1119] Some philosophers have generalized too far; they believed the principles
[L1120] were the whole science and consequently that the whole science was
[L1121] conventional.
[L1122]
[L1123] This paradoxical doctrine, called nominalism, will not bear
[L1124] examination.
[L1125]
[L1126] How can a law become a principle? It expressed a relation between two
[L1127] real terms _A_ and _B_. But it was not rigorously true, it was only
[L1128] approximate. We introduce arbitrarily an intermediary term _C_ more or
[L1129] less fictitious, and _C_ is _by definition_ that which has with _A_
[L1130] _exactly_ the relation expressed by the law.
[L1131]
[L1132] Then our law is separated into an absolute and rigorous principle which
[L1133] expresses the relation of _A_ to _C_ and an experimental law,
[L1134] approximate and subject to revision, which expresses the relation of _C_
[L1135] to _B_. It is clear that, however far this partition is pushed, some
[L1136] laws will always be left remaining.
[L1137]
[L1138] We go to enter now the domain of laws properly so called.
[L1139]

[L10] [5] Whoever seeks to derive new
[L11] knowledge from the excursions of a creature like Lumen into space,
[L12] confuses the time of an experience with the time of the objective event;
[L13] but the former can have a definite meaning only if it is founded on a
[L14] proper causal relation of space and time. In the above imaginary
[L15] experiment the order of the experiences in time is the reverse of that
[L16] of the events. And as far as causality is concerned, it is a scientific
[L17] conception that relates only to events ordered in space and time, and
[L18] not to experiences. In brief, the experiments with Lumen are swindles.
[L19]
[L20] [Footnote 5: Perhaps an analogy will serve to make this clear. Suppose
[L21] that a certain quantity of some foodstuff is consumed by ⅒ head of
[L22] population. The false inference would be that a population is possible
[L23] which has ⅒ heads! In the same way the statistics may be quite correct
[L24] in arriving at the figure ⅕ suicides, but if we leave the realms of
[L25] calculation, then the £ suicide loses its meaning entirely.]
[L26]
[L27] M.: I must resign myself to giving up these illusions. I must frankly
[L28] confess that I do so with a certain sadness, for such bold flights of
[L29] constructive fancy exert a powerful attraction on me. At one time I was
[L30] near outdoing Lumen by assuming a Super-Lumen, who was to traverse all
[L31] worlds at once with infinite velocity. He would then be in a position to
[L32] take a survey of the whole of universal history at a single glance. From
[L33] the nearest star, Alpha Centauri, he would see the earth as it was four
[L34] years ago; from the Pole Star, as it was forty years ago; and from the
[L35] boundary of the Milky Way, as it was four thousand years ago. At the
[L36] same moment he could choose a point of observation that would enable him
[L37] to see the First Crusade, the Siege of Troy, the Flood, and also the
[L38] events of the present day simultaneously.
[L39]
[L40] EINSTEIN: And this flight of thought, which, by the way, has been
[L41] indulged in repeatedly by others too, has much more sense in it than the
[L42] former one, because you may make an abstraction which disregards speed
[L43] altogether. It is only a limiting case of reflection.
[L44]
[L45] M.: I should like to touch on other limiting cases, in particular two
[L46] that I find it impossible to interpret. Lotze mentions them in his
[L47] Logic. The first concerns the infinitely long lever whose fulcrum, or
[L48] turning-point, is at the confines of the universe. According to the Laws
[L49] of Levers, a mass of magnitude zero will suffice to keep in equilibrium
[L50] at the end of the other lever-arm any weight, no matter whether it is a
[L51] million times heavier than the earth. Our imaginations cannot even
[L52] picture this. Yet I cannot feel satisfied with the mere explanation that
[L53] it is an exceptional case, an extension of a general law to a case in
[L54] which it is no longer applicable. The second example is still more
[L55] perplexing because it does not require a journey into other worlds, but
[L56] leads us into inconceivable consequences even if we remain on the earth.
[L57] Lotze considers this second limiting case easier; to me it seems more
[L58] difficult. It is this: The force that a wedge exerts is inversely
[L59] proportional to its thickness. If it is infinitely thin, this formula
[L60] gives an infinitely great result, whereas, actually, the force exerted
[L61] is nil. This very thin wedge, transformed finally into a geometrical
[L62] plane, should be able to split in twain any wooden or even steel block.
