[L72] Michelson's results did not accord with analogy. No difference in time
[L73] could be detected between the beam of light travelling up-and-down,
[L74] and across-and-back.
[L75]
[L76] But this was contrary to all reason if the postulate of an ether was
[L77] sound. Must we then revise our ideas of an ether? Perhaps after all
[L78] there is no ether.
[L79]
[L80] But if no ether, how are we to explain the propagation of light in
[L81] space, and various electrical phenomena connected with it, such as
[L82] the Hertzian, or wireless waves?
[L83]
[L84] There was another alternative, one suggested by Larmor in England
[L85] and Lorentz in Holland,--that matter is contracted in the direction
[L86] of its motion through the ether current. To say that bodies are
[L87] actually shortened in the direction of their motion--by an amount
[L88] which increases as the velocity of these bodies approaches that of
[L89] light--is so revolutionary an idea that Larmor and Lorentz would
[L90] hardly have adopted such a viewpoint but for the fact that recent
[L91] investigations into the nature of matter gave basis for such belief.
[L92]
[L93] Matter, it has been shown, is electrical in nature. The forces which
[L94] hold the particles together are electrical. Lorentz showed that
[L95] mathematical formulas for electrical forces could be developed which
[L96] would inevitably lead to the view that material bodies contract in
[L97] the direction of their motion. [8]
[L98]
[L99] "But this is ridiculous," you say; "if I am shorter in one direction
[L100] than in another I would notice it." You would if some things were
[L101] shortened and others were not. But if all things pointing in a certain
[L102] direction are shortened to an equal extent, how are you going to notice
[L103] it? Will you apply the yard stick? That has been shortened. Will you
[L104] pass judgment with the help of your eyes? But your retina has also
[L105] contracted. In brief, if all things contract to the same amount it
[L106] is as if there were no contraction at all.
[L107]
[L108] Lorentz's Plausible Explanation Really Deepens the Mystery. The
[L109] startling ideas just outlined have opened up several new vistas,
[L110] but they have left unanswered the two problems we set out to solve:
[L111] whether there is an ether, and if so, what is the velocity of the earth
[L112] in reference to this ether? Lorentz maintains that there is an ether,
[L113] but the velocities of bodies relative to it must forever remain a
[L114] mystery. As you change your position your distances change; you change;
[L115] everything about you changes accordingly; and all basis for comparison
[L116] is lost. Nature has entered into a conspiracy to keep you ignorant.
[L117]
[L118] Einstein Comes upon the Scene. Einstein starts with the assumption
[L119] that there is no possible way of identifying this ether. Suppose we
[L120] ignore the ether altogether, what then? [9]
[L121]
[L122] If we do ignore the ether we no longer have any absolute point of
[L123] reference; for if the ether is considered stationary the velocity of
[L124] all bodies within the ether may be referred to it; any point in space
[L125] may be considered a fixed point. If, however, there is no ether, or if
[L126] we are to ignore it, how are we to get the velocity of bodies in space?
[L127]
[L128] The Principle of Relativity. If we are to believe in the "causal
[L129] relationship between only such things as lie within the realm of
[L130] observation," then observation teaches us that bodies move only
[L131] relative to one another, and that the idea of absolute motion of a

[L149] "The properties of ether seem to be perfect. Matter is less so; it has

[L151] ether space. It doesn't wear out; there is no dissipation of energy;

[L154] that holds things together and acts as a cement. My business is to
[L155] call attention to the whole world of etherealness of things, and I
[L156] have made it a subject of thirty years' study, but we must admit that
[L157] there is no getting hold of ether except indirectly."
[L158]
[L159] "I consider the ether of space," says Lodge, in conclusion, "the one

[L166]
[L167] For the benefit of those readers who wish to gain a deeper insight
[L168] into the relativity principle, we shall here discuss it very briefly.
[L169]
[L170] Newton and Galileo had developed a relativity principle in mechanics
[L171] which may be stated as follows: If one system of reference is in
[L172] uniform rectilinear motion with respect to another system of reference,
[L173] then whatever physical laws are deduced from the first system hold
[L174] true for the second system. The two systems are equivalent. If the
[L175] two systems be represented by $xyz$ and $x'y'z'$, and if they move
[L176] with the velocity of v along the x-axis with respect to one another,
[L177] then the two systems are mathematically related thus:
[L178]
[L179]     $$x' = x - vt, y' = y, z' = z, t' = t,$$
[L180]
[L181] and this immediately provides us with a means of transforming the
[L182] laws of one system to those of another.
[L183]
[L184] With the development of electrodynamics (which we may call electricity
[L185] in motion) difficulties arose which equations in mechanics of type
[L186] (1) could no longer solve. These difficulties merely increased when
[L187] Maxwell showed that light must be regarded as an electromagnetic
[L188] phenomenon. For suppose we wish to investigate the motion of a source
[L189] of light (which may be the equivalent of the motion of the earth
[L190] with reference to the sun) with respect to the velocity of the light
[L191] it emits--a typical example of the study of moving systems--how are
[L192] we to coordinate the electrodynamical and mechanical elements? Or,
[L193] again, suppose we wish to investigate the velocity of electrons shot
[L194] out from radium with a speed comparable to that of light, how are we
[L195] to coordinate the two branches in tracing the course of these negative
[L196] particles of electricity?
[L197]
[L198] It was difficulties such as these that led to the Lorentz-Einstein
[L199] modifications of the Newton-Galileo relativity equations (1). The
[L200] Lorentz-Einstein equations are expressed in the form:
[L201]
[L202] $$x' = \frac{x-vt}{\sqrt{1-\frac{v^2}{c}}}, y' = y, z' = z, t' =
[L203] \frac{t-\frac{v}{c^2}\cdot x}{\sqrt{1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}}},$$
[L204]
[L205] c denoting the velocity of light in vacuo (which, according to all
[L206] observations, is the same, irrespective of the observer's state of
[L207] motion). Here, you see, electrodynamical systems (light and therefore
[L208] "ray" velocities such as those due to electrons) are brought into play.
[L209]
[L210] This gives us Einstein's special theory of relativity. From it Einstein
[L211] deduced some startling conceptions of time and space.

[L225] The ether of the general theory of
[L226] relativity is transmuted conceptually into the ether of Lorentz if
[L227] we substitute constants for the functions of space which describe
[L228] the former, disregarding the causes which condition its state.
[L229] Thus we may also say, I think, that the ether of the general theory
[L230] of relativity is the outcome of the Lorentzian ether, through
[L231] relativation.
[L232]
[L233] As to the part which the new ether is to play in the physics of
[L234] the future we are not yet clear. We know that it determines the
[L235] metrical relations in the space-time continuum, e.g. the configurative
[L236] possibilities of solid bodies as well as the gravitational fields;
[L237] but we do not know whether it has an essential share in the structure
[L238] of the electrical elementary particles constituting matter. Nor do
[L239] we know whether it is only in the proximity of ponderable masses
[L240] that its structure differs essentially from that of the Lorentzian
[L241] ether; whether the geometry of spaces of cosmic extent is approximately
[L242] Euclidean. But we can assert by reason of the relativistic equations
[L243] of gravitation that there must be a departure from Euclidean
[L244] relations, with spaces of cosmic order of magnitude, if there exists
[L245] a positive mean density, no matter how small, of the matter in the
[L246] universe. In this case the universe must of necessity be spatially
[L247] unbounded and of finite magnitude, its magnitude being determined
[L248] by the value of that mean density.
[L249]
[L250] If we consider the gravitational field and the electromagnetic field
[L251] from the stand-point of the ether hypothesis, we find a remarkable
[L252] difference between the two. There can be no space nor any part
[L253] of space without gravitational potentials; for these confer upon
[L254] space its metrical qualities, without which it cannot be imagined
[L255] at all. The existence of the gravitational field is inseparably
[L256] bound up with the existence of space. On the other hand a part of
[L257] space may very well be imagined without an electromagnetic field;
[L258] thus in contrast with the gravitational field, the electromagnetic
[L259] field seems to be only secondarily linked to the ether, the formal
[L260] nature of the electromagnetic field being as yet in no way determined
[L261] by that of gravitational ether. From the present state of theory
[L262] it looks as if the electromagnetic field, as opposed to the
[L263] gravitational field, rests upon an entirely new formal _motif_,
[L264] as though nature might just as well have endowed the gravitational
[L265] ether with fields of quite another type, for example, with fields
[L266] of a scalar potential, instead of fields of the electromagnetic
[L267] type.
[L268]
[L269] Since according to our present conceptions the elementary particles
[L270] of matter are also, in their essence, nothing else than condensations
[L271] of the electromagnetic field, our present view of the universe
[L272] presents two realities which are completely separated from each other
[L273] conceptually, although connected causally, namely, gravitational ether
[L274] and electromagnetic field, or--as they might also be called--space
[L275] and matter.
[L276]
[L277] Of course it would be a great advance if we could succeed in
[L278] comprehending the gravitational field and the electromagnetic field
[L279] together as one unified conformation. Then for the first time the
[L280] epoch of theoretical physics founded by Faraday and Maxwell would
[L281] reach a satisfactory conclusion. The contrast between ether and
[L282] matter would fade away, and, through the general theory of relativity,
[L283] the whole of physics would become a complete system of thought,
[L284] like geometry, kinematics, and the theory of gravitation.  An
[L285] exceedingly ingenious attempt in this direction has been made by
[L286] the mathematician H. Weyl; but I do not believe that his theory will
[L287] hold its ground in relation to reality.

[L297] This introduction of imaginary quantities might be expected,
[L298] possibly, to introduce difficulties; but, in reality, it is the very
[L299] essence of the simplicity of the geometrical description just given
[L300] of the rotation of the sets of axes. It thus appears that different
[L301] observers situated at different points in the universe would each have
[L302] their own set of axes, all different, yet all connected by the fact
[L303] that any one can be rotated so as to coincide with any other. This
[L304] means that there is no one direction in the four-dimensional space
[L305] that corresponds to time for all observers. Just as with reference to
[L306] the earth there is no direction which can be called vertical for all
[L307] observers living on the earth. In the sense of an absolute meaning
[L308] the words "up and down," "before and after," "sooner or later,"
[L309] are entirely meaningless.
[L310]
[L311] This concept of Minkowski's may be made clearer, perhaps, by the
[L312] following process of thought. If we take a section through our
[L313] three-dimensional space, we have a plane, i.e., a two-dimensional
[L314] space. Similarly, if a section is made through a four-dimensional
[L315] space, one of three dimensions is obtained. Thus, for an observer on
[L316] the earth a definite section of Minkowski's four-dimensional space will
[L317] give us our ordinary three-dimensional one; so that this section will,
[L318] as it were, break up Minkowski's space into our space and give us our
[L319] ordinary time. Similarly, a different section would have to be used
[L320] to the observer on Arcturus; but by a suitable selection he would
[L321] get his own familiar three-dimensional space and his own time. Thus
[L322] the space defined by Minkowski is completely isotropic in reference
[L323] to measured lengths and times, there is absolutely no difference
[L324] between any two directions in an absolute sense; for any particular
[L325] observer, of course, a particular section will cause the space to
[L326] fall apart so as to suit his habits of measurement; any section,
[L327] however, taken at random will do the same thing for some observer
[L328] somewhere. From another point of view, that of Lorentz and Einstein,
[L329] it is obvious that, since this four-dimensional space is isotropic,
[L330] the expression of the laws of electromagnetic phenomena take identical
[L331] mathematical forms when expressed by any observer.
[L332]
[L333] The question of course must be raised as to what can be said in regard
[L334] to phenomena which so far as we know do not have an electromagnetic
[L335] origin. In particular what can be done with respect to gravitational
[L336] phenomena? Before, however, showing how this problem was attacked by
[L337] Einstein; and the fact that the subject of my address is Einstein's
[L338] work on gravitation shows that ultimately I shall explain this, I
[L339] must emphasize another feature of Minkowski's geometry. To describe
[L340] the space-time characteristics of any event a point, defined by its
[L341] four coordinates, is sufficient; so, if one observes the life-history
[L342] of any entity, e.g., a particle of matter, a light-wave, etc., he
[L343] observes a sequence of points in the space-time continuum; that is,
[L344] the life-history of any entity is described fully by a line in this
[L345] space. Such a line was called by Minkowski a "world-line." Further,
[L346] from a different point of view, all of our observations of nature
[L347] are in reality observations of coincidences, e.g., if one reads
[L348] a thermometer, what he does is to note the coincidence of the
[L349] end of the column of mercury with a certain scale division on
[L350] the thermometer tube. In other words, thinking of the world-line
[L351] of the end of the mercury column and the world-line of the scale
[L352] division, what we have observed was the intersection or crossing of
[L353] these lines.

[L372] discover an exit elsewhere at the other end perhaps."

[L374] Perhaps poets of the future will busy themselves with this universe; not
[L375] lyrical poets, but descendants of Hesiod, Lucretius, or Rückert. They
[L376] will express in verse that Einstein's world offers a source of
[L377] consolation to tormented spirits which have sickened of Kant's
[L378] antinomies. For in this still almost immeasurable world the fateful
[L379] conception "infinite" has been made bearable for the first time. In a
[L380] certain way it relieves us from what is quite inconceivable, yet into
[L381] which we are usually driven, and forms a bridge between the thesis
[L382] "finite" and the antithesis infinite. We are brought to a common stream,
[L383] in which both conceptions peacefully flow together. There was no mention
[L384] of this in our talk, and I had good reason for being cautious about
[L385] following out the theme along these lines. I must not allow any doubts
[L386] to arise on this point: Einstein, himself, clings with unerring logic to
[L387] the strict mathematically defined conception of infinity, and allows no
[L388] compromise with the non-infinite.
[L389]
[L390] When I, on some previous occasion, sought to lead him on to a
[L391] compromise, involving a transition-boundary, it availed me nothing that

[L393] effort came to an abrupt end.

[L395]      *     *     *     *     *     *     *     *
[L396]
[L397] In pursuing these considerations about the universe, we arrived at

[L400] trying to trace out a connexion between the four-dimensionality that you
[L401] establish, Professor, and the four-dimensionality of certain spiritistic
[L402] pseudo-philosophers, yet it suggests itself to me that in such occult
[L403] circles efforts will be made to derive advantage from the fact that the
[L404] same word is used in both cases. This is more than a conjecture, indeed,
[L405] for there are no misgivings among the ignorant, and so we actually find
[L406] the name Einstein quoted in connexion with mediumistic experiments that
[L407] are flavoured with four-dimensionality."
[L408]
[L409] "It will not be expected of me," said Einstein, "to enter into
[L410] discussion with ignoramuses and misinterpreted. Discarding them, then,
[L411] let us confine ourselves to a brief consideration of the conception
[L412] 'occult,' as this has played a part in serious science. The chief
[L413] example of this in history is gravitation. Huyghens and Leibniz refused
[L414] to accept gravitation, for, so they said, according to Newton's view, it
[L415] is an action at a distance and hence belongs to the realm of the occult.
[L416] Like everything occult, it contradicts the causal order in Nature.

[L496] M.: This would be a very grateful task, judged from the literary point
[L497] of view. What a splendid colouring could be obtained by bringing these
[L498] two worlds of thought into conflict with one another, the Relative
[L499] against the Absolute, which has been established in tradition and dogma.
[L500] But we need not even call the historical fancy into action, for,
[L501] actually, the theory of the structure of the world is even now still at
[L502] variance with traditional ideas, that act with dogmatic violence. There
[L503] is no need to deny the fact that every person of education, who makes
[L504] the acquaintance of Lorentz's, Minkowski's, Einstein's ideas for the
[L505] first time, feels excited to offer contradictions, and becomes involved
[L506] in a tumult of pros and cons, and each one experiences in himself the
[L507] excitement of an inquisitorial tribunal. The triumph of the new theory
[L508] passes over the corpses of conceptions that lie at the cross-roads of
[L509] thought and, long after, retain a ghostly existence. Only very few of us
[L510] are aware of the further inner revolution that awaits us along the line
[L511] of development of Einsteinian ideas; we have only vague presentiments
[L512] that whisper to us that the end of forms of thought once considered as
[L513] irrefragable is drawing nigh. When once the principle of causality has
[L514] been set on a relative base, and all "properties" have been resolved
[L515] into occurrence, and all that is three-dimensional has come to be
[L516] recognized as an abstraction from the four-dimensional world that is
[L517] alone valid, then the time will have come to arrange for, the death
[L518] procession of all the philosophies that once served as the main pillars
[L519] of thought.
[L520]
[L521] A retrospect of the trials of Giordano Bruno and of Galileo Galilei
[L522] offers certain parallels other than those usually discovered by
[L523] scholars. And if, to-day, we proclaim Einstein as the Galilei of the
[L524] twentieth century, it must be added that in character he is fortunately
[L525] a Bruno and not a Galilei. For it is not true that the latter came out
[L526] of the persecution as a moral victor with an _eppur si muove_, rather,
[L527] in spite of the protection of influential prelates and dignitaries, even
[L528] of the entourage of the Pope, he lacked courage and bowed his head,
[L529] betraying his science and denying himself as well as Copernicus. Are we
[L530] to picture how Einstein would have acted under similar circumstances,
[L531] even if they cannot recur again?
[L532]
[L533] Whoever has even an inkling of his character will entertain no doubts.
[L534] At that time, three hundred years ago, the materials for a magnificent
[L535] scene, "one world _versus_ the other," lay ready. Only one condition was
[L536] wanting, the moral courage of the hero. The lack of this one factor
[L537] spoilt the final act for the history of that time. The fine ethical
[L538] feelings of later generations have had to be propitiated by improvising
[L539] a legend iridescent with beautiful colours.

[L569] But the problems raised by the electron and the quantum are not those
[L570] that the theory of relativity can solve, at any rate at present; as
[L571] yet, it throws no light upon the discontinuities which exist in nature.
[L572] The problems solved by the special theory of relativity are typified by
[L573] the Michelson-Morley experiment. Assuming the correctness of Maxwell’s
[L574] theory of electromagnetism, there should have been certain discoverable
[L575] effects of motion through the ether; in fact, there were none. Then
[L576] there was the observed fact that a body in very rapid motion appears
[L577] to increase its mass; the increase is in the ratio of =OP= to =MP=
[L578] in the figure in the preceding chapter. Facts of this sort gradually
[L579] accumulated, until it became imperative to find some theory which would
[L580] account for them all.
[L581]
[L582] Maxwell’s theory reduced itself to certain equations, known as
[L583] “Maxwell’s equations.” Through all the revolutions which physics has
[L584] undergone in the last fifty years, these equations have remained
[L585] standing; indeed they have continually grown in importance as well as
[L586] in certainty—for Maxwell’s arguments in their favor were so shaky that
[L587] the correctness of his results must almost be ascribed to intuition.
[L588] Now these equations were, of course, obtained from experiments in
[L589] terrestrial laboratories, but there was a tacit assumption that the
[L590] motion of the earth through the ether could be ignored. In certain
[L591] cases, such as the Michelson-Morley experiment, this ought not to have
[L592] been possible without measurable error; but it turned out to be always
[L593] possible. Physicists were faced with the odd difficulty that Maxwell’s
[L594] equations were more accurate than they should be. A very similar
[L595] difficulty was explained by Galileo at the very beginning of modern
[L596] physics. Most people think that if you let a weight drop it will fall
[L597] vertically. But if you try the experiment in the cabin of a moving
[L598] ship, the weight falls, in relation to the cabin, just as if the ship
[L599] were at rest; for instance, if it starts from the middle of the ceiling
[L600] it will drop onto the middle of the floor. That is to say, from the
[L601] point of view of an observer on the shore it does not fall vertically,
[L602] since it shares the motion of the ship. So long as the ship’s motion
[L603] is steady, everything goes on inside the ship as if the ship were not
[L604] moving. Galileo explained how this happens, to the great indignation
[L605] of the disciples of Aristotle. In orthodox physics, which is derived
[L606] from Galileo, a uniform motion in a straight line has no discoverable
[L607] effects. This was, in its day, as astonishing a form of relativity
[L608] as that of Einstein is to us. Einstein, in the special theory of
[L609] relativity, set to work to show how electromagnetic phenomena could be
[L610] unaffected by uniform motion through the ether if there be an ether.
[L611] This was a more difficult problem, which could not be solved by merely
[L612] adhering to the principles of Galileo.
[L613]
[L614] The really difficult effort required for solving this problem was in
[L615] regard to time. It was necessary to introduce the notion of “proper”
[L616] time which we have already considered, and to abandon the old belief in
[L617] one universal time. The quantitative laws of electromagnetic phenomena
[L618] are expressed in Maxwell’s equations, and these equations are found
[L619] to be true for any observer, however he may be moving.[3] It is a
[L620] straight-forward mathematical problem to find out what differences
[L621] there must be between the measures applied by one observer and the
[L622] measures applied by another, if, in spite of their relative motion,
[L623] they are to find the same equations verified.

[L633] For the theoretician such
[L634] an asymmetry in the theoretical structure, with no corresponding
[L635] asymmetry in the system of experience, is intolerable. If we assume
[L636] the ether to be at rest relatively to K, but in motion relatively
[L637] to K', the physical equivalence of K and K' seems to me from the
[L638] logical standpoint, not indeed downright incorrect, but nevertheless
[L639] inacceptable.
[L640]
[L641] The next position which it was possible to take up in face of this
[L642] state of things appeared to be the following. The ether does not
[L643] exist at all. The electromagnetic fields are not states of a medium,
[L644] and are not bound down to any bearer, but they are independent
[L645] realities which are not reducible to anything else, exactly like
[L646] the atoms of ponderable matter. This conception suggests itself
[L647] the more readily as, according to Lorentz's theory, electromagnetic
[L648] radiation, like ponderable matter, brings impulse and energy with
[L649] it, and as, according to the special theory of relativity, both
[L650] matter and radiation are but special forms of distributed energy,
[L651] ponderable mass losing its isolation and appearing as a special
[L652] form of energy.
[L653]
[L654] More careful reflection teaches us, however, that the special theory
[L655] of relativity does not compel us to deny ether. We may assume the
[L656] existence of an ether; only we must give up ascribing a definite
[L657] state of motion to it, i.e. we must by abstraction take from it the
[L658] last mechanical characteristic which Lorentz had still left it. We
[L659] shall see later that this point of view, the conceivability of which
[L660] I shall at once endeavour to make more intelligible by a somewhat
[L661] halting comparison, is justified by the results of the general
[L662] theory of relativity.
[L663]
[L664] Think of waves on the surface of water. Here we can describe two
[L665] entirely different things. Either we may observe how the undulatory
[L666] surface forming the boundary between water and air alters in the course
[L667] of time; or else--with the help of small floats, for instance--we
[L668] can observe how the position of the separate particles of water
[L669] alters in the course of time. If the existence of such floats for
[L670] tracking the motion of the particles of a fluid were a fundamental
[L671] impossibility in physics--if, in fact, nothing else whatever were
[L672] observable than the shape of the space occupied by the water as it
[L673] varies in time, we should have no ground for the assumption that
[L674] water consists of movable particles. But all the same we could
[L675] characterise it as a medium.
[L676]
[L677] We have something like this in the electromagnetic field. For we may
[L678] picture the field to ourselves as consisting of lines of force.  If
[L679] we wish to interpret these lines of force to ourselves as something
[L680] material in the ordinary sense, we are tempted to interpret the
[L681] dynamic processes as motions of these lines of force, such that each
[L682] separate line of force is tracked through the course of time. It is
[L683] well known, however, that this way of regarding the electromagnetic
[L684] field leads to contradictions.
[L685]
[L686] Generalising we must say this:--There may be supposed to be extended
[L687] physical objects to which the idea of motion cannot be applied.
[L688] They may not be thought of as consisting of particles which allow
[L689] themselves to be separately tracked through time. In Minkowski's
[L690] idiom this is expressed as follows:--Not every extended conformation
[L691] in the four-dimensional world can be regarded as composed
[L692] of world-threads. The special theory of relativity forbids us to
[L693] assume the ether to consist of particles observable through time,
[L694] but the hypothesis of ether in itself is not in conflict with the
[L695] special theory of relativity. Only we must be on our guard against
[L696] ascribing a state of motion to the ether.

[L706] Note 8 (page 59)
[L707]
[L708] That the conception of the "simultaneity" of events is devoid of
[L709] meaning can be deduced from equation (2) [see Note 4]. We owe the proof
[L710] to Einstein. "It is possible to select a suitable time-coordinate
[L711] in such a way that a time-measurement enters into physical laws
[L712] in exactly the same manner as regards its significance as a space
[L713] measurement (that is, they are fully equivalent symbolically), and
[L714] has likewise a definite coordinate direction.... It never occurred to
[L715] anyone that the use of a light-signal as a means of connection between
[L716] the moving-body and the observer, which is necessary in practice in
[L717] order to determine simultaneity, might affect the final result, i.e.,
[L718] of time measurements in different systems." (Freundlich). But that
[L719] is just what Einstein shows, because time-measurements are based on
[L720] "simultaneity of events," and this, as pointed out above, is devoid
[L721] of meaning.
[L722]
[L723] Had the older masters the occasion to study enormous velocities, such
[L724] as the velocity of light, rather than relatively small ones--and even
[L725] the velocity of the earth around the sun is small as compared to the
[L726] velocity of light--discrepancies between theory and experiment would
[L727] have become apparent.
[L728]
[L729]
[L730]
[L731] Note 9 (page 67)
[L732]
[L733] How the special theory of relativity (see Note 4) led to the general
[L734] theory of relativity (which included gravitation) may now be briefly
[L735] traced.
[L736]
[L737] When we speak of electrons, or negative particles of electricity,
[L738] in motion, we are speaking of energy in motion. Now these electrons
[L739] when in motion exhibit properties that are very similar to matter in
[L740] motion. Whatever deviations there are are due to the enormous velocity
[L741] of these electrons, and this velocity, as has already been pointed
[L742] out, is comparable to that of light; whereas before the advent of the
[L743] electron, the velocity of no particles comparable to that of light
[L744] had ever been measured.
[L745]
[L746] According to present views "all inertia of matter consists only of the
[L747] inertia of the latent energy in it; ... everything that we know of the
[L748] inertia of energy holds without exception for the inertia of matter."
[L749]
[L750] Now it is on the assumption that inertial mass and gravitational
[L751] "pull" are equivalent that the mass of a body is determined by its
[L752] weight. What is true of matter should be true of energy.
[L753]
[L754] The special theory of relativity, however, takes into account only
[L755] inertia ("inertial mass") but not gravitation (gravitational pull or
[L756] weight) of energy. When a body absorbs energy equation 2 (see Note 4)
[L757] will record a gain in inertia but not in weight--which is contrary
[L758] to one of the fundamental facts in mechanics.
[L759]
[L760] This means that a more general theory of relativity is required to
[L761] include gravitational phenomena. Hence Einstein's General Theory of
[L762] Relativity. Hence the approach to a new theory of gravitation. Hence
[L763] "the setting up of a differential equation which comprises the
[L764] motion of a body under the influence of both inertia and gravity,
[L765] and which symbolically expresses the relativity of motions.... The
[L766] differential law must always preserve the same form, irrespective of
[L767] the system of coordinates to which it is referred, so that no system of
[L768] coordinates enjoys a preference to any other." (For the general form
[L769] of the equation and for an excellent discussion of its significance,
[L770] see Freundlich's monograph, pages 27-33.)
[L771]
[L772]
[L773]
[L774]
[L775]
[L776]
[L777]
[L778]
[L779] TIME, SPACE, AND GRAVITATION [14]
[L780]
[L781] By Prof. Albert Einstein

[L791] Certainly any effect of refraction seems to be excluded.
[L792]
[L793] It is thus seen that the formulæ deduced by Einstein have been
[L794] confirmed in a variety of ways and in a most brilliant manner. In
[L795] connection with these formulæ one question must arise in the minds of
[L796] everyone; by what process, where in the course of the mathematical
[L797] development, does the idea of mass reveal itself? It was not in
[L798] the equations at the beginning and yet here it is at the end. How
[L799] does it appear? As a matter of fact it is first seen as a constant
[L800] of integration in the discussion of the problem of the gravitational
[L801] field due to a single particle; and the identity of this constant with
[L802] mass is proved when one compares Einstein's formulæ with Newton's
[L803] law which is simply its degenerated form. This mass, though, is the
[L804] mass of which we become aware through our experiences with weight;
[L805] and Einstein proceeded to prove that this quantity which entered as
[L806] a constant of integration in his ideally simple problem also obeyed
[L807] the laws of conservation of mass and conservation of momentum when
[L808] he investigated the problems of two and more particles. Therefore
[L809] Einstein deduced from his study of gravitational fields the well-known
[L810] properties of matter which form the basis of theoretical mechanics. A
[L811] further logical consequence of Einstein's development is to show that
[L812] energy has mass, a concept with which every one nowadays is familiar.
[L813]
[L814] The description of Einstein's method which I have given so far is
[L815] simply the story of one success after another; and it is certainly
[L816] fair to ask if we have at last reached finality in our investigation
[L817] of nature, if we have attained to truth. Are there no outstanding
[L818] difficulties? Is there no possibility of error? Certainly, not
[L819] until all the predictions made from Einstein's formulæ have been
[L820] investigated can much be said; and further, it must be seen whether
[L821] any other lines of argument will lead to the same conclusions. But
[L822] without waiting for all this there is at least one difficulty which
[L823] is apparent at this time. We have discussed the laws of nature as
[L824] independent in their form of reference axes, a concept which appeals
[L825] strongly to our philosophy; yet it is not at all clear, at first sight,
[L826] that we can be justified in our belief. We can not imagine any way
[L827] by which we can become conscious of the translation of the earth in
[L828] space; but by means of gyroscopes we can learn a great deal about its
[L829] rotation on its axis. We could locate the positions of its two poles,
[L830] and by watching a Foucault pendulum or a gyroscope we can obtain a
[L831] number which we interpret as the angular velocity of rotation of axes
[L832] fixed in the earth; angular velocity with reference to what? Where
[L833] is the fundamental set of axes? This is a real difficulty. It can be
[L834] surmounted in several ways. Einstein himself has outlined a method
[L835] which in the end amounts to assuming the existence on the confines
[L836] of space of vast quantities of matter, a proposition which is not
[L837] attractive. deSitter has suggested a peculiar quality of the space
[L838] to which we refer our space-time coordinates. The consequences of
[L839] this are most interesting, but no decision can as yet be made as to
[L840] the justification of the hypothesis. In any case we can say that
[L841] the difficulty raised is not one that destroys the real value of
[L842] Einstein's work.

[L852] This
[L853] isotropy and homogeneity is exactly expressed by Einstein’s law of
[L854] gravitation.”[14]
[L855]
[L856] [13] “Isotropy” means being similar in all directions—_e.g._, that a
[L857] foot rule is as long when it points north as when it points east.
[L858]
[L859] [14] _Mathematical Theory of Relativity_, p. 238.
[L860]
[L861] The limitations of knowledge introduced by the selectiveness of our
[L862] perceptual apparatus may be illustrated by the indestructibility
[L863] of matter. This has been gradually discovered by experiment, and
[L864] seemed a well-founded empirical law of nature. Now it turns out
[L865] that, from our original space-time continuum, we can construct a
[L866] mathematical expression which will have properties causing it to appear
[L867] indestructible. The statement that matter is indestructible then ceases
[L868] to be a proposition of physics, and becomes instead a proposition
[L869] of linguistics and psychology. As a proposition of linguistics:
[L870] “Matter” is the name of the mathematical expression in question. As a
[L871] proposition of psychology: Our senses are such that we notice what is
[L872] roughly the mathematical expression in question, and we are led nearer
[L873] and nearer to it as we refine upon our crude perceptions by scientific
[L874] observation. This is much less than physicists used to think they knew
[L875] about matter.
[L876]
[L877] The reader may say: What then is left of physics? What do we really
[L878] know about the world of matter? Here we may distinguish three
[L879] departments of physics. There is first what is included within the
[L880] theory of relativity, generalized as widely as possible. Next, there
[L881] are laws which cannot be brought within the scope of relativity.
[L882] Thirdly, there is what may be called geography. Let us consider each of
[L883] these in turn.
[L884]
[L885] The theory of relativity, apart from convention, tells us that the
[L886] events in the universe have a four-dimensional order, and that,
[L887] between any two events which are near together in this order, there
[L888] is a relation called “interval,” which is capable of being measured
[L889] if suitable precautions are taken. We make also an assumption as to
[L890] what happens when a little measuring rod is carried round a closed
[L891] circuit in a certain manner; the consequences of this assumption are
[L892] such as to make it highly probable that it is true. Beyond this, there
[L893] is little in the theory of relativity that can be regarded as physical
[L894] laws. There is a great deal of mathematics, showing that certain
[L895] mathematically-constructed quantities must behave like the things we
[L896] perceive; and there is a suggestion of a bridge between psychology and
[L897] physics in the theory that these mathematically-constructed quantities
[L898] are what our senses are adapted for perceiving. But neither of these
[L899] things is physics in the strict sense.
[L900]
[L901] The part of physics which cannot, at present, be brought within
[L902] the scope of relativity is large and important. There is nothing
[L903] in relativity to show why there should be electrons and protons;
[L904] relativity cannot give any reason why matter should exist in little
[L905] lumps. With this goes the whole theory of the structure of the atom.
[L906] The theory of quanta also is quite outside the scope of relativity.
[L907] Relativity is, in a sense, the most extreme application of what may
[L908] be called next-to-next methods. Gravitation is no longer regarded
[L909] as due to the effect of the sun upon a planet, but as expressing
[L910] characteristics of the region in which the planet happens to be.
[L911] Distance, which used to be thought to have a definite meaning however
[L912] far apart two points might be, is now only definite for neighboring
[L913] points. The distance between widely separated places depends upon the
[L914] route chosen.

[L924] Now anybody can verify, either by
[L925] trial or by a little arithmetic, that it takes longer to row a given
[L926] distance on a river upstream and then back again, than it takes to
[L927] row the same distance across the stream and back again. Therefore, if
[L928] there were an ether wind, one of the two light signals, which consist
[L929] of waves in the ether, ought to have traveled to the mirror and back at
[L930] a slower average rate than the other. Michelson and Morley tried the
[L931] experiment, they tried it in various positions, they tried it again
[L932] later. Their apparatus was quite accurate enough to have detected the
[L933] expected difference of speed or even a much smaller difference, if
[L934] it had existed, but not the smallest difference could be observed.
[L935] The result was a surprise to them as to everybody else; but careful
[L936] repetitions made doubt impossible. The experiment was first made as
[L937] long ago as 1881, and was repeated with more elaboration in 1887. But
[L938] it was many years before it could be rightly interpreted.
[L939]
[L940] The supposition that the earth carries the neighboring ether with it
[L941] in its motion was found to be impossible, for a number of reasons.
[L942] Consequently a logical deadlock seemed to have arisen, from which at
[L943] first physicists sought to extricate themselves by very arbitrary
[L944] hypotheses. The most important of these was that of Fitzgerald,
[L945] developed by Lorentz, and known as the Fitzgerald contraction
[L946] hypothesis.
[L947]
[L948] According to this hypothesis, when a body is in motion it becomes
[L949] shortened in the direction of motion by a certain proportion depending
[L950] upon its velocity. The amount of the contraction was to be just enough
[L951] to account for the negative result of the Michelson-Morley experiment.
[L952] The journey up stream and down again was to have been really a shorter
[L953] journey than the one across the stream, and was to have been just so
[L954] much shorter as would enable the slower light wave to traverse it in
[L955] the same time. Of course the shortening could never be detected by
[L956] measurement, because our measuring rods would share it. A foot rule
[L957] placed in the line of the earth’s motion would be shorter than the
[L958] same foot rule placed at right angles to the earth’s motion. This
[L959] point of view resembles nothing so much as the White Knight’s “plan to
[L960] dye my whiskers green, and always use so large a fan that they could
[L961] not be seen.” The odd thing was that the plan worked well enough. Later
[L962] on, when Einstein propounded his special theory of relativity (1905),
[L963] it was found that the theory was in a certain sense correct, but only
[L964] in a certain sense. That is to say, the supposed contraction is not
[L965] a physical fact, but a result of certain conventions of measurement
[L966] which, when once the right point of view has been found, are seen to
[L967] be such as we are almost compelled to adopt. But I do not wish yet to
[L968] set forth Einstein’s solution of the puzzle. For the present, it is the
[L969] nature of the puzzle itself that I want to make clear.
[L970]
[L971] On the face of it, and apart from hypotheses _ad hoc_, the
[L972] Michelson-Morley experiment (in conjunction with others) showed that,
[L973] relatively to the earth, the velocity of light is the same in all
[L974] directions, and that this is equally true at all times of the year,
[L975] although the direction of the earth’s motion is always changing as
[L976] it goes round the sun.

[L986] With the development of electrodynamics (which we may call electricity
[L987] in motion) difficulties arose which equations in mechanics of type
[L988] (1) could no longer solve. These difficulties merely increased when
[L989] Maxwell showed that light must be regarded as an electromagnetic
[L990] phenomenon. For suppose we wish to investigate the motion of a source
[L991] of light (which may be the equivalent of the motion of the earth
[L992] with reference to the sun) with respect to the velocity of the light
[L993] it emits--a typical example of the study of moving systems--how are
[L994] we to coordinate the electrodynamical and mechanical elements? Or,
[L995] again, suppose we wish to investigate the velocity of electrons shot
[L996] out from radium with a speed comparable to that of light, how are we
[L997] to coordinate the two branches in tracing the course of these negative
[L998] particles of electricity?
[L999]
[L1000] It was difficulties such as these that led to the Lorentz-Einstein
[L1001] modifications of the Newton-Galileo relativity equations (1). The
[L1002] Lorentz-Einstein equations are expressed in the form:
[L1003]
[L1004] $$x' = \frac{x-vt}{\sqrt{1-\frac{v^2}{c}}}, y' = y, z' = z, t' =
[L1005] \frac{t-\frac{v}{c^2}\cdot x}{\sqrt{1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}}},$$
[L1006]
[L1007] c denoting the velocity of light in vacuo (which, according to all
[L1008] observations, is the same, irrespective of the observer's state of
[L1009] motion). Here, you see, electrodynamical systems (light and therefore
[L1010] "ray" velocities such as those due to electrons) are brought into play.
[L1011]
[L1012] This gives us Einstein's special theory of relativity. From it Einstein
[L1013] deduced some startling conceptions of time and space.
[L1014]
[L1015]
[L1016]
[L1017] Note 5 (page 55)
[L1018]
[L1019] The velocity (v) of an object in one system will have a different
[L1020] velocity (v') if referred to another system in uniform motion relative
[L1021] to the first. It had been supposed that only a "something" endowed
[L1022] with infinite velocity would show the same velocity in all systems,
[L1023] irrespective of the motions of the latter. Michelson and Morley's
[L1024] results actually point to the velocity of light as showing the
[L1025] properties of the imaginary "infinite velocity." The velocity of
[L1026] light possesses universal significance; and this is the basis for
[L1027] much of Einstein's earlier work.
[L1028]
[L1029]
[L1030]
[L1031] Note 6 (page 56)
[L1032]
[L1033] "Euclid assumes that parallel lines never meet, which they cannot
[L1034] do of course if they be defined as equidistant. But are there such
[L1035] lines? And if not, why not assume that all lines drawn through a
[L1036] point outside a given line will eventually intersect it? Such an
[L1037] assumption leads to a geometry in which all lines are conceived as
[L1038] being drawn on the surface of a sphere or an ellipse, and in it the
[L1039] three angles of a triangle are never quite equal to two right angles,
[L1040] nor the circumference of a circle quite [pi] times its diameter. But
[L1041] that is precisely what the contraction effect due to motion requires."
[L1042]
[L1043]
[L1044]     (Dr. Walker)
[L1045]
[L1046]
[L1047]
[L1048] Note 7 (page 57)
[L1049]
[L1050] Einstein had become tired of assumptions. He had no particular
[L1051] objection to the "ether" theory beyond the fact that this "ether"
[L1052] did not come within the range of our senses; it could not be
[L1053] "observed." "The consistent fulfilment of the two postulates--'action
[L1054] by contact' and causal relationship between only such things
[L1055] as lie within the realm of observation [see Note 2] combined
[L1056] together is, I believe, the mainspring of Einstein's method of
[L1057] investigation...." (Prof. Freundlich).

[L10] Between a piece of orchestral
[L11] music as played, and the same piece of music as printed in the score,
[L12] there is a certain resemblance, which may be described as a resemblance
[L13] in structure. The resemblance is of such a sort that, when you know the
[L14] rules, you can infer the music from the score or the score from the
[L15] music. But suppose you had been stone deaf from birth, but had lived
[L16] among musical people. You could understand, if you had learned to speak
[L17] and to do lip-reading, that the musical scores represented something
[L18] quite different from themselves in intrinsic quality, though similar in
[L19] structure.[16] The value of music would be completely unimaginable to
[L20] you, but you could infer all its mathematical characteristics, since
[L21] they are the same as those of the score. Now our knowledge of nature is
[L22] something like this. We can read the scores, and infer just so much as
[L23] our stone-deaf person could have inferred about music. But we have not
[L24] the advantages which he derived from association with musical people.
[L25] We cannot know whether the music represented by the scores is beautiful
[L26] or hideous; perhaps, in the last analysis, we cannot be quite sure that
[L27] the scores represent anything but themselves. But this is a doubt which
[L28] the physicist, in his professional capacity, cannot permit himself to
[L29] entertain.
[L30]
[L31] [16] For the definition of “structure,” see the present author’s
[L32] _Introduction to Mathematical Philosophy_.
[L33]
[L34] Assuming the utmost that can be claimed for physics, it does not tell
[L35] us what it is that changes, or what are its various states; it only
[L36] tells us such things as that changes follow each other periodically,
[L37] or spread with a certain speed. Even now we are probably not at the
[L38] end of the process of stripping away what is merely imagination, in
[L39] order to reach the core of true scientific knowledge. The theory of
[L40] relativity has accomplished a very great deal in this respect, and in
[L41] doing so has taken us nearer and nearer to bare structure, which is
[L42] the mathematician’s goal—not because it is the only thing in which he
[L43] is interested as a human being, but because it is the only thing that
[L44] he can express in mathematical formulæ. But far as we have traveled in
[L45] the direction of abstraction, it may be that we shall have to travel
[L46] further still.
[L47]
[L48] In the preceding chapter, I suggested what may be called a minimum
[L49] definition of matter, that is to say, one in which matter has, so
[L50] to speak, as little “substance” as is compatible with the truth of
[L51] physics. In adopting a definition of this kind, we are playing for
[L52] safety: our tenuous matter will exist, even if something more beefy
[L53] also exists. We tried to make our definition of matter, like Isabella’s
[L54] gruel in Jane Austen, “thin, but not too thin.” We shall, however, fall
[L55] into error if we assert positively that matter is nothing more than
[L56] this. Leibniz thought that a piece of matter is really a colony of
[L57] souls. There is nothing to show that he was wrong, though there is also
[L58] nothing to show that he was right: we know no more about it either way
[L59] than we do about the flora and fauna of Mars.
[L60]
[L61] To the non-mathematical mind, the abstract character of our physical
[L62] knowledge may seem unsatisfactory. From an artistic or imaginative
[L63] point of view, it is perhaps regrettable, but from a practical point
[L64] of view it is of no consequence. Abstraction, difficult as it is, is
[L65] the source of practical power.

[L75] It is thought that a sufficient knowledge of the
[L76] geographical facts of the solar system throughout any finite time,
[L77] however short, would enable an ideally competent physicist to predict
[L78] the future of the solar system so long as it remained remote from other
[L79] stars. We are already in a position to calculate the large facts about
[L80] the solar system backwards and forwards for vast periods of time. But
[L81] in all such calculations we need a basis of crude fact. The facts are
[L82] interconnected, but facts can only be inferred from other facts, not
[L83] from general laws alone. Thus the facts of geography have a certain
[L84] independent status in physics. No amount of physical laws will enable
[L85] us to infer a physical fact unless we know other facts as data for our
[L86] inference. And here when I speak of “facts” I am thinking of particular
[L87] facts of geography, in the extended sense in which I am using the term.
[L88]
[L89] In the theory of relativity, we are concerned with _structure_, not
[L90] with the material of which the structure is composed. In geography,
[L91] on the other hand, the material is relevant. If there is to be any
[L92] difference between one place and another, there must either be
[L93] differences between the material in one place and that in another, or
[L94] places where there is material and places where there is none. The
[L95] former of these alternatives seems the more satisfactory. We might
[L96] try to say: There are electrons and protons, and the rest is empty.
[L97] But in the “empty” regions there are light waves, so that we cannot
[L98] say nothing happens in them. Some people maintain that the light
[L99] waves take place in the ether, others are content to say simply that
[L100] they take place; but in any case events are occurring where there are
[L101] light waves. That is all that we can really say for the places where
[L102] there is matter, since matter has turned out to be a mathematical
[L103] construction built out of events. We may say, therefore, that there
[L104] are events everywhere in space-time, but they must be of a somewhat
[L105] different kind according as we are dealing with a region where there is
[L106] an electron or proton or with the sort of region we should ordinarily
[L107] call empty. But as to the intrinsic nature of these events we can know
[L108] nothing, except when they happen to be events in our own lives. Our own
[L109] perceptions and feelings must be part of the crude material of events
[L110] which physics arranges into a pattern—or rather, which physics finds
[L111] to be arranged in a pattern. As regards events which do not form part
[L112] of our own lives, physics tells us the pattern of them, but is quite
[L113] unable to tell us what they are like in themselves. Nor does it seem
[L114] possible that this should be discovered by any other method.
[L115]
[L116]
[L117]
[L118]
[L119] CHAPTER XIII: THE ABOLITION OF “FORCE”
[L120]
[L121]
[L122] In the Newtonian system, bodies under the action of no forces move in
[L123] straight lines with uniform velocity; when bodies do not move in this
[L124] way, their change of motion is ascribed to a “force.” Some forces seem
[L125] intelligible to our imagination: those exerted by a rope or string,
[L126] by bodies colliding, or by any kind of obvious pushing or pulling. As
[L127] explained in an earlier chapter, our apparent imaginative understanding
[L128] of these processes is quite fallacious; all that it really means is
[L129] that past experience enables us to foresee more or less what is going
[L130] to happen without the need of mathematical calculations. But the
[L131] “forces” involved in gravitation and in the less familiar forms of
[L132] electrical action do not seem in this way “natural” to our imagination.
[L133] It seems odd that the earth can float in the void: the natural thing
[L134] to suppose is that it must fall.

[L144] The ether became still more
[L145] respectable when it was found to play the same part in electromagnetic
[L146] phenomena as in the propagation of light. It was even hoped that atoms
[L147] might turn out to be a mode of motion of the ether. At this stage, the
[L148] atomic view of matter was, on the whole, getting the worst of it.
[L149]
[L150] Leaving relativity aside for the moment, modern physics has provided
[L151] proof of the atomic structure of ordinary matter, while not disproving
[L152] the arguments in favor of the ether, to which no such structure is
[L153] attributed. The result was a sort of compromise between the two views,
[L154] the one applying to what was called “gross” matter, the other to the
[L155] ether. There can be no doubt about electrons and protons, though, as we
[L156] shall see shortly, they need not be conceived as atoms were conceived
[L157] traditionally. As for the ether, its status is very curious: many
[L158] physicists still maintain that, without it, the propagation of light
[L159] and other electromagnetic waves would be inconceivable, but except in
[L160] this way it is difficult to see what purpose it serves. The truth is,
[L161] I think, that relativity demands the abandonment of the old conception
[L162] of “matter,” which is infected by the metaphysics associated with
[L163] “substance,” and represents a point of view not really necessary in
[L164] dealing with phenomena. This is what we must now investigate.
[L165]
[L166] In the old view, a piece of matter was something which survived all
[L167] through time, while never being at more than one place at a given time.
[L168] This way of looking at things is obviously connected with the complete
[L169] separation of space and time in which people formerly believed. When we
[L170] substitute space-time for space and time, we shall naturally expect to
[L171] derive the physical world from constituents which are as limited in
[L172] time as in space. Such constituents are what we call “events.” An event
[L173] does not persist and move, like the traditional piece of matter; it
[L174] merely exists for its little moment and then ceases. A piece of matter
[L175] will thus be resolved into a series of events. Just as, in the old
[L176] view, an extended body was composed of a number of particles, so, now,
[L177] each particle, being extended in time, must be regarded as composed
[L178] of what we may call “event-particles.” The whole series of these
[L179] events makes up the whole history of the particle, and the particle is
[L180] regarded as _being_ its history, not some metaphysical entity to which
[L181] the events happen. This view is rendered necessary by the fact that
[L182] relativity compels us to place time and space more on a level than they
[L183] were in the older physics.
[L184]
[L185] This abstract requirement must be brought into relation with the known
[L186] facts of the physical world. Now what are the known facts? Let us
[L187] take it as conceded that light consists of waves traveling with the
[L188] received velocity. We then know a great deal about what goes on in
[L189] the parts of space-time where there is no matter; we know, that is to
[L190] say, that there are periodic occurrences (light waves) obeying certain
[L191] laws. These light waves start from atoms, and the modern theory of
[L192] the structure of the atoms enables us to know a great deal about the
[L193] circumstances under which they start, and the reasons which determine
[L194] their wave lengths. We can find out not only how one light wave
[L195] travels, but how its source moves relatively to ourselves. But when I
[L196] say this I am assuming that we can recognise a source of light as the
[L197] same at two slightly different times. This is, however, the very thing
[L198] which had to be investigated.

[L208] Hence the
[L209]     agency invoked through our observer’s mistake is
[L210]     described as a “field of force.”... _A field of
[L211]     force represents the discrepancy between the natural
[L212]     geometry of a co-ordinate system and the abstract
[L213]     geometry arbitrarily ascribed to it._[15]
[L214]
[L215] [15] _Mathematical Theory of Relativity_, pp. 37-38. Italics in the
[L216] original.
[L217]
[L218] If people were to learn to conceive the world in the new way, without
[L219] the old notion of “force,” it would alter not only their physical
[L220] imagination, but probably also their morals and politics. The latter
[L221] effect would be quite illogical, but is none the less probable on that
[L222] account. In Newton’s theory of the solar system, the sun seems like a
[L223] monarch whose behests the planets have to obey. In Einstein’s world
[L224] there is more individualism and less government than in Newton’s.
[L225] There is also far less hustle: we have seen that laziness is the
[L226] fundamental law of Einstein’s universe. The word “dynamic” has come to
[L227] mean, in newspaper language, “energetic and forceful”; but if it meant
[L228] “illustrating the principles of dynamics,” it ought to be applied to
[L229] the people in hot climates who sit under banana trees waiting for the
[L230] fruit to drop into their mouths. I hope that journalists, in future,
[L231] when they speak of a “dynamic personality,” will mean a person who
[L232] does what is least trouble at the moment, without thinking of remote
[L233] consequences. If I can contribute to this result, I shall not have
[L234] written in vain.
[L235]
[L236] It has been customary for people to draw arguments from the laws of
[L237] nature as to what we ought to do. Such arguments seem to me a mistake:
[L238] to imitate nature may be merely slavish. But if nature, as portrayed by
[L239] Einstein, is to be our model, it would seem that the anarchists will
[L240] have the best of the argument. The physical universe is orderly, not
[L241] because there is a central government, but because every body minds
[L242] its own business. No two particles of matter ever come into contact;
[L243] when they get too close, they both move off. If a man were had up
[L244] for knocking another man down, he would be scientifically correct in
[L245] pleading that he had never touched him. What happened was that there
[L246] was a hill in space-time in the region of the other man’s nose, and it
[L247] fell down the hill.
[L248]
[L249] The abolition of “force” seems to be connected with the substitution
[L250] of sight for touch as the source of physical ideas, as explained in
[L251] Chapter I. When an image in a looking glass moves, we do not think that
[L252] something has pushed it. In places where there are two large mirrors
[L253] opposite to each other, you may see innumerable reflections of the
[L254] same object. Suppose a gentleman in a top-hat is standing between the
[L255] mirrors, there may be twenty or thirty top-hats in the reflections.
[L256] Suppose now somebody comes and knocks off the gentleman’s hat with a
[L257] stick: all the other twenty or thirty top-hats will tumble down at the
[L258] same moment. We think that a force is needed to knock off the “real”
[L259] top-hat, but we think the remaining twenty or thirty tumble off, so to
[L260] speak, of themselves, or out of a mere passion for imitation. Let us
[L261] try to think out this matter a little more seriously.
[L262]
[L263] Obviously something happens when an image in a looking glass moves.
[L264] From the point of view of sight, the event seems just as real as if it
[L265] were not in a mirror. But nothing has happened from the point of view
[L266] of touch or hearing.

[L276] Such constituents are what we call “events.” An event
[L277] does not persist and move, like the traditional piece of matter; it
[L278] merely exists for its little moment and then ceases. A piece of matter
[L279] will thus be resolved into a series of events. Just as, in the old
[L280] view, an extended body was composed of a number of particles, so, now,
[L281] each particle, being extended in time, must be regarded as composed
[L282] of what we may call “event-particles.” The whole series of these
[L283] events makes up the whole history of the particle, and the particle is
[L284] regarded as _being_ its history, not some metaphysical entity to which
[L285] the events happen. This view is rendered necessary by the fact that
[L286] relativity compels us to place time and space more on a level than they
[L287] were in the older physics.
[L288]
[L289] This abstract requirement must be brought into relation with the known
[L290] facts of the physical world. Now what are the known facts? Let us
[L291] take it as conceded that light consists of waves traveling with the
[L292] received velocity. We then know a great deal about what goes on in
[L293] the parts of space-time where there is no matter; we know, that is to
[L294] say, that there are periodic occurrences (light waves) obeying certain
[L295] laws. These light waves start from atoms, and the modern theory of
[L296] the structure of the atoms enables us to know a great deal about the
[L297] circumstances under which they start, and the reasons which determine
[L298] their wave lengths. We can find out not only how one light wave
[L299] travels, but how its source moves relatively to ourselves. But when I
[L300] say this I am assuming that we can recognise a source of light as the
[L301] same at two slightly different times. This is, however, the very thing
[L302] which had to be investigated.
[L303]
[L304] We saw, in the preceding chapter, how a group of connected events can
[L305] be formed, all related to each other by a law, and all ranged about a
[L306] center in space-time. Such a group of events will be the arrival, at
[L307] various places, of the light waves emitted by a brief flash of light.
[L308] We do not need to suppose that anything particular is happening at the
[L309] center; certainly we do not need to suppose that we know _what_ is
[L310] happening there. What we know is that, as a matter of geometry, the
[L311] group of events in question are ranged about a center, like widening
[L312] ripples on a pool when a fly has touched it. We can hypothetically
[L313] invent an occurrence which is to have happened at the center, and set
[L314] forth the laws by which the consequent disturbance is transmitted. This
[L315] hypothetical occurrence will then appear to common sense as the “cause”
[L316] of the disturbance. It will also count as one event in the biography of
[L317] the particle of matter which is supposed to occupy the center of the
[L318] disturbance.
[L319]
[L320] Now we find not only that one light wave travels outward from a center
[L321] according to a certain law, but also that, in general, it is followed
[L322] by other closely similar light waves. The sun, for example, does not
[L323] change its appearance suddenly; even if a cloud passes across it during
[L324] a high wind, the transition is gradual, though swift. In this way a
[L325] group of occurrences connected with a center at one point of space-time
[L326] is brought into relation with other very similar groups whose centers
[L327] are at neighboring points of space-time. For each of these other groups
[L328] common sense invents similar hypothetical occurrences to occupy their
[L329] centers, and says that all these hypothetical occurrences are part of
[L330] one history; that is to say, it invents a hypothetical “particle” to
[L331] which the hypothetical occurrences are to have occurred.

[L341] The region so defined is found to move relatively to other such
[L342] regions, and its movements follow the known laws of dynamics. So far,
[L343] this theory provides for electromagnetic phenomena and the motions of
[L344] matter; and it does so without assuming that “matter” is anything but
[L345] systems of electromagnetic phenomena. In order to carry out the theory
[L346] fully, it would no doubt be necessary to introduce many complications.
[L347] But it seems fairly clear that all the facts and laws of physics
[L348] can be interpreted without assuming that “matter” is anything more
[L349] than groups of events, each event being of the sort which we should
[L350] naturally regard as “caused” by the matter in question. This does not
[L351] involve any change in the symbols or formulæ of physics: it is merely
[L352] a question of interpretation of the symbols.
[L353]
[L354] This latitude in interpretation is a characteristic of mathematical
[L355] physics. What we know is certain very abstract logical relations,
[L356] which we express in mathematical formulæ; we know also that, at
[L357] certain points, we arrive at results which are capable of being tested
[L358] experimentally. Take, for example, the eclipse observations by which
[L359] Einstein’s theory as to the bending of light was established. The
[L360] actual observation consisted in the careful measurement of certain
[L361] distances on certain photographic plates. The formulæ which were to
[L362] be verified were concerned with the course of light in passing near
[L363] the sun. Although the part of these formulæ which gives the observed
[L364] result must always be interpreted in the same way, the other part of
[L365] them may be capable of a great variety of interpretations. The formulæ
[L366] giving the motions of the planets are almost exactly the same in
[L367] Einstein’s theory as in Newton’s, but the meaning of the formulæ is
[L368] quite different. It may be said generally that, in the mathematical
[L369] treatment of nature, we can be far more certain that our formulæ are
[L370] approximately correct than we can be as to the correctness of this or
[L371] that interpretation of them. And so in the case with which this chapter
[L372] is concerned: the question as to the nature of an electron or a proton
[L373] is by no means answered when we know all that mathematical physics has
[L374] to say as to the laws of its motion and the laws of its interaction
[L375] with the environment. A definite and conclusive answer to our question
[L376] is not possible just because a variety of answers are compatible with
[L377] the truth of mathematical physics. Nevertheless some answers are
[L378] preferable to others, because some have a greater probability in their
[L379] favor. We have been seeking, in this chapter, to define matter so that
[L380] there _must_ be such a thing if the formulæ of physics are true. If we
[L381] had made our definition such as to secure that a particle of matter
[L382] should be what one thinks of as substantial, a hard, definite lump, we
[L383] should not have been _sure_ that any such thing exists. That is why
[L384] our definition, though it may seem complicated, is preferable from the
[L385] point of view of logical economy and scientific caution.
[L386]
[L387]
[L388]
[L389]
[L390] CHAPTER XV: PHILOSOPHICAL CONSEQUENCES
[L391]
[L392]
[L393] The philosophical consequences of relativity are neither so great nor
[L394] so startling as is sometimes thought. It throws very little light on
[L395] time-honored controversies, such as that between realism and idealism.
[L396] Some people think that it supports Kant’s view that space and time are
[L397] “subjective” and are “forms of intuition.” I think such people have
[L398] been misled by the way in which writers on relativity speak of “the
[L399] observer.” It is natural to suppose that the observer is a human being,
[L400] or at least a mind; but he is just as likely to be a photographic
[L401] plate or a clock.

[L411] Instead of acting through
[L412] waves of light or sound, the sun acquires its apparent power through
[L413] the fact that there are modifications of space-time all round the sun.
[L414] Like the noise of the tiger, they are more intense near their source;
[L415] as we travel away they grow less and less. To say that the sun “causes”
[L416] these modifications of space-time is to add nothing to our knowledge.
[L417] What we know is that the modifications proceed according to a certain
[L418] rule, and that they are grouped symmetrically about the sun as center.
[L419] The language of cause and effect adds only a number of quite irrelevant
[L420] imaginings, connected with will, muscular tension, and such matters.
[L421] What we can more or less ascertain is merely the formula according to
[L422] which space-time is modified by the presence of gravitating matter.
[L423] More correctly: we can ascertain what kind of space-time _is_ the
[L424] presence of gravitating matter. When space-time is not accurately
[L425] Euclidean in a certain region, but has a non-Euclidean character which
[L426] grows more and more marked as we approach a certain center, and when,
[L427] further, the departure from Euclid obeys a certain law, we describe
[L428] this state of affairs briefly by saying that there is gravitating
[L429] matter at the center. But this is only a compendious account of what
[L430] we know. What we know is about the places where the gravitating matter
[L431] is _not_, not about the place where it is. The language of cause
[L432] and effect (of which “force” is a particular case) is thus merely
[L433] a convenient shorthand for certain purposes; it does not represent
[L434] anything that is genuinely to be found in the physical world.
[L435]
[L436] And how about matter? Is matter also no more than a convenient
[L437] shorthand? This question, however, being a large one, demands a
[L438] separate chapter.
[L439]
[L440]
[L441]
[L442]
[L443] CHAPTER XIV: WHAT IS MATTER?
[L444]
[L445]
[L446] The question “What is matter?” is of the kind that is asked by
[L447] metaphysicians, and answered in vast books of incredible obscurity.
[L448] But I am not asking the question as metaphysician: I am asking it as a
[L449] person who wants to find out what is the moral of modern physics, and
[L450] more especially of the theory of relativity. It is obvious from what we
[L451] have learned of that theory that matter cannot be conceived quite as it
[L452] used to be. I think we can now say more or less what the new conception
[L453] must be.
[L454]
[L455] There were two traditional conceptions of matter, both of which have
[L456] had advocates ever since scientific speculation began. There were
[L457] the atomists, who thought that matter consisted of tiny lumps which
[L458] could never be divided; these were supposed to hit each other and then
[L459] bounce off in various ways. After Newton, they were no longer supposed
[L460] actually to come into contact with each other, but to attract and
[L461] repel each other, and move in orbits round each other. Then there
[L462] were those who thought that there is matter of some kind everywhere,
[L463] and that a true vacuum is impossible. Descartes held this view, and
[L464] attributed the motions of the planets to vortices in the ether. The
[L465] Newtonian theory of gravitation caused the view that there is matter
[L466] everywhere to fall into discredit, the more so as light was thought by
[L467] Newton and his disciples to be due to actual particles traveling from
[L468] the source of the light. But when this view of light was disproved, and
[L469] it was shown that light consisted of waves, the ether was revived so
[L470] that there should be something to undulate. The ether became still more
[L471] respectable when it was found to play the same part in electromagnetic
[L472] phenomena as in the propagation of light.

[L482] 3. That at a great distance from gravitating matter,
[L483]        we can transform our co-ordinates by mathematical
[L484]        manipulation so that the interval shall be what it
[L485]        is in the special theory of relativity; and that
[L486]        this is approximately true wherever gravitation is
[L487]        not very powerful.

[L489] Each of these postulates requires some explanation.
[L490]
[L491] We saw that a geodesic on a surface is the shortest line that can be
[L492] drawn on the surface from one point to another; for example, on the
[L493] earth the geodesics are great circles. When we come to space-time,
[L494] the mathematics is the same, but the verbal explanations have to be
[L495] rather different. In the general theory of relativity, it is only
[L496] neighboring events that have a definite interval, independently of
[L497] the route by which we travel from one to the other. The interval
[L498] between distant events depends upon the route pursued, and has to be
[L499] calculated by dividing the route into a number of little bits and
[L500] adding up the intervals for the various little bits. If the interval
[L501] is space-like, a body cannot travel from one event to the other;
[L502] therefore when we are considering the way bodies move, we are confined
[L503] to time-like intervals. The interval between neighboring events, when
[L504] it is time-like, will appear as the time between them for an observer
[L505] who travels from the one event to the other. And so the whole interval
[L506] between two events will be judged by a person who travels from one to
[L507] the other to be what his clocks show to be the time that he has taken
[L508] on the journey. For some routes this time will be longer, for others
[L509] shorter; the more slowly the man travels, the longer he will think he
[L510] has been on the journey. This must not be taken as a platitude. I am
[L511] not saying that if you travel from London to Edinburgh you will take
[L512] longer if you travel more slowly. I am saying something much more odd.
[L513] I am saying that if you leave London at 10 A.M. and arrive in Edinburgh
[L514] at 6.30 P.M. Greenwich time, the more slowly you travel the longer
[L515] you will take—if the time is judged by your watch. This is a very
[L516] different statement. From the point of view of a person on the earth,
[L517] your journey takes eight and a half hours. But if you had been a ray
[L518] of light traveling round the solar system, starting from London at 10
[L519] A.M., reflected from Jupiter to Saturn, and so on, until at last you
[L520] were reflected back to Edinburgh and arrived there at 6.30 P.M., you
[L521] would judge that the journey had taken you exactly no time. And if you
[L522] had gone by any circuitous route, which enabled you to arrive in time
[L523] by traveling fast, the longer your route the less time you would judge
[L524] that you had taken; the diminution of time would be continual as your
[L525] speed approached that of light. Now I say that when a body travels, if
[L526] it is left to itself, it chooses the route which makes the time between
[L527] two stages of the journey as long as possible; if it had traveled from
[L528] one event to another by any other route, the time, as measured by its
[L529] own clocks, would have been shorter. This is a way of saying that
[L530] bodies left to themselves do their journeys as slowly as they can; it
[L531] is a sort of law of cosmic laziness. Its mathematical expression is
[L532] that they travel in geodesics, in which the total interval between any
[L533] two events on the journey is _greater_ than by any alternative route.
